solution_summary: The team trained EfficientNet image classifiers at several resolutions and combined predictions through rank averaging and weighted blends with public baselines. Their CV-selected ensemble of 12 models achieved CV 0.9517 and private score 0.9451, outperforming their more complicated public-leaderboard-selected ensemble. Helpful choices included combined binary cross-entropy and focal loss, resolution matching, oversampling, external 2018 data, GridMask, and noisy-student training. Extensive blending and post-processing raised the public score to 0.9723 but generalized poorly.

The team trained multiple image backbones with subcenter ArcFace and dynamic margins, incorporating external FGVC8 images. They assigned competition labels to the external images through nearest-neighbor matching and hotel-level mean aggregation. Logit-based predictions worked better than nearest-neighbor inference under the train–test mask mismatch. Hotel50K data and gradient checkpointing did not work, and inference took about two hours.

solution_title: Why a Single Mechanism Attack Wins in Public and Collapses in Private
solution_summary: The author constructed deterministic attack candidates around a public guardrail's incomplete inspection of tool arguments and a separate confused-deputy weakness. Candidates reused successful phrasings from an earlier live search, with mixed designs adding mechanism diversity. Local replay favored a concentrated design for throughput, but it scored 30.47 publicly and zero privately, while hybrid and combo designs retained private scores of 5.27 and 5.01. The officially counted earlier baseline scored 1.68 privately because later submissions did not finish processing in time.

The solution combined a modified GraphNeT pulse graph model with an attention and GRU model through a trained MLP ensemble. The GNN improved through additional EdgeConv capacity, more neighbors, a wider feature projection, and direction classification instead of regression. The transformer used pulse and event features, length-grouped minibatches, and progressively longer, unaggregated pulse sequences. Complementary errors across the two architectures made ensembling particularly effective, producing a reported angular error of 0.976.

Useful additions included monthly transaction counts, ridge predictions from sparse entity TF-IDF features, and embedding similarities between historical and new transactions. Recursive feature elimination with a LightGBM random forest booster produced the largest reported improvement. An outlier-aware three-model postprocessing scheme used out-of-fold predictions to tune its threshold, and the final submissions also blended public kernel outputs.

The final prediction combined five RAINT+ sequence models with a LightGBM model using weighted averaging. The sequence models varied encoder and decoder depth, embedding combination, and inputs such as question frequencies and tags. LightGBM used 73 features describing user performance, question statistics, timing, and recent history. The ensemble achieved private AUC 0.805 and public AUC 0.803, with GPU online inference taking about three hours.

solution_summary: The solution fed frozen BERT-large representations into a small feedforward neural network adapted from an end-to-end coreference paper. Features comprised layer -6 vectors for the two candidates and pronoun, plus pronoun-to-candidate distances. Swapping the two candidates provided a reported improvement of 0.006. The team extracted CTransPath features from background-filtered 224×224 patches at 20× magnification and classified slides with a modified attention-based MIL model. Adding a 1D convolution before attention improved the public score by about 0.04. A second MIL model learned an Other class from synthetic slides assembled from stroma and necrosis patches, while a separate ViT-S addressed TMA classification at 10× magnification. The final predictions were the NaN-aware average of probabilities from both MIL models and ViT-S.

The author initially compared histogram gradient boosting, LightGBM, XGBoost, and CatBoost, with shallow CatBoost performing particularly well. Experiments added original-dataset meta-features and target encoding. The final ensemble combined five CatBoost variants and two RealMLP variants with Ridge as the meta-learner. Adding RealMLP improved local CV to 0.95572, with public and private scores of 0.95394 and 0.95532.

The author blended LightGBM, XGBoost, and CatBoost using just seven selected features. The main contribution was a stable validation scheme that kept earthquake cycles intact while balancing fold sizes and time-to-failure distributions. Four separate five-fold evaluations provided both an average MAE and an uncertainty estimate, which guided feature selection. Acoustic segments were mean-centered, and overlapping training segments were used without crossing cycle boundaries in validation.

The author proposed cropping whale flukes with bounding boxes, splitting each crop into halves, and horizontally flipping the right half. At test time, corresponding halves were compared and their results combined, while the training procedure itself was left unspecified. This doubled the training examples and increased effective image resolution, but depended on bounding boxes and split the object's center. Half-fluke modeling improved private/public scores from 0.93686/0.93642 to 0.95398/0.95214, and an ensemble achieved 0.95652/0.95722.

solution_title: 13th Place Solution Part I. My first gold medal
solution_summary: Training proceeded through selected training subsets, test-set pseudo-labeling, and five-fold training on augmented validation data. Soft targets and diverse training configurations supported a stack with more than 1,900 first-level features. Two StackNet models and a forward-selection ensemble reached post-processing, where multilingual curse-word rules increased predicted toxicity. Rank averaging combined the processed predictions, while PCA-based data selection experiments did not work.

The solution extracted time-series features with tsfresh after splitting each signal segment into six smaller pieces. Correlation and quasi-constant filtering reduced almost 8,000 features to 2,854, followed by recursive elimination to retain 501. A global LightGBM regressor provided initial predictions, while additional regressors specialized in different time-to-eruption ranges. The six predictions for each segment were combined using their median.

The solution used a pretrained language model to extract a small vector of entropy-based features from essays. A one-class SVM was trained exclusively on organizer-provided human-written essays. External DAIGT data guided feature selection. Among the language models tested, phi-2 performed best.

The solution trained Mask R-CNN models on modality-balanced stratified folds, using external nuclei datasets and cleaned annotations. Grayscale conversion, contrast adjustments, and standard geometric augmentation supported generalization, while ResNet50 was selected over ResNet101. Flip-based test-time augmentation and mask-overlap agreement rules were followed by majority voting across folds and hole filling. The reported stage-two score was 0.578; a later limited experiment with additional BBBC6 images scored 0.565.

The best reported RMSE was 0.70011, with slow execution identified as the main drawback.

solution_title: 4th Place Solution for the CAFA 6 Protein Function Prediction
solution_summary: The author developed several protein-function predictors, including Py-Boost, an attention-based TRGO model, and structure-based approaches. The successful selected submission was standalone Py-Boost trained on roughly 150,000 sequences, whereas the ensemble overfit the public leaderboard. Pretrained protein embeddings, annotation quality, and filtering infrequent GO labels were central experimental factors. The selected submission achieved a private weighted F-measure of 0.43883.

solution_title: 62nd Place solution and what I learnt and tried
solution_summary: The selected submission used simple averaging of models trained with toxic-comment and Ruddit data, with the closing description emphasizing DistilBERT and RoBERTa. External-data training used MSE loss, and some DistilBERT variants benefited from augmentation and activation changes. Model additions were guided by an ensemble validation strategy built from unioned folds. Weighted ensembles and a late DeBERTa variant performed better in some comparisons but were not selected; the chosen ensemble reported a private score of 0.80434.

solution_title: 2nd Place Solution for the Google - Fast or Slow? Predict AI Model Runtime Competition
solution_summary: The team trained five separate whole-graph SageConv networks from scratch, one for each competition subset. They removed duplicate configurations, filtered selected corrupted graphs, and repacked Layout data for much faster lazy loading. Ranking losses were central: Layout-NLP used ListMLE, Tile used their pairwise DiffMat loss, and Layout-XLA combined DiffMat with MAPE. Training used the supplied splits and fixed final checkpoints, while unstable XLA validation made many filtering and modeling experiments difficult to assess.

solution_title: [59th Place, Silver] ByT5-base + LLM Data Augmentation + Cross-Model MBR Ensembl
solution_summary: The solution trained ByT5-base models on approximately 10,700 filtered pairs assembled from official data, OARE extractions, and GPT-5.2 translations. Document-level training and source-specific prefixes helped accommodate the small dataset and varying source quality. Three models generated beam candidates for minimum Bayes risk selection using chrF++, BLEU, and Jaccard consensus, followed by repetition removal and cleanup. ByT5 substantially outperformed early mBART and NLLB experiments, while several normalization and refinement methods were excluded.

The team first estimated image scale using SSD detections and XGBoost, then counted sea lions using class heatmaps from pretrained CNN encoders with U-Net-like decoders. Scale supervision came from manually matching sea-lion sizes to a reference image, and inference refined scale in two passes. Counts were obtained by summing each class heatmap and dividing by the area of the training marker. Scale correction improved the reported score from about 23 to 15.9, and the final submission averaged ResNet50 and VGG16 predictions with second-level models.

The pipeline used six-channel cellular images enlarged with bicubic interpolation and several CNN backbones trained with mixed precision. Experiment-based three-fold validation, all control samples, gradual layer unfreezing, and cell-type-specific classes were central choices. Training combined CosFace, scheduled learning rates and scales, and domain adaptation using plate and cell-type labels. Predictions were balanced and progressively constrained to reflect one occurrence of each class per experiment, with an additional unspecified leak-based step.

solution_title: [9 Place] Recall, Rotate and Zoom in
solution_summary: The solution used a two-stage YOLO detection pipeline, first recalling candidates at a low threshold and then filtering them with zoomed and rotated crops. YOLOv8l and YOLO11l models were trained jointly on competition and corrected external data, including local crop models. Ensembles, multiple inference resolutions, optional SAHI patches, confidence bypassing, and midpoint refinement supported the final predictions, with selected submissions scoring 0.852 and 0.832 privately.

solution_summary: The solution used beam search across puzzle types, primarily expanding states with precomputed sequences that changed relatively few pieces. Large cubes were reduced by solving faces and edges separately before applying a 3×3 solver. Globes were solved in two-row units and merged with dynamic programming to share flips, while larger wreaths used beam search with deep DFS-based evaluation. Diverse transitions, efficient scoring, extensive multithreading and puzzle-specific parity rules made the searches practical and improved solution quality.

solution_summary: The pipeline removed human speech, converted audio to mel spectrograms, and trained heavily augmented EfficientNet CNNs with different pooling configurations. Pseudo-labeling unlabeled soundscapes and pretraining on historical BirdCLEF data improved the CNNs. The final ensemble combined three CNNs with publicly shared SED predictions through Quantile-Mix. solution_title: 10th Place Solution: Flux 1 Dev -> SVG optimization -> Postprocessing
solution_summary: The pipeline generated raster images with Flux 1 Dev, then converted and compressed them into SVGs under 10,000 bytes. HyperSD, Nunchaku, and 4-bit quantization enabled fast generation on a single T4, while geometric simplification and parameter search preserved SVG fidelity. Candidates were selected with VQA, aesthetic, and OCR checks, followed by a comparison with an optional silver-border variant. A separate prompt-rewriting submission performed better privately but was not selected.

solution_title: From GR Events to Structural Landmarks
solution_summary: The selected competition submission used an early classical spatial contact-spline model; the contact-spline family achieved best public and private scores of 13.018 and 13.592 on different submissions. A later GR-only neural coordinate model learned useful local changes but accumulated structural drift and performed substantially worse on Kaggle. Subsequent experiments used Typewell references and a convolutional probability model to preserve multiple plausible structural positions, with promising results under truthful-history conditioning. The proposed structural decoder remained unfinished, and the author did not claim an end-to-end result for the later model.

solution_title: 16th Place Solution for Santa 2023 - The Polytope Permutation Puzzle Competition
solution_summary: Small puzzles were solved optimally using breadth-first and bidirectional breadth-first search, with state compression extending the approach to larger wreaths. Medium globes used adaptive incremental search over masked subsets of cells. Larger globes combined a short-horizon search prefix with a large database of commutators and conjugates selected for moves saved per cell solved. Cube solutions additionally used greedy wildcard allocation and travelling-salesman ordering of independently solved orbits to maximize move cancellation.

solution_summary: The author trained four EfficientNet-B3 models, one for each MRI modality: FLAIR, T1w, T1wCE, and T2w. Validation used a split stratified by patient identity and class. Predictions were aggregated by patient, comparing the maximum and minimum predictions against the mean and retaining the prediction associated with the larger difference.

The author trained an 8-million-parameter neural network to imitate actions from high-scoring game episodes. Training progressed through increasingly selective episode datasets, with different fine-tuning settings and a final switch to SGD. The large feedforward network offered a better speed and performance tradeoff than the tested convolutional and recurrent alternatives. Most submissions used a single model, while some explored ensembles or averaged model weights.

The authors explored clothing attribute classification, initially using a 92-way classifier. They switched to an image-captioning approach that predicts each attribute from image features and preceding attributes, using an implementation of Show, Attend and Tell. Predictions often captured most attributes, but ambiguous labels and missing annotations caused otherwise plausible outputs to count as false positives.

The solution used a three-level ensemble with 24 baseline models, four second-level regressors, and a final weighted average. Its main engineered features measured pairwise interactions between the 53 brain scans for each patient. Strong batch normalization and dropout helped the MLPs generalize, while a 2D CNN used projections of the 3D scans. Simple KFold validation supported stacking, with a final local score of 0.1559 and private leaderboard score of 0.15742.

The final submission blended LightGBM, XGBoost, and two similar neural networks, achieving a private score of 0.69500. Gaussian mixture models split each original feature into sub-distributions, represented by value and binary indicator columns for neural network training. Input rescaling, target centering, regularization, and averaging predictions across late epochs supported the neural models. The final neural pipeline used four random seeds and ten folds, while ridge regression did not improve the blend.

The team split the Kaggle-only essays using stratified cross-validation and fine-tuned DeBERTa models of several sizes on PERSUADE 2.0 plus the Kaggle training split. They then continued training only on the Kaggle training split while validating on held-out Kaggle essays. The final blend assigned 90% weight to DeBERTa and 10% to a public LightGBM notebook, producing public and private scores of 0.82763 and 0.83743.

The pipeline first constructed a parent TVT trajectory, then used a dilated 2D residual network to score nearby depth corrections from gamma-ray evidence. A persistent-datum HMM selected one geological layer and smoothed local corrections, followed by a global alignment adjustment using genuine sensor measurements. Fold-pure references and five-fold out-of-fold evaluation yielded RMSE 5.706354, with the final alignment improving it from 5.758806. Fold predictions were averaged, and the final submission averaged this pipeline with another variant to achieve a private score of 6.8.

solution_title: GPT-OSS Browser Tool for Math Reasoning
solution_summary: The author generated independent Python-assisted solutions, then let a second-stage solver inspect those attempts through a simulated browser interface. A simpler variant placed candidate summaries directly in the prompt and performed at least as well in local testing. On Hard-50, browser-based sharing increased maj@8 from 66.0% to 73.7%, while concatenation reached 78.0%; both reduced pass@8. Competition runtime constraints limited the final submission to applying the second stage to tied cases, yielding a score of 36.

The solution combined a first-stage transformer with a second-stage GBDT, with the latter providing a large improvement. It encoded discourse type and boundary information through token type IDs and used masked-language-model pretraining. Topic-level score aggregates and combined discourse and essay embeddings strengthened the predictions. A post-competition experiment showed that putting discourse boundary and type markers directly into the token sequence significantly improved the weaker first-stage model.

solution_title: 164th Place Solution — NVIDIA Nemotron Reasoning Challenge
solution_summary: The solution warm-started LoRA training for NVIDIA Nemotron-3-Nano from an existing public adapter using Unsloth and curated chain-of-thought data. Training balanced problem categories across accumulation windows and used BF16 precision with an 8192-token sequence limit. The final adapter merged three independently trained checkpoints using DARE-TIES with density 0.7 and weights 0.35, 0.30, and 0.35. It achieved approximately 0.864 publicly, with merging described as providing modest stabilization rather than a dramatic gain.

The solution collected roughly 60 diverse models, including CatBoost, LightGBM, XGBoost, neural networks, and TabNet, and combined their out-of-fold predictions. A Ridge Classifier provided a fast stacking baseline, while a second ensemble used gradient-boosted trees as meta-models. Averaging these ensembles and blending with a strong public submission produced a reported score of 0.89780. Model diversity and CV improvement guided additions, while low Ridge weights guided pruning under substantial memory and GPU constraints.

solution_title: 15th Place Solution - A Beginner Data Scientist's Journey
solution_summary: The final pipeline filled five prediction slots with template-based modeling, two RNAPro configurations, and Protenix 2025, with the last two slots containing identical coordinates. Template selection combined sequence and ligand similarity with chain composition, while structural corrections improved the pure template predictions. Longer sequences were handled through sliding windows and stitching. Validation used the default validation set, USalign TM-score, and an interactive 3D dashboard that exposed structural problems. Protenix fine-tuning was abandoned because of seed variance and catastrophic forgetting.

The final TensorFlow solution ensembled four selected cross-validation models with one model trained on the entire competition training set. Both model variants used Transformer architectures with LayerNorm and float16 quantization; the full-data model additionally used flip augmentation. Optuna tuning, grouped stratified validation and strong label smoothing were useful, while distillation and several geometric or noise augmentations were unsuccessful. The five-model submission scored 0.73896 publicly and 0.82815 privately.

solution_title: 20th Place Solution (Private 0.95533) — Ridge Stacking + Weighted Rank-Average
solution_summary: The author selected two final ensembles built from CatBoost and RealMLP predictions: a Ridge stack of 12 models and a weighted rank average of seven models. The Ridge meta-model used an alpha of 14.375664881335657, while the rank ensemble doubled the weights of three RealMLP variants. Saving aligned out-of-fold and test predictions and examining rank correlations were central to keeping the ensembles stable. The reported private score was 0.95533, and weight exploration was deliberately limited to reduce overfitting.

solution_title: Part of the 18th place solution (Iafoss's model)
solution_summary: The solution trained a ResNeXt50 sequence segmentation model from weak clip labels, using full-sequence self-attention and temperature-controlled logsumexp pooling. A three-stage process generated pseudo labels, refined localization with confidence-masked segmentation training, and addressed domain mismatch using rainforest background audio. Five-second training chunks, soft-label focal loss, and audio augmentation supported this pipeline. Shifted-window prediction averaging and class-level post-processing improved inference, and a weighted two-model ensemble achieved public/private scores of 0.7736/0.6605.

GOCurator extended NetGO 3.0 with protein structure, descriptions, and scientific literature, combining component predictions through learning to rank. Its components included logistic regression on multimodal representations, structure-based nearest neighbors, extreme multilabel classification, and retrieval followed by semantic reranking. ESM-1b embeddings and species-aware validation were retained after comparing alternatives, while network predictions were restricted to well-annotated species. The reported private score was 0.61623.

solution_summary: The solution classified 20-second mel-spectrogram segments using ResNet101d and ResNeXt50d_32x4d backbones with GeM pooling and a 152-output classifier. Noise augmentation helped address domain shift, while MixUp, focal loss, and an Adam-based SAM optimizer supported training. Thresholds were tuned using public leaderboard feedback because validation-optimal thresholds transferred poorly. Combining thresholded predictions with logical OR achieved a private score of 0.7292, improving over the two component predictions.

The solution blended LightGBM, XGBoost, and CatBoost regressors across three feature sets combining tabular data and actigraphy summaries. Null Importance feature selection and Bayesian Ridge iterative imputation improved robustness to noisy and missing data. Evaluation and threshold optimization used three seeds of five-fold stratified cross-validation. The final model improved CV QWK from 0.475 to 0.501.

The solution used nested transformers: a cell transformer encoded tokens, and a notebook transformer modeled interactions between cells. Cell-type markers, code-position features, and learned attention pooling formed the cell representations. Joint pointwise rank regression and auxiliary next-cell classification improved validation performance, while inference used only predicted percentile ranks followed by code-order correction. The final ensemble combined CodeBERT, Deberta-large, Deberta-base, and DistilBERT backbones.

solution_title: 118th Place Solution for the Open Problems – Single-Cell Perturbations Competition draft
solution_summary: The post outlines a decomposition of gene-response prediction into gene ordering, curve shape, point location, and scale prediction. It proposes predicting gene ranks instead of directly predicting signed log-transformed p-values. Compound and cell-specific multipliers are discussed as a way to scale predictions. Implementation, validation, and numerical results are largely unspecified.

The approach appended original data only to training partitions so it would not affect validation accuracy. Five-fold cross-validation performed better than ten-fold validation and was selected. Experiments favored appending the original data four times for LightGBM and once for XGBoost. The author also introduced threshold optimization into their competition workflow.

The author modeled padded daily sequences using four related architectures built mainly from bidirectional LSTMs, with the strongest models using a U-Net structure and a transformer block. Minute-level sensor aggregations, a 15-minute-cycle feature, and explicit repeated-pattern detection supplied useful signals. Models predicted onset and wakeup probabilities at several temporal tolerances, followed by peak suppression and small timing adjustments. Six-fold validation, seed selection, and full-data refits supported the final approach, with local cross-validation around 0.833.

The agent used imitation learning from 11,681 episodes across ten agents, retaining winning games and matches. Separate U-Nets predicted map-level actions and unit-level sap targets, with agent conditioning to handle differing expert policies. A persistent global state addressed fog of war, while diagonal mirroring standardized the player viewpoint. Final submissions ensembled separate-head and DiT-head action architectures.

solution_summary: The solution first predicted contact with multiple CNNs, then combined their predictions with tracking and helmet features in second-stage classifiers. Temporal rolling statistics of CNN outputs were especially important, while spatial tracking features supplied additional signal. Four boosted-tree models and one neural network were averaged, with separate optimized thresholds for player-player and player-ground contact. Rectified signal regions were divided into four segments and processed by a modified U-Net that directly regressed short-lead and long Lead II waveforms. Domain-specific masked-autoencoder pretraining, auxiliary signal segmentation, synthetic external training images, and an SNR-based loss supported learning. The solution centered on feature frequencies computed over training data and genuine test rows, excluding identified fake test examples. It combined per-feature models, a heavily regularized neural network, a neural-feature-to-LightGBM pipeline, and joint LightGBM models using pivoted or masked features. Shared hyperparameters helped control overfitting across hundreds of individual models. A hill-climbing weighted blend achieved 0.927 cross-validation, while pseudo-labeling and several custom modeling variants were excluded after weaker holdout or leaderboard results.

solution_summary: The pipeline predicted basketball point differential with XGBoost and calibrated the resulting margins into win probabilities. Men's and women's games were pooled with a gender indicator, using season-level box score summaries, efficiency metrics, Elo ratings, GLM team quality, and seed differences. Leave-one-season-out predictions supported Optuna optimization of features, model parameters, and margin clipping. The solution blended simple MLPs with different output structures and network settings. Training was restricted to selected visit months, which improved agreement between cross-validation and the leaderboard. Visit timing, gaps, and patient visit counts supplied the main predictive information, with patient-relative NPX ratios providing limited protein features. Models either predicted 16 target and horizon combinations or predicted four UPDRS targets with the forecast horizon supplied as a feature.

The author found no convincing learnable signal in exploratory ML experiments and adopted a regularized statistical prediction based on a Kelly-optimal portfolio expressed through standardized ranks. Covariance regularization was guided by validation windows similar in length to the private test period. Preprocessing forward-filled prices before target construction and standardized ranks per day; a full-data submission outperformed one excluding 2020–2021. Late validation scores were around 0.4 with high variance, and the final score was 0.479.

The solution combined five architecture variants into an ensemble reported to contain 35 models. It included RoBERTa-base models with different heads, ExtraTrees regression on RoBERTa embeddings, and RoBERTa-large variants including mean pooling. All Hugging Face models underwent further pretraining on competition data before fine-tuning. Five-fold validation and seed reruns supported generalization, with seed averaging improving the public score by approximately 0.002.

The final ensemble combined Transformer, MLP, and GRU models with two variants of landmark sequences. Coordinate, motion, and distance features received separate embeddings, with pose and lip distances producing the largest reported feature gain. Selecting the less-missing hand and mirroring it into a consistent orientation also improved validation. Strong regularization and label smoothing were important, and switching to Keras simplified TFLite conversion.

The solution trained a universal image embedding model using a CLIP ViT-H/14 visual backbone, a dropout-equipped fully connected neck, and an ArcFace head. Training combined many external image datasets with class-size limits and light resampling. A progressively increased ArcFace margin helped, but the largest gain came from using a much smaller learning rate for the backbone. The final schedule fine-tuned the backbone for two epochs, froze it for one more epoch, and used flip augmentation to reach a reported score of 0.713.

solution_summary: The final ensemble combined 16 mostly LightGBM models with a few XGBoost models, selected by hill climbing and weighted using Nelder–Mead optimization. Cross-validation stratified on booking date, used 20 or 30 folds, and added the original dataset to each training fold. Duplicate-pair label structure enabled direct test prediction corrections, including opposite-label assignment for train–test pairs and an OOF-tuned common score for test–test pairs. Date repair and a small set of indicator features complemented the original features, and the author reported strong agreement between CV and the leaderboard.

It combined selected cross-validation folds and models trained on all data, using multiple image sizes and stochastic weight averaging. solution_title: 5th place solution, poisson blending,detection and tracking
solution_summary: The solution combined several object detectors trained and evaluated at different image resolutions. Copy-paste augmentation used Poisson blending and a real-versus-fake classifier to produce more plausible training examples. Five-fold validation grouped images by sequence. Homography-based box propagation and DeepSort tracking recovered missed detections, while track filtering and cross-model agreement reduced false positives before weighted boxes fusion.

The solution combined GRU and WaveNet outputs using cleaned signals. K-means cluster assignments supplied additional one-hot encoded features, and the model used focal loss. Dropout reduced overfitting, while concatenating the two model outputs improved the score. The reported public leaderboard score was 0.943.

The author trained a YOLOv5 animal detector from MegaDetector v4 detections and merged both detectors' outputs using weighted boxes fusion. This fusion achieved public and private leaderboard scores of 0.275 and 0.265. A custom inter-frame tracking approach targeted herd species, using autoencoder embeddings from DeepMac-mask-centered image chips together with spatial and temporal features. Although mask-guided chips improved matching representations, tracking failed to improve counting across the full dataset because herd-direction estimates and matching were unreliable.

The solution combined masked-language-model pretraining with two-stage training that emphasized Kaggle-only essays. It ensembled DeBERTa-v3 base and large backbones with multiple heads and sequence lengths. The reported CV, public, and private scores were 0.836, 0.832, and 0.839. Persuade Corpus 2.0 provided almost no benefit in an alternative submission, while prompt-grouped validation produced a substantial private-score drop.

solution_title: 12th place solution - MLP Based (Structured Keypoint Pooling network)
solution_summary: The solution used a modified Structured Keypoint Pooling MLP with separate joint and bone streams connected bidirectionally. Inputs combined lip, upper-body, and hand coordinates with motion over one and two frames, with long sequences resized to 64 frames. Geometric, temporal, and same-sign part-swapping augmentations improved validation, and training used cross-entropy with 0.4 label smoothing. Removing the lowest-confidence 1% of training examples improved the public score despite hurting cross-validation.

Temporal augmentation, heavy dropout, and validation monitoring supported training, while larger batches worked better than smaller batches with gradient accumulation. solution_summary: The solution expanded five features with sums, differences, and squares, then applied min-max normalization. It combined KNN, logistic regression, XGBoost, LightGBM, and a neural network. Five-fold cross-validation and oversampling of training data supported the base models, while a stacked network learned how to combine their predictions.

The solution combined pneumothorax classification with segmentation. Classification used a multitask U-Net trained on all images, with BCE plus focal loss for classification and BCE for segmentation. Separate U-Net and DeepLabv3 segmenters trained on positive images using Dice loss. SE-ResNeXt and EfficientNet backbones supplied model diversity, with stacking for classification and averaging for segmentation.

The solution computes within-row ranks across 424 training targets and averages each target's ranks over the training rows. Every inference call returns these fixed target-specific values without using the incoming test features or lagged labels. This deliberately simple approach was the author's best submission and finished with a reported score of 0.387.

The post links to the author's final submission notebook, described as containing only the inference portion. The author says most effort went into reducing runtime. No model, feature, training, or validation details are provided in the post.

The author adapted public notebook pipelines combining DeBERTa V3, LightGBM, and optionally autocorrect. Work focused on preprocessing and the LightGBM component, including Optuna parameter tuning. These changes did not improve on the original models. The listed submissions achieved private scores of 0.484–0.487 and public scores of 0.445–0.450.

The authors focused on orders and carts, sharing candidates generated through co-visitation, collaborative filtering, embedding retrieval, and a bi-graph method. They built retrieval, session, item, and session-item interaction features, including embedding and similarity-matrix statistics. XGBoost and CatBoost Ranker used five folds grouped by session and target-specific negative sampling. Added teammate features improved the reported public single-model score from 0.601 to 0.603, while a GNN approach did not help.

The author removed fake test samples and combined the remaining test data with training data to construct count encodings. Arithmetic features derived from 200 count-encoded columns improved the reported leaderboard score from 0.908 to 0.916. The final solution blended CatBoost and LightGBM, with GPU CatBoost training enabling rapid experimentation.
compute: GPU used for fast CatBoost training.

solution_summary: The pipeline used Wav2vec2 CTC speech recognition, a KenLM n-gram language model, and xlm-roberta-large punctuation restoration. Fine-tuning on filtered Common Voice and OpenSLR 37 improved the reported public error from 0.439 to 0.414. Oscar text, audio augmentation, and Optuna decoding searches also helped. The final language model was a trimmed 4-gram in ARPA format, while speech enhancement models failed to improve results.

solution_summary: The solution fine-tuned two 32B causal language models with QLoRA across five folds each, representing the 65 classes as special tokens. It corrected annotation errors, merged duplicate labels, simplified prompts, and averaged special-token logits across ten models. AWQ and vLLM supported inference, and question-specific post-processing redistributed merged labels, yielding private MAP@3 of 0.948.

solution_summary: The team improved shared baselines using image models and engineered tabular features, submitting both their best leaderboard model and best cross-validation model. Features included image texture statistics, within-patient nearest-neighbor averages, age and tile-type differences, and numeric quartiles. The best cross-validation pipeline selected roughly 50–100 features separately for CatBoost, LightGBM, and XGBoost. Both final submissions scored 0.183 publicly and 0.171 privately, while past data, pseudo-labeling, and FTTransformer were unsuccessful.

The pipeline trained multiple CNN variants to predict left-ventricle contours using Sunnybrook data and manually labeled images. Averaged contour areas were converted into volumes, then simple fitted models corrected systematic errors. The final prediction averaged sex-age, largest-slice, four-channel, and CNN-derived models. The full approach scored 0.00936 on train plus validation and 0.009485 on test; a reduced CNN configuration was faster with slightly worse scores.

solution_summary: The solution combined five LightGBM models differentiated by imputation strategies and parameter settings using linear regression without an intercept. Original data was appended to each training fold while validation remained restricted to synthetic data. Feature preparation used logarithmic transforms and geometry-based rules to fill related values. The models included a baseline, three iterative LightGBM-imputed variants, and a linear-regression-imputed variant, with Optuna tuning the baseline parameters.

The solution used a single CatBoost model configuration with predictions averaged across ten folds. Feature engineering captured game properties such as board shape, piece types, randomness, and rule complexity, while agent swapping provided effective augmentation. Rewriting pandas operations with Polars reduced feature processing from about 410 seconds to 7 seconds. Scaling predictions by 1.2 produced public and private scores of 0.416 and 0.423; a more complex augmentation ensemble did not help.

solution_title: How we did it: David Slate and Peter Frey on 9th place in Elo comp
solution_summary: The team treated chess outcomes as a forecasting task using a home-grown Ensemble Recursive Binary Partitioning method. Its best submission used 22 engineered predictors covering iterative skill rankings, chronological Elo-like ratings, opponent strength, activity, and common-opponent results. Parameter and feature choices were explored through more than 1,100 runs with leaderboard feedback and temporal holdouts. The best reported official test score was 0.699472.

solution_title: 44th Place Solution for the Stanford Ribonanza RNA Folding Competition
solution_summary: The solution adapted a ResNet RNA structure predictor that converts one-hot sequences through 1D and 2D feature-extraction stages. Provided base-pair probabilities were added as a channel, and column sums converted the interaction representation into nucleotide-level predictions. Training retained sequences with SNR above 0.5, with sequence-cluster splits designed to reduce similarity leakage. The final prediction averaged five models, three trained only on cluster medoids; removing BPP substantially worsened average public performance.

solution_title: 35th place: rtklib tweaking and factor graph approach
solution_summary: The final submission combined an RTKLIB solution and a global factor graph solution using a weighted average. RTKLIB benefited from preserving receiver cycle slip flags and weighting measurements by signal strength and pseudorange uncertainty. The factor graph combined pseudorange, motion, Doppler, and time-differenced carrier phase constraints, with outlier handling and acceleration constraints to improve trajectories. Both approaches used Kalman smoothing, while ambiguity resolution and ensembling alternative RTKLIB weighting schemes did not improve results.

The author's individual model combined wavelet-denoised signals, a basic RNN, and engineered peak features. Peak features reduced overfitting and included counts and statistics of peak heights and widths. Feature outliers were converted to missing values and filled with group means based on a correlated attribute. Training ran for 25 epochs with validation-loss checkpoint monitoring, and the final submission ensembled this model with two publicly shared approaches.

The solution retrieved landmark images using EfficientNet-B5/B6/B7 and ResNet152 embeddings trained with ArcFace and progressively larger images. Training expanded from cleaned GLDv2 to a larger subset containing the same landmark classes. SuperPoint, SuperGlue, and geometric verification improved matching, while non-landmark suppression rules and a learned reranking model produced substantial further gains. The final model ensemble added only a modest improvement relative to its complexity.

solution_title: The 440th solution of the 'Open Problems – Single-Cell Perturbations' competition
solution_summary: The approach reduced gene-expression targets with PCA and encoded drug chemical strings into structural features before applying support vector regression. A separate tensor-completion approach represented drug, gene, and cell-type relationships with warm-start values for missing entries. The author used the provided test sets without creating an additional validation split and discussed CPA without implementing it. Weighted combinations of publicly available submission datasets performed better than the individual files.

The team combined three RoBERTa-large question-answering models using majority voting after model-specific thresholding. Two models were first fine-tuned on SQuAD2.0, and all competition models trained for one epoch with Adam. Sliding-window span predictions were mapped into document-level matrices with span-length restrictions. Quantile-based four-way thresholding was particularly important, while a larger inference stride, FP16 predictions, and multiprocessing made the ensemble fit the kernel limits.
compute: Two home PCs with 3 GTX1080Ti and 2 GTX1080Ti; RoBERTa1 training took 35h, SQuAD2.0 fine-tuning 30h, and subsequent competition fine-tuning about 24h.

solution_summary: The solution diversified image resizing, augmentation, tokenization, and CNN-transformer or vision-transformer architectures. Progressive pseudo-labeling retained valid test InChIs, and a string-level ensemble combined predictions from models with incompatible tokenizers, improving scores to about 0.67. A three-class ResNet50 corrected m0/m1 suffixes and improved the score to 0.65. Fine-tuning on long InChIs, test-time augmentation, and a specialized ensemble for the longest 100,000 predictions brought the final score to about 0.61.

The solution corrected GNSS positions using reference-station observations through RTKLIB and RTKLIB-py. It estimated velocity directly from accumulated delta range using weighted least squares, falling back to Doppler when necessary. Position estimates were then smoothed using both Kalman smoothing and cost minimization. Ensembling across implementations, smoothing methods, and parameter settings improved accuracy, while relaxed satellite-selection rules reduced missing velocity estimates.

The pipeline extracted DOI and accession-number candidates with regular expressions. It recovered whitespace-corrupted DOI URLs by retrieving PDF link targets and matching whitespace-tolerant versions against the document text. SciBERT classified marked reference contexts into Primary, Secondary, and Not_Labeled using a ±200 context window. Rules then adjusted DOI labels, restricted Primary accession labels to SAMN entries, and excluded selected DOI patterns.

The solution used MuRIL Large after intermediate fine-tuning on SQuAD v2. Training data also included the competition dataset, MLQA, and XQuAD. The author fine-tuned ten folds for two epochs each, using a maximum sequence length of 384, a document stride of 128, and a learning rate of 1e-5. Final predictions were a simple average of the ten folds.

solution_title: 4th Place Solution [Source Codes & Submission Notebook Released!]
solution_summary: The solution detects particle centers through Gaussian heatmap regression using two complementary 2.5D UNet architectures with ConvNeXt Nano and ResNetRS-50 backbones. Depth pooling, efficient decoding, and a balanced MSE loss supported accurate and efficient volumetric prediction. The final submission combined four models from one architecture and three from the other, with TensorRT and parallel inference on dual T4 GPUs. Local maxima were filtered by particle-specific thresholds and converted back to physical coordinates; leaderboard feedback guided method selection because CV correlated poorly with it.
compute: Dual T4 GPUs for parallel inference in a Kaggle Notebook

solution_summary: The author's contribution combined neural networks, XGBoost, LightGBM, and models based on a shared repository, with Gaussian event targets. Neural networks processed patched long sequences using transformer, WaveNet, or 1D CNN layers followed by GRU, while overlapping windows and seeds were averaged. Features captured standardized motion, repeated daily patterns, heuristic sleep episodes, and temporal lags. Weighted averaging and a confidence-reduction post-processing method produced a component CV of 0.825 and private score of 0.840; the team's final submissions used a teammate's refined post-processing.

The final agent used a three-stage heuristic pipeline that scored long-term ship tasks, assigned coordinated plans, and translated those plans into actions. Distance-decayed scores and conflict handling maintained consistent targets and coordinated base returns. Specialized mining, construction, defense, hunting, and rescue rules were combined with online estimates of opponent behavior and multistep safety checks. Deep reinforcement learning was abandoned after a month of unsuccessful experimentation, while chase detection and rescue logic helped beat a strong benchmark.

solution_title: 21st place solution [LB 0.948] on simplified data only
solution_summary: The solution rendered simplified drawings as 128×128 images with three channels encoding line order, stroke counts, and a constant intensity. Several deep CNN architectures were trained using cosine learning-rate annealing, checkpoint averaging, and gradient accumulation to reach a batch size of 1024. A LightGBM stacker classified candidate classes using the networks' probabilities and class identifiers, improving validation performance over simple averaging. The final LightGBM ensemble achieved a reported public leaderboard score of 0.948.

The solution recovered leaked targets by matching shifted feature sequences across 113 sets of 40 features. Reconstructing row groups enabled manual inspection that added missing leaks and corrected misaligned targets, yielding 7,897 test leaks. Correcting unusual three-step offsets improved an older blend's private score from 0.53679 to 0.52115. The authors also investigated aggregate relationships among feature sets and observed target censoring.

The solution averaged three unmodified nnUNetResEncUNetL models trained with different patch sizes. Sliding-window inference used mirroring augmentation for two models, followed by direct probability averaging. Most gains came from anisotropic diffusion and adaptive hysteresis with connectivity restricted to the z direction. Diffusion improved local validation by about 0.005, and the stronger diffusion setting was retained for stability despite a slightly worse public score.
compute: Three models trained for 500 epochs each; hardware unspecified.

solution_title: A simple approach and only 2 cell-wise models to get a silver [LB Private 0.436]
solution_summary: The author trained cell-wise EfficientNet-B0 and EfficientNet-B1 models on RGB images from competition and external data. Cell tiles were generated using code similar to a linked sample-balanced tile notebook, and the CNN inputs were 224 × 224 pixels. Models used five folds and were trained for five epochs, but the first-epoch checkpoint was consistently selected because it performed better on the leaderboard. The author also observed a relationship between local loss and leaderboard score and shared training code and an inference notebook.

The solution combined category-specific Longformer-base experts with a publicly available Deberta-large model. A Longformer first learned all PII labels, then separate experts were fine-tuned from that checkpoint while other categories were relabeled as O. Public datasets supplemented competition data, and final inference concatenated predictions from the experts and Deberta. A Deberta-large LoRA experiment performed worse than Longformer-base for individual categories.

solution_summary: The final solution combined six DynEdge and LSTM models using weights optimized for held-out mean angular error. Models directly predicted unnormalized three-dimensional direction vectors and minimized their Euclidean distance from the true unit vector. Random pulse selection and averaging four sampled predictions improved accuracy, while skipping redundant evaluations on small events limited the inference overhead to about 15%. Training used batches 1–100 with batches 601–602 held out, and the best reported individual LSTM and GNN scores on batch 602 were 0.9859 and about 1.001.

solution_title: Silver medal from lucky ensemble public kernels
solution_summary: The author built a submission by ensembling public kernels. They report that hardware limitations constrained their participation. The post links the ensemble notebook but provides no model, validation, or weighting details.

solution_summary: The team describes a location matching pipeline with candidate generation, transformer blocking, and GBDT/BERT stacking. The post links to detailed explanations and two inference notebooks. Reported leaderboard scores were 0.972 and 0.955, while the authors felt leaks dominated the competition outcome.

The post celebrates the success of a simple public kernel and congratulates the deepflash2 team and other winners. It links to a public deepflash2 ensemble submission. It provides no technical account of the author's own pipeline.

The author used blending for the final submission, with limited pipeline details provided in the post. A voting classifier helped a single LightGBM model achieve a public leaderboard score of 0.81851. Two final blending variants used the saga and liblinear solvers, and the liblinear variant was submitted because the saga run took longer. The referenced final blending notebook reports a score of 0.81875.

The final pipeline used Hierarchical-Localization with SuperPoint features and SuperGlue matching, with input resolution increased to 2000. Raising resolution from 1024 to 2000 increased the public score from 0.24 to 0.46, making resolution the central improvement. Feature augmentation, SIFT fusion, alternative matchers, and multiple resolutions did not provide clear additional gains. Repeated runs varied by as much as 0.04 on the public leaderboard, and increasing geometric-verification trials did not resolve this instability.

solution_title: Congratulations to every participant.....🙌😍😍🙌🙌  Once again my late and newly discovered "Ensemble Technique" paid off in the last minutes.
solution_summary: The author reports using a personally developed ensemble technique discovered shortly before the competition ended. The post provides no model choices, ensemble formula, or feature details. Local cross-validation guided submission selection, including one choice supported by the public leaderboard and another trusted by the author.

The solution initialized tree packings from a dense lattice whose basic unit was a pair of trees, then refined them with custom simulated annealing. Initialization varied with tree count, and temporarily freezing core trees substantially improved efficiency for larger packings. Tournament selection concentrated compute on promising configurations, while a final annealing variant compressed valid layouts or relaxed invalid ones. Optimized CPU geometry routines supported an improvement from roughly 69.43 to 69.22.

solution_summary: The solution combined template-based RNA modeling with Protenix inference under a two-T4 GPU budget. Templates were aligned using sequence and ViennaRNA secondary-structure information, with independent chain matching solved by linear assignment. Protenix candidates were generated within sequence-length and runtime limits, then used to replace weaker template candidates. Missing-chain filling and averaging of closely aligned structures helped candidate quality, while several alignment and coordinate-refinement experiments failed to improve scores.

solution_summary: The final submission used a single LightGBM model with 140 features, including 21 user-level aggregations. A custom transaction-linking script identified users and imputed missing D1 values. Validation combined a downsampled final-period holdout with month-grouped folds, emphasizing December performance. User-level maximum predictions and setting predictions to one for users whose last training transaction was fraudulent improved the reported AUC pairs from 0.956246/0.930972 to 0.958303/0.936062.

solution_summary: The author explored XGBoost with diverse target encodings and original-dataset aggregate features, alongside competitive TabM models. Standalone neural networks underperformed tree models, but a neural stacker combining diverse public-model predictions improved results. Exponential learning-rate decay and early stopping raised stacking CV to 0.95569. The final prediction equally blended that neural stack with another participant's ensemble, providing a small boost and more stable private performance.

The efficiency-focused pipeline combined text cleanup, rule-based PII detection, and a trained SpaCy model. Regular expressions handled several PII types, while a model based on en_core_web_lg predicted student names, usernames, and street addresses after pretraining on competition data and training with public supplementary data. Predictions were converted back to BIO labels and filtered with rules such as capitalization requirements for student names. Special-character preprocessing, adding ID numbers to the SpaCy model, and an additional token-checking model were unsuccessful.

solution_title: [9th solution] Ensemble of 5 external dataset transformers
solution_summary: The solution averaged prediction ranks from five RoBERTa models trained on different toxicity datasets and objectives. Exhaustive subset selection reduced an initial pool of 14 models to the strongest five-model ensemble. Validation used majority-voted competition annotations, and local scores ultimately guided decisions because public leaderboard scores were unstable. The ensemble achieved 0.7605 CV and 0.779 LB.

The solution combined four EfficientNet models with different input resolutions. All models used an 80% training split because alternative folds performed worse, and the author suspected the selected validation fold was unusually favorable. Five-pass test-time augmentation reduced both public and private scores. Both selected ensembles achieved about 0.92 private kappa, while the author also reported training on the previous competition's training and test data.

The author treated species detection as a multilabel problem and manually annotated additional overlapping calls in five-second audio chunks. The final ensemble combined 15 sound-event detection models trained with different losses, with Dense161 performing well. Training used multilabel-stratified folds, audio augmentations, and warmup followed by cosine learning-rate scheduling. Minority oversampling and majority undersampling worsened leaderboard performance, while an example Dense161 model scored 0.95548 publicly and 0.96300 privately.

The post describes a post-processing optimization that assigns camera labels while enforcing image-count constraints. It maximizes the sum of predicted probabilities for binary image-to-class assignments. The constraints exploit nearly equal camera-type proportions, equal counts of manipulated and unaltered images, and a timestamp-based public/private split. The author reports that the optimization runs in under a second.

Inference pooled 40 candidates from four folds and selected translations through minimum Bayes risk decoding, with character constraints and domain-specific normalization. The reported ensemble score reached 36.0 while fitting within the nine-hour inference limit.

solution_title: 17th Place Solution: An Alternative Rectification Workflow
solution_summary: The solution used a single-fold pipeline comprising template alignment, grid rectification, line segmentation, and signal regression. OpenCV keypoint matching supplied the initial homography, followed by learned grid detection and a nonrigid warp. A CNN–Transformer regressor converted predicted line intensity masks into subpixel signal coordinates. Pretraining achieved 30 dB validation SNR with ground-truth masks, while predicted masks limited fine-tuned performance to approximately 25–26 dB.

solution_summary: The solution uses a deep convolutional neural network to denoise document images. It maps a single input channel to a single output channel through six convolutional layers, with 96 channels in the intermediate layers. The architecture combines 3×3 and 1×1 convolutions with Leaky ReLU activations.

The team built a CatBoost approach centered on frequency encoding. They removed fake test rows before calculating frequencies jointly over training and test data. Original features were supplemented with versions that replaced singleton-frequency values by the median, followed by augmentation and stacking. They reported successive score improvements but noted that they forgot to include their neural network's weight in the stacking or blending models.

solution_title: preliminary LB 16th solution——Self-examination of a violator
solution_summary: The final solution extended a public LightGBM baseline and retained a single model after weighted averaging failed to improve the public score. Useful additions included city-item and country-item sales aggregates, recent missing-value counts, and feature pruning. The team divided forecast horizons into three groups with different training cutoffs to exploit more recent observations, then removed validation sets for final training. The reported public score improved from 0.514 to 0.508, with a final private score of 0.516; the post also discloses disqualification for extra-account submissions.

solution_title: REPRO: The Scored Attack Surface Collapses to a Single Primitive
solution_summary: The authors applied REPRO, an evolutionary prompt optimizer using failure-directed LLM mutation, semantic crossover, and Pareto selection with the benchmark scorer as fitness. Search converged on a simple exfiltration primitive that performed strongly against the public guardrail but failed against the held-out defense. A separate confused-deputy approach transferred approximately one-to-one between public and private evaluation, with a best private score of 19.065. Their recorded final score was zero because unset Final slots caused automatic selection of public exfiltration submissions.

solution_summary: The pipeline combined public ECG normalization and rectification stages with a public U-Net-style trace segmentation model. Source-aware preprocessing and selection between processed and unprocessed alignment outputs improved robustness. The largest individual improvement came from subpixel waveform extraction, interpolated gaps, and confidence-aware spike removal. Ensembled 1D signal refiners added further gains, producing a final private leaderboard SNR of 19.59 dB; rebuilding segmentation from scratch did not beat the public baseline.

solution_summary: The team combined ResNet200d, EfficientNetB7, and ResNet50d models using simple prediction averaging. Their main approach used three-stage training followed by soft-label pretraining and fine-tuning on competition and external chest X-ray datasets. Multi-head attention produced their best single model, with CV 0.9767 and private leaderboard score 0.972. The solution combined handcrafted specialists for cropping, tile repair, symmetry repair, and several isolated transformation tasks. Cropping used a manually constructed decision tree with elaborate scoring, while symmetry repair searched for complete or partial regularities. Some tasks first repaired symmetry and then cropped the recovered missing piece. Together these components solved seven direct cropping tasks, five direct symmetry-repair tasks, and two combined tasks, with four further tasks handled by separate methods.

The author modified a public CTC-based fingerspelling notebook with two small dropout changes. They reduced the dropout rate from 0.4 to 0.35 and added another dropout layer. The stated goal was to make learning easier without increasing the number of epochs, and the author reports that the changes worked.

The solution combined LightGBM and XGBoost models with neural networks. Tree models used original values, rarity-masked values, count encodings, and mean target encodings, with engineered features excluding fake test data. The neural network processed features independently while sharing dense-layer weights among features with similar target-conditional distributions. This weight sharing was critical to accuracy, while RAPIDS accelerated feature exploration and generation.

solution_summary: The solution combined variations of XGBoost and TabM, including TabM models trained to predict residuals from the original data-generating function. Seven models were blended with hill climbing, then TabM was retrained using test pseudo-labels generated by that ensemble. solution_title: KDD Cup 2013 - Author Paper Identification Challenge

solution_title: 26th Place Solution – MITSUI&CO. Commodity Prediction Challenge Writeup

solution_summary: The solution first trained a dilated ResNet-18 classifier on small patches, then removed its classification output to extract dense spatial features. Class-wise 1×1 convolutions mapped those features to normalized Gaussian density fields, and a simplified ResNet-18 converted ten density channels into five count predictions using RMSE loss. An auxiliary VGG-16 binary classifier filtered empty tiles to reduce the burden of the expensive dense network. Density regression alone worked well on synthetic data but suffered from class confusion and body-shape-related density overestimation on sea lions, motivating the final count-regression stage.

The final submission used a single Cascade Mask R-CNN with a ConvNeXt-tiny backbone and multi-scale TTA with NMS. Training proceeded through several stages, using initial models to pseudo-label Dataset 3 and later a Dataset 1-focused model to regenerate high-confidence labels for Datasets 2 and 3. Trusting expert-reviewed Dataset 1 annotations, training only the blood-vessel class, and scaling images were central decisions. Larger models, flip augmentation, weighted boxes fusion, and ensembles with other models did not improve the approach.

solution_title: 5th place | 24/27 | Lessons from my first CTF + how GPT4 can help
solution_summary: The author solved a range of AI security challenges using prompt injection, automated endpoint probing, image perturbations, and language-based search. GPT-4 helped explain unfamiliar tasks, generate attack code, and interpret experimental results. Successful approaches included structured-output prompts, gradient ascent with an image border, and Markov-generated phrases refined through word replacement. Extensive querying and brute force were central to several solutions, while Hush and Granny 3 remained unsolved.
compute: Close to 100 hours spent on Granny 3; over 200,000 endpoint requests for Inversion and over 10 million trials for Granny 3.

solution_title: Hosted Evaluator Reproducibility for Multi-Step Agent Security
solution_summary: This post is a methodological note about reproducibility and evidence management for hosted agent-security evaluations. It reports that a byte-identical candidate received public scores of 35.635 and 27.970, while leaving the cause unresolved. It advocates richer run identities, evaluator-era metadata, preregistration, and preservation of negative results, but does not disclose an operational competition solution.

The solution fine-tuned official joint-BERT variants in TensorFlow 1.15 using Google Cloud TPUs. Whole-word-masking weights and revised negative sampling were the strongest improvements, with SQuAD pre-tuning contributing to the best single model. Full-development-set validation guided checkpoint selection, thresholds, and three-model probability averaging. Larger inference strides reduced runtime, while yes/no thresholds and increased context coverage improved final development F1 to 67.0.

solution_summary: The author explored several attack families and selected a structured-mapping candidate and a source-free confused-deputy candidate for final submission. Local tests measured both tool-sequence completion and scoring throughput, revealing different execution behavior for GPT-OSS and Gemma. The structured-mapping selection scored 93.375 publicly but zero privately, while the confused-deputy selection scored 21.590 in both evaluations. Public scores failed to transfer across some attack families but preserved the ordering of four closely related confused-deputy variants, including a stronger candidate that was not selected.

solution_summary: The author extended a statistical text-normalization approach with five-word context matching and selective skipping of punctuation and short words. Custom parsers handled dates, simple URLs, and structured numbers, with num2words covering other numeric cases and a dictionary handling endings. Transliteration was the main difficulty: a CMU-based phonetic approach performed poorly, while transliterate plus over 40 manual rules reached 50% training accuracy.

The solution combined competition data with the original dataset and engineered hour, day, and division features. A CatBoost model used a custom focal loss, with predictions averaged across ten stratified folds. Optuna tuned model parameters and the focal-loss gamma parameter over roughly 50 trials.

The submitted solution equally averaged ranked predictions from two logistic regressions, a PyTorch MLP, CatBoost, and two RealMLP variants. The logistic regressions used target-encoded feature pairs or triplets transformed into logits and polynomial features, while the custom MLP embedded categorical values and original-data target statistics. Local cross-validation guided development because public notebooks were overfitting the public leaderboard. The ensemble achieved CV 0.95583 and private score 0.95532; post-competition analysis identified leakage in the second logistic regression, whose removal improved the private score to 0.95534.
compute: Nvidia GPU used for PyTorch MLP, CatBoost, and RealMLP; Nvidia cuML logistic regression.

solution_title: Open Contribution Award — Best RL Method
solution_summary: The final solution sequentially trained one Nemotron LoRA adapter with supervised fine-tuning and direct preference optimization. Diverse reasoning sources were normalized, filtered, and deduplicated, while generated answers were verified to build a small preference dataset. DPO used 105 training pairs and improved public and private scores from 0.836/0.852 to 0.844/0.856. Online GRPO and GSPO implementations remained experimental because of synchronization, runtime, dependency, and memory constraints.

solution_summary: The solution adapted the second.pytorch PointPillars implementation to the Lyft dataset and removed a problematic Spconv dependency. Validation held out the final 20% of data by scene. Extending point-cloud coverage, object anchors, and detection filtering from roughly 50 to 100 meters materially improved performance. The retrained model achieved validation mAP of 0.072 and private leaderboard mAP of 0.078.

solution_summary: The author trained a LightGBM model with a Poisson objective on all labeled data, without a validation split. The configuration used 700 iterations, 80 leaves, a learning rate of 0.1, and feature and row subsampling. The author emphasized avoiding overfitting and did not apply prediction multipliers. No numerical score was reported.

solution_summary: The final system trained 12 sparse MLPs across three differently preprocessed datasets, prioritizing input diversity over architectural variety. Text concatenation, character n-grams, stemming, numerical vectorization, and binary input variants improved the ensemble. Training combined increasing batch sizes, decreasing learning rates, and regression or soft price-bucket classification objectives. Lasso selected blending weights, and CPU-efficient implementations produced private scores of 0.37758 with MXNet and 0.38006 with TensorFlow.
compute: CPU training with four models in parallel, one core per model; 12 models with hidden size 256 and about 200k features.

solution_summary: The solution treated Persuade and non-Persuade essays as distinct scoring domains and assumed the test set consisted entirely of non-Persuade samples. Training used source tags, an auxiliary source classifier, source-specific scoring heads in some models, and early stopping on non-Persuade performance. The final ensemble averaged 45 predictions from three model families, five folds, and three random seeds. Optimizing thresholds on OOF predictions increased non-Persuade QWK from 0.818 to 0.827, while dynamic micro-batching and a modified DeBERTa implementation improved efficiency.

The final ensemble used weighted rank averaging across an attention-based LSTM–GRU, BERT Base and Large, GPT-2, and boosted trees trained on BERT features. RNN embeddings combined fastText or GloVe with fastText trained on the competition data. Preprocessing varied by model family, while all neural models used weighted focal loss and subgroup negative weighting. Translation-based augmentation, past competition data, statistical features, and several other feature and input experiments did not help.
