solution_title: What is you actual best model?
solution_summary: The post describes model selection using the final six weeks of training data and a reservation-data adjustment, without specifying the model architecture. Splitting validation into the first six days and remaining 33 days exposed a mismatch between public and private performance, leading the team to stop relying on public scores. Removing reservations made less than about ten days before visits reduced dependence on information that becomes scarce during the test period and improved the private score by about 0.002. A model with private score 0.508 was left unselected because it performed slightly worse on their validation window.

The solution used mathematical light-curve modeling to predict a single average transit depth and uncertainty per planet. Transit boundaries came from local linear fits to the white light curve, while depth estimation fitted a flux-drop model with cubic sensor drift. Uncertainty combined variation over time and wavelength, with conservative fallbacks for anomalous curves or failed phase detection. A 100-configuration ensemble improved the local score from 0.437 to 0.440 without improving leaderboard scores, and wavelength-dependent depth prediction performed worse.
compute: Preprocessing reduced from about 6 hours to roughly 2 hours through Numba acceleration.

solution_title: 9th Place Solution [ResNeSt might be the key]
solution_summary: The final submission averaged two EfficientNet-B0 models and two ResNeSt50 models trained with label smoothing and ordinal regression, with GeM pooling used for ResNeSt50. Training used 36 tiles of 256×256 pixels from level 1, represented either as tile lists or a single tiled image. Combining the stronger public-scoring EfficientNet models with the more stable ResNeSt models mattered more than favoring EfficientNet with larger ensemble weights. A progressive-resizing SE-ResNeXt50 experiment produced promising private results but was excluded because compute limits prevented training at larger image sizes.

solution_summary: The author improved a public essay-scoring baseline that incorporated DeBERTa-v3-large features, training LightGBM on 501 selected features. Repeating competition-only essays emphasized data believed to resemble the test distribution, while removing train-validation overlap made cross-validation more informative. The final setup used 30 stratified folds, regularized shallow trees, early stopping, and adjustments to quadratic weighted kappa parameters. The best final submission scored 0.836 privately, 0.826 publicly, and 0.8275 in cross-validation.

The solution repeatedly trained AutoGluon on selected out-of-fold predictions, using feature importance to refine the inputs between rounds. Strong pairwise interactions and target/categorical encoding mattered more than most handcrafted features. The final selections included a seeded AutoGluon ensemble and an average of four AutoGluon runs. The selected individual run achieved 0.97790 private ROC AUC, while additional blending improved CV without materially improving leaderboard performance.

solution_summary: The agent was initialized through behavioral cloning and then trained with PPO against a fixed collection of public-kernel opponents. A KL divergence term stabilized reinforcement learning. Self-play with league training enabled further improvement while limiting self-play collapse. The final agent included a small rule-based defensive patch.

The solution classified blood-containing image tiles using a frozen ImageNet-pretrained EfficientNetB0 and a single fully connected head. Clinic-based validation addressed institutional differences, while strong color jitter and random sharpness adjustments were central to generalization. Six fold models formed the final ensemble, with test-time augmentation and a neutral prediction for images without usable tiles. The reported CV metric was 0.63738 and the private leaderboard metric was 0.66421.

The final submission averaged 50 XGBoost models trained through five-fold stratification repeated ten times with fixed hyperparameters. TimeSeriesSplit supported local hyperparameter tuning, and original-data fraud examples were added to the synthetic training set. Daily-mean-centered V features improved the private score, while matching V14 and V21 pairs allowed 466 test predictions to be set to zero. Including original fraud examples ultimately hurt generalization; excluding them would have yielded a reported score of 0.8333.

The author modified a U-Net to predict shared nucleus boundaries, nucleus regions, and background using a heavily weighted pixelwise loss. Grayscale intensity normalization and overlapping image splits reduced appearance differences and geometric distortion. Six grouped folds supplied averaged predictions, followed by marker-based random-walker segmentation with watershed fallback. Boundary prediction was central to separating adjacent nuclei, while preprocessing and postprocessing alone raised the reported stage-one score from 0.263 to 0.457. Teammates also contributed mosaic reconstruction and stronger augmentation.

solution_title: 15th Place Solution: CAM & Semantic Segmentation approach
solution_summary: The solution used weakly supervised semantic segmentation, first training image classifiers and then generating CAM-based pseudo labels for segmentation models. Normal CAM and sub-category CAM were combined with instance masks from the HPA cell segmentator. Sub-category CAM improved scores at 512×512, while flip and scale test-time augmentation also improved CAM predictions. The best reported segmentation model achieved a public score of 0.491, and channels-last training reduced training time substantially.

solution_title: [Bronze, 262/4348] Honest held-out eval for Nemotron LoRA: server-like scoring,
solution_summary: The author fine-tuned NVIDIA Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B-BF16 with rank-32 LoRA on public chain-of-thought data and submitted an adapter-only archive. A deterministic, category-stratified 10% holdout was excluded from all reasoning generation and training records. Local scoring reproduced boxed-answer extraction and numeric tolerance, while category-level analysis exposed weak cryptarithm performance. Synthetic cryptarithm generation was explored, and the public baseline was calibrated around a 0.84 leaderboard score.

solution_summary: The approach combined sensor-based pedestrian dead reckoning with absolute positions inferred from Wi-Fi fingerprints. Fingerprint matching incorporated neighboring observations along path segments, shifting their coordinates using relative motion estimates. Iterative snapping to training waypoint grids refined whole paths and corrected adjacent points that collapsed onto the same waypoint. The team's submission used a different, more advanced post-processing method that this post does not describe.

14th Place: A Hierarchical U-Net Stack with Seed Averaging
solution_summary: The submitted pipeline combined a 30-checkpoint U-Net blend with an engineered-feature tree model through a hard per-well gate, then added width-difference and seed-averaged correction directions. Error analysis showed that per-well offsets dominated squared error, motivating these corrections. Fixed whole-well folds, nested fitting of ensemble parameters, and well-level bootstrap tests governed evaluation across hundreds of experiments. The final model achieved CV RMSE 6.2518 and private RMSE 6.329, while an earlier, simpler ridge-combined U-Net ensemble achieved a better private RMSE of 6.266 despite weaker CV.

solution_title: 6th Place Solution: Enhancing Features with Binned and RMSE-Optimized CatBoost Predictions
solution_summary: The solution generated additional features from CatBoost classification probabilities and RMSE-optimized regression predictions. Target binning and treating classifier inputs as categorical improved the classification-derived features, while feature engineering strengthened the regression-derived features. Out-of-fold LightGBM and XGBoost predictions were combined with these features in a stack, producing a private leaderboard score in the 1.023 range. Adding the original dataset was rejected because its target distribution hurt performance.

The solution emphasized diverse feature views built with traditional engineering, autoencoder representations, genetic programming, and PCA. Base learners used different feature subsets, single seeds, and five-fold cross-validation, with a Ridge stack guiding development. Only features with zero initial XGBoost importance were removed. Shared RealMLP predictions improved experimental scores, but the author states that the final Ridge stack used exclusively their own generated out-of-fold predictions.

The solution prioritized generalization to misconceptions absent from the training set through synthetic question generation, generated misconception descriptions, and targeted retrieval. LoRA-tuned Qwen retrievers combined embeddings from 14B and 32B models, retrieving both general candidates and additional unseen-misconception candidates. Three rerankers were formed by merging fold-specific LoRA components and then ensembling their outputs; including a reranker trained on generated data improved the private score by 0.01. Final post-processing multiplied scores for training-seen misconceptions by 0.40.

solution_title: [Kent AI Lab | Ding Han | Renan] 5th place solution (code available)
solution_summary: The solution treated salt detection as classification plus segmentation because many images had empty masks. It combined ResNet34 U-Net and ResNeXt-family models with spatial/channel excitation, hypercolumns, and an Object Context Module. Cosine annealing and snapshot ensembling produced 200 models, with higher-resolution fine-tuning and simulated leaderboard shakeups used to select the most stable 100. Final predictions averaged sigmoid outputs and used majority voting for binary decisions; distribution-based thresholding and jigsaw rules offered little private-leaderboard benefit.

solution_title: [LB25] Improvements to the progress prize submission
solution_summary: The author improved a Nemotron reasoning system by correcting validation prompts, shortening numeric-equation tasks, and adding synthetic training examples. Cipher training included prefix examples to address spelling weaknesses, while bit-manipulation reasoning was reorganized. Repeated submissions scored between 0.864 and 0.872. Attempts to improve cryptarithm reasoning did not succeed because the trained model repeated guesses.

solution_title: 7-th place solution from AlphaGoal Team [2.5D CenterNet, 3D CNN]
solution_summary: The pipeline combined helmet detection, impact classification, and duplicate suppression. Four fold-specific 2.5D CenterNet detectors processed eight-frame clips with DenseNet121 encoders and test-time augmentation. A single-fold 3D ResNet50 impact classifier improved the leaderboard score by roughly 0.05 when stacked with CenterNet predictions. IoU-based helmet tracking retained the frame with the highest impact probability, and the best classifier approach achieved an F1 of 0.57 after post-processing.

solution_title: 10th Place Solution: XGB with Autoregressive RNN features
solution_summary: The author treated short customer histories as sequences missing their most recent months and used an autoregressive GRU to reconstruct them. The GRU learned feature prediction from both training and test data, after log transformation and zero imputation. Completed 13-month histories were flattened into monthly features for seven XGBoost models. Their ensemble achieved 0.7993 CV and 0.799 public leaderboard performance before being averaged with a strong public solution.

The pipeline extracted DOI and accession identifiers from parsed documents using regex and corpus mining, then classified reference types with separately fine-tuned models. External unofficial data improved type classification, while SAMN identifiers were assigned Primary directly. A contextual positive-versus-negative filter learned which mined identifiers matched the hosts' annotation patterns and improved the public score to 0.748. The final submission used a single fine-tuned type classifier and limited post-processing after stacked models, fine-tuned LLMs, and several local-validation heuristics failed to improve leaderboard performance.

solution_summary: The solution stacked two MLP variants, a tabular 1D CNN and LightGBM, reducing standardized first-level predictions before feeding them to the second level. It blended variants with different feature extraction, dimensionality reduction and losses, and averaged results over 15 random seeds. Citeseq used PCA or truncated SVD and correlation-selected RNA features, while Multiome omitted selected features and compressed targets before training. Simple five-fold validation supported the approach, and direct stacking without dimensionality reduction performed worse.

The team combined three face classifiers with different architectures and training samples, using CenterNet detection and IoU tracking to handle videos containing multiple faces. Folder-based validation, noisy-face filtering, larger crop margins, and fine-tuning with random erasing helped improve generalization. Face predictions were combined using a conditional two-score ensemble, then aggregated with detection-confidence weights and a maximum across face tracks. The final ensemble achieved approximately 0.294 public leaderboard loss, but its submissions were removed because they used FaceForensics++ external data.

Training progressed from lower-resolution images using 2019 and 2020 data to 512-pixel training on 2020 data, followed by low-learning-rate fine-tuning. SAM with Adam and then AdamP, label-smoothed Taylor cross-entropy, a later combo loss, and strong augmentation defined the training recipe. The average achieved 0.905 public and 0.9013 private accuracy, with the author crediting SAM plus AdamP for generalization.

solution_title: 18th Place Solution - Simple Improvement of Public Kernel
solution_summary: The solution improved a public LightGBM one-step-ahead forecasting kernel with additional averaging and aggregation features. Store-level and item-level sales and transaction summaries supplemented the original store-item time-series features. Forecasts for nearer dates used more recent history, and the final model was retrained with two additional weeks of data after validation. These changes improved the reported private score from 0.523 to 0.516 and public score from 0.515 to 0.508.

solution_title: Team BNR: 12th Place Solution, Exploring Various Custom Architectures
solution_summary: The solution combined five EEG modeling approaches, including learnable convolutional frontends, a ResNet–Transformer–GRU model, trainable wavelets, and spectrogram models. Patient-grouped stratified validation, strong augmentation, and two-stage training with noisy and pseudo labels were central to performance. Hill climbing selected ensemble weights, which were reused for full-data models trained with three seeds. The final ensemble achieved approximately 0.215 CV and 0.23 leaderboard scores.

solution_title: 251 Place Solution for the NVIDIA Nemotron Model Reasoning Challenge Competition
solution_summary: The approach fine-tuned Nemotron-3-Nano-30B with LoRA using reasoning traces emitted by verified programmatic solvers. Corpus design was the main driver: each line expressed one reproducible operation, traces were length-filtered, and sample weights balanced task families. Training Mamba in_proj adapters at rank 64 and compressing them to rank 32 with SVD added a reproducible 0.01 leaderboard gain. Light GRPO improved already strong supervised models, with the best reported held-out accuracy reaching 93.8%, while clean-derivation methods failed on the coupled cryptarithm family. The author also found that public-leaderboard selection could disagree with held-out validation.

The solution averaged three LightGBM models trained for rising, falling, and relatively stable markets. Its most valuable feature measured the difference between the latest close and a Hull moving average. Other features used Fibonacci-based lag windows, a simple historical return proxy, and an aggregate market indicator. Parameters were largely defaults, and submission execution took around six hours.

solution_summary: The author combined a compact BigGAN with StyleGAN mechanisms, particularly style conditioning and blur, to generate 96×96 dog images. Using 24 generator and discriminator channels and a batch size of 32 proved effective, while attention and style mixing were excluded. Training on square dog crops achieved a public score of 12.4; probabilistically adding resized original images scored 13.4 but was preferred for potential generalization. The reported improvements came from changing multiple experimental settings rather than a controlled ablation study.

solution_summary: The submitted solution used a single CatBoost model trained on the competition training data combined with the original dataset. Its preprocessing combined filled columns, dropped columns, and grouped categorical values, although the supplied code omits the column names and constants. A broader notebook framework tracked datasets, models, and cross-validation results. The submission was selected automatically by its public leaderboard score.

The solution combined a binary nocall detector, a ResNeSt multilabel spectrogram classifier, and a LightGBM candidate classifier. Nocall probabilities refined weak training labels, while the tabular stage combined bird predictions with temporal context and recording metadata. The authors optimized a decision threshold on train_soundscapes and improved scoring by allowing nocall to coexist with predicted birds. Retrospectively, an unselected two-model ensemble would have performed better.

solution_title: 520th Place Solution for the ICR - Identifying Age-Related Conditions Competition
solution_summary: The solution adapted a public gradient boosting ensemble with basic preprocessing and a weighted blend of CatBoost, XGBoost, and LightGBM. Training used 10 folds instead of 20, and models with stronger cross-validation scores received larger blend weights. The approach emphasized stability under distribution shifts and improved its relative standing on the private evaluation.

solution_summary: The solution used a CNN–BiLSTM to combine helmet-centered video crops with player tracking data, then passed neural logits and engineered features to LightGBM and XGBoost classifiers. Temporal overlap averaging, player-order swapping, and diverse backbone and sequence-length combinations supplied robustness. Forward selection chose six model configurations, whose five-fold predictions were blended and thresholded. The final submission achieved CV 0.8016, public score 0.7902, and private score 0.7913.

solution_summary: The strongest submission was an initial baseline combining three LightGBM models and two XGBoost models tuned with FLAML. Weight-ratio features and synthetic training samples did not improve performance. Attempts to identify age outliers manually or generate additional old-crab samples also failed. Submission bookkeeping mistakes meant the author did not select the strongest baseline for the final submission.

The system retrieved candidates from past session events, weighted co-visitation, and an SRGNN before ranking them with four blended binary classifiers. SRGNN improved weighted candidate recall to 0.695 while slightly reducing the average candidate count relative to the co-visitation baseline. Ranking used session, item, temporal interaction, and embedding similarity features with grouped cross-validation and negative downsampling. Sessions with insufficient candidates were supplemented using unrestricted co-visitation and recent popular items.

solution_summary: The final predictor took the median of three ensembles, each formed from a learned linear combination of ten XGBoost fold models. Symmetric-game agent swapping, AdvantageP1 interaction features, and aggressive feature removal supported generalization. Validation grouped games by ruleset and stratified discretized targets, while column subsampling and selected early stopping constrained overfitting. Learned ensemble weights amplified predictions before clipping to the target range, and the selected submission scored 0.425 privately.

solution_summary: The solution first predicts coarse masks with a standard U-Net on 320×480 images, then refines boundaries using 256×256 tiles and a deeper U-Net. Overlapping tiles provide repeated predictions for boundary pixels, reducing tile-edge errors. Augmentation, Dice loss, and batch normalization support training, with batches drawing tiles from multiple images. The single model scored 0.9970 and a fold ensemble reached 0.9971, although some severely incorrect first-stage test masks remained uncorrected.

solution_title: 37th place solution - T0m part [Segment Copy-Paste & Progressive Learning]

Segmentation-guided copy-paste added small starfish, with RGB mean matching to harmonize pasted objects and backgrounds. Progressive learning increased image size and augmentation strength during training, and inference used TTA and tracking. The selected full-data retrained ensemble scored 0.696 privately, below the unselected ensemble's 0.711.

The solution combined Wikipedia retrieval with a DeBERTa large multiple-choice model. Article IDs from two Wikipedia datasets were used to collect article text through MediaWiki, producing roughly 22 million subsection texts after filtering. An e5-base-v2 retriever searched a sharded Faiss index and refined the retrieved context at the line level. Including competing answers in context and shuffling answer options for test-time augmentation improved performance, while RAG delivered the largest reported CV gain of 0.1.

Four-bit QLoRA training and quantized inference enabled the large-model ensemble within the available resources. solution_title: 2nd Place Solution Write-up for AIMO3 Competition
solution_summary: This inference-only solution served GPT-OSS 120B through vLLM and ran eight parallel tool-assisted reasoning attempts per problem. The most impactful modification was a stronger prompt emphasizing answer constraints, modular reduction, and independent verification. Final answers were extracted only from boxed integers and selected through voting supplemented by tail-window entropy and median confidence. Dynamic budgeting and early stopping conserved runtime, with 50 problems taking approximately four to five hours on one H100 80GB.

solution_summary: The author constructed the solution mathematically by separating sequences into mandatory sequences, their relatives, and all remaining sequences. A cyclic length-to-coverage argument established a relaxed lower bound of 2400 without wildcards. Carefully assembled base permutations produced three sequences of length 2440, then six wildcard substitutions reduced the objective to 2428. The author argued that each wildcard could save at most six characters within this construction, while acknowledging that this was not a complete proof of global optimality.

The author focused on the efficiency stream and chose LightGBM to balance predictive performance with fast inference. Feature engineering used Polars, Numba, and Joblib to reduce processing time, with Polars reported as faster than Pandas. Important features came from reconstructed essays and aggregates of differences in down_time and event_id between events. The provided text does not preserve numerical scores or execution timings.

The final system combined six lightweight Conv1D models with two transformer variants and test-time augmentation. Landmark normalization, varied body-part inputs, and strong spatial and temporal augmentations mattered more than architectural complexity. Same-label body-part recombination and CutMix improved training, while transformers combined coordinate and motion embeddings. The six-model convolutional ensemble achieved 0.8711 private score before transformers were added; additional WLASL data was tested but excluded.

solution_title: There is a silver solution hidden in public notebooks!
solution_summary: The post compares public RTK baselines and highlights how phone-specific performance explains public and private score differences. The Python RTK baseline performed poorly on Pixel4 devices but strongly on Samsung and Pixel5, which dominated the private paths. The authors also report improving taro's baseline from 3.027 to 2.66, without describing the modifications. They suggest replacing Pixel4 predictions from the Python RTK baseline with another public baseline, estimating a public score near 2.6.

The solution combined gradient-boosted trees with diverse neural models through hill climbing. Keras factorization machines treated every feature as categorical, using rounding to reduce cardinality and bigram interactions to improve their predictions. These models complemented the trees particularly well, raising ensemble CV from about 0.9275 to about 0.928. Several neural models and learned stackers improved CV without improving leaderboard performance, making ensemble overfitting a central difficulty.

solution_title: [47th place solution] Pytorch Lightning Framework + Column-wise Ensemble
solution_summary: The solution used transformer encoders trained with PyTorch Lightning and a 90/10 training-validation split. Rotary positional encoding improved the public score by approximately 0.005, and the best single model scored 0.751 publicly and 0.744 privately. Feature-specific transformations and scaling were combined with an Optuna-tuned ensemble that assigned separate model weights to each target column. KAN embeddings and clamped-label training did not improve standalone converged performance but supplied models for the final ensemble, while alternative output heads increased overfitting.

The solution combined two encoder-decoder Transformers trained on sequences of 500 user interactions, with users held out for validation. Engineered timing and repeated-question features improved convergence and AUROC, while container-aware attention masks prevented answer leakage and allowed appropriate within-container context. A time-aware ensemble skipped inference on the first 20% of the test stream and used both models as much as the remaining runtime allowed. The smaller Transformer outperformed the larger model, and training used distributed execution and mixed precision.

solution_summary: The pipeline used a two-tower MPNet recall model to identify likely code positions for markdown cells, followed by pairwise and context-based DeBERTa rankers. Recall predictions guided candidate selection, markdown grouping, training sampling, and additional context-model inputs. CatBoost and LightGBM combined scores from the three neural models. Recall-guided context selection was especially valuable, and the author reported a final score of 0.9170 without external data.

solution_title: [6th] RL + league + search with a custom edge attention transformer
solution_summary: The solution trained separate two-player and four-player transformer policies using self-play, with league play added for four-player games. Relative inputs, custom planet-to-planet attention, and extensive forward-prediction features were central to sample efficiency and stable behavior across starting positions. Training used asynchronous PPO, transferred knowledge from a smaller model, and averaged selected checkpoints. A greedy two-step rollout search improved two-player performance by roughly 30–40 points, while compute limits and weaker four-player opponent coverage remained constraints.

solution_summary: The author initially trained raw-waveform 1D CNNs with person-grouped ten-fold validation and manually reviewed errors to identify silence and mislabeled recordings. After teaming up, the approach shifted to high-resolution mel spectrograms with VGG-like and later ResNet-like networks. Heavy noise augmentation, with noise up to twice the signal level, was the largest improvement and raised a single model to 0.898 public leaderboard score. The final submission ensembled several additional models, while the original 1D model was dropped.

solution_title: Graph Transformer With Minimal FE, with code
solution_summary: The author implemented a compact Keras transformer with distance-based attention over player embeddings and a multi-head attention block. It combined a direct cumulative-probability output with a custom piecewise-logistic distribution output, using isotonic regression to enforce monotonicity. Time-based validation and reduced weighting of 2017 samples improved agreement with the leaderboard. Augmenting plays with projected future positions and averaging their predictions improved cross-validation by almost 0.00010 and produced a public score of 0.01299. Later notebook updates added encoder-decoder attention, squeeze-and-excitation, and better data cleaning.

solution_summary: The team modeled the 15 largest products using one general model and dedicated models for cco and reca. The general model used 12 product-history lags, while the dedicated models used five lags and selected historical months to capture seasonality. Dedicated and general predictions were combined by taking the maximum probability for each targeted product. Leaderboard-driven calibration in logit space materially improved the score, and previous product usage dominated other features.

solution_title: [79th]Shakeup: transfer analysis for a hidden guardrail[Working Note]

The surviving submission used marker-free CONFUSED_DEPUTY prompts and unique recipients on the fixture's dominant internal domain. Harmony framing and wrap-up suppression reduced generation costs for gpt_oss. The sentinel-based public submission failed privately, consistent with the predicted pattern-filter outcome. Conservative candidate-count sizing limited the surviving submission's score.

solution_title: 14th Place Solution: The Almost Golden Defenders
solution_summary: The team built a four-level stack combining LightGBM, text ridge models, and neural networks. The final layer used nonnegative Lasso models trained separately by parent category, capturing category-specific error patterns. Lower layers diversified categorical encodings, regression objectives, text representations, and model versions. The final stack improved the public score from about 0.2149 to 0.2148, with category-specific Lasso providing a very small additional gain.

solution_title: 8th place - Trust the CV - 409 jump in places on the private ds :)
solution_summary: The best single model was XGBoost trained after adding the original dataset and manually removing extreme outliers. Feature preparation included scaling, removal of perfect collinearity, cardinality reduction, and power transforms. A custom binned cross-validation optimization procedure selected feature engineering choices before tuning XGBoost. A second submission used an ensemble of different models and versions, with submission selection guided by local validation.

solution_title: Public 9th/Private 331st Place Solution - A Non-Bioinformatician's Journey in CAFA
solution_summary: The approach combined protein embeddings with sequence properties, species information, and UniProt metadata in diverse MLPs, a 1D CNN, and nearest-neighbor models. Feature filtering, label updates, and aspect-specific GO term selection supported the pipeline. Multilabel stratified validation and averaging across different fold counts were especially important, reportedly improving CV by 0.03–0.04. The best CV ensemble used different model weights for each functional aspect, while ridge regression received zero weight.

The author initially built hundreds of models, but blending them provided little improvement because they captured similar information. Most gains came from late feature generation with Claude and ChatGPT, followed by forward and backward selection and Optuna tuning. The strongest reported single XGBoost and logistic regression models reached OOF scores of 0.94666 and 0.94661. Logistic regression blending was selected for the final submission, although hill climbing produced better reported OOF and private scores.

The author trained a model on examples with efs equal to one. Predictions were then multiplied by the probability that efs equals one. The approach was discovered two days before the deadline, leaving little time for analysis; the model architecture and numerical results are not described in the text.

The final solution averaged three multilevel ensembles built with 5-, 7-, and 10-fold splits. Its pipeline combined diverse base predictions, engineered meta features, logistic-regression stacking, and self-distilled student models. RealMLP was the strongest base family, while using original data as extra rows versus derived columns supplied complementary signals. Conservative blends and averaging across parameter settings helped limit dependence on optimistic stacking CV scores. The final ensemble achieved public and private scores of 0.95462 and 0.95487.

The team combined whole-grapheme classifiers with separate component models to improve generalization to unseen graphemes. Grapheme probabilities were converted into component scores by averaging across graphemes sharing each component value, reducing frequency bias. FMix, synthetic graphemes, and validation that withheld entire graphemes supported this approach. The final seven-model ensemble used component-specific blending and inverse-frequency consonant weights.

These included LSTMs, transformers, convolutional models, NetVLAD and Fisher-vector variants, and class-conditioned XGBoost models. The final submission averaged segment-model scores and smoothed predictions using neighboring segments. Filtering raised public leaderboard mAP from 84.3 to 84.4.

The agent ensembled three imitation-learning models: a decreasing-learning-rate model, a toad model, and a U-Net model. It selected actions using the highest softmax probability rather than the most frequent model vote. A separate U-Net learned city-tile actions. solution_title: 15th Place Solution : 8 days of Hard Work

Their ensemble combined EfficientNet B5, B7, EfficientNetV2-M, and ECA-NFNet-L0, using only ON observations and light augmentation to preserve weak signals. Stratified five-fold validation guided training, while the final tuning stage used lower learning rates and fewer epochs. solution_title: [ods.ai] Power Fist solution and data explanation (11th public -> 43rd private)
solution_summary: The solution used U-Net-like segmentation networks, with SE-ResNeXt50 offering the preferred accuracy and speed tradeoff. Upscaled images, decoder attention blocks, an auxiliary mask-presence output, Lovasz loss, and cosine scheduling with RMSprop improved training. Pseudo-labeling strengthened the final ensemble, which averaged predictions from 15–21 checkpoints across eight folds. Puzzle reconstruction exposed dataset leakage and enabled heuristic corrections, while masks containing fewer than ten predicted pixels were removed.

The solution engineered features from value counts and the bimodal distributions found among values occurring exactly once. It created singleton and peak-membership masks, then calculated distances to peak locations for singleton values and to count-group means for other values. Three feature groups were constructed for ensembling, and the author attributed substantial gains to these features. LightGBM with data augmentation achieved reported scores of 0.92475 public and 0.92367 private.

Team members independently engineered features and generated out-of-fold predictions throughout the competition. They then pooled their features and generated additional predictions using different parameter settings and feature subsets. More than 150 out-of-fold prediction sets supported diverse one-layer stacking models, followed by tuning and blending. The post emphasizes feature engineering dashboards drawing on public kernels and the team's own ideas, but gives no specific model families or scores.

solution_title: 37th Place Solution - Prompt to shorten thinking
solution_summary: The submission adapted a public notebook and focused on prompting gpt-oss to solve integer-answer mathematics problems efficiently. The prompts organized problem solving into understanding, exploration, planning, execution, verification, and answer extraction. They emphasized exact arithmetic, targeted checks, and selective Python tool use to reduce errors and unnecessary reasoning. No numerical evaluation results were reported.

solution_title: LLM + Online Learning is all you need
solution_summary: The team built a translation pipeline around data extraction and cleaning, supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, and online learning from test-set pseudo-labels. Gemini extracted aligned sentence pairs from publications, while retrieval over these pairs supported pseudo-labeling and training-data repair. The strongest online-learning gains came from alternating between LLMs and ByT5 rather than training models repeatedly on outputs from the same architecture. Predictions from the resulting online-trained models were ensembled for the final submission.

solution_summary: The solution blended diverse neural networks and tree models with Ridge regression, relying on 10-fold cross-validation to guide progress. Neural models included FT-Transformers, ResNet-style MLPs, and plain MLPs with multiple embedding strategies, using log transformations and standardization. Duplicate handling depended on label noise and leakage, with noisy non-leaking duplicates averaged and noisy leaking duplicates removed. The selected submission scored 0.05646 publicly and 0.05853 privately, while an unselected submission achieved 0.05847 privately.

This repository contains team X's Galaxy Zoo competition implementation. It trains convolutional neural networks using Torch and qlua and includes a visualization of training. Configuration is controlled through config.lua, but the text gives no architecture details, validation procedure, or performance results.

A two-layer LSTM denoising autoencoder learned representations from scaled sensor sequences using both training and test inputs with swap noise. Selected intermediate representations were combined with the original sensor data to train predictive neural networks. The final blend used ElasticNet-derived weights and was driven mainly by PyTorch DAE runs, TensorFlow TPU runs, and LightGBM. Subject-grouped ten-fold validation supported model comparison, and the combined model achieved 0.9918 CV and 0.99249 private score.
compute: Kaggle GPU and TPU; best DAE: approximately 8 hours pretraining plus 5.5 hours predictive training over 10 folds.

solution_title: [38th Place] Single Stage Single Model Efficientnetv2
solution_summary: The pipeline used a pretrained EfficientNetV2-L with nine input channels formed from three CT windows across three neighboring slices. It predicted middle-slice fracture probabilities and vertebra presence, using study-grouped, fracture-stratified five-fold validation. Inference advanced by two slices for speed, and patient-level probability used a complement-of-products formula. Sequence models, a sampled-slice 3D classifier, and XGBoost aggregation failed to improve patient-level prediction.

solution_title: 3rd Place - Using Only Rules Achieves LB 0.590!
solution_summary: The author's individual solution generated candidates from co-visitation rules and reranked them with XGBoost. Twenty co-visit matrices captured different temporal windows, event types, sequence distances, and user segments, supplying both candidates and interaction features. The rules alone achieved 0.590 on the leaderboard, and reranking added about 0.011 to reach 0.601. The team combined its independently developed models by summing prediction ranks for each user and target type.
compute: Nvidia 4x V100 32GB GPUs; under 1 minute per co-visit matrix

solution_summary: The author proposed a model called Triplet Update for scalar-coupling prediction. Its hidden layers represent combinations of three atoms. The architecture generalizes Edge Update and is described as similar to higher-order graph neural networks. The post links implementation code but provides no training details or numerical results.

The solution combined an encoder-decoder WaveNet with three averaged decoders and a short-window encoder-decoder RNN using convolutional attention features. The RNN was weaker alone but improved cross-validation performance when blended equally with WaveNet. Random temporal windows, normalized-series scaling, and bagging across training runs addressed the small dataset and training variance. The best private score came from adding a LightGBM model with corrected reservation features, while a later WaveNet retraining with weekend and holiday flags improved local validation.
compute: Under one hour for both models to complete training.

solution_title: Rank17 approach - diverse models and blend
solution_summary: The solution combined extensive feature engineering with a diverse collection of tabular models and a multistage ensemble. More than 800 candidate features captured arithmetic interactions, categorical statistics, original-data information, and driver and race history. Five-fold validation stratified jointly by year and target guided model comparison and blending. Approximately 130 single models and two stacking rounds produced a pipeline with more than 200 models, retaining weaker individual models for their complementary predictions.
compute: L4 Colab and A100 Colab (80GB) for XGBoost/LightGBM; A6000Ada for CatBoost and other models; A100 (80GB) for TABM/RealMLP.

solution_summary: The author trained a simple neural network on approximately 1400 features per series, mostly spectra after DC removal and features with low frequencies filtered out. Quaternion derivatives provided angular-velocity information. The largest improvement came from linking series within runs using orientation and group information, exploiting temporal continuity and changes in behavior. The reported score rose from 0.67 to 0.87, with corresponding private scores of 0.79 and 0.99.

The team ensembled two versions of a seven-layer bidirectional LSTM with batch normalization and concatenated line-fitting features. Sensor sequences used time intervals and added coordinate differences, while TFRecord storage reduced memory use and accelerated training. Validation guided model selection and ensemble weights, although the post reports differing ensemble counts. Raising category probabilities to a power of 1.35 before direction aggregation reduced mean angular error by about 0.002.

The solution adapted Matterport Mask R-CNN with a ResNet101 backbone for small-nucleus instance segmentation. Corrected annotations, external H&E data, training-image mosaics, and extensive augmentation improved generalization, while validation was stratified by image modality. Training used partial initialization from ImageNet ResNet50 weights and Adam over 75 epochs with decreasing learning rates. Horizontal-flip prediction fusion, scale-down retries, overlap removal, and morphological hole closing improved the final masks.
external_data: ["External H&E data with mask annotations", "Konstantin Lopuhin's DSBowl 2018 dataset fixes", "ImageNet"]

solution_title: Private 9th | Public 2nd solution - Fight against randomness
solution_summary: The solution centers on a domain-pretrained EfficientNetV2-S sound-event detector using 10-second windows and a soundscape-specific class-interaction module. Waveform MixUp, rare-class upsampling, EMA, and additional species recordings supported training, while noisy validation required repeated seed comparisons. Final submissions combined four to six model groups, including pseudo-labeled models and an alternative backbone, with taxon-aware smoothing and file-level probability reinforcement. These submissions scored 0.956 privately, while a simpler post-competition ensemble of two raw EfficientNet models achieved 0.958.

solution_title: Avito Winner's Interview: 1st place, Owen Zhang
solution_summary: The solution used XGBoost exclusively, supported by extensive manual feature engineering and model tuning. Useful features included entropy measures and query-level information such as the number of other displayed ads. XGBoost outperformed FFM and VW on this dataset. The implementation was written in R, with training and prediction taking about 20 hours.
compute: About 20 hours for training and prediction.

solution_summary: The solution combined two segmentation stages with two classification stages, using pseudo labels in both pipelines. Segmentation predicted tubes, tube tips, and tracheal bifurcations, and the resulting masks were concatenated with images for classification. Patient-linked folds and deduplication supported the use of 28,000 external tube-containing images. Diverse model ensembles and selective ranking of five output columns produced a classification cross-validation score of 0.97606.
external_data: ["NIH ChestX dataset", "Dr. Konya's 5k trachea bifurcation annotations"]

solution_title: 34th Place. CatBoost with MultiRMSE plus public solutions.
solution_summary: The final ensemble combined AutoGluon on a Kaplan–Meier target, an event-masked pairwise-ranking neural network, monotonic XGBoost, and a three-target CatBoost model. CatBoost used MultiRMSE and different sample weights for observed events and censored cases, which improved performance. Ensemble weights were optimized with scipy.minimize, producing the author's best cross-validation and private leaderboard results.

solution_title: MoA solution - Tried to keep it simple
solution_summary: The final ensemble combined two neural networks and one TabNet model, each averaged across random seeds. TabNet used no feature engineering, while the neural networks used target-correlation filtering, distribution of correlated features across seeds, variance filtering, and quantile transformation. PCA features were also derived from raw inputs, and all feature processing was fitted using training data only.

The author built a compact Cfish-based chess engine whose strength primarily came from a small neural evaluation network. Data selection and a two-stage curriculum using Stockfish and Leela Chess Zero positions were central to network quality. Compression-aware feature layouts, weight encoding, and nested archive compression kept the submission within the 64 KB limit. Engine changes were measured through Elo testing, while hash size and time management were tuned for the competition environment. The resulting neural networks were reported to be substantially stronger than handcrafted evaluation despite compressing to about 20 KB.
compute: Competition environment: 5 MB RAM limit; final engine hash size 896 KB
external_data: ["Previously generated Stockfish NNUE training data", "Leela Chess Zero T77 and T79 training-run data"]

solution_summary: The final solution was a weighted average of two LightGBM models, with DART boosting reported to be faster and more accurate than standard GBM in their experiments. Features included click time deltas, counts, unique counts, and IP click frequency, with feature extraction from the test supplement providing a substantial improvement. They validated on the last 25 million training rows and selected features in batches, ultimately using 34 features. Post-processing improved the score by 0.0002, while factorization machine experiments produced no useful results; the final submissions nevertheless showed a substantial public-to-private leaderboard drop.

solution_title: Synthetic data for 0.945 public LB solution (no training data used at all)
solution_summary: The author generated unlimited synthetic training sequences by combining simulated single-channel signals and learning a transformation from ground truth to observed measurements. The final model combined a six-layer convolutional branch with a histogram network describing an entire 100,000-sample segment. Balanced synthetic training and removal of phase-aligned 50 Hz interference supported a single-model public score of 0.945. Random offsets and variable amplification helped, while variable Gaussian noise and an L2 model did not.
compute: 3 GPUs, approximately 8 hours of training.

solution_summary: The solution combined public XGBoost and Keras models trained on many engineered versions of the data. Generating diverse datasets improved performance more than tuning individual models, while out-of-fold predictions enabled optimized linear stacking. Models with mismatched training and test prediction distributions were removed, and ensemble weights were optimized for MAE with L1 regularization. A later variation fitted separate weights within three prediction-PCA segments, although its benefit was uncertain.

The author used the DeepState forecasting estimator in GluonTS to jointly model the sales time series. The approach uses a neural network and covariates to estimate latent state-space components such as trend, level, and seasonality, allowing information sharing across series. The data fit GluonTS's built-in representation with little preparation. Training 30,490 series took about 20 minutes, forecasting took about an hour, and the complete run took approximately 1.5 hours.
compute: 30,490 series: about 20 minutes training, about 1 hour forecasting, approximately 1.5 hours total runtime; hardware unspecified.

solution_summary: The author describes a solution based on neural networks, gradient boosting, and k-nearest neighbors. The post links to a code repository and embeds a conceptual diagram. The supplied text does not explain features, training, validation, or how the model families were combined.

solution_title: 26th Place Solution: SDXL Flash + Optimized img2svg + TIFA QA Generation
solution_summary: The pipeline generated images with SDXL Flash and converted each image into two SVG candidates using custom contour simplification and VTracer. A fine-tuned SmolLM2 generated evaluation questions, and PaliGemma-3B selected the best SVG using those questions. Color quantization, size-constrained simplification, an OCR-mitigating watermark, and adaptive allocation of generation attempts were central components. Final submissions were chosen using a synthetic validation set, although that choice missed a candidate with a better private score.
models_pretrained: ["SmolLM2-1.7B-Instruct", "SDXL Flash", "PaliGemma-3B", "Gemini", "Claude", "Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct-AWQ", "SDXL Hyper", "SD", "SDXL", "Flux Schnell", "Juggernaut XL V9", "Playground 1K Aesthetic"]

solution_title: Argus solution TGS Salt Identification Challenge
solution_summary: The team used a U-Net-like segmentation network with an SE-ResNeXt50 encoder, custom FPN-style decoder layers, and an auxiliary empty-tile classifier. Biharmonic padding and image augmentation supported training with Lovasz hinge and auxiliary binary classification losses. Final predictions averaged models from random folds and mosaic-grouped folds. Mosaic reconstruction, histogram matching, corner completion, and mask-hole filling improved the final masks, while careful cross-validation limited public leaderboard overfitting.

solution_title: 28th Place - Quick writeup - Improving the baseline
solution_summary: The final approach improved a public two-stage baseline by replacing stage-one b0 models with b6 models and aggregating predictions across both stages. Inference was optimized by caching public-test predictions and traversing the stage-one dataloader only once. Stage-two model and loss changes provided an additional boost, while ResNeXt101 and a parallel GRU–LSTM alternative did not help. The selected submission respected label-consistency requirements; an unselected version ignoring those requirements would have scored 0.177 on the private leaderboard.
compute: Z8 desktop; submission inference varied from 7 hours to over 9 hours

solution_summary: The solution models sales as a product of country GDP, product trends, store and weekday effects, COVID disruption, annual seasonality, and holiday effects. Product trends are smoothed with low-frequency Fourier filtering. Linear regression estimates seasonal coefficients, while ridge regression estimates amplitudes for shared Gaussian holiday response shapes.

The solution trains a 3D U-Net with a pretrained ResNet200 encoder to predict downsampled Gaussian motor heatmaps. It combines corrected competition annotations and external tomograms with heavy augmentation, deep supervision and a pooled auxiliary loss. Inference slides only along depth with substantial overlap, downweights window edges and combines eight seeded models. Motor presence is decided by ranking tomograms by peak confidence and removing the lowest quantile, which was more stable than a fixed probability threshold. Depth-only sliding was four times faster, and final inference took about ten hours.
compute: Final eight-seed ensemble inference: approximately 10 hours
external_data: ["CryoET Data Portal tomograms", "CryoET flagellar motors dataset with corrected annotations"]

solution_title: [5th Solution] - housuke's part - Private 0.572, Public 0.566 with single model
solution_summary: The solution treated discourse effectiveness as token classification using DeBERTa backbones, discourse boundary markers, type embeddings, discourse max pooling, and inverse-length token loss weights. Masked language model pretraining, random token masking, and SiFT perturbations improved training, while soft pseudo-labeling benefited from removing masking and perturbations in the author's experiments. Predictions passed through an LSTM discourse-sequence stack and then an XGBoost stack, with discourse length and type added as features. Using third-stage predictions as pseudo-labels, final five-fold DeBERTa models achieved private scores of 0.574 and 0.572, each reported in 27 minutes.
compute: 27 minutes reported for each final five-fold model; hardware and timing scope unspecified.

solution_title: 988th Place solution (4th on Public) - GNN and domain adaption. 800Kb model.
solution_summary: The author replaced molecular fingerprints and XGBoost with a compact graph attention network using rich atom and bond annotations from RDKit. Precomputed cross-validation folds stored on SSD made single-GPU training practical, and the shared-building-block model was trained on one fold before fine-tuning on the full dataset. For non-shared building blocks, a domain adaptation objective used embedding cosine similarities to generate soft labels, improving the public score from 0.498 to 0.517. Despite those gains, the approach generalized poorly to the private leaderboard.
compute: Single GPU; approximately 12 hours preprocessing per split; 1 TB storage; approximately 800 KB model.

solution_summary: The author trained YOLOv5x detectors at image size 640 using labels grouped by annotator agreement. Weighted boxes fusion merged annotations and detector outputs, while scale and horizontal-flip augmentation improved inference. Final selections combined detectors trained with at least one or two annotators' agreement and a disease-only detector, with one selection also including public notebook predictions. A no-finding score was derived from detection confidence; the selected submissions scored 0.297 and 0.303 privately, while an unselected ensemble including the strictest labels reached 0.306.

The author adapted Stockfish 16's handcrafted evaluation engine to the competition's memory and runtime constraints. A compact three-layer MLP learned the difference between NNUE and handcrafted evaluations from positions sampled during approximately 70,000 games. Adding half of the neural correction improved strength by about 30 Elo, compared with less than 10 Elo for the full correction. Both handcrafted-only and neural-enhanced agents were submitted, while memory reductions and efficient search execution helped control resource usage.
compute: Kaggle GPU environment for training; CPU cores in Kaggle TPU environments for some game-generation notebooks

solution_summary: The submission provides a short reproduction workflow for the DecMeg2014 challenge. It requires placing the challenge data in a data folder and installing the covariance toolbox. The workflow runs a preprocessing script followed by a final submission script in MATLAB, without describing the model or reporting numerical results.

solution_title: 131st Place: The 20.220 Hedge That Beat Our 114.570 Public Winner
solution_summary: The team selected two distinct sandbox attack mechanisms: a high-public marker-exfiltration router and a clean-email confused-deputy specialist. The surviving specialist used short templates, per-model live probing, predicate-specific validation, unique synthetic recipients, and conservative deadline budgeting. Its public and private scores were both 20.220, whereas the marker router scored zero privately. The key decision was preserving mechanism diversity despite the specialist's much lower public score.
compute: Kaggle-hosted T4 used for separate model/SDK validation

solution_title: Ablation study on the 1st place solution: effect of ensemble, tick-size leak and normalization
solution_summary: This ablation writeup examines a final ensemble of five LightGBM models, three 1D CNNs, and three MLPs. Its central feature design combined seven nearest-neighbor searches across timestamps and stocks using recovered real prices, volatility, and trade size. The full ensemble achieved 0.19545 private RMSPE, while a single LightGBM achieved 0.19699. Feature diversity mattered more than model diversity, and removing rank normalization had almost no effect.

solution_title: "I don't even see the top" solution | .776/.733
solution_summary: The pipeline first generated candidates using 15 two-dimensional U-Net models trained on provided positives. These comprised five folds each of ResNet34 models at two patch sizes and a ResNet18 model. Threshold-based false-positive mining supplied examples for a second-stage 2.5D discriminator ensemble containing ten models. GRU discriminators reduced performance and were excluded, while mask-derived voxel spacing estimation was intended to normalize samples to a reference spacing of 13.1.

The team built a diverse ensemble dominated by EfficientNet models trained on multiple image sizes, data-year combinations, and lesion crops. Five-fold validation on 2020 data guided model selection, while surrogate-label pretraining, augmentation, and test-time augmentation supported individual models. They filtered 91 models down to 58 using prediction-correlation discrepancies and adversarial validation. Their strongest submission blended averaged predictions with stacking using metadata and prediction statistics, achieving CV AUC 0.9532 and private leaderboard AUC 0.9459.
external_data: ["2017/2018/2019 competition data", "Unspecified external data for surrogate-label pretraining"]

solution_title: 21st Place Solution : So close Yet So Far
solution_summary: The final approach combined multi-head classifiers with spatial attention and a four-stage ResNet200d model. Models used ResNet200d, EfficientNet B5, and SE-ResNet152d backbones at image sizes of 640 and 768, with fine-tuning on pseudo-labeled NIH, SIIM, and test images. The final submission blended eight models using weights optimized by Optuna on out-of-fold predictions. Many more elaborate attention, training, preprocessing, and augmentation experiments improved cross-validation without meaningful leaderboard gains, so the team favored simpler models.

The team combined LightGBM, XGBoost, and a neural network, with stacking also used. Merging teammates' feature sets brought a major improvement; features included images, Russian-stemmed TF-IDF, ridge predictions, and aggregates. The neural network processed categorical, numerical, image, and text inputs in separate branches before dense layers, with a CNN on 32-by-32 images providing a significant gain. The three main models each achieved public scores near 0.2185–0.2186, and ridge features were regenerated using consistent folds to avoid leakage.

The author shares a processing framework capable of generating more than 3,000 features across the full dataset without running out of memory. The repository includes three methods for restoring decision dates and multiple preprocessing steps. It also provides memory-efficient LightGBM training with more than 1,000 features and feature-selection approaches including PSI. The best single model scored 0.598 publicly and 0.522 privately.

The final submission ensembled strong submissions from several different approaches, including medical reasoning, cluster engineering, and dimensionality reduction. A CatBoost baseline trained directly on the data without preprocessing or feature engineering was excluded from the final ensemble. The ensemble achieved a private score of 0.502, compared with 0.481 for its best individual component. Adversarial validation indicated that leaderboard movement was likely, but the author did not develop a strategy to avoid it.

The pipeline first estimated issue difficulty and skipped issues whose probability of being easy was below 0.5. A single quantized DeepSeek model handled difficulty estimation, repository search, patch generation, and verification, with a LoRA adapter for difficulty classification. Multiple search and patch candidates were checked through LLM judgment, patch parsing, and dry-run application. Avoiding incorrect submissions was central because the competition heavily penalized wrong answers.

The post provides code for inspecting a secret-sloth image in the frequency domain. It computes a two-dimensional Fourier transform and displays its magnitude with logarithmic color normalization. It provides no broader pipeline or quantitative results.

The solution trained eight different base learners with hyperparameters selected through local cross-validation. Gaussian mixture models supplied additional clustering features, while early stopping controlled LightGBM overfitting. A second LightGBM model combined the predictions and powered out-of-fold predictions. The author's strongest submissions did not use pseudo-labeling.

The author used a stacked ensemble with ridge regression in the second modeling stage. The post emphasizes selecting strong, diverse base models and checking validation performance when adding public predictions. It also discusses regularization and reviewing prediction sources for leakage. Exact base-model membership, preprocessing, and numerical results are not provided.

The pipeline extracted roughly 80 candidates per session and reranked them with XGBoost. Most of its 744 features aggregated candidate-to-session-item similarities using weights based on position, timestamp, and interaction type. Recovering sessions excluded by the original split improved carts and orders, while heavy downsampling enabled GPU training. Clicks used a single model, whereas carts and orders used small XGBoost blends; combining these with teammates' predictions reached a private leaderboard score above 0.603.
compute: 32 GB V100 for batched feature computation; GPU training after heavy downsampling.

solution_title: Rank 172, sharing code for the first time.
solution_summary: The author adapted Konstantin Yakovlev's code for forecasting. They constructed store-specific holiday features. The final 28-day forecast combined store-level and state-level predictions through weighted fusion.

solution_title: 26th short solution（Listwise stage2 model to transform stage1 scores)
solution_summary: The solution used a two-stage retrieval and score-transformation pipeline. Stage one learned rankings with in-batch negatives and a hard negative from the same channel, with sentence-pair pretraining that added an LSTM head. Stage two used listwise transformer models, where stage-one scores mattered much more than the content text. The final ensemble combined 17 stage-one models and three stage-two models, reporting an LB score of 667 with 90-minute inference.
compute: 90 minutes online inference for 17 stage-one models and three stage-two models.

solution_title: When the Leaderboard Scores One Axis
solution_summary: The final attack build hedged exfiltration with confused-deputy and additional attack predicates, informed by a local simulator over reconstructed guardrails. Selecting the higher-public-scoring hedge produced 2.595 private points, while another held build would have scored 3.960. The writeup also evaluates reconstructed defenses using the SDK defense track, finding that blocking the deputy channel can deny legitimate email traffic. A population analysis of submission histories supports the conclusion that public-score optimization often harmed private transfer and final selection.

solution_summary: The solution combined feature engineering with LightGBM. The author reported relatively stable public and private scores. Cross-validation was emphasized as especially important for this synthetic-data competition, although specific features and validation settings were not described.

The author restricted inputs to measurements available at test time, using only the initial FVC and percent values. FVC was normalized so its initial value equaled one, and the starting week was shifted to zero. A linear regression of normalized FVC against shifted weeks produced the author's best private leaderboard submission.

The post provides reproduction instructions for the team's submission. The listed pipeline runs three preprocessing scripts, three model-fitting scripts, and a final blending script. It reports a private leaderboard score of 0.71881, but does not explain the underlying features or model architectures.

solution_title: Artifact Verification and LoRA-Alpha Calibration for a Nemotron Reasoning Adapte
solution_summary: The submission reused a public rank-32 LoRA adapter for NVIDIA Nemotron rather than training new weights. A verification notebook checked archive integrity, required root files, adapter metadata, rank limits, and base-model compatibility. A second notebook reduced lora_alpha from 64 to 62 while preserving all learned weights, lowering the adapter contribution by 3.125%. The writeup presents this as a controlled calibration experiment and does not report a measured performance improvement.

solution_title: Solo silver (302nd): 3-min video of my solution
solution_summary: The final entry expanded a public Raptor and R6 blend with 18 knee-centered ConvNeXt and EfficientNet models. It averaged standardized logits rather than percentile ranks. Ten added models learned from expert-graded OAI knees after translating grades into competition labels. The resulting submission achieved 0.944 private AUC.

The selected approach concatenated NFNet image embeddings with several text representations and perceptual hashes, alongside TF-IDF matching. Concatenating image and text embeddings, SAM optimization, and resize plus center-crop test-time augmentation worked well. The selected model achieved a private score of 0.728, while an unselected CurricularFace variant achieved 0.729. Swin, ViT, RoBERTa, and mode-specific thresholds did not help.

The author inferred essay prompts with a shared prompt classifier and trained DeBERTa-v3-large using five stratified folds. DeBERTa predictions were then stacked with public-notebook features into an ensemble of LightGBM and XGBoost trained using seven-fold prompt-grouped validation. This strategy produced relatively stable agreement between cross-validation and leaderboard results, although the author retained concerns about leakage from DeBERTa. Additional ensembles, threshold tuning, and adding PERSUADE data did not help.

The detailed component used a ResNet34 tile encoder on medium-resolution slides after white-background cropping and artifact cleaning. Tile features were reshaped into a square, passed through a squeeze-and-excitation block, pooled, and trained with classification and regression heads. Slide-level and tile-level augmentation, bounded regression outputs, and staged training from 49 to 81 tiles improved learning; only regression outputs were used for prediction. The final team submission averaged four model components, while the detailed five-fold ResNet34 component achieved 0.911 CV.
compute: Medium-resolution images stored on SSD; tile augmentations performed on GPU.

solution_title: 19th Place - Single Model LB 860 Without Pseudo
solution_summary: The team trained large image backbones on six crop datasets using separate ArcFace heads for species and individual identity. Each model produced six embeddings per image, whose weighted average was optimized on cross-validation for nearest-neighbor matching. An eight-fold validation setup supported threshold tuning, and voting across 96 fold models achieved an LB score of 0.868. Post-competition retraining of two ensemble models with pseudo labels improved the private score by 0.016.

solution_title: 2nd place solution ： Segmentation + 2.5D CNN + GRU Attention
solution_summary: The pipeline first segmented vertebrae with a 2.5D EfficientNetB0 U-Net trained on 87 annotated studies. Predicted masks then defined separate cervical-vertebra crops, each represented by 24 uniformly sampled slices. A CNN, bidirectional GRU, and attention classified these sequences using EfficientNetV2-S and ResNeSt50d backbones. Limited disk capacity led the team to store crop coordinates and DICOM references instead of full cropped volumes.
compute: Disk capacity was insufficient to store high-resolution cropped volumes; crop coordinates and DICOM references were stored instead.

solution_title: How to win a gold medal with basic DL technics and a simple stacking
solution_summary: The pipeline generated diverse neural-network predictions with varying fold counts, test-time augmentation, and selective pseudo-labeling. Networks trained on Fourier-transformed bands provided a substantial gain, while SVM or logistic regression on CNN features added diversity. A second level used 25 LightGBM and XGBoost ensembles over random subsets of predictions and additional features. Final predictions were averaged, power-calibrated, and clipped, with calibration improving log loss by about 0.003.

The approach used four image models—DINOv2-small, BEiTv2, EfficientNetB0, and EfficientNetB3—without test-time augmentation. Training combined mixed precision, repeated negative downsampling, a one-class formulation, and stepwise cosine annealing. Grouped cross-validation produced out-of-fold predictions and guided checkpoint selection across 20 epochs. The reported CV, LB, and PL scores were 0.182, 0.183, and 0.170, and adding EfficientNetB3 reduced private performance.
compute: 20 epochs per model; approximately 1–5 minutes per epoch.

solution_summary: The solution trained an Xception-based motion predictor using offline-rendered images stored as PNG-compressed TFRecords. Validation splits separated map regions using agent-center y positions to avoid similar maps appearing on both sides. The model predicted four trajectory modes and retained the three with highest confidence, using the official multimode metric as an angle-weighted training loss. Multiplicative Gaussian target noise and random removal of history frames improved robustness, while Colab memory limits prevented use of the full training data.
compute: Free Colab TPU; approximately 2 TB of rendered data in Google Cloud Storage; Colab memory limited preprocessing.

solution_summary: The solution averaged two XGBoost models built through successive feature-selection stages, with the second model using a stacked predictor from the first. Engineered interactions, grouped cumulative binary sums, recoded categories, and ID supplied the initial feature set. Thirty-fold cross-validation guided training rounds and feature selection, although its mean scores were optimistic. A small set of interactions dominated feature gain, and the final average scored 0.55551 on the private leaderboard.
compute: Desktop i7-3770 @3.40 GHz, 8 cores, 16 MB RAM as reported; approximately 8 minutes to train both models, 6 seconds preparation and 2 seconds for 4,209 predictions.

solution_summary: The final submission combined three 2.5D Unet++ models and three ResidualUNet3D models with nearly equal weights. Case-grouped cross-validation used different splits across model configurations to improve diversity. Auxiliary annotation-presence classification addressed inconsistent slice annotations, while questionable boundary slices were excluded from segmentation loss. The ensemble scored 0.880 on the private leaderboard; omitting the last added model would have scored 0.883.

The solution aggregated extensively engineered session features into user-level predictors. A purchase classifier generated out-of-fold probabilities that became features for a LightGBM revenue regressor, with results averaged across four seeds. Validation used the previous year's matching holiday period, although the author later questioned that seasonal assumption and the use of stratified folds. The reported regression RMSE was 0.320785.
external_data: ["Country GDP data", "Country official-language information", "Bing Maps city coordinates", "Country and city timezone information", "Google Analytics Demo Account exports before the reset"]

solution_summary: The solution combined SVR models trained on concatenated pretrained image features with five directly trained image models, using only competition images. GPU-accelerated SVR made forward selection over many pretrained feature combinations practical, yielding three complementary feature sets. The image branch combined Swin, BEiT, and EfficientNet models trained with BCE, augmentation, and cosine warm restarts. Their final weighted blend achieved 16.81 CV RMSE and 16.82 private RMSE.

solution_summary: The main solution combined DeBERTa models and SVR with pseudo-labels from FB1 and argumentative-element metadata from FB2 models. The author optimized the weights of 13 models using L-BFGS-B. The efficiency solution distilled this ensemble into deberta-v3-xsmall with a maximum sequence length of 512 and uniform length batching. Validation used four multilabel-stratified folds based on targets and BERTopic topics, followed by training on all available training data.

The author combined models from public notebooks and concentrated on ensemble optimization rather than developing new architectures. The decisive change was a constant +40 adjustment to predicted glass transition temperature, addressing a target-specific distribution shift. A Celsius-to-Fahrenheit transformation was rejected during the competition because it hurt the public score, but later inspection showed substantially better private performance. Postcompetition experiments showed that correcting this single target could match or surpass the final ensemble even with a simple ExtraTrees model.

The author iteratively estimated monthly player strengths using a modified Chessmetrics-style rating procedure, then predicted game outcomes from rating differences and a rating-dependent white advantage. Ratings incorporated time-weighted opponents, artificial opponents, and penalties for limited playing experience. The procedure used later results when estimating earlier strengths and also used game participation information from the missing months to adjust predictions. Parameters were tested using historical cutoffs, but the post leaves parts of the strength-estimation algorithm unexplained and reports no numerical evaluation score.

The solution used iterated local search with restricted k-opt moves and custom kicks to escape local optima. Candidate moves excluded reversals and limited moving subsequence lengths to keep expensive scoring manageable. Problem-specific kicks moved or swapped words between structural groups, helping achieve a score of 28.5 on Problem 5. Multiple starts and exhaustive choices for the final word also improved results on other problems.
compute: 4090 GPU; about 18 minutes to test all restricted moves on Problem 5, with full convergence taking longer.

solution_summary: The solution used hourglass CenterNet models to predict car locations and poses, with perspective transforms reducing differences in apparent car size and covering outliers. Camera rotation was the most important augmentation for controlling overfitting on the small training set. Six models with different heads and transforms were combined with test-time augmentation and weighted averaging. Metric probing informed extensive post-processing, including global roll prediction, coordinate shifts, selective filtering, and duplicate removal.

solution_summary: The solution relied on online training using test-provided examples and ensembled diverse classification, embedding, and instruction-tuned language models. Rule-specific contrastive models scored rule–body cosine similarity, while classifiers and LLMs used varied prompts and body-only tasks. Hard pseudo-labels from confident ensemble predictions enabled additional BERT and LLM training, with earlier LoRA weights reused to reduce training time. solution_title: Draper Satellite Image Chronology: Pure ML Solution | Vicens Gaitan
solution_summary: The pipeline registered satellite images using matched local keypoints and trained XGBoost to predict signed time differences between matching patches. Registration parameters and matching quality supplied additional features, while connected image sets were kept together in cross-validation. Image ordering came from averaging patch predictions and iteratively incorporating evidence from overlapping sets. Local validation scored 0.83 ± 0.05, while public and private scores were 0.76786 and 0.69209; tuning aggregation parameters on public feedback caused some overfitting.

solution_title: Source Code for Bryan Gregory & Miroslaw Horbal
solution_summary: This post announces the release of the team's competition code under the BSD-3 OSI license. It lists repositories for the ensemble and individual models. The solution enriched tabular inputs with target statistics from the original Heart Disease dataset, periodic and interaction features, and fold-aware encodings. Diverse boosted trees and tabular neural networks were trained with ten-fold stratified validation, with RealMLP providing the strongest individual models. Confident test predictions supplied hard pseudo-labels for teacher-student variants, and ridge models stacked out-of-fold predictions. Hill-climbing blending achieved an OOF ROC-AUC of 0.955805; allowing negative weights slightly improved validation but produced the same private leaderboard score as positive-only blending.

The solution uses a six-member ONNX ensemble for multilabel bioacoustic identification and achieves a private macro-AUC of 0.92041. Shared log-mel inputs, GeM pooling, and an attention-based sound-event head support CNN backbones trained through supervised fine-tuning, Noisy Student self-training, and Perch v2 distillation. Soundscape adaptation and ensemble error diversity mattered more than increasing backbone size. BatchNorm recalibration, probability-space blending, and selective augmentation enabled complete CPU inference within the competition budget.
