SVD alignment and sub-trip alignment error provided the strongest match scoring, and match counts became classifier features. Dynamic time warping and network-based features offered little improvement, while distributed EC2 computation enabled faster iteration and helped push the reported score above 97%.
compute: About 20 hours on an i7 quad core; EC2 basic runs took 1–2 hours. A 16-machine run used eleven 32-core and five 36-core machines for two algorithms in about 3.5 hours.

solution_summary: The solution retrieved 25 misconception candidates and reranked them with an instruction-tuned Qwen model. Retriever training progressed from pretrained embeddings through Qwen models using contrastive learning and randomly sampled hard negatives. GPT-4o generated additional questions for unseen or rare misconceptions, while reranker training varied the number of candidate options. Predictions from two pipelines were merged by averaging scores for overlapping IDs and retaining unique candidates, improving the score by about 0.02 and yielding 0.553 private and 0.617 public.

The pipeline routes images between separate seen-grapheme and unseen-grapheme models using ArcFace. The seen model uses little augmentation and decomposes its grapheme prediction into three components, while the unseen model uses heavy augmentation and predicts components directly. A minimal pair of EfficientNet-B1 models trained at 128×128 achieved over 0.935 private leaderboard score. Larger EfficientNet backbones, higher resolution, longer training, and more model pairs were described as the route to scores above 0.950.
compute: Minimal kernel pipeline: seen model ~5 hours, unseen model ~8.5 hours, submission ~20 minutes; 30 epochs at 128×128.

solution_summary: The solution uses LightGBM classifiers with inexpensive features extracted from astronomical light curves. Bayesian flux denoising, magnitude-normalized flux features, and measurements around light-curve peaks provided the largest improvements. Class probabilities were adjusted for the competition metric after optimizing ordinary log loss. The pipeline scored 0.84070 on the private leaderboard and took around six hours on a laptop.
compute: 24 GB laptop; around 6 hours for feature calculation, training, and prediction

solution_summary: The author proposes solving ARC tasks through executable procedures generated by language models. They create a partial collection of golden solutions and use those solutions to guide reinforcement learning. The attempt achieved zero evaluation accuracy, with no claimed improvement even on training data.

solution_title: 8th Place Solution: Implementing Multimodal Data Augmentation Methods (last updated 05/28)
solution_summary: The solution used eca_nfnet_l0 models with sound detection guided preprocessing and several mixup strategies designed to preserve plausible acoustic combinations. Training progressively shifted from global spectrogram context to local features. Validation used a simple holdout with bootstrapped five-second segments and excluded recordings with secondary labels. An ensemble of six models using different mel resolutions achieved public and private scores of 0.83616 and 0.75285.

The solution combined Wikipedia context retrieval with an optimized ensemble of DeBERTa multiple-choice models, including one model without context. Retrieval used bge-base-en-v1-5 and LuceneSearcher, with BM25 context changes providing the largest reported score gain. Ensemble weights were optimized on 200 competition training examples and 300 additional high-quality samples. Uncertain predictions were revisited with Platypus 70B after retraining its language-model head, using the remaining inference time; this step was particularly effective on the private leaderboard.
compute: 9-hour inference window; approximately 800 samples reprocessed per 2 hours remaining.
external_data: ["radek1 datasets with retrieval context", "yalickj 300 high-quality samples", "nbroad 60k dataset", "Full Wikipedia dataset and self-parsed full set", "mbanei 270K Wikipedia article set"]

solution_summary: The solution fitted a projection pursuit regression baseline to log-transformed sales for each item-store pair, then modeled residuals with a lasso linear model in Vowpal Wabbit. Calendar indicators and interactions captured weekday effects, monthly patterns, and Black Friday fluctuations. Predictions were converted back to sales and forced to zero under several historical zero-sales rules. Successive-zero handling provided a small final improvement, while weather features contributed little.

The solution combined ResNeSt50-fast-4s2x40d and EfficientNet models trained with different recipes, selecting two ensembles using CV and public leaderboard scores. Label smoothing, external 2019 data, and test-time augmentation helped, while pseudo-labeling improved CV without improving the reported private score for the compared model. Ensemble weights were optimized on CV, although the author suspected this contributed to poor generalization. The reported overall scores were 0.907 publicly and 0.898 privately.
compute: Kaggle GPU; training recipes used 10–20 epochs.

solution_summary: The author used a teammate's candidate set and concentrated on improving item-to-item collaborative filtering features. Counts, time differences, sequence differences, weighted variants, and aggregations produced hundreds of final features. XGBoost and CatBoost formed the modeling stage, with first-stage prediction and pseudo-event features also included. The team combined results by rank, and cuDF and cuML enabled extensive experimentation.

The team initialized tours with LKH and refined them using a custom Rust implementation of Lin–Kernighan search. Nonsequential moves, especially 4-opt, gradual penalty increases and penalty-aware merging of tours were central to improvement. They used random kicks and regional penalty perturbations to escape local optima, distributing search across many cores. A 72-core machine could produce a score in the 15141xy range in a day, while the best kernel scored 1514637 with substantial run-to-run variation.
compute: 48- or 72-core machines; LKH ran for a couple of days; approximately one day on 72 cores to reach the 15141xy score range.

solution_summary: The solution compares observed horizontal gamma-ray slices with candidate trajectories and uses constrained beam search to recover TVT paths. Candidate scores come from physical similarity measures and lightweight dilated 1D CNNs, with predictions combined across architectures and slice lengths. The final ensemble contains two heuristic models and multiple CNN groups, with inference taking about eight GPU hours. The best reported single CNN achieved 8.2 ft private RMSE, and the author's best private submission omitted the neighboring-well constraint.
compute: CNN training usually under 5 minutes; final inference about 8 hours on GPU.

solution_summary: The solution combined extensive feature engineering with a diverse ensemble of tree models and neural networks. A LightGBM meta-model stacked first-level predictions, and blending with an earlier submission improved the score by 0.02. Separate galactic and extragalactic LightGBM models used importance-selected features, with microlensing and astrophysics-inspired features particularly valuable. Observation subsampling improved neural-network validation, while pseudo-labeling and modeling hostgal_specz did not work.

The solution addressed severe label imbalance with weighted sampling and binary cross-entropy that emphasized positive labels. At prediction time, it used softmax outputs with a fixed 0.04 threshold across classes to improve generalization under label distribution shifts. Training batches were normalized using statistics calculated from the full training data. The final ensemble contained two models trained from scratch, each taking around two weeks on one P100 GPU.
compute: Single P100 GPU, around two weeks of training per model for two models.

solution_title: [16th place] A pure self-play reinforcement learning approach to the Santa 2020 challenge
solution_summary: The team trained deep reinforcement learning agents using a GPU-parallel game environment that greatly increased simulation throughput. Their strongest agent used per-bandit event histories and a set-based residual network that combined each bandit's features with the mean features of other bandits. Training used a dense zero-sum reward based on the difference in expected pull rewards, with A2C and AWAC giving the best results. Self-play produced continuing improvements, but internal match results did not reliably predict performance against the broader field.
compute: Single-GPU home desktop; GPU-parallel simulation ran a 10,000-game match in 12 seconds versus over 30 minutes with multiprocessing.

solution_summary: The solution combined a dual-head cell model, whole-image classifiers, and cell classifiers trained with image-level labels. The dual-head architecture jointly learned cell and image predictions, while the other pipelines averaged predictions across multiple models and inference views. External HPA data, extensive augmentation, and refined cell segmentation supported the approach. The dual-head ensemble alone scored 0.550 on both public and private leaderboards; an antibody ArcFace approach helped publicly but did not transfer well privately.
compute: A single B3 model at 256 resolution took about 30 hours on one RTX3090.
external_data: ["External data shared by Phil and API rare-class samples", "HPA official website data", "HPA antibody-ID XML metadata"]

solution_summary: The agent extended an existing deterministic football script through rules refined by watching replays. Defensive changes restricted blind clearances, improved evasion and tackle timing, and made the last defender track the leading attacker against overhead balls. Offensive changes anticipated first contact to issue repeated quick passes or shots and ignored defenders sufficiently far behind during dribbling. The dribbling adjustment helped substantially, while game randomness and slowly converging leaderboard scores made parameter tuning difficult.

This post describes four waveform augmentations rather than a complete detection pipeline. Zebra mixup interleaved alternating samples from two waveforms and reportedly improved the score by 0.001. Other successful augmentations reversed negative waveforms, replaced individual channels with channels from other negative examples, and swapped the two LIGO channels.

The solution combined five-fold EfficientDet D2 models trained at 1024×1024 with five-fold D4 models trained at 512×512. Heavy augmentation, five-way test-time augmentation, and weighted boxes fusion formed the ensemble pipeline. One round of pseudo-labeling trained for one epoch with training data and doubled pseudo-labeled test data, improving the private score from 0.6956 to 0.7050. Bounding-box cleaning, gradient accumulation, CutMix, Mixup, and several threshold or loss adjustments did not help.

The pipeline used a bi-encoder retriever followed by a multi-option LLM reranker. Retrieval benefited from generated explanations of incorrect answers, filling missing misconceptions, and removing unseen training examples. Both models were adapted with LoRA, and reranker training used out-of-fold retrieval candidates with single-token answer labels. Two overlapping candidate windows were reranked and merged, with the complete pipeline taking 210 minutes.
compute: Pipeline runtime: 210 minutes; 140 minutes with one prediction pass.

solution_summary: The pipeline replaced baseline helmet detections with a trained YOLOv5 model and linked detections into tracks for player assignment. A two-head ResNet34 jersey reader supplied high-precision corrections to the geometric mapping. Cluster-level confidence aggregation and framewise linear regression completed the helmet-to-player assignments. A custom tracker performed worse publicly but produced the team's best private submission.
compute: Helmet detector training: 15 epochs at image size 640, followed by 5 fine-tuning epochs at image size 1280.

solution_summary: The team modeled 19 product targets with separate models trained on June 2015 and May 2016 data to capture seasonality and recent trends. Features included historical target averages, prior product ownership counts and patterns, encoded raw attributes, and new-product flags. Product-specific ensemble weights were the key improvement, raising the reported score from 0.0303 to 0.0306. Ten-fold cross-validation tracked leaderboard performance, while bagging and parameter tuning offered no improvement; a shared script scored approximately 0.03102 on the private leaderboard.

The post announces an updated solution notebook that runs on Kaggle. The author says the notebook includes descriptions and output. It links to the solution code but provides no technical approach in the post itself.

solution_title: 2nd Place and 2nd Place Solution to Kaggle Landmark Recognition and Retrieval Competition 2019
solution_summary: The post announces that the team's solution has been released on arXiv. It links to the paper and a GitHub source-code location. It also thanks the organizers and indicates plans to open the source code, without describing methods or results.

The team built around 100 models, dominated by LightGBM and XGBoost, and organized them into two ensembles using different cross-validation schemes. Categorical dummy variables worked well, while neural networks used scaled and log-transformed numerical inputs and simplified genetic-programming features. A simple neural stacking model improved on a linear blender by about 0.001, and the two ensembles were combined through rank averaging. Extensive validation experiments produced limited private-leaderboard gains, and the authors felt broader model exploration would have been more valuable.

The solution uses a single AWQ four-bit DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-14B model with vLLM and FlashInfer. Generation uses one prompt without a system message and allocates tokens and sequences equally across problems. Repeated local validation on 50 handpicked math problems guided configuration choices, with throughput favored over public leaderboard tuning. The reported scores were 25/50 public and 29/50 private.

The solution removed the known trajectory contribution from TVT and anchored predictions at the end of each well's known section. A convex blend of sequence and row-wise models supplied the baseline, with a small correction based on nearby wells' geological changes relative to their anchors. Reference wells from the evaluated fold were excluded, and corrections were restricted by proximity to both the query and anchor. Selection emphasized well-level OOF results, spatial robustness, shuffled-information controls, and private-test compatibility. The final correction reduced OOF RMSE from 9.9775 to 9.7080 and achieved a private score of 8.861.

The final ensemble combined nine submodels from NetVLAD, Deep Bag of Frames, Fisher Vector, and recurrent network families. Multilayer knowledge distillation and partial 8-bit weight quantization helped fit strong models within the size constraint. Weight averaging improved smaller models, while inference sampling ensured every frame was represented. A held-out subset guided model selection and random-search optimization of ensemble weights.
compute: Single GPU per model; 1.5–3.5 days per model; approximately 60 GPU-days for all models.

solution_summary: The solution averaged eight diverse audio classifiers trained on standardized mel spectrograms with extensive augmentation. Manually completing and checking recording labels was central, supplemented by hand-labeled external frog recordings and some pseudolabels. Training used five-second samples, recording-level multilabel folds, and different losses for confidently complete versus incomplete labels. Overlapping-window maximum predictions and a species-specific threshold completed inference; the author's best single model scored 0.970 publicly.
external_data: ["Dryad frog recordings, DOI 10.5061/dryad.c0g2t, manually labeled", "Freesound50k", "Cornell Competition species recordings, rejected distractor augmentation"]

solution_summary: The team combined complementary sensor models using an equal-weight ensemble, later replacing probabilities with class ranks before averaging. Both approaches emphasized separate sensor or feature branches, with shallow convolutions and recurrent extractors limiting overfitting. Handcrafted IMU features, mixup, and sensor or channel dropout were important components. Postprocessing improved predictions by enforcing at most two gestures per subject orientation and suppressing unseen orientation–gesture combinations.

solution_title: 4th place sharing and tips about having a good teamwork experience
solution_summary: The team built trend features and trained more than 200 diverse models on feature subsets and the combined feature set. Predictions saved during Bayesian parameter optimization also supplied out-of-fold inputs for stacking. Selecting stacking features before fitting LightGBM improved CV by about 0.0005. A final manual correction adjusted high predictions for revolving loans; stacking achieved CV 0.8055 and private leaderboard score 0.804.

The solution adapted a public DeBERTa-v3-large and LightGBM baseline notebook. The author increased the number of folds from five to six and changed the reported cross-validation splits from 15 to 18. These small changes formed the reported solution, with no additional modeling details or scores provided.

The solution classified cell type before applying specialized instance segmentation models and post-processing for each type. LIVE_CELL pretraining and pseudo labels from semi-supervised images supported staged training with cell-specific data. It combined two-stage detectors for cort cells and merged semantically reranked masks for shsy5y cells, while using one astro model. Classwise filtering, overlap removal, and astro contour reconstruction refined the final masks.

solution_title: 119th Place Solution: Transformer is much much better than GRU!
solution_summary: The author trained landmark-based GRU, bidirectional GRU, and Transformer models with Conv1D components on preprocessed data without normalization. Validation used participant-based splits, and training ran for 100 epochs with Adam and plateau-based learning-rate reduction. The selected submission ensembled the three model types and achieved a private score of 0.82339, while an unselected Transformer scored 0.82484. FP16 TFLite quantization reduced model sizes by about half, and positional embeddings and recurrent attention masks caused overfitting.

solution_title: 18 place write up  (short meditation on results)
solution_summary: The team used a ResNet-101 Mask R-CNN at 1024×1024 resolution and combined predictions from multiple snapshots, retaining the most confident overlapping detections. Image classifiers filtered object predictions using optimized thresholds, while class-specific segmentation networks refined masks and provided the largest gains. Attribute classifiers used separate mask-crop and full-image inputs with outputs grouped by attribute co-occurrence, and their predictions were retained only with strong ensemble agreement and confidence. Attribute modeling improved the score by only about 0.005, which the authors considered a poor use of their limited resources.
compute: Two machines with 2×1080 Ti each and one machine with a GTX 1080; one fold of 1024×1024 ResNet-101 Mask R-CNN took 5 days.

solution_summary: The solution ensembled VoxNet and PointNet variants with XGBoost models using distance and position features. VoxNet processed voxelized atom counts, while PointNet consumed atom-level spatial and chemical descriptors; both incorporated organizer-provided features in their final dense layers. Evaluation used 24-fold cross-validation, and the selected ensemble achieved CV 0.0464 and private score 0.0573. A late PointNet++ addition slightly improved private performance but was not selected.

solution_title: Wow, Removing AdaptableSnail fps=25 Wins 2nd Place!
solution_summary: The author performed a postcompetition experiment removing all predictions for AdaptableSnail test videos recorded at 25 frames per second. This increased the private leaderboard score from 0.523 to 0.535. The post provides submission filtering code and attributes the improvement to reportedly incorrect evaluation targets. The adjustment was not applied to the author's final competition submission.

solution_title: 12 flags only - my solutions and approaches to some of the unsolved
solution_summary: The author solved several capture-the-flag tasks using model-output analysis, brute force, synonym search, and tailored prompts. For Cluster 1, filtering high-confidence false positives within the Tech-support occupation produced a successful subset. Language-model tasks were solved through contextual framing, indirect requests, follow-up questions, and searching responses for flag prefixes. Evolutionary word searches failed on Passphrase because the optimization target was wrong, and similar searches did not solve Semantle Level 2.

The solution first built a meta-model from 18 five-fold models spanning CatBoost, LightGBM, XGBoost, neural networks, and AutoGluon. AutoFeat and Optuna helped create diverse model conditions, followed by further feature exploration and a hill climbing ensemble that selected six additional models. The final CV score improved from 0.05893 to 0.05885. Public leaderboard results were ignored because of unstable CV correlations, and adding the original dataset to training was rejected after insufficient CV improvement.

The agent searched object names alphabetically early in the game and switched to frequency-based, Huffman-like questioning once the candidate set became small. Its responder used extensive regular-expression rules for spelling and membership questions, falling back to a Llama 3.1 model for other questions. Candidate objects came from caption datasets, Amazon reviews, and WordNet, with Gemini Flash filtering nouns. Guesses prioritized the remaining keyword with the highest word frequency.

solution_title: 12th place solution: UNet with mask scoring head
solution_summary: The solution combined segmentation at image size 896 with classification at size 768, removing masks with low probability. Segmentation used an EfficientNet-B4 U-Net with an auxiliary mask-quality scoring head and a combined segmentation and score-regression loss. Two SE-ResNeXt101 classifiers supplied embeddings, which were concatenated with DICOM metadata for an Optuna-tuned LightGBM classifier. Classification training incorporated CheXpert data after ambiguous labels were removed, and inference used horizontal-flip augmentation.

The team trained modified ResNets on standardized six-channel images with cropping, flips and right-angle rotations, limiting receptive fields to emphasize individual cells and nearby neighbors. ArcFace loss with tuned gamma and Adam with warmup and staged learning-rate reductions supported training, including positive and negative controls from test plates. Post-processing centered embeddings by plate, averaged sites and matched wells to training centers through cosine similarity and leak-constrained label assignment. Filtering out inconsistent test predictions before pseudo-label training improved the ensemble's private score from 0.9957 to 0.9967.

The final submission ensembled six token-classification models and one sequence-classification model using several DeBERTa variants. Successful methods included MLM pretraining, text encoding fixes, masking, adversarial training, recurrent layers, and pseudo-labeling. An LSTM second-stage stacker gave a substantial benefit, followed by a smaller improvement from an XGBoost third-stage stacker. The reported final losses were 0.5609 on CV, 0.555 on the public leaderboard, and 0.560 on the private leaderboard.

The team combined EfficientNet B0–B6, ResNeSt, and ResNeXt models trained at multiple image sizes and aspect ratios. Useful methods included heavy test-time augmentation, CutMix, coarse dropout, stochastic weight averaging, label smoothing, and checkpoint prediction averaging. Their submissions blended PyTorch models with context, TensorFlow models without context, and metadata-only predictions. The combined framework submission scored 0.9470 privately, while a more aggressively postprocessed blend overfit the public leaderboard.

solution_title: Solution for 21st place and a PyTorch kernel
solution_summary: The team skipped the competition training dataset and trained on segment-labeled validation data using temporal average pooling followed by an MLP with a 1,000-class softmax classifier. Hyperopt selected the network widths, and the hidden layers used batch normalization and Swish activations. Combining ten folds improved the public leaderboard score from 0.750 to 0.760, while blending four similar models reached the final score of 0.761. Converting labeled data to NumPy arrays accelerated training, and submission-generation optimizations reduced that step from five hours to five minutes.
compute: Training took less than one minute per epoch; the shared kernel achieved 0.753 public LB in less than one hour including submission generation. Submission generation was reduced from five hours to five minutes.

solution_title: 1790th Place Solution - code details, attempts and insights
solution_summary: The author trained LightGBM to classify awake, sleep, onset, and wakeup states using sensor measurements, a one-step angle lag, and cyclic hour features. Validation used a holdout of 56 series against 221 training series. The final submission extracted peaks from onset and wakeup scores and achieved an AP of 0.004. Adding an enmo lag reduced performance, while detecting valleys in awake and sleep scores produced a score of zero.

solution_title: 21st place - Pseudo Labels, Feature Engineering and stable validation scores
solution_summary: The final ensemble combined two Gemma2-9b-it models with a maximum input length of 4096, selected for complementary features, training data, and tie-versus-winner behavior. The largest improvement came from fold-aware pseudo-labeling and an equal mixture of original labels and soft predictions. One model received rounded text statistics appended to its input, and supplementary preference datasets improved stability. Dynamic padding and length-dependent batch sizes made inference fast enough to run both models, with dynamic batching adding about an 18% speedup.
compute: Full training experiments took about 20+ hours before results could be assessed.

solution_title: 14 th solution (that could have been 6 th )
solution_summary: The team used validation splits that train on three product groups and validate on the remaining two, covering all ten combinations. This addressed differences between training and test measurement modalities and helped avoid leaderboard overfitting. Their ensemble included TabNet, logistic regression, LightGBM, a neural network, XGBoost, CatBoost, and KNN, with TabNet reported as the best single model. After the competition, they discovered that CatBoost class predictions had been used instead of probabilities; correcting this improved the ensemble's private score from 0.59090 to 0.59110.

solution_title: 240 place with simple model, no kfold, no combining networks
solution_summary: The best solution was a single FPN with a pretrained SE-ResNeXt101 encoder, trained without folds or architecture ensembling. It used RAdam, BCE-Dice loss, batch size six, and gradient accumulation over two steps. Resizing and geometric augmentation were followed by class-specific probability thresholds and minimum mask sizes. The model achieved public and private scores of 0.65803 and 0.65038, respectively.
models_pretrained: ["ResNet18, ResNet34, ResNet50, ResNet101, ResNet152", "SE-ResNeXt50_32x4d, SE-ResNeXt101_32x4d", "EfficientNet-B0, EfficientNet-B1, EfficientNet-B2, EfficientNet-B7"]

solution_title: [28th Place Solution] Pre Training on Supplemental Data gives 0.01 LB Improvement
solution_summary: The solution extended an open-source CTC pipeline with more model blocks, 256-frame inputs, and 128 selected landmark indices. Retaining frames unless all selected parts were missing and choosing extra face and pose landmarks by variance were important improvements. Training combined CTC with KL-based label smoothing and used supplemental-data pretraining before main-data training. Motion features and 120 main-data epochs brought the public score to 0.782.
compute: Training notebook designed for Google Colab; hardware and elapsed training time unspecified

solution_summary: The team ensembled six DeBERTa-large models and one DeBERTa-xlarge model by weighted token probabilities. Diversity came from tagging schemes, MLM pretraining, random masking, LSTM heads, learning rates, and multitask objectives. A LightGBM classifier filtered candidate discourse spans using token-probability aggregates and length features. Additional span rules completed postprocessing, with LightGBM filtering improving public/private scores from 0.716/0.724 to 0.719/0.727.

The solution averaged three pseudo-labeled LSTM position models, including building-specific modeling, and refined their predictions with dynamic programming. Its path-level objective balanced proximity to regression predictions, sensor-derived relative motion, and neighboring paths from the same device. Device metadata hashes linked paths, with path prefixes used when metadata was unavailable. The candidate grid was expanded with off-grid predictions and intermediate points before exact optimization.

The pipeline first extracted vascular regions with a fast tri-axial 2D nnU-Net, then classified uniformly resized volumes using a 3D nnU-Net with auxiliary vessel and aneurysm segmentation. Cross-attention pooling, modality supervision, improved annotations, and rare-class balancing supported stable learning across diverse scans. Left-right augmentation required corresponding label swaps, and eight-view test-time augmentation was combined with a two-fold ensemble. Encoder-only classification inference kept execution near nine hours on two T4 GPUs, with reported private performance around 0.8673.
compute: Two T4 GPUs; approximately 9 hours for final two-fold ensemble inference.
external_data: ["TopCoW Training Data and External Testsets, excluding LargeIA", "TopBrain annotations"]

solution_title: Public LB 10th Place - NN vs. GBM
solution_summary: The team developed neural-network and LightGBM models in parallel, with the neural network ultimately performing better. Their best neural network scored 0.01265 on the leaderboard, compared with 0.01297 for LightGBM, and runtime constraints prevented combining them. Geometric features, forward simulation of plays, label clipping, and a holdout containing each team's last three games helped both approaches. Bagging substantially improved the neural network, while several preprocessing and augmentation choices transferred poorly between model families.

solution_title: #9 Solution: model with only atom type and distance
solution_summary: The solution represented each molecule as a fully connected graph using only atom types and interatomic distances. A modified message-passing network predicted couplings from propagated atom states through separate output layers for the eight coupling types. Radial basis distance encoding and an edge update network with GRU updates produced substantial improvements. Hyperparameter tuning and an ensemble of ten differently initialized models brought the reported leaderboard score to about -2.98.

solution_title: Solutions of team "liveinparis" with codes (6th place)
solution_summary: The agent learned from scratch through PPO self-play against a growing pool of saved opponents. A hierarchical action space, situation-dependent action masks, and zero-sum reward shaping made exploration more efficient. Player representations used a 1D convolutional architecture selected through learning-curve comparisons. Synchronized distributed training maintained on-policy rollouts, and the final agent achieved a 92% win rate against the hard rule-based AI.
compute: 30 CPU cores (AMD Ryzen Threadripper 2950X), 1 RTX 2080 GPU, 370 hours; approximately 450,000 episodes

solution_summary: The solution combined three DINOv3 ViT-Huge architectures with LocalMamba fusion across four folds. Its main improvement was stabilizing dead biomass prediction through a dead-to-total ratio, auxiliary losses, and a state-specific bias. Training used collection-session grouping and stratification by clover and dead biomass presence. Fold weighting and target-specific postprocessing improved the ensemble's private score to 0.65179, although the ratio-based model alone scored 0.65329.
compute: Ensemble submission with TTA exceeded 9 hours; TTA was omitted.

solution_title: 37th place approach in the G-Research Crypto Forecasting Competition.
solution_summary: The solution focused on asset-specific technical indicators across multiple timeframes, with periods capped at 1,440 minutes to meet inference limits. Predictions came from an ensemble of two XGBoost and two LightGBM models with different seeds and minor configuration differences. Per-asset quantile cutoffs handled extreme values, and manually selected bullish, bearish, and intermediate periods supported validation. The two submissions used the same pipeline trained on different datasets, and Polars with TA-Lib supported efficient feature computation.

The solution combined seven classifiers into three weighted probability ensembles, then selected the modal class across their predictions. Models and ensembles were tuned and evaluated using 10-fold out-of-fold accuracy. The final mode ensemble achieved 0.835124 accuracy with a fold standard deviation of 0.004098, slightly exceeding each individual ensemble. Feature engineering was tested but did not improve performance.

The solution combined fine-tuned DINOv3 ViT-Huge regression with a semantic tabular branch based on SigLIP embeddings. It predicted Green, Dead, and Clover components, deriving aggregate targets through deterministic relationships to enforce consistency. A left-right image split captured spatial variation, while semantic features and GBDT models provided complementary predictions. Weighted ensembling combined four-fold DINO models with the semantic branch, achieving weighted R² of approximately 0.62.

The final submission used a single BERT model with answer-type classification, span boundary heads, and a bilinear head scoring token pairs. Preprocessing retained simplified HTML structure, processed entire documents, and heavily subsampled negative examples. The model was first fine-tuned on SQuAD 2.0 and then trained on Natural Questions, with development data used to set answer thresholds. It scored about 0.71 publicly and 0.69 privately.
compute: TPU; 2 epochs, batch size 64, learning rate 2.5e-5

solution_summary: The solution used linear regression on transit depth and shape features derived from polynomial fits to light curves. Features combined SNR-weighted AIRS measurements, adjacent-frequency windows, and FG1 measurements, with slope and percentile features providing substantial gains. Edge transits received a separate Ridge model, while very poor transits were excluded from training and assigned larger uncertainties at inference. Bootstrap prediction variability was combined with cross-validation uncertainty estimates, producing a private score of 61.2.

solution_title: 87th place private and 1st place public solution
solution_summary: The team reduced 270 engineered signal features to 90 using recursive elimination with LightGBM permutation importance. Six model outputs were combined through nonnegative linear stacking optimized for MAE, although this performed similarly to the strongest individual models. Validation used stratified grouped five-fold splits with overlapping boundary segments removed. Merging two short earthquakes was the decisive change, while adding public test segments labeled through leaderboard probing had limited apparent impact.

The solution combined LightGBM models with neural networks for the Cite and Multi tasks. Centered log-ratio normalization, alternative count transformations, and row-wise standardization were important preprocessing choices. LightGBM out-of-fold predictions were compressed with truncated SVD and supplied as neural-network meta features. Three-layer MLPs and GRU variants used several activation and loss functions, while out-of-day validation checked whether features remained useful under temporal shift.

solution_title: 3rd Place Solution: An Open Secret - Gather, Ridge, Repeat
solution_summary: The author collected public out-of-fold predictions and repeatedly expanded a Ridge regression stack, eventually reaching 77 OOF inputs. AutoGluon and hill-climbing ensembles were also explored, and some ensemble OOF predictions became inputs to subsequent stacks. Original data and GAN-generated KaggleX data were tested, with KaggleX helping public scores but not private scores. The selected standalone ensemble scored 62958 privately, while blending it with a public notebook improved the public score but yielded 62977 privately.
compute: AutoGluon experiments used CPUs, P100 GPUs, and T4 GPUs.

solution_title: A top solution note for everyone.
solution_summary: This post collects lessons from other competitors rather than describing the author's own final solution. It emphasizes target-permutation feature selection, temporal and grouped aggregations, and domain-informed credit features. Summarized modeling approaches include convolutional and bidirectional LSTM processing of time series, nested LightGBM predictions, and separate models for data blocks. Additional ideas include interest-rate proxies, neighbor-based target statistics, and encoding combinations; no original experimental results are reported.

The solution used only RoBERTa base, ensembled across five folds. Recovering original labels, cleaning problematic text, and correctly finding all label occurrences were central to the pipeline. solution_title: 35th Solution - HRNet-W18 encoder, U-Net++ decoder, and Heatmap/GRU prediction

solution_summary: The solution developed reasoning supervision through five stages while keeping a largely stable LoRA training framework on Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B. solution_summary: The author assembled out-of-fold predictions from diverse models and ultimately used Lasso to combine 81 prediction sets. Missing-value-derived features and approximately 140 OpenFE-generated features improved the base models, while CatBoost configuration changes and neural networks added diversity. The strongest individual model was a 30-fold CatBoost run, and the selected Lasso ensemble scored 1.02765 privately. An AutoGluon ensemble completed after the deadline and achieved a better private score of 1.02582.
compute: MacBook; Ridge/Lasso ensembling took minutes, AutoGluon about an hour, and hill climbing several hours.

solution_summary: The solution combined TF-IDF, DistilRoBERTa, an LSTM/Transformer CNN model, and DeBERTa through weighted averaging. The neural hybrid included readability and sentiment features, while DeBERTa-v3-large used 900,000 training rows, randomized truncation, and label smoothing. TF-IDF received half of the ensemble weight. The final ensemble scored 0.921 privately and 0.970 publicly.

The final solution blends a large collection of gradient boosting, neural, and linear models trained with two feature sets. Target-encoded, pseudo-labeled, residual-based, and scratch-trained variants increased model diversity. Stratified K-fold validation supplied out-of-fold predictions, which were converted to ranks before GPU-accelerated hill-climbing ensemble selection. The final cross-validation score was 0.919911.
compute: GPU-accelerated hill-climbing ensemble optimization; hardware unspecified

solution_summary: The final submission was a weighted average of five models with weights 0.25, 0.2, 0.25, 0.2, and 0.1. The four main components used either nearly all features with some outliers removed or a selected feature set informed by genetic programming. Two components also used sequential PCA, Gaussian random projection, sparse random projection, and ICA, feeding each transformation's outputs into the next. The final component came from a public LightGBM stacking and XGBoost averaging kernel; changing the order of the feature transformations worsened leaderboard performance.

solution_title: 50th Place Solution for the Kaggle - LLM Science Exam Competition
solution_summary: The team combined two retrieval approaches with an ensemble of eight models. Earlier experiments found that gte-small improved leaderboard performance by about 0.02 over other sentence transformers, but a newly published retrieval method reduced that advantage. They fine-tuned multiple DeBERTa-v3-large models with varied learning rates, epochs, and datasets, froze the first 18 layers, and used weighted ensembling. Wikipedia data supported training, and an alternative submission using additional stop words and different models scored 0.912.

solution_title: 22th Place - Lessons learned from a beginner
solution_summary: The final solution ensembled six-fold segmentation models using ResNet34 and EfficientNet B2/B5 encoders with U-Net, FPN, and LinkNet decoders. Models used BCE plus Dice loss and several image resolutions. Three post-processing thresholds were tuned on validation predictions from all six folds to binarize masks, remove small components, and binarize again. The chosen solution achieved 0.6651 CV and 0.66498 privately, while a discarded approach with a separate model per mask type later proved stronger.

The final approach used separate XGBoost models for men's and women's games, with normalized basketball statistics, seeds and derived features. Weighted averages over the current and previous two seasons helped smooth unusual team performance. Model selection used a held-out final season alongside repeated five-fold cross-validation, and predictions were submitted without post-processing. The private score was 0.17525, close to the author's expected range.

The solution enriched phrase-pair inputs with other targets sharing the same anchor and CPC context or sector, excluding the current target. Transformer backbones were augmented with bidirectional LSTM heads and linear attention pooling, trained using Pearson loss and adversarial weight perturbation. Validation grouped anchors, stratified scores, and kept overlapping anchor/target words together. The final weighted ensemble combined five-fold and full-data models, with output scaling and stronger weighting for full-data models, reaching a reported private score of 0.8782.

The solution extracted transit spectra using calibrated, spatially selected signals and polynomial curve fitting with wavelength averaging. Derivative-based transition detection and fitting trends over wider wavelength ranges improved transit-depth estimation. Dynamics-dependent spectrum corrections and empirical uncertainty estimates were followed by per-star PCA using five components. Additional Taurex samples improved the private score by 0.005, while PCA reduced training RMSE from 4.3e-5 to 3.3e-5 and added 0.015 to the leaderboard score.
compute: Approximately 1.5 hours on the test set using 4 CPU processes.

solution_summary: The solution ensembled customized U-shaped segmentation networks with CoaT, NeXtViT, EfficientNetV2, and SAM-B backbones. Ash false-color inputs, increased spatial resolution, pixel-shuffle decoding, and soft annotator labels addressed thin contrails and noisy masks. Low-resolution temporal feature mixing improved sequence models, with LSTM performing best, while externally pseudo-labeled images strengthened single-frame models. Validation used the provided holdout because ordinary training-set splits appeared optimistic, and flips were excluded because shifted masks made them harmful. The final eight-model ensemble achieved 0.7140 validation Dice and 0.72304 private leaderboard performance.
compute: Per fold: CoaT/NeXtViT took 2 hours single-frame or 8 hours multi-frame on 2×RTX4090; EfficientNet took 3 hours 45 minutes per 100 epochs on 8×V100; SAM took 16 hours on 2×A6000. P100 inference took 35 minutes for 5 multi-frame folds, 20 minutes for 6 EfficientNet folds, and 48 minutes for 5 SAM folds.

solution_title: 2nd Place Solution for the Open Problems – Single-Cell Perturbations
solution_summary: The solution combined four transformer regressors trained with different feature sets and sampling strategies, using weights of 0.5, 0.25, 0.25, and 0.3. One-hot categorical inputs and cell-type/drug target statistics were encoded separately before fusion, with 128 reported as the best model dimension. Target-cluster-based validation, Huber loss, Lion optimization, and extensive regularization supported training on the small dataset. Target SVD underperformed direct regression, while mean and standard-deviation features were valuable.
compute: Laptop GPU; training up to 20,000 epochs.

solution_summary: The team concatenated embeddings from transformer and EfficientNet models trained with ArcFace variants to retrieve landmark images. Training progressed across cleaned and larger datasets, often increasing image resolution and freezing batch normalization. Label based reranking first sorted retrieved images by landmark agreement and then inserted same-landmark candidates missed by image similarity. This reranking increased public/private scores from 0.31324/0.32614 to 0.39905/0.43219.
compute: Z8G4 workstation with dual RTX6000 GPUs used for PyTorch DDP training; a ZBook with RTX5000 GPU was also sponsored.

solution_summary: The solution merged roughly 45 DBSCAN clustering outputs built with different helix features and z-shifts. Each output underwent aggressive hit and track outlier removal, followed by helix and straight-track extension. Tracks were divided by curvature consistency and merged from strong to weak using overlap-based heuristics. Careful merge ordering and track extension mattered substantially, while simple longest-track-wins merging degraded scores with many models.

solution_title: 43rd place and my best local tested approach
solution_summary: The final agent learned by imitation from Team Durrett replays with center actions included. Local matches guided the selection of models for each map size, and training used replay filtering, augmentation, mixed precision, and resumed random-batch training. Models were exported to ONNX for fast CPU inference, with a smaller model used when the remaining time budget became short. Reinforcement learning did not outperform imitation learning and was abandoned.
compute: Inference environment: 1 CPU, 3 seconds per frame; 60-second cumulative time limit.

solution_title: [64th Place] A simple low computation model
solution_summary: The author describes constructing forecast-period features by copying the last 28 observed sales days into the next 28 days. These copied values supplied rolling and lagged features without recursive prediction or separate models for each horizon. Three years of history supported two years of training rows with rolling windows up to 365 days, and training was split across hobbies, household, and foods. Under the author's WRMSSE calculation, repeating 28 days performed better than repeating the last seven days four times.

The team combined diverse LightGBM models built with different feature engineering approaches, using stratified 10-fold validation. Applicant-level transaction aggregates over time, delinquency buckets, and zero-filled missing values improved the author's baseline. Combining teammates' features and adding out-of-fold predictions from individual tables as meta features produced models with local CV around 0.800 and public scores up to 0.809. Percentile-ranking predictions before stacking or blending was essential, and the final results supported trusting local validation.

solution_title: Single Model Transformer - LB 0.112 - Gold Medal
solution_summary: The post presents one strong TensorFlow transformer from a broader team solution. The model uses encoder layers only, which outperformed experiments with decoders and out-of-fold prediction inputs. It achieved CV 0.133 and LB 0.112 when inference used 32 models described as folds, each trained on all training data.

A single Temporal 3D U-Net jointly learned cell detection, backward motion, and division from dense shared features. Training progressed from detector initialization through mixed real and synthetic supervision to sparse real-data fine-tuning. After freezing the network, calibration tuned candidate extraction and integer linear programming costs to reconstruct lineages. The fine-tuned model with tuned ILP achieved 0.94905 Public and 0.94743 Private; additional submitted post-processing slightly reduced both scores.

solution_title: 5th Place - by standing on the shoulders of Giants
solution_summary: The solution built article–dataset candidate pairs from Europe PMC and Data Citation Corpus v3, then filtered accession families against the training labels. Qwen models classified references using XML context, linked references, table rows, and dataset metadata, with most effort focused on DOI and SAMN identifiers. Their predictions were combined with a CPU submission through majority voting. The corpus-based baseline scored 0.82 publicly and 0.70 privately, and a final accession filter was retained based on CV despite no leaderboard improvement.

solution_title: Vote of Thanks and Lessons Learnt
solution_summary: This post thanks the organizers and community and reflects on lessons learned during the competition. The author says rereading discussions helped uncover a bug late in the competition. It recommends broad experimentation, reviewing kernels, version control, and cloud backups, but provides no concrete modeling pipeline.

solution_title: [1st place solution] Transformer model with Dynamic positional encoding + CNN for BPPM features
solution_summary: The solution combined nucleotide embeddings with EternaFold base-pair probability matrices in a 12-layer transformer. Convolutional blocks processed structural features and injected them into attention logits, while Dynamic Positional Bias supported generalization to longer sequences. Signal-to-noise-weighted sampling and additional SGD training improved performance. The final ensemble averaged 27 models and lightly blended a separate DMS-to-2A3 predictor into its 2A3 outputs.
external_data: ["RMDB RNA Mapping Database 2023", "Predicted 3D structures of 100k training sequences"]

solution_title: Now that the competition is over - what everyone used?
solution_summary: The final model used gradient boosting to predict the logarithm of useful-vote counts. About 20–30 engineered features emphasized review age, user voting history, user and business activity ratios, rating differences, and business clusters. The approach relied primarily on user and business characteristics. Text extraction, location features, and bag-of-words review clustering worsened results.

The solution adapted an existing CLIP training pipeline using Open CLIP ViT-H/14 pretrained on LAION-2B. The main improvements were feeding 64-dimensional vectors into ArcFace, linearly reducing the learning rate, and fine-tuning the backbone for one epoch at a low learning rate without augmentation. The author retained the original datasets after failing to find better alternatives. Random submission out-of-memory errors prevented adoption of more complex architectures.

solution_title: The REAL UserID, different from CardID
solution_summary: The post presents an algorithm for reconstructing users who transact with multiple cards, extending an earlier card identification method. Transactions connect card groups through matching amounts, devices, browsers, and IP-related fields, with shared transactions serving as bridges. Examples show that these groups can collect isolated fraudulent transactions into larger patterns, although some groupings may contain errors. The author proposes additional features based on card counts and changes in devices, IP addresses, or emails, but does not describe a complete predictive pipeline or validation score.

The author shares a competition solution and links its source code. The approach builds on the community's Bench Stacked Generalization and Blah-XGB scripts. It achieved a private leaderboard score of 0.394519, but the post provides no further implementation details.

solution_title: Rossmann Store Sales, Winner's Interview: 1st place, Gert Jacobusse
solution_summary: The solution combined over 20 XGBoost models with historical sales averages and calendar features. Rolling averages covered several time horizons and were conditioned on factors such as weekday and promotions. A single time-based holdout reliably guided improvements and helped avoid overfitting public leaderboard feedback. Feature engineering, feature selection, and ensembling received substantially more attention than model tuning.
compute: Laptop; about two hours per model with three models running in parallel; estimated under 24 hours for the ensemble.

solution_title: 9 Place solution: pretrain & semi-supervised & postprocessing & Trust both cv and lb
solution_summary: The team pretrained on LIVECell with all cells treated as one class, then generated pseudo-labels for the provided semi-supervised data. A Cascade R-CNN with a ResNeXt152 backbone reached 0.338 on the leaderboard after this training. Five-fold ResNet34 classification constrained segmentation outputs to the image's predicted cell class. The final pipeline relied heavily on mask repair, overlap-based mask merging, and category-specific weighted non-maximum weighting.

The final submission combined 15 models trained with four folds, with orthogonal initialization, last-layer reinitialization, and layer-wise learning rate decay across all models. Mean pooling was particularly effective, while weighted loss modestly improved some models and added diversity. SiFT and MIXout helped smaller DeBERTa variants despite failing on the base variant. The ensemble averaged target-wise weights optimized with Optuna on out-of-fold predictions and weights adjusted manually using leaderboard feedback.

The solution combined cloud segmentation with separate classifiers that removed false-positive masks. The classifiers included a multiscale Xception network and a jointly supervised mask-and-label model, reaching 78% classification validation accuracy together. Segmentation used an EfficientNetB2 U-Net with crop augmentation, test-time augmentation, and ensembles across folds and initializations. The final solution achieved 0.663 on both cross-validation and the private leaderboard.

solution_title: Code sharing, 13th place, no external data
solution_summary: The author shared an XGBoost notebook that used no external data. The post also described a stronger single-model variant incorporating Google Trends, state information, and weather, but excluded those sources from the shared model over real-world usability concerns. The script required about 8 GB of RAM and several hours, and the author reported selecting submissions based on public leaderboard scores.
compute: About 8 GB RAM; several hours runtime
external_data: ["Google Trends daily searches for Rossmann in Germany", "State data by dune_dweller", "Weather data per state"]

solution_summary: The team trained separate image and title embedding models, concatenated their vectors, and refined embeddings using nearby matches. Nearest-neighbor retrieval produced candidate pairs that GPU XGBoost models scored using embedding distances, ranks, and TF-IDF similarities. A second model used percentage ranks to reduce sensitivity to dataset size, and probability-based agglomerative clustering formed the final matches. Joint image-text representation learning did not improve validation, and the team's two similar kernels could not be combined within the time limit.
compute: GPU used for second-stage XGBoost.

solution_summary: The author built an Excel model that regressed standardized pre-tournament metrics against historical results scored using the ESPN points scheme. Regression coefficients determined metric weights and produced a power rating for each team using the 2018, 2019, and 2021 tournaments. Features covered efficiency, shooting, pace, rankings, seeds, schedule strength, and win/loss indicators. TeamRankings supplied additional statistics for the final three games before the tournament.

The solution retrieved DOI and accession candidates through article-ID lookups in V4 and external Europe PMC text-mined terms, then checked that candidates appeared in the article. DOI type classification used author information where available and a distilled 7B context classifier otherwise. Accession classification combined distilled 7B and 14B models with identifier-specific rules and majority voting. Two rule variants behaved differently on public and private evaluations, while an additional EPI author-information approach was not selected.

solution_title: 13th Place Solution for the Google - Fast or Slow? Predict AI Model Runtime Competition
solution_summary: The approach used separate multilayer perceptrons for layout and tile configuration ranking. The layout model combined configurable-node features with parent and sibling information, averaged node representations, and added graph and subset descriptors. Pairwise hinge loss, balanced graph batches, careful normalization, and deduplication stabilized training, while three independent runs formed the final ensemble. Compressed TFRecords and strict graph-size limits kept training within 16 GB RAM and 4 GB VRAM.
compute: 16 GB RAM, 4 GB VRAM

solution_title: [86th place solution] How a beginner became a expert !
solution_summary: The solution combines public choice and give9 prompt attacks with a custom give9_python attack. The choice attack repeats the topic in option nine, while the Python variant asks the evaluator to output the answer to code and includes a temperature instruction. Multiple seeds were submitted to select stable attacks because local verification and seed consistency were difficult. The reported selected configuration scored 23.749 publicly and 23.319 privately.

solution_title: Bronze Medal Solution for the Vesuvius Challenge - Surface Detection Competition
solution_summary: The final pipeline generated CT surface probabilities with TransUNet, refined them using a lightweight residual UNet, and extracted ridges through orientation-aware relaxed non-maximum suppression. Anisotropic closing and connected-component filtering then repaired gaps and removed fragments. Replacing skeleton thinning with relaxed NMS delivered the largest reported public-score improvement, from 0.555 to 0.570. The final private score was 0.582.

solution_title: 5th Place Solution: Features are all you need!
solution_summary: The team emphasized features describing reconstructed essay structure, punctuation, cursor behavior, and writing activity. Their final system combined four tabular neural networks, a 1D CNN, and LightGBM, CatBoost, and XGBoost models. Score-stratified validation and five shared seeds helped maintain agreement between cross-validation and leaderboard results. Neural and tree ensembles were weighted separately with Optuna and then combined equally, producing a final CV score of 0.5858 and private score of 0.560.

The post announces that the author is attaching source code and documentation to comply with the competition rules. The supplied text contains no description of the approach. It provides no methods, implementation details, or results to extract.

The author combined XGBoost models trained on different time periods to capture product seasonality and longer-term trends. Historical ownership averages, lag features, and customer tenure features helped, while training was restricted to customers acquiring products to fit limited memory. The final blend averaged multi-output and product-specific predictions, adjusted product odds using leaderboard feedback, and incorporated the teammate's predictions with conditional weights.
compute: Computer with 8 GB RAM

solution_summary: The team adapted shared training code with extensive data augmentation and changed the backbone to EfficientNet V2 B3. They trained 10 models using 10-fold cross-validation and a learning rate of 0.0001, reaching approximately 0.92 CV and 0.71 leaderboard scores. Flip-based test-time augmentation with corresponding output-index remapping added about 0.005 to the leaderboard score. They also built a YOLO-based alternative, although its role in the final submission is unspecified.

The solution used a single TensorFlow 2.0 BERT-large model with separate outputs for short-answer boundaries and long-answer locations. Matching the empty-answer sampling ratio to the full dataset was the main improvement. Custom HTML tokens helped slightly, and SQuAD-finetuned whole-word-masking weights performed best among the tested initializations, reaching about 0.73 on the leaderboard. Final training took a little over two hours on TPUs, excluding tokenization and post-processing.
compute: TPUs; final training a little over 2 hours excluding tokenization and post-processing; local machine had 2 x 1080 TI.

solution_summary: The solution refined a weighted least-squares baseline by repeatedly removing measurements with large residuals. It estimated relative motion from GNSS measurements and a convolutional model using IMU data, then combined those estimates with pseudoranges over a 21-timestamp optimization window. Downtown predictions used nearby ground-truth road points with robust residual scoring and medoid selection. A final convolutional error-correction model and aggregation across stationary periods and phones further improved predictions.

solution_title: 11th Place - GRU, CNN, Transformer - GPU Deep Learning!
solution_summary: The solution combined a CNN–Transformer–GRU model using 80 features with a deep GRU using two features. Training windows always contained one onset and one wakeup, allowing a question-answering-style softmax head to predict event minutes. Producing 30 progressively downweighted guesses per night added approximately 0.050 to CV, while auxiliary models reranked event confidence scores. Non-maximum suppression and weighted box fusion combined the diverse event predictions.

solution_title: 7th place solution - the power of randomness
solution_summary: The solution combined transformer models predicting one score per text with token models predicting multiple targets in a shared anchor-context group. Randomly permuted related targets supplied additional context, and balanced encoding was preferred at inference. Token scores combined simple and prediction-weighted averages, while text models mainly used target-masked attention heads. Final submissions used positive-coefficient linear regression ensembles fitted to out-of-fold predictions, with alternative handling of a model that had produced NaNs.
compute: Only Kaggle resources; many experiments used one fold for one epoch.

solution_title: The code of my best submission
solution_summary: The solution blended gradient boosting models. Categorical variables were represented with binary vectors, while dates were decomposed into year, month, and day using both categorical and scalar representations. The implementation used scikit-learn, and the author shared the code for the best submission.

solution_title: 11th Place Solution: Supervised Contrastive Pretraining + Query and Database expansion
solution_summary: The final retrieval ensemble combined two EfficientNetV2-M models with SE-ResNeXt101 and EfficientNet-B6 models. Class-balanced supervised contrastive pretraining followed by AdaCos fine-tuning improved convergence, while a second training pipeline used GeM pooling and ArcFace. Weighted concatenation of normalized embeddings outperformed combining ranked retrieval lists. Query expansion and class-based database reranking improved the leaderboard score by approximately 0.07, with the concatenation experiment reaching 0.455.
compute: GPU augmentation and Faiss postprocessing; hardware unspecified.
external_data: ["GLDv2 cleaned and full datasets", "Google repository index and test validation data"]

solution_summary: The final pipeline allocated one prediction slot to TBM, two to RNAPro, and two to BPP-Protenix, with plain Protenix handling targets unsuitable for BPP features. BPP-Protenix projected EternaFold base-pair probabilities into the initial pair representation of a pretrained Protenix model and was trained on 619 RNA-only PDBs. A simple linear projection outperformed more elaborate binned and Pairformer-based embeddings. The final ensemble scored 0.504 publicly and 0.492 privately, while local analysis found benefits even for targets containing pseudoknots.

The post develops a hypothesis about how the dataset was generated rather than describing a complete modeling pipeline. The author argues that negative examples include Gaussian noise and that the test set contains both real and shuffled fake samples. They propose computing counts using training data and real test samples, then interpreting those counts together with each value's position in its feature distribution. Distinguishing noise from real observations is presented as the key challenge, while the final classifier and measured results are unspecified.

The post announces that the team's solution is available on Docker Hub. It provides a command to launch the container with nvidia-docker. It gives no details about the modeling pipeline, training, or results.

The repository provides the team's competition solution through three contributor-specific code folders. Reproduction requires following the instructions in each folder. The resulting models are combined using a supplied blending script, but the text gives no model architectures or scores.

The system retrieved 200 candidates per session using tuned co-visitation matrices, then reranked them with LightGBM, XGBoost, and CatBoost. Roughly 500 user, item, and interaction features captured activity counts, time patterns, co-visitation, embedding similarities, and BPR scores. Validation used shared datasets with separately fitted validation and full-data retrieval representations to avoid leakage. CatBoost was the strongest ranker, and Optuna optimized a weighted ensemble against local recall@20.
compute: Ensemble weight evaluation took 700 ms per trial for 60 million cart samples.

solution_summary: The solution decomposed survival prediction into censored and uncensored regressions combined through class probabilities. Race-specific target transformations enabled binary cross-entropy regression, while neural networks used a tuned constant for censored cases. Repeated four-fold validation across many split seeds guided model selection and public/private score estimation. The final ensemble blended regressors and stacked classifiers with logistic regression, reaching a reported private score of 0.69937.

The solution combined six image channels, normalized images by experiment, plate, and channel, and added train and test controls as extra classes. DenseNet121 was the main model, alongside EfficientNet-B1, SE-ResNet101, and DenseNet169, with five-fold validation and models at two image resolutions. Batch-level mixup and cutout were particularly helpful, while training also used pseudo-labels, label smoothing, mixed precision, and learning-rate schedules. Predictions used cosine similarity to experiment-level average training logits, test-time augmentation, plate leakage, and prediction balancing.

The submission generated transferable adversarial examples using a momentum iterative attack. Its update accumulates normalized gradients and applies clipped sign-based perturbations. The attack used an ensemble of eight models, many adversarially trained. The writeup also describes a 1,000-image ImageNet validation subset and a Cleverhans implementation.

The post describes feature engineering for volatility prediction rather than a complete modeling pipeline. It generalizes weighted average price to multiple order-book levels and derives liquidity measures from the minimized price objectives. Alternative WAP features provided little benefit, but trade volume divided by liquidity was highly informative, with a reported log-space correlation of about 0.88 with volatility. Strong features combined trade volume over long windows with recent liquidity and sometimes aggregated across stocks.

The pipeline detected helmets with YOLOv5-l, tracked them using optical flow, and classified motion-corrected video crops with Temporal Shift Module networks. Consistent crop scaling and velocity compensation helped isolate acceleration associated with impacts. Predictions from multiple architectures and four folds were averaged, with fast models filtering most easy negatives first. Tracking-based temporal suppression was applied separately by predicted impact type, yielding a small additional validation improvement.
compute: TSM classification models took an hour to a few hours each to train.

solution_title: 25th Place Solution for DAIGT (Public LB: 0.966 Private LB: 0.927)
solution_summary: The team combined typo correction, trained BPE tokenization, and TF-IDF features with an ensemble of four conventional classifiers. LoRA-tuned Mistral-7B predictions were used for difficult cases, alongside a public transformer model described inconsistently as DistilBert and DistilRoberta. Confident predictions supplied pseudo-labels for an additional semi-supervised component, and the resulting predictions were blended. Typo correction and pseudo-labeling reportedly improved the private score by about 0.01 and 0.02 respectively.

The solution used extensive weighted ensembles of CatBoost, LightGBM, and XGBoost models, including stacks with glmnet. Diversity came from random seeds, training subsets enriched for positive examples, and independently generated synthetic features. Repeated random holdouts guided model and hyperparameter choices, while categorical encoding and numerical standardization prepared the inputs. The best selected submission scored 0.29144, and a related unselected ensemble scored 0.29157 on the private leaderboard.
compute: Multiple Intel Xeon workstations totaling 74 physical cores and 448 GB RAM, running Ubuntu Linux 16.04.

solution_title: 3rd place solution - attack the opponent's second shipyard
solution_summary: The agent extended an existing solution with analytical rules for mining, shipyard construction, defense, and attacks. Its main strength was identifying safe opportunities to capture the opponent's second shipyard using a 25-turn simulator and estimates of available attackers, defenders, and future ship production. It merged allied fleets along attack routes and retained ships through mining decisions to create more attack opportunities. Reinforcement learning was abandoned after limited benefits, while accurate attack decisions contributed strongly to winning matches.
compute: About three weeks preparing reinforcement learning and about one week of learning before abandoning it.

solution_title: Neural networks architectures and training methods
solution_summary: The solution used neural networks over approximately 11,000 sparse features, processing feature types separately through one layer before fusion. This fusion strategy improved log loss by about 0.02, and the best individual network achieved 0.61 log loss. The author averaged that network and eight additional neural architectures with one XGBoost model. Numerous alternatives, including autoencoder pretraining and additional recommendation features, produced no major gains.

The solution combined KeyNet, AffNet, and HardNet with a two-stage AdaLAM matching pipeline. Initial candidate matches guided a second local matching pass over ten nearest neighbors, improving feature-track connections across overlapping images for SfM. OriNet was enabled, the feature count was increased to 8,192, and images were resized to a 1,600-pixel longer edge. Grid grouping produced low scores, while DBSCAN matching offered limited gains and multiscale descriptor concatenation remained incompletely tested.

The solution generated purchase candidates through repurchases, collaborative filtering, and global or segmented popularity, then reranked them with LightGBM LambdaMART. Time-decayed ItemkNN provided the largest gain, while candidate ranks were important reranking features. Negative sampling and positive-sample ratios became increasingly important as candidate volume grew. Processing moved to BigQuery and training to GCP Vertex with high-memory machines; the best model scored 0.03861 locally and 0.03252 on the private leaderboard.
compute: Initially a GPU notebook; later parallel experiments on GCP Vertex high-memory machines with up to 512GB RAM.

solution_summary: The solution used two RetinaNet detectors with ResNet-50 and ResNet-101 backbones to predict pneumonia bounding boxes. Training and validation data came from the Stage 1 training labels, without training on the Stage 2 set. The author manually selected snapshots from several training runs using precision and maximum Youden index.
compute: Dell Precision T5500; 3.07 GHz Intel Xeon X5675 CPU; 12 GB NVIDIA Titan Xp GPU; 16 GB DDR3 RAM; 512 GB HDD

solution_summary: The author detected helmets with YOLOv5 and matched detections to tracking data using a coordinate-regression network. This network paired an EfficientNetB0 encoder with a U-Net decoder and predicted x/y coordinate masks from two-channel 256×256 inputs. Training used L1 loss only where tracking labels existed, with an additional segmentation channel providing guidance. DeepSORT and SiamRPN tracking postprocessing increased CV from about 0.7 to 0.9 and the private score from 0.7 to 0.86.

The solution used a combinatorial geometric tracking algorithm that repeatedly seeded, extended, ranked, and pruned candidate tracks. Idealized helices predicted subsequent hits, with training-derived corrections and nearest-neighbor searches guiding extensions. Tracks were committed in quality order to resolve shared hits, and the process repeated on unused hits. Hyperopt tuned the many heuristic parameters, and the final score was 0.86395 with approximately three minutes of single-threaded processing per event.
compute: Intel Core i7-3667U @ 2GHz notebook; about 3 minutes per event using one thread.

solution_title: How some small changes on the public notebook had gave you a 55th place!
solution_summary: The solution modified a public notebook into a manual ensemble of Multinomial Naive Bayes, an SGD classifier, two LightGBM classifiers, and two CatBoost classifiers. Sequential fitting and probability accumulation reduced memory use and allowed additional models. Lower iteration counts helped reduce overfitting, and changing the training objective to log loss was another important adjustment.

solution_title: Best Single Model: 0.915 (Private LB score) with nearly zero pre-processing
solution_summary: The author describes a compact CNN with fewer than 1.5 million parameters and five folds. Preprocessing consists only of silence removal and audio chunking, while unspecified feature engineering is credited with much of the model's strength. The best single model scored 0.915 on the private leaderboard and 0.921 publicly. Mixup increased the public score to 0.925 but reduced the private score to 0.907, and the author says these results were omitted from the final submission and technical report.

The author summed scores from seven models varying RoBERTa encoders, classification heads, datasets, losses, and seeds. Training used either binary cross-entropy or a custom batchwise ranking loss over adjacent examples sorted by label. Large-batch TPU training used a constant learning rate of 1e-4. Model selection relied on one-fold validation and its voting version, with leaky toxic-data comments removed; including OLID was reported to hurt performance.
compute: 8-core TPU; batch size 384

solution_summary: The pipeline fine-tuned google/matcha-base image-to-text models in two phases: synthetic-data adaptation followed by separate scatter and non-scatter specialization. A diverse collection of 700,000 self-generated plots formed the foundation, supplemented by public synthetic data, corrected pseudo-labels, and ICDAR images. Extracted and other real plots were heavily oversampled during specialization. solution_summary: The solution emphasized a large engineered feature store and diverse tabular models for irrigation-need classification. solution_summary: The approach focused on correcting noisy bounding boxes and removing very small annotations. Pseudo-label training used 1024-pixel images after excluding noisy training images and incorporating test images. A 512-pixel model performed better publicly, while an unselected 1024-pixel submission achieved a reported private score of 67.13.

Whole-slide images were downsampled sixfold and tiled, with background removal and learned tile selection reducing the workload. An ImageNet-initialized EfficientNetB0 feature extractor was trained through iterative clustering-based tile pseudo labels, including a noncritical tile category. Attention-based slide aggregation and maximum tile predictions fed a random forest classifier using the 25 darkest tiles. Tile balance and hue augmentation mattered, while the author reported that robust end-to-end validation remained unresolved.

The post asks whether another participant shared a writeup and encourages them to explain their approach. It specifically expresses interest in a reported CatBoost result using few features. It provides no account of the author's own solution.

The author combined outputs from public kernels and simple ensembles using a weighted mean. One example assigned half the weight to the best public kernel and half to the mean of the source predictions. A subsequent rule replaced predictions above 0.75 with the maximum source prediction and those below 0.25 with the minimum source prediction.

The final solution averaged predictions from 14 EfficientNet-B4 models, with checkpoint weights averaged within each model. Diversity came from input preprocessing, training subsets, loss weighting, hard-example mining, external data, and postprocessing. Very strong color, crop, stain, and organ-size augmentations combined with long training raised scores from below 0.6 to consistently above 0.75.
