solution_summary: The author expanded impact bounding boxes and manually labeled helmet, shoulder, body, and ground regions to provide more context. Head annotations included both helmets, and detections from two models were compared using overlap. Only cases with at least two detections exceeding an IoU of 0.1 were retained, aiming to suppress isolated false positives. The author reported that the overall attempt did not go well.

The team ensembled three complementary components, with this post detailing a genetic search over grid-transformation programs. Programs combined global DSL operations with cellular automaton rules, and late support for splitting and merging grids substantially improved results. Search used mutation and crossover, scored through overall accuracy, per-output accuracy, and exact color matching. The author trained a ship-wise imitation-learning bot using winning replays from strong players. solution_summary: The team combined public and locally trained CaFormer and ConvNeXt predictions using a weighted median, obtaining a private leaderboard MAE of 24.57. Family-weighted L1 loss and removal of an all-zero trace row were additional training changes. Each subset underwent feature selection and transformation to a standard normal distribution before training LightGBM, XGBoost, and a very small neural network. Features described spectral power, entropy, spectral edge power, and cross-channel correlations and eigenvalues in both frequency and time domains. Squared versions of all features were added, and training used all data marked safe. The reported submission achieved 0.79458 on the private leaderboard and 0.79650 on the public leaderboard.

This smartphone-addiction classifier relied on extensive feature engineering and a diverse pool of more than 400 candidate models. A store of over 600 engineered features supported models trained on different subsets, with RealMLP the strongest individual model and TabM close behind. solution_title: 93rd Place Solution for the SenNet + HOA - Hacking the Human Vasculature in 3D
solution_summary: The competition submission equally ensembled two ImageNet-initialized 2D U-Nets with ResNeXt50 backbones trained at crop sizes of 1024 and 512. Training and inference used slices from all three spatial axes, with tiled inference, four-rotation TTA, a fixed probability threshold, and majority voting across projections. Preserving native image resolution and avoiding mask cleanup helped retain tiny vessels, while several postprocessing and multislice experiments failed. After the competition, revised normalization, a boundary/Dice/focal loss, an upscale layer, and stronger resolution-aware augmentation improved the private score to 0.682.

solution_summary: The solution used a five-layer bidirectional LSTM with concatenated skip connections and engineered breath-level time-series features. Inputs included logarithmic airflow, lagged values, cumulative quantities, and first and second derivatives, with robust scaling fitted on inspiratory rows. solution_title: 40th Place Solution for the ICR - Identifying Age-Related Conditions Competition
solution_summary: The solution uses a LightGBM pairwise classifier inspired by contrastive learning to address the small training set. Pair features include absolute feature differences and summary statistics, with sampled pairs providing many training examples. Validation is stratified by Alpha, and AUC determines the training rounds. At inference, each observation is compared with all training observations, and classwise average similarities are normalized into a final probability.

The solution combined full-context TabPFN-3.5 models, generator-aware logistic regression, and nested stacks of tree and neural models. GPT-2 token features, label-free generator statistics, and likelihood-ratio features from distilgpt2 trained on the original dataset supplied the strongest complementary signals. A constrained blend optimized a smoothed pairwise AUC objective using histogram convolution and FFT, improving nested validation over the earlier log-loss combiner. Model selection relied on fixed nested folds and statistical gain gates; the second final submission deliberately relaxed those gates for an expanded refit and achieved 0.94588 private AUC. Experiments fitted directly to public leaderboard scores substantially harmed private performance and were excluded.

The approach transformed raw anglez, enmo, and hour inputs into a wavegram using a CNN feature extractor. A two-dimensional U-Net produced heatmaps, which a one-dimensional U-Net decoded into sleep, onset, and wakeup probabilities before post-processing. Stratified five-fold validation, balanced sampling, and label smoothing supported training. Post-processing lowered a species threshold throughout an audio file when any clip produced a confident detection.

solution_title: 9th place solution: RL with LookAhead, Floodfill, and Rules
solution_summary: The team combined a customized HandyRL policy and value network with alpha-beta minimax lookahead, floodfill space analysis, and hand-crafted survival and aggression rules. solution_summary: The solution represented typewell depth and horizontal position as a twelve-channel alignment image and predicted a depth class for every horizontal column. ImageNet-pretrained image models were pretrained on physically consistent synthetic wells and then fine-tuned on real wells with additional augmentation and synthetic batches. A coherent trajectory-bank decoder enforced consistency across each whole well. Three image models were blended with a weaker but complementary 1D candidate-verification pipeline. Selection used grouped cross-validation alone, with final pooled CV RMSE of 5.097 and private score of 6.319.

The solution combined YOLOX-s with a ConvNeXt-base Cascade R-CNN detector. Validation trained on videos 0 and 1 and evaluated on video 2, including background images, while final training used all data. YOLOX-s used high-resolution multiscale inference and weighted boxes fusion for test-time augmentation. Weighted boxes fusion combined the detectors, achieving 0.795 cross-validation and 0.726 private leaderboard scores.

The author handled uncertain RNA structures by encoding BPPS matrices as bond-specific color images and extracting sequence-aligned CNN embeddings. Predictions for the three most likely foldings of each test RNA were averaged according to folding probability. They built 109 model variants from recurrent, graph, and autoencoder-based starter pipelines, removed suspicious predictions, and formed a hierarchical weighted ensemble. Multiplying final predictions by 1.04, selected through public leaderboard probing, also helped the private submission.

The solution combined a metadata encoder, a bidirectional GRU light-curve encoder, and a spectroscopic-redshift predictor. Their outputs fed two fully connected layers for class prediction. The light-curve encoder was pretrained as an autoencoder on test data, while the redshift predictor was pretrained on test objects with available spectroscopic redshifts. Gaussian perturbations and observation dropping augmented training, and the top submission averaged five cross-validation runs of three network variants.

The solution combined five U-Net models with 3D SEResNet101, 3D ResNet34, and SegFormer-b3 backbones. It used spatial and depth augmentations, staged training at larger image sizes, and fragment-based validation. Inference averaged rotated and depth-window predictions while excluding patch edges and invalid regions. Fixed-threshold and percentile-threshold submissions achieved private scores of 0.65 and 0.63 respectively.

Mutual information filtering, hierarchical clustering, and iterative permutation importance reduced 4,778 initial features to small target-specific subsets. Inputs were scaled and mixed with PCA, while targets were log-transformed and robust-scaled, with a temperature offset where needed. Architecture and hyperparameters were selected using a custom R2-and-MAE score, followed by repeated fitting and selection of a single best model. Neighbor-sequence features failed, and adding leakage features again at the meta-model stage caused overfitting.

The solution combined BERT, XLNet, and GPT2 models with custom heads and auxiliary tasks. Training used bucketed sequence collation and a custom loss that combined overall binary cross-entropy with subgroup-specific terms. Stochastic weight averaging and checkpoint ensembling were also used. The final ensemble averaged prediction ranks from two XLNet models, two BERT models, and GPT2 medium.

The solution used 120 log-mel filterbanks and a CNN that processed time and frequency differently, preserving temporal resolution until the final pooling step. Windowed peak-volume standardization, time stretching, and vocal tract length perturbation improved performance. A single model achieved 90.9% on the private leaderboard. The author also averaged square roots of probabilities from model variants, though ensembling delivered limited benefit.

solution_title: Result of Late Submission: 2D-CNN + XGB + 1D-CNN (Private LB: 0.78703)
solution_summary: This post reports post-competition improvements to a staged XGBoost and CNN contact-detection pipeline. A five-channel 2D CNN, stricter folds with less player duplication, and lagged and grouped prediction features drove major gains. solution_summary: The solution calibrated the observations with adjusted AIRS and FGS binning and refined transit boundaries through signal fitting. It extracted seven transit-depth estimates per wavelength using different wavelength grouping scales. A neural network combined wavelength convolutions with stellar information and residual blocks to predict the spectrum. Linear regression on spectrum variability, white-curve variance, and mean predicted spectrum improved uncertainty estimates.

The pipeline selected SuperPoint/SuperGlue or COLMAP SIFT separately for each scene using mean image memory consumption. Large scenes used SIFT, while other scenes used SuperGlue with images capped at a 2560-pixel longest edge. COLMAP incremental reconstruction selected the model with the most registered images and filled missing poses with scene averages. The author combined XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost with averaging across ten seeds. The pipeline used balanced undersampling, removed EJ, constructed ratios from highly correlated features, and added Epsilon_year without imputing missing values. Validation used ten stratified folds based on Class, EJ, and BN. CV scored 0.1172, compared with 0.19 public and 0.40 private scores, and the author reported poor agreement between validation and leaderboard results.

The bot combined heuristic shipyard conversion, role-based ship behavior, spawning policies, and danger-aware navigation. Its main miner policy assigned ships to targets using rewards for mining, attacking, guarding, depositing, and area control. Genetic optimization tuned policy parameters, while an alternative spawning policy imitated leading teams with a small multilayer perceptron and achieved 98% accuracy. Dijkstra navigation and movement priorities supported collision avoidance and friendly position swaps.

The author describes their contribution using LightGBM and XGBoost with fixed tree counts, Huber or gamma objectives, and sample weights. Around 200 features summarize STFT frequency-band energy and raw-signal statistics, with augmentation based on 30,000-sample chunks. Validation holds out one earthquake, and shifting time-to-failure labels for long earthquakes improved cross-validation. To address distribution shift, the team optimized two evaluation measures under possible test distributions; the submission with the weaker public score performed better privately.

The team ensembled diverse pretrained language models with attention, recurrent, convolutional, and masked-sum heads. Validation used multilabel stratification on anchor and score, and training selected BCEWithLogitsLoss after comparing prediction distributions. Useful inputs included natural-language combinations of anchor, target, and context, plus frequent claim words grouped by context. The two final submissions used ridge-derived coefficients for 14 models and Optuna weight search for 15 models, achieving private scores of 0.8641 and 0.8638.

solution_title: 3rd Place Public - We Should Have Trusted CV - 118th Private
solution_summary: The team built a diverse ensemble of 12 model types, including TabNet, denoising autoencoders, DeepInsight EfficientNet, MX10 transfer learning, and PyTorch neural networks. Each model used about 30 folds, producing 360 trained models for inference, and some DeepInsight models used UMAP image layouts for additional diversity. The submitted predictions were postprocessed by reducing probabilities for common targets and increasing them for rare targets that models could not recognize. This improved public log loss by 0.00011 but worsened private log loss by 0.00008; the unprocessed ensemble selected using the best cross-validation results achieved a reported private score of 0.01603.

solution_title: 4th Place Gold - Single Model RAPIDS cuML SVR!
solution_summary: The final model was a TensorFlow MLP trained only on clinical data, using visit month and ten indicators of whether visits occurred at particular months. Indicators distinguished observed visits, observed absences, and unknown future visits, while training rows were expanded to reproduce the forecast horizons. Visit timing supplied the useful signal; protein and peptide features improved validation no more than random features. The MLP achieved CV 55.0, public score 54.9, and private score 60.1.

Features combined raw arithmetic relationships, scaled sizes, imbalance and urgency measures, temporal differences, lags, rolling statistics, and historical target information. Feature groups and individual features were retained based on local cross-validation improvement. Training emphasized recent observations, included two online retraining updates, and applied a weighted zero-sum correction to predictions.
compute: GPU training for XGBoost and LightGBM comparisons; hardware and runtime unspecified.

solution_summary: The solution combined more than ten independently initialized models trained on the complete training dataset, each using a small bidirectional LSTM followed by a pointwise convolution and global max pooling. It used blended GloVe and para embeddings, extensive embedding lookup rules, and a few statistical features. Batch-specific padding and truncation at the 95th length percentile made the ensemble feasible within the runtime limit. Predictions were combined by averaging ranks, with a fixed threshold selected through ensemble-aware cross-validation for stable F1 performance. The best final submission ran in about 6,000 seconds, and its score matched expectations from cross-validation.
compute: Best final submission runtime: 6,000 seconds; hardware unspecified.

solution_summary: The solution used image-plus-metadata classifiers to generate prediction features for LightGBM and CatBoost models. Training combined historical ISIC data with the 2024 dataset, keeping shared patient IDs in the same validation fold. EfficientNet B1 at 128 pixels and B3 at 192 pixels were selected, and the image task was changed from binary to nine-class classification using modified iddx_3 labels. The ensemble combined two seeds of the tree models with weights based on cross-validation, while an alternative pipeline applied the slower B3 model only to the 70,000 highest-scoring samples. The best reported result was 0.173, and the author emphasized that cross-validation correctly favored B3 despite its weaker public leaderboard score.
external_data: ["Historical ISIC 2017–2020 records from Triple Stratified Leak-Free KFold CV data"]

solution_summary: The selected submissions combined two attention-based sound event detection models with one CNN. Prior-year BirdCLEF pretraining, offline and online pseudo-labels, knowledge distillation, and filter augmentation drove the main improvements. Hard mixup, weighted binary cross-entropy, inference augmentation, and prediction smoothing provided additional gains. Removing lower-rank power postprocessing raised the ensemble's public score from 0.916 to 0.924, and both versions were selected.
compute: Single EfficientNetV2-B3 SED model running time: approximately 21 minutes

solution_summary: The solution concatenated frozen BirdNET V2.2 embeddings with CNN features from two different backbones. The CNNs were pretrained on BirdCLEF 2021 and 2022 data, then trained on BirdCLEF 2023 with extensive audio augmentation and oversampling. Predictions from the two models were averaged, with ONNX conversion and threaded inference used to meet the submission time limit. The reported scores increased from 0.71 private and 0.80 public for the baseline to 0.75 private and 0.83 public for the complete pipeline.
compute: Two-hour submission inference time limit; models converted to ONNX to meet it.

solution_title: March Machine Learning Mania 2026: 1st Place Solution
solution_summary: Separate men's and women's XGBoost regressors predicted wins from a small set of team-difference features. Seed differences, quality wins, and a custom efficiency rating carried most of the signal, with manual injury adjustments applied only to men. Leave-one-season-out predictions supported isotonic calibration, reducing combined CV Brier score from 0.1620 to 0.1590. Predictions at or beyond 97% and 3% were rounded to certainty, and the final competition Brier score was 0.1097454.
external_data: ["Rotowire college basketball injury report", "EvanMiya player ratings", "AP Poll data from Nishaan Amin"]

solution_title: Farmcore: a one-pass transformer trained on what the engine executed
solution_summary: The final agent used pure behavioral cloning from public strong-player replays, with labels reconstructed from actions actually executed by the engine. A transformer drafted the entire turn, then a six-layer corrector revised unit and market decisions jointly. Broad pretraining followed by single-team fine-tuning and weight averaging produced larger gains per GPU-hour than PPO. Engine-derived safeguards, logit adjustment, and checkpoint selection by paired-seed game money further improved play, with final training costing about 5.5 A100-hours.
compute: Final model approximately 5.5 A100-hours; 1–2 university A100-80GB GPUs plus free cloud compute; approximately 19,000 paired-seed evaluation games on CPU; FP32 inference on two CPU threads.

solution_title: From Public LB #3762 --> Private LB #80... How I got there
solution_summary: The author used a fast.ai tabular model with Poisson loss and avoided recursive forecasting. Lag, rolling, and window features were adapted to that forecasting setup, with attention to limiting overfitting on intermittent sales. Averaging models trained from different starting dates improved the score by about 0.1. MAE, MSE, and a prediction multiplier were tried but did not improve on the selected approach.
compute: 1–2 hours per fast.ai tabular model run; hardware unspecified.

solution_summary: The final solution combined LightGBM, XGBoost, and CatBoost with equal weights using about 210 engineered features. Important inputs described sentence, word, and paragraph structure, pauses, timing, word counts, cursor positions, and punctuation. Larger feature sets, neural networks, TabNet, and classification-based adjustments did not produce satisfactory results. The author identified weak correlation between cross-validation and leaderboard scores as a major limitation.

The solution treated markdown ordering as regression, anchoring code cells to relative positions between zero and one while allowing markdown predictions beyond that range. CodeBERT encoded each cell, and a transformer encoder-decoder combined code context with markdown representations before regression. A differentiable ranking loss inspired by Spearman correlation outperformed MSE and MAE. Larger models and inputs helped, ensembling gave marginal gains, and cell-splitting or merging augmentation did not work.

solution_title: 3rd Place Solution for the Regression with an Abalone Dataset Competition
solution_summary: The final solution combined six model groups built with AutoGluon, boosted-tree ensembles, and a shared LightGBM ensemble. Customized OpenFE generated features, followed by cross-validated recursive elimination to retain 30 features. One AutoGluon component also used pseudo-labeled data, while other components used Optuna-tuned weights or a voting regressor. Reliable local validation guided model selection, and neural networks were excluded because they offered no significant local improvement.

solution_title: Hybrid TBM & Chunked Protenix Pipeline with Physics-Informed Refinement
solution_summary: The pipeline combines template-based RNA modeling with Protenix diffusion inference for partially covered or long targets. It expands and scores templates using sequence, structural quality, GC content, and ligand similarity, then rethreads low-identity loops. Chain-aware chunks are stitched and aligned to a secondary-structure-derived global scaffold, followed by confidence, thermodynamic, and ligand-based reranking and geometric refinement. The author reports scores of 0.38621 on the public set and 0.50941 on the private set.
compute: Dual Tesla T4 GPUs with parallel inference and bf16 activations.

solution_title: Solution high light and how to choose submission
solution_summary: The approach retrained Gaussian mixture models using pairwise averages of fitted means as new initializations to avoid local minima. It corrected class-mean estimates for an assumed 5% target-flip rate and augmented samples by reflecting them around the corrected means. Synthetic-data experiments suggested an overall AUC near 0.975. Based on that expectation, the author selected a lower-public-score model as one submission.

The author improved a neutrino-direction prediction pipeline through learning-rate tuning, sensor features, and models specialized by pulse count. Batch-wise data loading with shuffled batch order enabled more practical multi-GPU training, while EuclidianDistanceLoss provided a substantial improvement. Splitting events into roughly equal pulse-count buckets was especially effective for events with at least 145 pulses. The final team blend averaged direction coordinates with 60/40 weights and normalized them to unit length, yielding reported scores of 0.976/0.975.
compute: Rented 3x3090 host: 1 day 6 hours on the first 200 batches; rented 4x3090 machine: approximately 2 days for events with 145–2000 pulses.

solution_summary: The post asks whether anyone obtained a good private leaderboard score using Apache Spark ML. It requests that successful participants share their solution or strategy. No approach or experimental result is supplied.

solution_title: Document and code for the 3rd place finish
solution_summary: The post points readers to an attached document. It also links to a GitHub repository containing code. The supplied text does not describe any methods or results.

The team built a 1.92M-parameter transformer policy that encodes visible cards and selects arbitrary legal actions through a pointer decoder. Behavioral cloning on replay decisions initialized both policy and value predictions before self-play with PPO, Phasic Policy Gradient, and an Actor-Critic Hedge objective. Measured opponent pools and matchup matrices guided training and the selection of Dragapult and Crustle specialists. The final agents used a single forward pass, with checkpoint combinations and value-based reranking rejected after controlled tests; the two decks won 57.9% and 58.9% of their rated games.
compute: One shared NVIDIA A100 limited to 15 vCPUs; submitted Dragapult network trained on about 29 million decisions.

solution_summary: The final prediction was a weighted average of three DeBERTa-v3-large models and a LightGBM model using neural outputs plus handcrafted features. The baseline transformer used title, question, prompt text, and summary, with validation grouped by prompt ID. Two additional transformer models used mask augmentation, all training data, and different seeds; mask augmentation stabilized loss without improving cross-validation. Layer freezing helped, while text cleaning, adversarial weight perturbation, and back translation did not; the ensemble achieved a private score of 0.459.

The author trained an R random forest with 199 trees and a minimum node size of 25 on roughly 110,000 rows. Training combined a 10% sample with all observations close to alert-state transitions, and features were simplified through correlation filtering and targeted discretization. True held-out validation was more useful than the misleadingly optimistic out-of-bag error. Subsampling and larger terminal nodes improved generalization, while lagged values and moving averages were rejected.

The author describes a straightforward blend built from public ResNet, SVM, and TabNet pipelines. They replaced the SVC component with ridge regression and fed its outputs into TabNet. TabNet predictions were then averaged with a two-headed ResNet. This candidate was intended as a starting point for further blends and was not selected for submission because its public score was weaker.

solution_title: [2nd Place] Winning based on ID Shift Analysis
solution_summary: The solution addressed distribution and concept shifts by validating on the training tail and emphasizing both tail samples and the original dataset. A diverse ensemble combined boosted trees, neural networks, logistic regression, and a generalized additive model. Feature variants included tail-based target encoding, interaction features, feature removal, and pseudo-labeling with distribution correction. Bagged hill climbing selected the final ensemble weights and achieved a cutoff validation AUC of 0.70771.

The solution treated the task as 37-class misconception classification after removing correctness prefixes. Seven Qwen models were fine-tuned with 4-bit Q-LoRA and ensembled, mixing deduplicated data, modest text augmentation, pseudo-labelled duplicates, and synthetic examples for rare categories. Qwen3-Embedding-8B was the strongest initial classification approach, and synthetic data plus pseudo-labels produced a 0.949 public single-model score. Both an augmented-data model and a weaker alternate-seed model improved the ensemble through complementary predictions.
compute: A5000/A100 GPUs on Jarvis Labs

solution_summary: The solution averaged 20 pretrained image classifiers spanning SE-ResNeXt-101, Inception-ResNet-v2, and PNASNet-5-Large. Training used 320-pixel random crops, mixup, and random erasing, with models trained on selected folds from a 40-fold split. Inference used two test-time augmentations and a per-image threshold equal to the maximum class probability divided by seven. This adaptive threshold improved the leaderboard score by about 0.005, while graph convolutional networks, soft and pseudo labels, and EfficientNet did not work for the author.

The pipeline transformed waveforms into the DCT domain, applied a trainable band-pass filter, and reconstructed signals before neural modeling. The best single model used a 1D CNN followed by ResNet34 and achieved 0.8810 on the private leaderboard with one fold and test-time augmentation. Separate waveform shifts and phase changes provided augmentation. Fine-tuning on cropped waveforms supplied additional models for blending.

The submission uses pretrained gpt-oss-120b without further training and concentrates on inference under a sequential five-hour evaluation budget. It dynamically allocates 300–900 seconds per problem, launches up to eight reasoning attempts, and stops when four answers agree. Python tools support reasoning, with entropy-weighted voting resolving cases without consensus. A locally constructed validation set and repeated tests of hard-problem order guided parameter selection for robustness rather than peak single-run performance.
compute: Final inference: one H100 80GB under a five-hour notebook budget, no training. Tuning: local machines with 64 H100 80GB GPUs.

solution_summary: The solution trains ArcFace recognition models on YOLOv5-derived fullbody and backfin crops, using EfficientNet-b7 and ConvNeXt-L backbones. Better crops were especially important, while auxiliary species classification, pseudo-labeling, and teacher-feature distillation supported training. Eight models are ensembled by averaging cosine-similarity matrices, with a fixed new-individual threshold and class-balancing adjustments to top predictions. The best single fullbody model achieved a private leaderboard score of 0.781.
compute: Single A100 GPU; 30 epochs take about 30 hours for a fullbody model and 15 hours for a backfin model.

solution_summary: The author combined manual code golfing with iterative refinement by language models. OpenAI Codex Web was the main tool used for the automated refinement. The post links a GitHub repository but provides no further implementation details or quantitative results.

solution_title: 1st PLACE - WINNER SOLUTION - Gilberto Titericz & Stanislav Semenov
solution_summary: The solution used three levels: diverse base models and engineered features, three second-level learners, and a weighted final blend. Shared five-fold splits generated base-model predictions, while four-fold validation guided second-level selection and blend tuning. XGBoost, neural networks, KNN, and t-SNE features contributed most, with extensive bagging stabilizing predictions. The reported cross-validation score was approximately 0.3962, with public and private scores of 0.38055 and 0.38243.
compute: CPU and GPU used for Lasagne neural networks; hardware specifications and elapsed time were not stated.

solution_summary: The author used spaCy tokenization while retaining all tokens and punctuation. Stemming, lemmatization, and spelling correction helped locate word vectors for tokens. The model included two global max-pooling layers, and checkpoints were ensembled. Reliable local cross-validation guided hyperparameter tuning.

The author started with a rank blend of several public notebook predictions, including CatBoost models. The main improvement exploited repeated feature rows by adding out-of-sample target encodings and training-row occurrence counts. CatBoost and a public ensemble pipeline used these features, with their application restricted to test rows matching training rows.

The pipeline combined YOLOv7-X detection with a ResNet and bidirectional LSTM OCR model. Linear interpolation generated training coordinates for chart data points and converted detected coordinates back into numerical series at inference. Geometric heuristics filtered detections and inferred tick locations from label boxes. Additional OCR data improved accuracy from 84% to 89%, but mismatched prediction counts caused roughly a quarter of predictions to score zero.

The final submission used a single XGBoost model with extensive handcrafted features and confidence-filtered pseudo-labeling. Validation grouped examples by WEEK_NUM, although the team found no strategy that aligned reliably with the leaderboard. Count encoding, rare-category collapsing, and selective recovery of highly missing features improved performance. The most influential final adjustment reconstructed test weeks from a date feature and modified predictions over weeks 92–130 to exploit the competition metric.

solution_title: Jumped from 45th to 42nd place? What happened?
solution_summary: The post asks why the private leaderboard changed after the competition ended. The author observes movement in their own position while noting that gold medal positions appear unchanged. It provides no modeling approach, implementation details, or experiments.

The solution split chart extraction into chart classification, component detection, text-orientation classification, OCR, and chart-specific post-processing. ConvNeXt xlarge classified chart types, while TrOCR read detected axis labels. Scatter detection benefited from jointly detecting ticks and using larger images with predictions fused across four inference sizes. Extensive rules converted coordinates into values and corrected OCR symbols, while submission-time fine-tuning on generated scatter images did not improve the score.
compute: About 8 extra hours available during submission for fine-tuning experiments

solution_title: Feature Engineering and Ensemble Architecture (7th place)
solution_summary: The author describes their contribution as NLP feature extraction, feature selection, and ensemble design. Feature engineering improved the performance of multiple models. The post links to the full technical account and mentions attached R examples for RFE and Boruta, but provides no model configurations or quantitative results.

The solution combined a tree-based pipeline using engineered text and event-log features with language models trained on reconstructed essays. Consecutive runs of anonymized q characters were replaced by their lengths, preserving word-length sequences and punctuation structure for the language models. DeBERTa-v3-base and DeBERTa-xlarge predictions were combined using weights. The author reported a private leaderboard error improvement from 0.568 to 0.565 when adding this approach to the public notebook baseline.
The post announces a presentation about the author's competition solution and experience. It links to slides hosted on SlideShare. No methods or results are described in the supplied text.

solution_title: My 9th place solution to the September Tabular competition
solution_summary: The solution combined missing-value-count features, tuned gradient-boosted trees, and a large stacking pipeline. Linear regression worked well as a meta-model over out-of-fold predictions from 34 base models, while seed replication improved individual LightGBM and XGBoost predictions. Training on all available data with more estimators than cross-validation suggested provided further gains. The final submission blended a first-level stacking prediction, five full-data model predictions, and a shared submission.

The author's models use ResNet50 with ArcFace, experiment-based validation, image augmentation, and cell-type-specific training. Dynamic soft pseudo-labels exploit plate restrictions and one-to-one sirna structure, while feature mean normalization reduces experiment bias and incremental hard pseudo-labeling locks confident assignments. Predictions combine 16 test-time transformations and geometric-mean aggregation across sites, folds, runs, and teammates. Iterative probability-matrix normalization and mixed integer assignment enforce unique sirna predictions. Public-score constraints also enabled leaderboard probing, whose estimated private benefit was at most 0.001.
compute: PyTorch on TPUs; $600 in GCP credits used; Cplex solves each assignment matrix in a couple of seconds.

solution_summary: The agent used hand-written rules for factory placement, production, watering, and robot behavior. Factory placement considered resource proximity, rubble density, and distances to friendly and opposing factories. Heavy and light robots had different task priorities, with collision avoidance favoring heavy robots. Late in the game, light robots targeted opposing lichen, while occasional random movement encouraged exploration.

solution_title: 10th solution & thoughts - Part2. LB 0.61 [ Think out of the box version ]
solution_summary: The solution supplemented a TNT/ViT/CAIT ensemble with molecular OCR and an object detector that reconstructed molecules using chemistry rules. A ResNet34 U-Net enhanced images before MolVec OCR, while EfficientDet-D3 detected atom groups and bonds for a custom molecular builder. Replacement rules compared molecular formulas, edit distances, and agreement between OCR and the builder, with OCR used broadly for large images. Updating 7,679 invalid predictions improved the leaderboard score from 0.71 to 0.61.

The agent combined a replay-derived opening book with daily heuristic replanning rather than machine learning. Simulated annealing and beam search drove planning after the opening. Development began from a public shop-routing notebook and evolved through AI-assisted heuristic improvements and local matches. The final opening book used public replays from M & M & P & Q.
compute: Cloud instances with many CPU cores for batches of agent matches
external_data: ["M & M & P & Q public replays", "DECEM and DSM public replays"]

solution_title: 723rd Place Solutions for the AI Village Capture the Flag @ DEFCON31
solution_summary: The author extended a public notebook by solving two additional capture-the-flag tasks. For cluster1, manual filtering in Excel followed by iterative filter removal identified people aged 19–39 working in tech support as the target subgroup. For cluster2, enumerating integers against the scoring endpoint revealed the answer 4. A t-SNE exploration of cluster3 embeddings did not recover all the text, and the final public and private scores were both 3.

The final prediction averages three greedy hill-climbing ensembles and one Ridge stacking ensemble built from a diverse model pool. Each hill-climbing ensemble contains 21–26 models and permits negative weights to correct correlated errors. All predictions use seven-fold cross-validation, with no final calibration or post-processing. Aggressive optimization improved CV but raised overfitting concerns; final public and private scores were 0.05536 and 0.05564.

The solution created features for each level group and also reused features from previous level groups. It trained LightGBM and XGBoost models separately for each level, tuning XGBoost hyperparameters at that same granularity. CatBoost, probability features for stacking, sample weights, per-level F1 threshold tuning, and Word2Vec event-sequence features did not work for the author. Knowledge-tracing ensembles and per-level LightGBM tuning remained untried.

solution_title: private 20th | public 3rd solution: RAFT-refined GR↔typewell matcher
solution_summary: The solution blends a single-well gamma-ray registration transformer with particle-filter residual models and geometry-only predictors. Its strongest component uses shared encoders, a nonuniform drift grid and RAFT refinement, supported by extensive real and synthetic well augmentation. Distance-dependent blending reduces reliance on neighboring geology for isolated wells, while well-grouped validation guides selection. The two selected ensembles achieved private scores of 6.639 and 6.500, and local validation proved more useful than the noisy public leaderboard.
compute: GPU particle filtering with 64 seeds × 500 particles; GPU model and runtime unspecified

solution_summary: The solution used DeepLabV3+ with ResNet and ResNeXt backbones and group normalization at high image resolutions. Models trained on all images with weighted binary cross-entropy were combined with models trained only on positive images using soft Dice loss. The ensemble used segmentation-derived classification scores to scale positive-only predictions, then averaged them with other segmentation predictions. Horizontal-flip augmentation at inference and removal of small predicted masks improved results, yielding a stage-two private score of 0.8627.

solution_title: How I did it: Jeremy Howard on finishing second
solution_summary: The solution used monthly TrueSkill Through Time inference and adjusted player ratings using opponents' average ratings and uncertainty. Predictions came from a cumulative Gaussian with spread controlled by black's skill. Discarding the earliest 40 months and incorporating test-set match counts brought the reported score to 0.653. The author emphasized substantive modeling changes over fine parameter tuning and reported a strong relationship between public and final submission scores.

solution_title: 12th place solution (mysteriously disqualified) - Single ConvNeXt CascadeRCNN
solution_summary: The author used a single ConvNeXt base Cascade R-CNN detector in MMDetection, validated with video-based splits. Training combined bounding-box-centered multiscale crops with balanced sampling of empty and nonempty images, improving CV by about 3% over full-image training. Inference used 3840×2160 images, validation-based thresholds, and temporal detection-cluster filtering to remove false positives. The reported public and private scores were 0.632 and 0.718.
compute: One week spent on the challenge; training hardware and runtime unspecified.

solution_summary: The solution built on an existing Siamese network and exploited prediction diversity across many training variants. Roughly 40 prediction sets from different image sizes, color modes, and training continuations were combined through position-wise hard voting and score averaging. Adding classification and prototype models provided further diversity. The combined voting and averaging approach reached 0.941 on the public leaderboard before the final additions.

solution_title: What is your approach and what is your local CV
solution_summary: The author describes feature experiments with a local ten-fold cross-validation log loss of approximately 0.77. Useful features included topic and sentiment representations of selected text sections, clusters of document embeddings, and reduced character TF-IDF representations of variations. The document embeddings were converted into cluster identifiers and distances rather than used directly. Word2vec inputs to a one-dimensional CNN and experiments with an RNN did not produce good results.

The solution extracted image features from a pretrained Inception network and aggregated them into business-level representations. One branch averaged all images for each business, while another clustered similar images before averaging them. Each branch trained nine binary classifiers, and a neural network combined their predictions to capture label dependencies. Adding softmax-layer features provided a small improvement.

The solution combined competition and original datasets, memory-conscious preprocessing, and factorized interaction features. Its final ensemble contained 24 CatBoost, LightGBM, TensorFlow, XGBoost, and LightGBM-based random forest models trained with different data and feature configurations. Ten-fold evaluation guided model comparisons, and hill climbing optimized a linear blend for ROC-AUC. CatBoost was the strongest individual model, reaching 0.895819 with original data included, and the final blend received additional post-processing.

A single SE-ResNet-101 was trained from scratch on human-labeled Open Images data using all 18,000 labels, then fine-tuned on 1,000 stage 1 tuning images. Fine-tuning addressed the substantial difference between training and test label distributions. The author introduced a multilabel softmax cross-entropy loss and used random crops and horizontal flips during training. Ten-crop inference and leaderboard-tuned prediction thresholds and label-count limits improved results; the model without test-time augmentation scored 0.32601 on the private leaderboard.
compute: Used 1×1080; approximately 10 days training and 1.5 hours for stage 2 predictions. Inference without TTA was 10 times faster.

solution_summary: The solution stacked 29 models using an Optuna-tuned ridge classifier. Its meta-features included class probabilities, predicted classes, and Chris' exact formula. Base learners used multiple feature views, including categorical encodings, feature combinations, numerical bins, digit features, and original-data target encoding, with five-fold validation. Bias tuning improved cross-validation but hurt private leaderboard performance.
compute: Laptop used during the competition.

solution_summary: The team validated models on week 9 and formed the final submission as a weighted average of seven models. Their candidates included XGBoost with more than 100 lag-combination features, LR, and libFM using sparse features. To handle unavailable week-11 lag-one values, they trained some models without those features and others using week-10 predictions as week-11 lag inputs. Their best single XGBoost model scored approximately 0.433x on the public leaderboard.

solution_title: [Working Note] 79th Place Solution and Suggesting a Robust Guardrail Design
solution_summary: The submission induced benign business email actions that triggered the competition's confused-deputy scoring predicate. It locally tested attacks against both target models and several hypothesized private guardrails, then selected between single-email and same-domain multi-recipient templates at startup. Recipient uniqueness and a pool of 2,000 candidates supported novelty and throughput within the evaluation budget. The main submission scored 24.090 publicly and 24.060 privately, whereas high-scoring public exfiltration variants scored zero privately.

The solution detects image panels and text with YOLOv8-m, then finds duplicated regions through classical SIFT matching and affine RANSAC. Synthetic training images and manually corrected text annotations support preprocessing that excludes misleading graphs and captions. Low-threshold keypoint extraction, adaptive matching, and image-type-specific geometric filtering make matching viable on low-texture biological images. Two-stage cluster merging and bidirectional geometric mask refinement were essential for accurate instance segmentation.

The solution uses a modified U-Net with inception blocks, strided convolutions, residual skip connections, batch normalization, and an auxiliary nerve-presence head. It trains with Adam and batch-averaged Dice loss, using image augmentation and augmented-image prediction. Random validation splits replaced an unsuccessful patient-based split, and final predictions combine presence estimates from the classification and segmentation branches. The best single model scored 0.694, while an ensemble of six cross-validation ensembles reached 0.70399.
compute: GeForce 1080 or Titan X; batch sizes 64 and 128 respectively. Titan X: about 6 minutes per epoch, early stopping at 15–30 epochs. Batch size 64 requires 6 GB GPU memory.

solution_summary: The pipeline first localized the brain and Circle of Willis, then extracted slice features with separate 2.5D vessel-segmentation and aneurysm models. Sequence models combined those features across depth, with an ensemble of LSTM, GRU, and BERT variants producing scan-level predictions. Hard-negative mining, OOF self-distillation, EMA, and heavy mixup supported training. Two submissions achieved CV AUCs of 0.8909 and 0.9035, but substantially lower private scores; dual-T4 parallel inference processed 11 aneurysm models and 45 sequence models within 12 hours.
compute: 2x T4; inference of 11 aneurysm models and 45 RNN models within 12 hours
external_data: ["Zenodo CT and MRI subset of TotalSegmentator training data", "CoWSeg"]

solution_title: # 28 Solution | Problem with private LB score
solution_summary: The submitted solution combined eight model families in an Optuna-tuned weighted ensemble trained with ten-fold cross-validation. It reused public feature engineering and added binary hydration, osmo, and calc status features. Outlier removal was a particularly influential component, and the author found public scores unreliable for selecting improvements. An unsubmitted variant removed KNN and GradientBoosting and changed the quantiles used for outlier handling, producing a better private result.

The final submission averaged six EfficientNet B0 models trained on Mel spectrograms from the first five seconds of labeled recordings. Its main improvement came from iterative target-domain pseudo-labeling, mixing unlabeled soundscape segments into training audio with randomized amplitudes and maximum-combined targets. Checkpoint soups and variation in spectrogram settings, input sizes, data subsets, and pseudo-label probabilities supported the ensemble. Neighboring-window smoothing completed inference, and the selected stage-two ensemble achieved public and private AUCs of 0.72528 and 0.69035.
compute: Six-model inference could exceed two hours; a two-model notebook took approximately 1 hour 10 minutes.

solution_title: Bronze: from MuZero to a measured hybrid agent
solution_summary: The final agent extended a strong public V78/V79 script with gated rules for garden labor, sheep management, feed recovery, and rival market behavior. MuZero, PPO, imitation learning, and a scripted-planner hybrid were explored, but compute limits, noisy gradients, and rollout distribution shift prevented them from surpassing strong scripts. Exact simulation, paired seat-swapped comparisons, and pinned ladder replays determined which additions survived. Across 252 replayed rated games, the added layers converted 32 losses to wins without reversing any wins and increased average margin by $571.
compute: 96-core Google Cloud VM for PPO/MuZero; smaller Azure VM; Kaggle TPU sessions with 96-core EPYC and 396 GB memory; local 6-core PC with WSL. CPU throughput was 460,072 environment steps/s versus 2,440 with the network.

solution_summary: The author adapted a public cancer subtype classification pipeline with two modifications. They trained a MaxViT Base model, reporting 0.48 on both public and private testing. At inference, they applied a threshold to the maximum mean softmax probability, although the supplied code omits the threshold and fallback output.

solution_title: Bronze Medal Solution - No ML Model
solution_summary: The author built a simple prediction approach based on a public starter kernel. It aggregated historical game results to estimate the probability that a lower-seeded team defeats a higher-seeded team. The post provides no further implementation details or numerical performance metrics.

The best approach extracted pretrained VGG16 features from 512×512 patches and fed them to five gradient-boosted regression trees, one for each sea-lion type. It scored 23.9 on the private leaderboard. Earlier HOG/SVM and six-class CNN approaches produced too many false positives, while adding nearest-sea-lion distances failed at test time. A two-stage CNN detector and count regressor looked promising visually but scored only slightly better than predicting zeros.

The final ensemble combined 32 models, almost all drawn from public solutions, including two notebooks by the author. A GPU logistic regression stacker reached about 0.9702 out-of-fold balanced accuracy, improving to 0.97032 with additional models. A weighted mean of TabPFN-3 and logistic regression stacker outputs reached 0.97043. The best individual RealMLP and boosting models achieved about 0.9691.
compute: GPU used for logistic regression stacking; hardware and runtime unspecified.

solution_title: 6th Place - PF, PF, PF, PF, Physics and Row-Level Bagging
solution_summary: The solution generated 91 TVT candidate trajectories using diverse, tuned particle filters and fused them with a neural candidate-curve ensembler. Accuracy depended primarily on complementary GR references, a geometry-based physical prior, and full-interval smoothing. Strict out-of-fold construction of the prior and neighbor pools made validation more reliable than public leaderboard ordering. A small global gain corrected amplitude shrinkage, and the final solution achieved CV 5.4577 and private score 5.984.

solution_title: 2nd Place Solution for the LLM 20 Questions Competition
solution_summary: The agent combined alphabetic binary search with an online Llama 3.1 8B strategy using eight-bit quantization and no fine-tuning. Its alphabetic component searched a frequency-ranked 120,000-word vocabulary before using the LLM to propose noun phrases. The online questioner progressed through category, location, size, and candidate-splitting questions, while a running natural-language summary supported guessing and recovery from inconsistent answers. Channel-specific contrast and geometric transformations provide augmentation. Averaging predictions for detected test duplicates improved LB by 0.004–0.005. Training both components together within each validation split addresses leakage from separately pretraining the supervised encoder. Gaussian noise, swish activation, batch normalization, dropout, and hyperparameter tuning support the proposed pipeline.

A single model combined sequence embeddings, a convolution over the probability matrix, and twelve relative-position Transformer blocks to produce two outputs per position. solution_title: 22nd Place Solution — Five Engines and a Hard Lesson About Leaderboards

A 2.5D CNN and attention-equipped RNN first learned from slice windows, then a new RNN was trained on full studies with the CNN frozen. Study-wide cropping and consistent augmentation reduced irrelevant variation without using fracture bounding boxes. The final ensemble combined six resnest50d and four seresnext50 weight sets, with inference taking about 4.5 hours.

The agent developed sophisticated resource control and long-term strategies but retained weaknesses in fuel budgeting and recovery from losing positions.

The final submission used a single CatBoost model without hyperparameter tuning. Adversarial-validation analyses highlighted substantial differences between the competition training, test, and original datasets. The author supplemented training with only 132 positive examples from the original data whose Time exceeded 120580, aiming to cover a region absent from the supplied training set. Cube and globe solutions relied on short move sequences that affect few pieces, inserted throughout a growing solution using efficient conjugate calculations. Greedy or beam search reduced mismatches, with explicit center alignment and parity correction before completing remaining pieces. Cube subproblems were separated into 24- or 48-position groups, and external solvers finished corners. Small wreath puzzles used bidirectional breadth-first search, while large wildcard wreaths used a specialized ring-correction algorithm with randomized preprocessing. About one million preprocessing trials produced a solution of length 681.

The solution used three- and four-hidden-layer neural networks alongside XGBoost. Random Indexing and Transposed Random Indexing generated projected features with controlled sparsity. Five model types paired these representations or feature-value counts with the classifiers. solution_title: [38th solution]My attempt at simulating private leaderboard

solution_title: Sharing My ARC Prize 2024 Code (31 Points in the final submission)
solution_summary: The author trained custom transformer architectures from scratch and combined them in an ensemble that achieved 31 points. Active inference and reverse augmentation were central improvements over an early version that scored about four private-test points. Specialized grid positional encoding and a compact 19-token vocabulary supported the architecture. A transformer mask modification was disabled in the final submission, while the impact of a progressive head remained uncertain because of bugs.

The final solution used XGBoost with frequency features computed from training data and real test rows, excluding fake test rows from the frequency reference. Counts were normalized by the maximum count and multiplied by the original variables to create interaction features. These features and parameter tuning raised the public score to 0.916. Augmentation reduced performance, and investigations of timestamps and customer IDs were unsuccessful.

The solution used SE-ResNeXt50 with three component prediction heads, an auxiliary 1,292-grapheme head, and an ArcFace loss. A frozen binary mapping connected component logits to grapheme logits, while the grapheme loss received substantially more weight than the other losses. Sample-wise CutMix was the most useful augmentation, supplemented by progressively introduced grid shuffling. Self-training on 300,000 unlabeled Ekush images with soft targets and grapheme-balanced sampling improved generalization, and predictions from four randomly split folds were ensembled.

solution_title: Dato Truly Native? Winner's Interview: 2nd place, mortehu
solution_summary: The solution combined a linear SVM on hashed word skip-grams and HTML semantic features with XGBoost on frequent substrings and a Unix timestamp feature. A memory-efficient custom SVM implementation supported 79 million features, with per-class regularization selected through 10-fold cross-validation. The second model used 30,000 selected substrings, while date-related clues exploited differences in when positive and negative documents were downloaded. Combining six times the SVM predictions with the XGBoost predictions achieved a private leaderboard score of 0.99017, compared with 0.98519 and 0.98856 for the individual models.
compute: HTML preprocessing for 400,000 documents took under 5 minutes; compact feature matrix exceeded 25 GB; SVM training took 32 minutes excluding tuning; substring mining took about 10 minutes; XGBoost training took almost 5 hours.

solution_title: 30th Place Solution - ChatGPT can be helpful for quick idea realization
solution_summary: The final approach ensembled two models with different landmarks, feature sets, and parameters, with diversity providing a substantial benefit. Features captured facial and pose landmarks, hand geometry, and motion, with both landmark-level and global normalization. Training used heavy and similarity-aware label smoothing, scheduled late dropout, and parallel transformers sharing embeddings. The best single-fold submission scored 0.76 publicly and the best ensemble reached 0.7791; attempts to add a third model repeatedly ran into the inference time limit.

solution_title: 18th place solution: single xgboost with custom AUC loss
solution_summary: An early neural-network and GBDT blend achieved a private score of 0.90577. The later approach used XGBoost with a custom AUC loss, engineered features, and forward feature selection, reaching 0.90395 privately. Validation combined six folds equivalent to grouping by year with shuffled five-fold splitting, and submission selection favored the highest CV-minus-public-score difference. Adding the public dataset helped only about half of simulated private evaluations, so it was excluded.

The solution used a multiplicative sales model combining GDP per capita, store and country effects, periodic factors, holidays, and a time trend. Holiday effects were modeled with delayed Gaussian responses, and a separate model handled Kenya. Parameters were jointly optimized with SciPy, using six yearly validation folds before training on all available data. solution_title: 6th place solution : GNN and Transformer part

GraphNet was progressively trained on more batches, with pulse and edge dropout, charge noise, gradient accumulation, a corrected pulse-length feature, and an added MSE loss. Its reported score improved from 1.018 for baseline weights to 0.989 for a seven-model ensemble. The transformer used two prediction heads, flip-z test-time augmentation, and an early-checkpoint ensemble, reaching reported public/private scores of 0.983/0.984.

solution_summary: The author describes a simple neural network created as part of the competition submission package. It uses median visits over the last eight weeks together with site, access method, and calendar features. The model achieved a score of 36.78 and was described as robust. Its code was uploaded to the author's repository.

The solution first trained image-level CNNs and saved their global average pooling features. It reconstructed CT studies by sorting slices by z-position, then trained study-level bidirectional GRUs on the saved features. Seven CNN models used different training-validation splits, extensive augmentation, and input resolutions between 384 and 512 pixels.

The final solution averaged LightGBM, CatBoost, and CNN predictions, benefiting from their different feature representations. The CNN processed interpolated multiband time series alongside detection-weighted flux and interpolation-distance channels, then combined its representation with metadata from a small MLP. Training used sample deletion, flux-error noise, cyclic shifts, and channel scaling across four folds with learning-rate changes and best-weight averaging. Three neural variants scored 0.857, 0.857, and 0.814 individually, while their average scored 0.791; test-time augmentation degraded leaderboard performance.

The final submission combined CT models, tabular neural networks, and Bayesian ridge regression, with the ensemble selected by cross-validation. The CT pipeline used Concatenate Tile Pooling with ResNeXt50 and ResNet18, first training on masked lungs and then fine-tuning on original scans. It modeled FVC and uncertainty over time with a carefully initialized Laplace log-likelihood objective, while tabular validation controlled leakage and evaluated the last three visits. CT models alone performed modestly, while the final ensemble achieved reported private/public scores of 6.8385/6.8884.
compute: Inference for a single four-fold model took 10–20 minutes on Kaggle.

solution_summary: The final prediction blended a pseudo-labeled ensemble of three DeBERTa-v3-base models with a separate 22-model stack. The stack combined trained transformer predictions with regressors fitted to frozen transformer text embeddings. Four-fold out-of-fold predictions fed a Lasso stacker, with log transformation and robust scaling providing a small validation improvement. The stacked model achieved CV 0.4473 and leaderboard score 0.43, while a frozen DeBERTa-v3-large embedding model reached CV 0.4518.

The author trained separate LightGBM quantile models for each forecast horizon and quantile across all aggregation levels. Sales were normalized by their nonzero mean and detrended with horizon-lagged rolling means so forecasts remained independent across horizons. Calendar, price, rolling, and target-encoded features supported the models, with normalized and clipped WSPL training weights. Memory and runtime limits required restricting training dates and weekdays, while validation on only two horizons raised concerns about overfitting.

solution_title: 1st Place Solution - Track me if you can
solution_summary: The solution combined WiFi localization and three sensor models through discrete trajectory optimization over known and generated waypoints. A custom beam search minimized penalties for WiFi similarity, movement, distance, temporal consistency, and grid preferences. Time and device leaks supported floor prediction and estimates of sensor reliability. Selecting among three waypoint grids improved the score by about 10 cm, and a fixed trajectory holdout tracked private leaderboard performance well.

solution_title: Taylor-made NN for 0.285 PLB (part of solution of 8º)

Careful parameter tuning, classifier dropout, embedding regularization, and positive oversampling supported training. Smaller training portions allowed finer stopping decisions because the network overfit very quickly. Predictions were averaged across five folds and up to 20 seeds, and this network was the strongest individual component of the team's ensemble.

Replacing the reference with the well's own labeled landing log and preserving the measured initial dip were major improvements. Five well-level folds and a separate 77-well holdout guarded against overfitting, although later stacking made cross-validation optimistic. This raised the public score to 0.8507 and reportedly improved private scores by more than 0.0005.

Name replacement augmentation, length-ratio stratification, and minimum Bayes risk decoding support the final pipeline, which also mentions ridge regression and an Onomasticon. solution_summary: The team trained three DenseNet201 models on roughly 7,000 images after removing poor-quality and duplicate images. One model used 448-pixel crops with test-time random cropping and flipping, while two used 512-pixel inputs and modified fully connected layers. Majority voting combined the three models, producing public and private scores of 0.962 and 0.969. Switching from Keras with Theano to PyTorch enabled training within their limited compute budget.

solution_summary: The solution used rule-based dataset-name extraction without training a predictive model. Keyword-specific extractors examined surrounding tokens using spaCy, and the author refined their rules by inspecting frequent extracted mentions. Document-frequency filtering reduced the candidate list before a second document search. Searching longer names first and masking matched text prevented redundant predictions of shorter names embedded within them.

solution_summary: The team trained football agents with distributed off-policy reinforcement learning, combining self-play with games against a changing mixture of opponents. Supervised learning from top-player replays and early knowledge distillation accelerated training before reinforcement learning took over. The model combined player attention, action-history GRU features, player-interaction CNN features, and separate policy, value, and return heads. Expanded directional pass and shot actions and varied starting states improved play, and the final model reached roughly a 90% win rate against hard built-in AI. A weighted policy ensemble performed best locally but could not be submitted before the deadline.

Approximately 4,000 CPUs and 20 GPUs were used in parallel during the last three days; the final agent trained on approximately 700,000 games.

solution_title: Fast and Simple: Ranker fine-tuning + Embeddings + Classifier
solution_summary: The approach fine-tuned multilingual-e5-base for ranking rule-violating comments, then used its embeddings as classifier inputs. Features combined subreddit, rule, and comment embeddings with a rule-to-comment similarity score. An equal-weight voting ensemble of five conventional classifiers achieved column-averaged AUC of 0.89437. The author emphasized inference efficiency and CPU deployment as practical advantages.

Candidate subqueries were constructed to retrieve only target patents, allowing the objective to focus on target coverage. Compact query syntax, frequency filtering, and candidate deduplication reduced query and search complexity. GPU-accelerated intersections with CuPy were two to three times faster than Python set intersections and enabled broader field coverage.

A competition-adapted model generated pseudo-labels for additional datasets, which were incorporated into renewed training before final competition fine-tuning. Soft label distributions were crucial because hard labels did not provide satisfactory improvements. Inference used sequence-length-dependent dynamic batching and selective response-swap augmentation for uncertain predictions.

solution_summary: The solution combined three largely out-of-the-box 3D nnUNet models trained with default, aggressive, and no augmentation. Models were trained at 256x384 and fine-tuned at full resolution, with mixup, label smoothing, AdamW, and a Noam scheduler among the successful choices. Class thresholds, a minimum area of 100, and a pixel threshold of 0.3 controlled predictions. A reported alternative class-three threshold achieved public and private scores of 0.92016 and 0.90819.

solution_title: 13 Robust Features: Bridging 15 Years of Manufacturing Experience with Machine L
solution_summary: The approach used LightGBM with a deliberately restricted set of 13 features for a stable and explainable pipeline. Inputs combined coordinates, five photometric bands, redshift, categorical metadata, spherical coordinate transformations, and a logarithmic delta feature. Optuna supplied systematic hyperparameter tuning in Kaggle Notebooks. The post does not report a score or validation results.

The author built interactive software for manually adjusting competition configurations. Objects can be translated by dragging and rotated with the mouse scroll button, while square distance is displayed. solution_summary: The solution combined Qwen 14B instruction and coder retrievers with a Qwen 32B AWQ reranker. Retrievers first learned from 7,000 GPT-4o-generated examples and then were fine-tuned on competition data using LoRA. The reranker treated the top 25 candidates as multiple-choice options and optimized cross-entropy over their answer characters. Five-fold LoRA fusion was used, while attempted distillation from a 72B model showed no offline improvement.

The author shared a simple public notebook using regression models for the task. The approach was inspired by Chris and the author's recent work on CIBMTR. The notebook was not selected as a final submission, and the post provides no model specifications or numerical results.

The solution ensembles Mask R-CNN models with ResNet-50 and ResNet-101 backbones. It averages masks and combines scores using proximity-based weights. Training stopped after a few epochs despite continued improvement because training, inference, and prediction generation were time-consuming on images exceeding 4K resolution. The ensemble offered less benefit than expected, and the authors believed more training epochs would have been a better use of their time.

solution_summary: The solution used separate U-Net segmentation models for each class, with collage-level white balancing and channel alignment. Positive and negative sampling, class-specific model settings and cross-validation helped address sparse classes. Water was segmented jointly and then divided into lakes and rivers using contour size and proximity rules. Vehicle predictions averaged up to 15 models and were cleaned using other class predictions, while final polygons required topology-preserving simplification.

solution_summary: The solution combined a rotation-resistant matching model with Alike-LightGlue and scene-specific adjustments. Center cropping and filtering nearly stationary keypoint matches helped transparent objects, while detecting keypoints in four image sections targeted finer church details. The final submission used a simple-radial camera model for every scene. End-to-end matchers, matched-point region cropping, and CLAHE were excluded because of runtime limits or poor results.
The post links to a video discussing the author's solution and other leading solutions. It also includes an image. The supplied text contains no technical description of the approach.

The solution combined two CatBoost models, one LightGBM model, and one neural network using weights chosen from cross-validation performance. Feature engineering adapted public code, rescaled date differences into years, and added features inspired by the previous Home Credit competition. Validation mixed week-grouped stratified folds with stratified folds using week-based sample weights. Linear shifting and week-number restoration were tried, but the better private result came without metric hacks.

solution_title: Solution - Single transformer without val dataset
solution_summary: The author used a shallow transformer with modified embedding and fully connected layers, label smoothing, learning-rate warmup, and late dropout. Landmark preprocessing normalized handedness, standardized sequence length, and added motion and hand-joint distance features. Small rotations provided some benefit, while a later two-seed ensemble improved after an inappropriate learning-rate reduction was reversed. The corrected ensemble achieved 0.7683 public and 0.8445 private scores.

The solution combined aggregated time-series features and deep autoencoder representations with feature engineering and LightGBM. Rows without targets were removed, and Optuna optimized the three prediction thresholds. The final submission used models and thresholds obtained in Google Colab with voting across manually varied seeds, although a single model performed better than seed averaging.

solution_title: AIMO3: a collection of delightful side quests
solution_summary: The final solver used a layer-wise distilled clone of Nemotron-Cascade-2-30B-A3B, selectively quantized to FP8. It generated eight parallel Python-assisted rollouts and combined answers with entropy-weighted majority voting, achieving a private score of 41. Validation used 50 hard IMO-AnswerBench problems under a five-hour single-H100 budget with three fixed-seed orderings. Pairwise self-verification did not beat the simpler harness, and substantial speculative-decoding work remained outside the final submission.

solution_summary: The final blend combined two ResNeXt models and two ResNeSt models trained on five-second audio crops. Aggressive noise augmentation, modified mixup with union targets, and additional recordings helped address the mismatch between training and test audio. Post-processing applied a 0.5 threshold, site-specific temporal aggregation, and limits on the number of predicted birds. Validation was unreliable, and the five-fold ResNeXt50 alone ultimately produced their best submission.

solution_title: 38th solution, data driven to find embedding weights
solution_summary: The approach combined three pretrained embeddings with data-driven weights of 0.5 for GloVe, 0.4 for para, and 0.1 for wiki. Learned embedding weights were averaged across five folds, and text was lowercased after case-preserving lookup proved ineffective. The author evaluated blended predictions within each validation fold and examined correlations to assess model diversity. Focal loss achieved 0.712 single-model local CV, but its ensemble validation was not completed.

The author presents neural network outputs estimating ventricular volume at 1 mm intervals along the left ventricle's long axis. The region of interest comes from the intersection of four-chamber and two-chamber views. They manually labeled 200 hearts and bootstrapped from those annotations to hearts 1–700. Illustrated failures include incorrect ventricular localization and insufficient short-axis coverage near the heart's end.

The author trained a U-Net imitation learning policy using 1,100 episodes from three Toad team submissions. Improvements included a city action model, flip and rotation augmentation, wider U-Net channels, and a hybrid stochastic and deterministic action policy. The final submission used separate early-, mid-, and endgame models with different loss weights and stacked current and previous states. Limited compute and time led the author to focus on imitation learning instead of pursuing reinforcement learning.
compute: Less than 3 weeks available; Kaggle compute quota and a 1060 GPU with 6 GB memory.

solution_summary: The author trained a RoBERTa named entity recognition model with concatenated output layers, convolutional layers, and Dice loss. An initial model trained on dataset-containing token crops generated approximately 3,000 candidates for manual review. The final model was retrained using positive and negative examples from those candidates, then filtered using prediction length, confidence, keywords, and duplicate merging. Dataset co-occurrence clusters supported validation and sampling, although validation remained unreliable; the reported public and private scores were 0.497 and 0.347.

The solution combined several ImageNet-initialized CNNs with two additional layers of tree models. CNN top-five predictions and duplicate-image hashes generated candidate classes, turning the large multiclass problem into binary candidate verification. Class-frequency priors, including frequencies among nearby product IDs, exploited a slight dataset leak. Weighted third-layer predictions and averaging two inference pipelines improved the ensemble, while pseudo-labeling hurt downstream stacking despite improving individual models.

The solution searched over a three-stage pipeline that extracted parts from an input, transformed those parts, and recombined them into candidate outputs. Each stage allowed an identity operation, enabling simpler solutions such as cropping or recoloring alone. The large combinatorial search was refined through submission feedback, with unhelpful functions removed because the public and private evaluations were the same.

GPU hill climbing selected a weighted ensemble of seven models from hundreds of diverse candidates. The selected models combined target-encoded and arithmetic-feature XGBoost models, CatBoost with categorical bins and group statistics, and two residual-learning pipelines. Five-fold out-of-fold predictions determined ensemble weights, after which models were retrained on all training data and averaged across seeds. Diversity mattered more than individual model scores, and the final ensemble achieved 0.05880 CV RMSLE and 0.05841 private leaderboard RMSLE.
compute: GPU used for candidate modeling and hill climbing; hardware model and runtime not specified.

solution_summary: The author used EfficientNet-B7 and an ensemble of EfficientNet-B6 and B7, with Ben Graham preprocessing and an image size of 299. EfficientNet performed better than the tested DenseNet and ResNet architectures, while batch size and learning rate tuning were important. Three- and five-fold validation were unreliable, so the author used macro F1 to assess model quality instead of quadratic kappa. Focal loss did not help, external data was excluded after experimentation, and pseudo-labeling remained untested because time ran out.

solution_title: A OK solution without peeking test data --  we are hiring talented:)
solution_summary: The author combines original numeric variables with cumulative target encodings and uses a LightGBM classifier. The encoding sorts each variable's values and computes cumulative target sums divided by cumulative counts, with five stratified folds generating out-of-fold training features. Test features are encoded using training labels, without exploiting the true-versus-fake test split discussed by other teams. The reported score is approximately 0.912, although the model training loop is omitted.

solution_title: Congrats to STRAYA, NCCU and adamaconguli!
solution_summary: The best submission combined GBMs that incorporated time and historical teacher behavior. A particularly useful feature described teachers' own donations, rather than donations they received. Teachers who donated to exciting projects were more likely to post exciting projects themselves. The author believed stronger time decay would have helped and reported choosing the wrong submission.

The solution used a DenseNet121 ArcFace identifier with bounding boxes and landmarks predicted by five cross-validated models. Identity and test representations were formed by taking the centers of multiple embedding vectors and comparing them with cosine similarity. Training included singleton identities, mixed aligned and unaligned images, and treated horizontal flips as separate identities while masking their competing logits. New-whale predictions were calibrated to an expected proportion of 0.276, and the final reported private scores ranged from 0.965 to 0.968.
