solution_summary: The solution used XLM-RoBERTa-large models trained with translations of the supplied data and combined them through rank averaging. Translation into the target languages was the main reported training improvement. Language-specific scaling of intermediate ranked predictions, supported by repeated CV split experiments, improved global AUC. The full post-processing routine added roughly 0.004, with a further small benefit from averaging predictions for similar texts.

solution_summary: The solution combined embeddings from six ECA-NFNet-L0 image models with TF-IDF title matching. Image training used ArcFace, GeM pooling, limited augmentation, and validation-driven checkpoint selection with a custom weight-averaging procedure. Titles were cleaned and translated from Indonesian to English before image and text matches were retrieved separately and their unique labels combined. A second TF-IDF pass over predicted label sets helped make matching rows more consistent.

solution_title: Child Mind Institute PIU 3rd Place Solution
solution_summary: The solution used LightGBM with 100 repetitions of stratified five-fold cross-validation to stabilize results on a small, noisy dataset. Features summarized actigraphy measurements, activity streaks, and light exposure, alongside selected public-notebook features and custom instrument features. Training data was augmented through missing-value injection and Gaussian noise after simple imputation. Models predicted PCIAT totals, which were converted to sii classes using thresholds optimized on repeated out-of-fold predictions, then combined by majority vote. The stable approach achieved validation QWK of 0.454–0.456 and optimized QWK near 0.470; later fixed-seed leaderboard tuning worsened private scores.

solution_title: Part of 2nd place solution (only kaggle/colab TPU were used)
solution_summary: The author trained an EfficientNet-B3 regression model on large mosaics assembled from slide tiles. The central improvement was using MSE for Karolinska samples and Huber loss for noisier Radboud samples, limiting overfitting to noisy labels. Training used extensive image augmentation, cosine learning-rate scheduling, and checkpoint selection based primarily on Karolinska validation. The single model achieved 0.891 overall validation QWK and 0.927 private QWK, and contributed to a diverse team ensemble.
compute: Kaggle/Colab TPU; 40 training epochs

solution_summary: The solution combined more than 200 CNN models with clustering and post-processing driven by incidence angle. Incidence-angle patterns separated a consistently iceberg-only group from a second group with mixed labels. Retraining CNNs exclusively on the second group improved ship detection by reducing distracting signal. Cross-validation guided clustering thresholds and conservative probability adjustments to control log-loss risk.

The pipeline converted pathology slides into image tiles and trained five-fold base models to identify noisy training labels from held-out predictions. It then retrained two model families on cleaned data, including a cleaning variant that removed 20% of Radboud labels. Final inference combined EfficientNet-B0 and EfficientNet-B1 models, with only folds 1, 4, and 5 used for the second family. The competition submission achieved public/private scores of 0.904/0.940, and a fixed-seed reproduction achieved 0.894/0.939.

solution_summary: The submission combined GPT-120B, Eagle3 speculative decoding, and an adaptive Tree-of-Thoughts solver with 8–16 parallel attempts. Reinforcement attempts restored earlier conversation and Jupyter state, while quadratic resource scaling and effort-weighted answer selection managed constrained inference. The final model was fine-tuned by freezing the model head and training the last transformer layer on cached hidden states. The final structured-prompt SFT submission scored 36 public and 38.5 private, below the base model's 39–41 public results with a simpler prompt.

solution_summary: The team generated approximately 2,400 descriptions and held out 268 for validation. A category classifier routed descriptions to category-specific generation settings using SDXL Turbo with HeunDiscreteScheduler. Candidate SVG evaluation combined a weighted three-question pseudo-VQA score with an adopted OCR hallucination prevention function, restricting OCR checks to top candidates. Geometric transformations, category-specific pseudo-VQA questions, and score distribution calibration did not help.

The approach constructed three training variants using sliding target windows of 14, 28, and 42 days. Historical visitor and reservation aggregates were grouped by restaurant, weekday, holiday, area, and genre over multiple lookback periods. LightGBM, XGBoost, and neural-network predictions were blended within the approach. Averaging the three target-window variants improved the offline score by 0.002, substantially more than blending model types.

solution_title: 85th place solution; 0.906 public and private scores; our 2nd back to back medal; kaggle experts now !
solution_summary: The authors fine-tuned all layers of DeBERTa v3 large with context lengths of 512, 768, and 1024 using external question datasets with context. They combined the three models with weights of 0.2, 0.6, and 0.2 separately on Wikipedia 6M retrieval contexts and STEM 270K parsed and unparsed contexts. The final blend weighted these two ensembles at 0.2 and 0.8, respectively. They reported that the inference notebook could achieve 0.908 on both public and private scores, but unresolved out-of-memory errors and exhausted submissions prevented its submission before the deadline.

solution_title: My scalable and industrializable solution with Scala+Spark
solution_summary: The post links to an external blog describing the author's competition work. It claims the implementation is ready for industrial use and can scale to massive datasets. The supplied text provides no concrete modeling, preprocessing, or validation details.

The solution reduced instrument noise before estimating transit boundaries and screening unreliable samples with simple polynomial fits. A custom nonlinear limb-darkening model then jointly fitted all wavelength channels using sparse nonlinear least squares. A staged increase in system-polynomial order reduced degeneracy between instrument effects and limb darkening. A four-fold gradient-boosting ensemble predicted uncertainty, followed by wavelength scaling, smoothing, and PCA refinements.

solution_title: From ARC Rules to Tiny ONNX Graphs: Our NeuroGolf Bronze
solution_summary: The team solved individual visual reasoning tasks as compact, exact ONNX programs, optimizing stored parameters plus intermediate-tensor memory. Direct-output operations, quantized arithmetic, algebraic color classifiers, and initializer reuse reduced costs across many tasks. Every replacement underwent runtime, sanitizer, correctness, and stress validation before entering a known-good submission bundle. Accumulating verified improvements raised the reported score from about 5,554.69 to 7,454.84.

The team used online adversarial validation and concluded that training and test data were randomly split. A denoiser trained with no-margin cosine loss cleaned the training data while preserving the validation set, and MSE loss helped handle label noise. Thirteen models were blended or stacked, achieving CV scores of 0.908 and 0.910 but private leaderboard scores of 0.899. Scaling healthy-class predictions by 0.9 improved the private score to 0.901.

The final solution combines six LightGBM models and one neural network in a weighted ensemble, followed by graph-based probability recalibration. The models use shared graph and NLP features, with one LightGBM consuming thousands of features including sparse n-gram vectors. Multiple text representations were especially useful because they captured different kinds of similarity. The single model using the full feature set scored approximately 0.116–0.117 on the leaderboard, while the author highlighted distribution artifacts and noisy labels as limitations.

solution_title: Expert Pruning, Masked TIR and Stream Arbitration
solution_summary: The pipeline pruned GPT-OSS-120B experts using routing frequencies measured on math reasoning traces under the submission prompting setup. Dynamic pruning retained a layer-specific set of experts and was favored over fixed pruning because it preserved quality without additional recovery training. Masked tool-integrated reasoning SFT improved aggressively pruned checkpoints, but its added complexity was not retained in the central approach. At inference, eight parallel tool-assisted reasoning streams were governed by a vote-based stopping policy under a 15-minute per-problem cap.

solution_title: Scaling Inference-Time Compute for Mathematical Reasoning
solution_summary: The final pipeline served GPT-OSS-120B through vLLM and generated eight parallel tool-using reasoning attempts per problem. It aggregated answers using inverse weights from a five-component token-entropy score and stopped early when an answer collected four votes. A short prompt, temperature 1.0, a 65K context window, and FP8 KV cache formed the stable configuration, which scored 41/50 after an earlier version reached 42/50. A post-competition reference run solved 10/10 problems in 31 minutes, while verbose prompts, Bayesian voting, and a mismatched fine-tuned model reduced performance.
compute: Single NVIDIA H100, 4.8-hour competition budget; post-competition H100 80GB SXM reference run took 1869 seconds and cost $5.50.

solution_summary: The team averaged PrecTime and LSTM-Unet models, including multiple five-fold model sets and additional single models. They used 28 input features and predicted central sequence regions from longer overlapping inputs to improve boundary accuracy. PrecTime modifications added transformers and residual connections, while dynamic programming postprocessing handled overlapping event predictions. Selected submissions reported public/private scores of 0.75/0.8 and 0.759/0.803.

The team manually developed and shortened Python programs for individual grid tasks, accumulating many small task-specific improvements. Common constructions included recursive rotation, cellular propagation, bitwise encodings, regular expressions and brute-force expression searches. Compression optimization explored zlib and zopfli settings as well as variable names and deliberately repetitive source forms. LLM assistance was generally unhelpful, so most final progress came from manual reasoning and testing.

The author started from publicly shared pretrained models and used a three-stage training strategy. Training progressed from a classifier for all classes to classifiers for each class, then introduced heavier augmentation. Annotation-based mixcut erased annotated regions and their labels and filled those regions with non-label images. Selectively dropping test-time augmentation kept inference within 8 hours 59 minutes, with reported public and private scores of 0.970 and 0.973.

solution_summary: The author moved from a heavily engineered random forest to a linear stack of approximately 58 pretrained models. A classifier predicting seven target quantile regions supplied probabilities for adjusting the stack's predictions toward regional anchors. The final blend trusted these adjustments more when classifier confidence was high and the base models agreed. This gating step produced the largest reported improvement, while gate and model hyperparameters were left untuned.

The solution combines a squeeze-and-excitation CNN, an attention-based sequence model, gated GRUs, and boosted trees. Physics-informed IMU features and statistical sensor features support both neural and tree models. Ensemble weights adapt to confidence, sensor availability, data quality, and Dirichlet posterior estimates. Subject-aware validation is reported, with individual scores of 0.820–0.835 for the neural components and a target ensemble score of 0.856.

The author shares training and inference notebooks alongside the original Colab implementation. A single-seed model reportedly trained in about 20 minutes and had 17 ms latency. Kaggle TPU-VM training was approximately twice as slow as Colab. A four-seed model often encountered submission scoring errors, and a three-seed alternative was suggested without a confirmed improvement.

solution_title: Making my (not submitted) 5th place solution public

The author describes a competition project that produced ten machine learning models and several analyses of the Santander data. The work included a stacked autoencoder, development of a KLIEP covariate-shift correction algorithm, and investigation of hidden time-series structure. Many models loaded HDF5 versions of the datasets to improve read speed. This repository overview does not identify the final submitted model, its validation procedure, or its predictive score.

solution_title: Rank 28 approach - diversity and CV prevail!
solution_summary: The author trained more than 70 models with diverse tree algorithms and different amounts of replicated training and original data. Shuffled ten-fold validation guided model selection, with a depth-eight XGBoost model performing best individually. AutoGluon and neural network stackers were combined with single models using a GPU hill-climbing blender. The final blending approach achieved cross-validation scores of approximately 0.382–0.383.
compute: A5000 for tree models and Torch NN; A6000 Ada for XGBoost; Google Colab L4 for AutoGluon and stackers; local RTX 4090 for hill-climbing blending.

solution_summary: The solution combined agent-swapping data generation, manual and OpenFE-generated features, and CatBoost-centered regression models. Validation grouped games and stratified by target and agent identity, while nested cross-validation supplied leakage-safe predictions for second-stage models. A weighted ensemble achieved the best local validation score, but a separate CatBoost submission adjusted to the public prediction distribution performed better on the private test. That distribution-matched submission achieved 0.417 publicly and 0.422 privately.
compute: OpenFE feature generation took around 30 hours on a 10% subsample using 1 CPU.

solution_summary: The solution combined three Cascade Mask R-CNN models for 275 leaf classes with a separate model for 23 parent classes, expanding predictions through the class hierarchy. Class-dependent oversampling and undersampling addressed severe imbalance, while small validation subsets guided learning-rate changes and checkpoint selection. Multi-scale and flip inference combined detections with NMS and averaged instance masks, followed by mask-level NMS to merge parent predictions from both sources. Increasing the leaf ensemble's detection limit on part of the test set produced final public/private scores of 0.5383/0.4922.
compute: 4 Tesla T4 for training; 8 Tesla T4 for TTA inference. Four models took approximately 22, 18, 10, and 5 days to train; leaf TTA required about 525 T4-hours.

solution_title: 376th → 92nd: the signal was non-monotonic, and one model beat every blend
solution_summary: The final submission used a single FT-Transformer with Periodic–Linear–ReLU numerical embeddings and exact-value target encoding. Diagnostics showed reproducible non-monotonic signal at individual numeric values, explaining why histogram-based trees plateaued and why richer value representations helped. Training used fold-specific transformations, class-weighted cross-entropy, mixed precision, and stratified five-fold validation. The model achieved 0.95057 OOF balanced accuracy and 0.95099 public score, outperforming blends whose small OOF gains did not transfer.
compute: HistGradientBoostingClassifier training took approximately 2.5 minutes.

solution_summary: The solution centered on reconstructing multiple user identifiers from D features and card information, combining strict identities with more flexible variants. User-level sequence encoding, target encoding of past records, and aggregate features drove substantial improvements. LightGBM supplied most predictions, with a small Regularized Greedy Forest contribution and diversity from seeds and encoding fold counts. Validation moved from unshuffled five-fold CV to a final-period holdout, and the reported private score was 0.941338.

The author solved the CTF tasks with a mix of statistical analysis, model inspection, adversarial inputs, and manual search. K-means and PCA recovered cluster counts and dimensions, while PCA followed by distance sorting decoded hidden tokens. Other tasks used autoregressive character generation, targeted image optimization, input perturbations, and exploitation of scoring logic. Inspecting data and implementation details often mattered more than sophisticated modeling.

The solution generated recommendation candidates and reranked them with one XGBoost ranker per target, without ensembling. Candidates came from session history, co-visitation matrices, Word2Vec similarities, and item popularity. The rankers used 53 features describing ranks, interaction history, co-visitation weights, popularity, and embedding similarity. Separate data constructions controlled leakage, and the approach achieved 0.574 overall validation recall@20 and 0.586 on the public leaderboard.

The author combined three complementary approaches built around Google Perch v2 representations. One used contextual state-space models and MLP probes, while another distilled Perch features into EfficientNet-B0 with an attention-based sound event detection head. Taxonomy-aware smoothing, asymmetric loss, audio augmentation and dual MixUp addressed noisy and imbalanced data. A third model used high-confidence pseudo-labels selected per class, with stratified folds incorporating pseudo-label provenance. Perch inference was accelerated from roughly 90 to 23 minutes, while BirdNET+ experiments and improved insect validation scores did not translate into better leaderboard performance.
compute: Perch inference accelerated from approximately 90 minutes to 23 minutes.

solution_summary: The solution used three stages: diverse base predictions, two MLP stackers, and a simple average of their outputs. Base learners included LightGBM variants, custom CNNs, a public transformer, and Gaussian naive Bayes, with consistent five-fold out-of-fold predictions. Random architecture search selected two MLPs with hidden sizes 52/94 and 10/20. The better selected submission scored 0.80833 private and 0.80074 public, while an unselected variant with an additional MLP scored slightly higher privately.

solution_title: A type of solution I was expecting some to try
solution_summary: The author proposes decomposing gift allocation into a prefix containing twins and triplets and a base containing individual children. One variant generates candidate prefixes, computes the remaining gift supplies, and solves each corresponding base using minimum-cost flow. A reverse variant solves the base first and allocates the remaining gifts afterward. These are unverified proposals, and the author explicitly notes that they do not guarantee an optimum.

An EfficientNet-B5 crop classifier learned embeddings and ISUP probabilities from 512×512 level-0 crops containing cancer. Slide-level embedding statistics, probability statistics, class counts, and probability-weighted embedding sums fed a LightGBM classifier. Mixing embeddings from compatible slides expanded the slide-level training dataset from 10,000 to 200,000 rows. Inference averaged predictions from random embedding subsets, then converted expected ISUP scores into grades using fixed thresholds. The author acknowledged feature leakage from training the crop model on the full training set and considered its effect small because of strong augmentation.

The solution combined single-stage and multi-stage spine classifiers with condition-specific weights applied to logits. DINOv2 supplied global image context, while LSTM layers mixed information across MRI slices. The two-stage pipeline localized key points, projected them across imaging sources, and classified cropped slice stacks using ConvNeXtv2 or DINOv2. CLAHE normalization, SPIDER pretraining, and losses approximating the competition metric supported an ensemble CV score of 0.379.

The solution adapted a public baseline with group-based validation balanced by event count and clipping enmo at 1. Predictions from models trained with seeds 0, 21, and 42 were averaged before find_peaks post-processing, producing reported scores around 0.73–0.735. Extending input windows from 8 to 24 hours and adjusting Gaussian labels did not improve results. Tuning peak-finding parameters and removing low-score predictions were also unsuccessful.

The author trained two models using maskrcnn-benchmark without modifying the library or applying test-time augmentation or post-processing. Class imbalance was addressed by selecting a fixed number of training images per class. Class hierarchy was handled through separate datasets and models for root classes and deeper classes, with annotation conversion, removal, and gray masking of selected non-target objects. Each model required about 14 hours on eight V100 GPUs.
compute: Two models, approximately 14 hours each using 8 V100 GPUs.

solution_title: Some of the 3rd place solution history (Danijel|Matias)
solution_summary: The team combined XGBoost, glmnet, and neural-network models, with a regularized Keras network providing the strongest individual model for devices with events. TF-IDF representations of device metadata and app labels, along with brand and model frequencies, improved performance. Fold prediction averaging and separately optimized ensembles for devices with and without events were useful. The final approach applied a matching-based leak only to devices without events; the best individual event-device model scored 2.23452 on the leaderboard.

The solution averaged signal probabilities from 108 sigmoid neural networks using three architectures in equal proportions. All features were retained and standardized, with simple missing-value imputation rules distributed equally across the ensemble. Training used cross-entropy, batches of 10, and unweighted early epochs followed by weighted epochs. A signal threshold of 0.5575 was selected using cross-validation and the public leaderboard.

solution_summary: The solution ensembled CatBoost, LightGBM, XGBoost, and neural networks using 75 selected features. CatBoost was the strongest model, and intraday trailing features were the most influential feature group. Model tuning used five-fold rolling-window validation, with MAE and information ratio guiding selection. A final submission incorporating a model trained on original and unscored data outperformed the version without unscored data.

solution_title: Summary of things I've learned in get to my moderate 13th place
solution_summary: The author trained random forest, XGBoost, and k-nearest-neighbor models within geographic grids after abandoning an overlapping place-group strategy. Feature tuning, time-based sample weighting, rare-place filtering, and per-place outlier removal supported the individual models. The final combination retained six candidates per model and normalized their probabilities before voting. Individual scores were between 0.58 and 0.59, while the combined model achieved 0.605 on the private leaderboard.

solution_summary: The author used pointwise ranking based on association rules, with user click history and historical relevance for the current query providing the strongest signals. Domain associations were more useful than URL associations, and query trigrams also helped. Validation used 900,000 sessions from Day 26 with randomly sampled test queries. Restricting in-memory model data to test users and queries made inference manageable, but further additions stopped improving the score beyond approximately 0.798.

solution_summary: The pipeline used DKM correspondences to locate overlapping image regions, then ensembled matches from LoFTR, SE2-LoFTR, and SuperGlue on those crops. Original-image LoFTR matches compensated for regions missed by cropping. Multithreaded processing, spatial keypoint suppression, and weighted sampling reduced matching and estimation costs. Difficult image pairs triggered SGMNet augmentation or a DKM-only fallback, with these rules guided by custom validation.

solution_title: 2nd Place solution: The Godaddy Microbusiness Data Cleaning Challenge
solution_summary: The solution combined public leaderboard probing, reversion forecasts for anomalous counties, and an XGBoost model for smooth changes. Large jumps in active counts were removed by shifting the historical series, which gave the best cross-validation performance among the cleaning methods tried. The model used lagged signals and demographic, geographic, labor, and neighboring-county features with attention to their historical availability. Recursive one-month forecasts performed better than direct three-month forecasts, and predictions were rounded to integer active counts.

solution_summary: The team combined pretrained EfficientNets with experiment-based validation, experiment-specific image normalization, and strong augmentation. Class co-occurrence constraints and Hungarian assignment substantially improved raw network predictions, while train and test controls were added as extra classes. A second training iteration used soft pseudo labels with balanced experiment splits and added larger EfficientNets, although B6 did not converge well in time. The initial B0/B1/B2 blend achieved a private score of 0.990, and final inference used both imaging sites with eight flip/rotation variants each.

solution_summary: The team trained several CNN backbones and extracted their bottleneck features for product-level image aggregation. Padded groups of up to four image features were processed using LSTM, GRU, dense models, and NetVLAD, then averaged across aggregation models and backbones. This ensemble reached around 0.77, compared with roughly 0.69–0.72 for the baseline CNNs. Off-the-shelf EAST text detection and CRNN OCR supplied character n-gram features, adding about 0.01 without retraining the OCR models or correcting their output with a language model.

The post shares links to reverse-engineering notebooks for difficulty levels 3 and 4. It also links the notebook that produced the final submission. The author thanks another participant for kernels and a difficulty 2 solution, but provides no methodological details in the post itself.

solution_title: Was there an issue with the selected submission?
solution_summary: The post reports an issue encountered during submission. It refers readers to an attached photo. The supplied text contains no solution methods or results.

The solution used an ImageNet-pretrained CNN adapted to predict three possible vehicle trajectories over five seconds. Direct optimization of multimodal negative log-likelihood, matching the test agent filtering, and training on the full dataset were the main improvements. The reported seresnext26 model used two history frames because of time constraints and achieved a test score of 11.377.

solution_title: 20th place solution based on custom sample_weight and data augmentation
solution_summary: The solution combined store-and-calendar target encodings, weather features, customized sample weights, and imputed monthly statistics. Validation held out the final month and separated its first six days from the remainder to assess public-like and private-like performance. Sample weights combined recentness with annual similarity, while regression ensembles filled missing May statistics. Randomly dropping historical observations before target encoding and averaging the resulting predictions improved robustness to differing store observation histories.

The team used a frozen DINOv3 Large backbone with four overlapping image patches, Local Mamba fusion, and patch attention. Validation grouped sampling dates and stratified states across four folds. Color augmentation, artifact inpainting, state conditioning, multiscale instances, and state-specific expert heads addressed domain differences. Backbone unfreezing and TTA hurt performance, while WA-based dead-biomass scaling improved public results but performed worse privately than omitting it.

The solution relied on stacking approximately 40 out-of-fold prediction sets. Combining many predictions was the central strategy described. The author credited shared notebooks and community contributions but provided no base-model or training details.

solution_title: SegFormer  + Depth Pro -> DinoV3Base w/Lora -> Learned Fusion module
solution_summary: This approach fuses DINOv3 image representations with 18 auxiliary features derived from segmentation, depth, and texture. Separate heads predict green, dead, and clover biomass, with total biomass computed as their sum. Training combines LoRA adaptation, increased weighting for high-biomass samples, and component-specific losses. Inference uses horizontal-flip augmentation and differential-evolution-tuned component corrections, including adjustments for occlusion and saturation.
compute: Training on the full dataset for 50 epochs

solution_summary: The approach averaged lightweight 3D segmentation models and converted predicted masks into particle centroids using CC3D. Customized particle mask radii, segmentation losses, balanced crop sampling, and augmentation were central to training, while InstanceNorm3d and PReLU improved stability in several architectures. Public leaderboard scores guided ensemble selection, with selected submissions scoring 0.78283 and 0.78381 on the private leaderboard. Post-processing used a shared probability threshold of 0.15 and removed small clusters; synthetic data, second-stage classification, and heavyweight transformers did not improve results.

The author built a largely automated pipeline using cross-validated models from multiple neural network architectures with basic augmentation. The implementation included test-time augmentation, threshold search, several ensemble approaches, and multiple loss functions. Single models scored about 0.55–0.57 on the public leaderboard, while the large ensemble reached 0.601. The author concluded that improving individual models would have been more valuable than adding many weak models.

The solution combined five CNN architectures trained with five-fold multilabel iterative stratification. Training used binary cross-entropy followed by three to five epochs of F2 loss, with only the last two layers and classifier trained. Aggressive learning-rate reduction and logits drawn from the last two layers helped improve performance while keeping training efficient. A weighted model average reached 0.658 on the public leaderboard; test-time augmentation and gradient accumulation did not help.

The author shared useful components of a solution built largely on @mrkmakr's public kernel. Features included trigonometric speed components, distances, and an exponentially weighted measure of defender proximity to the rusher. Simulating player positions one second ahead provided additional derived features. Symmetry flips and coordinate noise improved training, while validation grouped samples by week.

solution_title: Some Useful external Datasets Used helped boost score
solution_summary: The post shares links to prepared datasets for post-competition experimentation. These include BIMCV, VinBig, RICORD, RSNA images and metadata, and pseudo-labeled test data. The author reports that using 500 RSNA normal images improved the leaderboard score by 0.001, but does not describe a modeling pipeline.

The pipeline detected helmets, projected them onto a bird’s-eye map, and registered the resulting points to player tracking data. Team classification and temporal tracking improved player assignments, while a four-detector ensemble combined assignment matrices before Hungarian matching. The mapping and registration modules were especially important, achieving approximately 0.8 using helmets.csv alone. The team classifier achieved approximately 97% validation accuracy.
compute: Mapping and registration approach runs faster than 10 frames/sec on an unspecified GPU.

solution_summary: The solution blended four neural networks, one CatBoost model, and predictions from public kernels. All neural networks used the same compact feature set: categorical conversion and label encoding, plus ordinal encodings for ord_1 through ord_5. The networks combined CTR components such as CIN, factorization machines, product networks, cross networks, DNNs, and AutoInt through Deeptables. Additional feature-processing methods overfit, while the strongest individual neural network achieved a public score of 0.78672.

solution_title: What is the difference between a good and a great solution?
solution_summary: The author reviews other teams' approaches while identifying strengths and weaknesses in their own retrieval pipeline. Their solution used HuggingFace Wikipedia dumps and passage-level retrieval, but approximate search was considered a costly accuracy compromise. They identify better Wikipedia parsing and accurate retrieval as major opportunities for improvement. The post also discusses model training and inference improvements reported by other teams without claiming to have used them.

The solution handled accession identifiers with keyword rules filtered by embedding similarity, while DOIs followed a multistage zero-shot Qwen extraction and classification pipeline. Corpus lookup and repository-specific rules supplemented the DOI predictions. Postprocessing capped certain accession predictions and removed identifiers appearing in textual ranges. The two selected submissions scored 0.729 and 0.745 on the private leaderboard.

The author used XGBoost tuned with 10-fold cross-validation and generated predictions from each fold. Experiments compared training with and without original fraud examples, while validation scores were calculated only on synthetic examples. Features included indicators for zero and one dollar amounts, hourly time bins, and day and hour-of-day indicators. Random undersampling maintained five non-fraud examples per fraud example, reducing runtime without an apparent loss of useful information.

solution_title: [Working Note] Two transfer failures: instruction complexity & a wasted signal
solution_summary: The final strategy emphasized simple single-action email.send candidates in the competition sandbox because that mechanism transferred to the private guardrail better than marker-based attacks. Packing eight actions into each candidate worked on the local 8B proxy but produced empty or malformed outputs on the real 26B target. The most transferable submission scored 3.720 privately versus 3.900 publicly. The author identified throughput and proxy-to-target instruction transfer as major limitations and observed, but did not systematically exploit, grading-time signals.
compute: 12GB GPU with an 8B local proxy; real-target email submissions took roughly 24 hours to grade.

solution_summary: The solution separately predicted the probability of no event and the normalized rank of event time, then combined these outputs with a tuned nonlinear function. Classifiers included boosted trees, neural networks, TabM, and graph models, while regressors used boosted trees with event-status features and sample weights. Shared ten-fold splits supported model comparison, and fold prediction shifts were corrected for ranking models. An Optuna-weighted ensemble of 27 classifier–regressor combinations achieved approximately 0.6965 CV stratified concordance.

The final solution combined 218 first-level models using NVIDIA cuML logistic regression fitted to their logit-transformed predictions. The blend used five-fold out-of-fold predictions and drew on extensively tuned XGBoost, CatBoost, LightGBM, RealMLP, TabM, and TabICLv2 models alongside many additional model families for diversity. An autonomous Codex workflow ran feature-engineering and hyperparameter experiments on four A100 GPUs while tracking cross-validation results. The selected submission achieved a private leaderboard score of 0.95502; the author explicitly reports using neither pseudo-labels nor models trained on other models' predictions.
compute: 4x A100 GPUs running experiments in parallel; improved single-model CV scores within a few hours

solution_title: Quan Sun on finishing in second place in Predict Grant Applications
solution_summary: The author addressed concept drift by concentrating training on applications from 2007 and 2008. Extensive application-level statistics and categorical frequencies supported a greedy ensemble selected using later-year validation data. A separate Rotation Forest used M5P trees and Gaussian random projections. Averaging the two approaches improved final test AUC to approximately 0.963.
compute: Home PC with AMD 6-core CPU, 16 GB RAM, Windows; used for most experiments.

solution_title: 7th place Pure Magic thanks Radek solution: classification
solution_summary: The post links to an external solution article and a cleaned-up code repository. It also points to a separate metric-learning account by team members. The supplied text contains no substantive pipeline description.

solution_title: 15-th plcae solution: sphereface, image alignment and multi-layer fusion
solution_summary: The team used angular-margin classification with SphereFace, multi-layer feature concatenation, and SE-ResNeXt/ResNeXt backbones. A custom keypoint detector enabled affine image alignment, raising the best single-model score to 0.943. Ensembling aligned and unaligned models at two resolutions reached 0.953, and playground pseudo-labeling plus a new-whale suppression loss increased the ensemble score to 0.954.
external_data: ["Paul Johnson's 1000 Hand-Annotated Humpback Whale Fluke Keypoints dataset", "Playground images"]

solution_summary: The solution ensembles four LightGBM models that predict user-product purchase probabilities using different features, datasets, and parameters. Training includes each user's last two prior orders, which improved the score by about 0.001. Features describe product diversity, repeat-order behavior, recent purchase history, and unusual ordering times. The probability of purchasing nothing combines a calibrated product-based estimate with a separate order-level model.

The final blend used two CatBoost models, seven LightGBM models, two random forests, and a model from a public notebook. LAD regression combined predictions, with the intercept disabled, and this model set achieved the author's best cross-validation MAE. Random forest out-of-bag predictions served as substitutes for out-of-fold predictions, while ExtraTrees did not improve results. The author relied on cross-validation and submitted final variants with and without a public post-processing trick.
compute: Random forest training took approximately 10 minutes on a Kaggle notebook.

solution_summary: The solution blended five detector families using weighted boxes fusion and temporal tracking. Models trained at 1152×2048 using only images containing boxes, with varied augmentation including background mixing. Tracking raised weak detection confidences using stronger detections on the same track and improved local performance by about 0.01. Subsequence validation correlated with the public leaderboard but failed to predict private performance, while tighter-box adjustments also failed to generalize as expected.

The solution combined recurrent models and GNN–Transformer models, including variants with autoencoder pretraining. Inputs included sequence, structure, loop type, base-pair probability summaries from multiple RNA algorithms and temperatures, and Shannon entropy. Training used signal-to-noise sample weights, while validation retained SN-filtered examples. Predictions were averaged across three ten-fold validation schemes, with ensemble weights chosen using public leaderboard scores.

The author trained Qwen3-14B with four-fold cross-validation under two random seeds, producing eight models. Inputs included possible answers and question-specific misconceptions, and training used QLoRA for two epochs. Averaging the eight models helped address noisy labels, and submission selection relied on out-of-fold scores. Adversarial weight perturbation improved local validation but was not submitted.

The solution combined EfficientNet image encoders with transformer or LSTM sequence decoders, using multiple image resolutions. Predictions were ordered by local validation performance, and the first valid InChI was selected for each image from more than 20 outputs. Orientation correction, border cropping, and oversampling long formulas were important preprocessing and training choices. Training used plateau-based restarts, while checkpoint blending improved the best transformer model by about 0.04. Long training times restricted most experiments to a single split, and later validation problems led the team to rely mainly on leaderboard feedback.
compute: One DGX Station and up to three DGX-1 servers; later one and then two DGX A100 stations with 4 A100 GPUs each. An epoch took 2–12 hours depending on architecture and resolution.

solution_summary: The author averaged three BERT-based configurations using different combinations of question title, question body, and answer text, with separate or joint target prediction. Training first fitted the regression head with BERT frozen, then fine-tuned the full network for three epochs using five-fold validation grouped by question title. The decisive post-processing step used DBSCAN to replace nearby predictions with a shared cluster median, creating ties relevant to the ranking metric. Tuning its distance threshold on validation predictions improved public scores from 0.39X to 0.42X and private scores from 0.37X to 0.39X.

solution_title: Private 28th, Public 8th, Thank you all, my first medal!
solution_summary: The solution ensembled EfficientNet B4 with Noisy Student weights, SE-ResNeXt50, and a base Vision Transformer. Training incorporated the 2019 dataset, scheduled augmentation strength, CutMix, MixUp, and bi-tempered logistic loss with label smoothing. Seed ensembling and combining original-image predictions with test-time augmentation strengthened otherwise modest individual models. Equal averaging of original predictions and nine augmented views achieved 0.908 publicly and 0.901 privately.

solution_title: 4th Place Solution - Nikhil's Part (Modified Unet + Transformer and Weighted Box Fusion)
solution_summary: The solution regressed normalized Gaussian onset and wakeup targets from day-long sensor sequences using modified U-Nets with transformer and recurrent blocks. Four models combined two LSTM and two GRU variants, using sensor, timestamp, and derived features with series-grouped validation. The final submission blended the author's predictions with a teammate's predictions after a power transform, then applied a custom WBF-style peak extraction procedure. The final ensemble scored 0.835 CV, 0.793 public, and 0.845 private, although WBF slightly hurt private performance.

The solution applies a 30 Hz high-pass filter and normalizes each observation by its absolute mean. Training augmentation includes temporal rolls, amplitude scaling, and sign inversion. All three models share a WaveNet frontend, followed by EfficientNet B3, WaveNet with GRU, or WaveNet modeling. Implemented in TensorFlow and trained on TPU, the models report CV scores ranging from 87.79 to 88.07.
compute: Trained on TPU

solution_summary: The team combined complementary LightGBM solutions, using different models and blends for Investment and OwnerOccupier properties. Extensive cleaning, suspicious-price removal, area-normalized features, and price-per-square-meter modeling improved robustness. Time-period normalization, validation, and leaderboard probing informed prediction scaling. Comparing model disagreements exposed incorrect property locations, and targeted address corrections contributed about 0.004 to the public score.

The solution used out-of-the-box Distance Weighted Discriminant classification without feature selection. The penalization parameter C was tuned using 10-fold cross-validation and ROC area. Performance saturated around C=300, which was used for the submission.

The author used an eight-layer BERT token model for joint regression of RNA reactivity targets. Pretraining predicted four per-token summaries of base-pair probabilities using the combined competition training and test sequences. Fine-tuning added a two-layer probing head over concatenated backbone layers and used filtered competition labels together with external targets. The final ensemble averaged 16 fine-tuning runs, used stochastic weight averaging for some models, and clipped predictions below one.
external_data: ["External RNA dataset from a discussion post (unspecified)"]

solution_summary: The solution engineered workflow-aware batch features from exact and approximate duplicates, including duplicate counts and within-batch ID ranks. A two-level stack combined XGBoost models trained on different feature subsets and station groups, then trained second-level models only on the identified batches. The final predictions averaged XGBoost, random forest, ExtraTrees, and Keras outputs. Batch-grouped validation and a conservative MCC-based threshold selection emphasized robustness, with performance ordering consistent across validation and both leaderboards.

The solution combines an attention-based MLP with a smaller logistic regression contribution using extensive play-level and player-level features. Bounded Voronoi geometry, relative player positions, and projected future movement were important engineered inputs. Grouped and temporal validation were considered together, while coordinate-flip TTA improved predictions. Final submissions used four-seed MLP averaging, with one submission also blending five-fold logistic regression predictions.
compute: MLP submission: approximately 9000 seconds including 4000 seconds training; blended submission: approximately 10500 seconds including 5000 seconds training.

solution_title: Looking back at my approach 1284 pos [0.8952 private leaderboard and 0.8950 public leaderboard]
solution_summary: The solution combined ImageNet-initialized ResNeXt50-style and EfficientNet-B4 models trained on the full training set after five-fold stratified model selection. Strong image augmentation, particularly CutMix, improved the difficult classes, while plain cross entropy worked as well as its weighted variant. Training used SGD with cosine annealing, and inference averaged ten randomly augmented predictions per image. A 0.6/0.4 soft-voting ensemble achieved approximately 0.8952 accuracy on both public and private leaderboards.

Images were tiled into 512×512 RGB patches, with 16 instances selected per image. The central improvement was pretraining an ImageNet-initialized ResNet152 on competition images labeled Unknown or Other before learning CE/LAA classification. Training used binary cross entropy with balanced class weights. The selected submission ensembled this model with EfficientNetB0 and Xception, although the single pretrained ResNet achieved the author's best private score of 0.65726.

The solution trained four image-text models using Swin or EfficientNet image backbones and BERT-family text backbones with ArcFace. Each model produced joint, image, and text embeddings, and predictions combined 24 votes across models, embedding types, and distance measures. Validation used five folds grouped by product label, with submission thresholds adjusted from CV settings. Forcing singleton predictions to contain two items improved CV and leaderboard scores by 0.01, while removing matches with inconsistent units further refined results.

solution_title: Do not trust the LB,  trust your CV.  (5th/8th in public/private LB)
solution_summary: The team combined ship-presence classifiers with several segmentation models. ResNet34 and SE-ResNeXt50 classifiers trained on all images, while U-Net and Mask R-CNN variants trained on ship-containing images. A further U-Net variant used deep supervision and all images, and the final submission combined these model families. The author emphasized trusting cross-validation and reported that pseudo-labeling worked, with a single-model private score described as 853.

The solution combined neural networks, ODST variants, and gradient boosting models trained on survival targets. CNN and dense neural models fitted both a CoxPHFitter-derived target and a custom target designed to separate event and censored cases. ODST improvements included replacing unseen categories with training modes, adding public notebook features, and weighting fold predictions. Two classification trees provided post-processing.

The solution combined three DINOv3 Huge pipelines with weights of 50% for subspace-alignment test-time adaptation, 30% for species-aware prediction, and 20% for DINOv3–SigLIP feature fusion. Scaling the pretrained backbone and carefully stabilizing fine-tuning mattered more than increasing image resolution. Target reformulation, predicted species probabilities, and a deeper MLP head improved the biomass models. Validation used five stratified folds based on biomass bins and species after date-grouped validation proved unhelpful. The final ensemble scored 0.760 publicly and 0.652 privately.
compute: A100 GPU; memory constraints influenced backbone and image-size choices.

solution_summary: Fully connected networks processed descriptors and fingerprints for individual building blocks, with some models also using tokenized SMILES embeddings. Binding sites were capped to distinguish and align them, and swapping the second and third building blocks provided augmentation. Training retained all binding molecules and sampled one fifth of nonbinding molecules. Scaffold-based validation guided binary model selection for the ensemble, followed by a rule that zeroed predictions for unsupported building-block combinations.

solution_title: 4th place solution. Boundary DoU Loss is all you need!
solution_summary: The main pipeline equally averaged a multiview 2D EfficientNet-B5 UNet++ model and a 3D DynUNet model, with D4 test-time augmentation. It used percentile-based stack normalization, sparsity-aware sampling, external pseudo-labels, and BoundaryDOULoss. A vessel ROI derived from 2D predictions suppressed false positives in the 3D output, while Canny-based kidney masking improved public results but severely damaged private performance. The main ensemble scored 0.712 privately, although the author reports that their best private submission was a simpler mixture of 2D and 2.5D models.
compute: 2D training: 30 epochs. 3D training: 500 epochs with 2000 samples per epoch.

solution_title: 24th place solution - 2 stage Autogluon and XGB, no post-processing
solution_summary: The solution combined molecular fingerprints, descriptors, graph features, and ChemBERT embeddings with target-specific AutoGluon and XGBoost models. Initial AutoGluon runs used all features and then importance-selected subsets, while a second stage learned pseudo-labels and incorporated predictions for other targets. The final submission selected different models for each target using leaderboard scores, including an average for Density. It scored 0.66 publicly and 0.86 privately; a more conservative median ensemble performed worse privately.
compute: GPU notebooks with a 12-hour budget for AutoGluon runs and feature selection.

solution_summary: The final solution combined six DeBERTa models, comprising two base and four large variants, with a LightGBM regressor on top of each model and a late-fusion ensemble. Variants differed in whether prompt text and questions were included and whether external Feedback Prize data was used for pretraining. Handcrafted prompt-text features in LightGBM substantially improved models that omitted prompt inputs. The ensemble achieved approximately 0.4734 cross-validation MCRMSE and 0.468 private leaderboard MCRMSE.

solution_title: 554 Place Solution for the ICR - Identifying Age-Related Conditions Competition
solution_summary: The solution combined XGBoost and LightGBM models trained with cross-validation. Preprocessing distinguished categorical columns from other features and applied no normalization. GridSearchCV tuned the models using balanced log loss. The final submission averaged the two models' predicted probabilities equally.

solution_title: 516th solution with the one which is supposed to win Copper medal in private score
solution_summary: The author modified two public notebook approaches by changing the datasets they used. Two variants of the Jelal notebook were chosen as final submissions based on slightly stronger public scores. A Coleridge MLMv2 variant that was not submitted achieved a better private score of 0.228, compared with 0.196 for the reported submitted variant.

solution_title: 72nd Place: Training-only Site Bias and Image-reading LLM Labels
solution_summary: The final model used an ImageNet-pretrained 2.5D ConvNeXt-B with hierarchical per-finding attention over MRI windows and series. Label quality drove most improvements: source-specific out-of-fold teachers were combined with multimodal LLM image-and-report labels. A training-only site bias absorbed reporting differences and was removed at inference, improving private AUC by 0.007. The final single-seed model achieved 0.949 private AUC, outperforming the attempted ensembles.
compute: Image-label generation: 128 parallel calls, about 45 minutes, about 21k tokens per study; image training: 30 epochs.

solution_summary: The final solution equally blended two sensor sequence pipelines with substantially different architectures. One used modality-specific residual CNNs, cross-modal attention, a bidirectional LSTM, and auxiliary tasks; the other used gated sensor streams, attention pooling, and random sensor masking. Sensor alignment, motion features, and sequence augmentation helped standardize the small dataset. Combining the pipelines improved public performance from about 86.5 individually to 87.6, while manual upside-down corrections and leaking OOF distillation exposed weaknesses in validation.

The solution used seven weighted models based on a pretrained ResNet-50 FCN, varying image resolution, loss, folds, and test-time augmentation. All layers were fine-tuned with Adam, using restrained geometric augmentation and primarily binary cross-entropy minus log Dice loss. Geometric mask cleanup repaired antennas, filled selected holes and concavities, and removed stray contours. Post-processing increased the reported private score from 0.997010 to 0.997209.
compute: GTX1080Ti and GTX1080; GTX1070 for inference/TTA. GTX1080Ti used for 1918x1280 and 2010x1340.

solution_summary: The task was treated as direct multiclass classification using 15 QLoRA-fine-tuned Qwen models across three backbones and five folds. Data corrections and keeping near-duplicates together supported reliable validation, while focal and smoothed cross-entropy losses with delayed class weights addressed noisy, long-tailed labels. Inference used quantized models, including a GPTQ 32B base with a separate FP16 classifier head executed through vLLM. A weighted logit blend achieved private MAP@3 of 0.948.
compute: Single RTX 4090 for 8B models, four epochs; A800-40GB for the 32B model, three epochs.

solution_summary: The solution localized lungs with an EfficientNet-B0 detector trained on manually annotated boxes, then classified neighboring CT slices with SE-ResNeXt50 and SE-ResNeXt101 models. A second stage processed image embeddings and their neighboring differences with a bidirectional GRU to predict image-level and study-level labels. A single holdout of 1,000 studies guided tuning before models were retrained on the full training set. Final predictions were adjusted to satisfy label consistency constraints, producing a small local validation improvement.
compute: 576x576 localized inputs were the largest size that allowed the models to finish within 9 hours.

solution_summary: The solution represents each well as an image over candidate vertical depths and measured depth, with whole-well U-Nets predicting categorical depth distributions. Autoregressive tracking, a physics-guided HMM, segmented beam search, and posterior fusion provide complementary predictions. Seeded grouped cross-validation supports entropy-weighted test-time augmentation and a position-dependent nonnegative stack with disagreement calibration. The selected combination achieved 5.28 strict cross-validation RMSE and 6.251 private leaderboard RMSE.

The final solution ensembled two DeBERTa-v3-large models, including one with masked-language-model pretraining on FB2 data at a 0.4 masking probability. Adversarial weight perturbation and target-specific attention pooling had the strongest impact, with layer-wise learning-rate decay also helping. MLM slightly improved single-model CV while worsening leaderboard scores, but its inclusion appeared to improve the ensemble. The final ensemble achieved CV 0.44582 and public/private scores of 0.439025/0.435032; smooth-L1 loss, masking augmentation, and recurrent heads did not help.

The pipeline trained YOLOv5l on overlapping image tiles with balanced foreground/background sampling and strong augmentation, then detected objects on full images at higher resolution. Experiments included pseudo-label relabeling, scale and flip TTA, and fold-model fusion with WBF. Post-processing removed unreliable edge boxes and applied an online adaptation of Seq-NMS over the previous 20 frames. The strongest reported late submission used original labels and a five-fold ensemble, reaching 0.737 with Seq-NMS.
compute: Tesla T4 16GB on an EC2 g4dn.xlarge instance; training for 45–60 epochs.

solution_title: 6th Place Solution: Multi-view Multi-lateral Multi-stage Approach
solution_summary: The team used ConvNeXt-based mammography models with VOI-LUT processing, breast-region cropping, and extensive augmentation. YOLOX supplied training crops, while simpler rule-based cropping reduced inference time. Auxiliary prediction losses and weight averaging improved training stability, and the final approach combined models. A submission scoring 0.53 on the private leaderboard was left unselected because its validation and public scores were weaker.

solution_title: Silver medal solution: ViT-L/14 with test time augmentations
solution_summary: The solution used an OpenCLIP ViT-L/14 encoder pretrained on LAION-400M with aspect-ratio-preserving image resizing. A projection layer trained with ArcFace on Products-10k substantially improved the embeddings. Test-time augmentation combined predefined crops and masked pixel dropout. The final reported scores were 0.628 public and 0.631 private.

solution_title: 6th Place Solution for the NeurIPS 2023 - Machine Unlearning Competition
solution_summary: The team performed machine unlearning by resetting the original model's first and last layers, warming up through teacher-student distillation, and fine-tuning on retained data. Fine-tuning combined hard-label cross-entropy, soft cross-entropy, and KL divergence with cosine learning-rate scheduling. The method did not require the forget set and retained the starter notebook's preprocessing. Restricting warm-up to validation classes 0 and 1 achieved a private score of 0.07831, compared with 0.07219 using all validation classes.

solution_summary: The final blend combined three BERT models and one XLNet model, using a simple BERT baseline without text preprocessing or loss weights. The main improvement came from selecting about 475,000 training records containing valid identity annotations or positive toxicity labels. Selecting identity-annotated records outperformed random selection, while including all toxic comments helped address class imbalance. Two epochs on this subset achieved a reported leaderboard score of 0.94299, and XLNet improved the blend despite implementation bugs.
compute: Trained approximately 475,000 records for two epochs in a Kaggle Kernel; hardware and runtime unspecified.

solution_title: Solution and experience sharing - 4th place (should have been 2nd)
solution_summary: The solution combined 16 XGBoost variants spanning four modeling methods, two public-script feature sets, and two post-processing approaches. It mixed linear, Poisson, multiclass-derived continuous predictions, and an undisclosed heuristic method, with offsets or cutoffs used to map predictions to ordinal classes. Weighted ensembling delivered substantial gains, and the final blend also included a variant that post-processed predictions after aggregation. Five-fold validation and public leaderboard results sometimes disagreed, while a genetic programming model was excluded despite later showing complementary value.

The final solution combined 37 submission files, including 30 generated by the author and seven from public kernels. Diversity came from different combinations of face embeddings, VGGFace versus Facenet features, and fully connected layer configurations. The strongest individual model combined features from both extractors and scored 0.893 on the public leaderboard. Weighted combination performed slightly better than simple averaging, with model quality and low correlation driving the ensemble gains.

The pipeline retrieved candidate image pairs with DINOv2/Base and cheaply filtered them using ALIKED descriptor distances before expensive LightGlue matching. It pruned the match graph to reduce reconstruction cost and improve opportunities to reconstruct small clusters. NetworkX clustering preceded repeated pycolmap incremental reconstruction, followed by native COLMAP map merging and bundle adjustment. The reported public and private scores were 43.53 and 43.34.
compute: GPU used for descriptor-distance matrix computation; hardware and runtime unspecified

solution_title: 54th Place Solution: All I Need Is fastai, timm, and DINOv3
solution_summary: The solution fine-tuned DINOv3 Huge and Large vision transformers for image-based biomass regression and averaged 42 models across seeds, folds, and target configurations. Validation used three-fold StratifiedGroupKFold with species-based strata and Sampling_Date plus State groups. Auxiliary biomass, height, and NDVI targets supported representation learning, while final total biomass and GDM predictions were derived from three primary components. The ensemble achieved reported CV of 0.773948 and public score of 0.75, with a private score of 0.63. TTA, MixUp, CutMix, and several alternative models did not improve validation.
compute: Early validation: 2× T4, 15GB, 15 min/fold. Later Google Colab Pro training: A100 80GB, 45 min/fold for Huge; A100 40GB, 25 min/fold for Large; approximately $25.

solution_summary: The final approach trained convolutional networks with mixup and random frequency/time masking on curated data and two pseudo-labeled datasets. Pseudo-labels came from high-confidence windows selected using the ratio of top-k activations to total activations, with a second dataset assigning clip-level labels from selected windows. Training combined separate losses for curated data and both pseudo-label sets, and inference used the same window-scanning strategy. Test-targeted fine-tuning reached about 0.76 but was deliberately excluded from the final submission.

The solution used batch-separated cross-validation, with nine Citeseq folds and twelve Multiome folds, and found that local gains closely tracked leaderboard gains. PCA and truncated SVD supplied reduced representations, while shallow LightGBM models selected target-specific Citeseq features. Citeseq combined single-target and multi-target neural networks with LightGBM and CatBoost; Multiome used three multi-target neural networks and CatBoost. A simple blend restricted weights to 0, 1, 2, or 3 and achieved local scores of 0.9039 for Citeseq and 0.669 for Multiome.

solution_title: 24th (-2.633) - haha nice - pairs of pairs of ...
solution_summary: The solution modeled interactions between molecular connections using shared neural networks over connection types and Euclidean distances. Pointwise convolutions and summation produced features invariant to connection ordering, translation and orthogonal transformations. A second interaction stage captured pairs of aggregated pair features, improving the reported score from -2.126 to -2.473. The best submission blended predictions and scored -2.633, while a further interaction stage could not be trained sufficiently within the available time.

solution_summary: The post describes a lightweight field-aware factorization machine implementation based on libffm. Its stated focus is optimized out-of-core performance. The implementation contributed to the competition solution, while further details are deferred to an accompanying PDF.

The solution rasterized raw and simplified strokes into three-channel images encoding stroke order, motion, and timing information. ImageNet-pretrained InceptionResNetV2 was the strongest single model, achieving a local validation score of 0.9516 with 139×139 inputs from raw drawings. Training used Adam, followed by a stage with gradient accumulation and a loss combining 10% categorical cross-entropy with 90% top-three loss. The final ensemble combined InceptionResNetV2, Xception, and ResNet50 predictions using weights based on local validation scores and correlations between predicted classes.

The solution used a single EfficientNet-B0 with an FPN and an auxiliary four-class defect classifier sharing encoder features. Training proceeded through three stages, adding pseudo-labeled test images and Dice loss before incorporating validation data for final training. The final weights averaged five checkpoints, and training used 256×512 crops. Inference skipped decoding when the classification head predicted no defect, used a fixed 0.5 classification threshold, and applied TorchScript tracing without test-time augmentation.

solution_title: LB61th PB72th solution & Please tell me your opinion!
solution_summary: The solution combined CWT image classifiers and raw-signal 1D CNNs using weights derived from out-of-fold ridge coefficients. Larger image inputs and EfficientNet models performed well, while ViT and Swin improved ensemble diversity despite lower individual validation scores. Positive ensemble weights were preferable on the private leaderboard, with the ensemble reaching 0.8783. CQT, a convolutional transformer encoder, and autoencoder anomaly detection did not improve results.

solution_title: 4th place solution - LB probing, acronym detection, and NER
solution_summary: The solution combined rule-based acronym extraction, string matching against several dataset-name inventories, and NER-based detection of name variants. Leaderboard probing estimated hidden-test properties and guided submission selection by evaluating predictions with training-label matches removed. A spaCy NER model learned from training labels, extracted acronyms, and external government dataset names, then supplied variants filtered by Jaccard similarity. Adding training-name and acronym matches produced final public and private scores of 0.614 and 0.513.
external_data: ["U.S. government dataset names", "Rich Context competition data"]

solution_summary: The final TensorFlow 2.0 solution combined BERT joint large and base models through weighted averaging of their logits. Removing duplicate answer spans and suppressing YES/NO answers improved predictions, while validation selected separate long- and short-answer thresholds. A cross-window span selection method improved private performance but was omitted from the chosen submission because it did not improve the public score. Experiments ran on free Colab TPUs, while late PyTorch TPU experiments were not completed.
compute: Google Colab free-tier TPUs for all experiments

solution_title: [5th Place Solution in Efficiency Prize] 327th Place in Private LB
solution_summary: The solution adapted a public baseline with Byte-Pair Encoding and an ensemble of three ComplementNB variants, three SGDClassifier variants, and one LGBMClassifier. Training data came from the DAIGT V2 dataset, with ten sources selected according to leaderboard improvements and prompt restrictions applied to three sources. SGD models used class weights, while LightGBM's n_iter was reduced to 300 to shorten inference. The author also tried batching tokenizer input to accelerate processing, although its benefit was uncertain.

The team built its optimization loop largely from public code and submissions. It accelerated some code with AI assistance, randomized run arguments, and repeatedly merged results from short parallel runs. The solution improved the best solution in 11 boxes by about 0.0002 overall, although it added little beyond another strong public solution.
compute: Primarily a newer 16-core miniPC and parallel Kaggle CPU runs.

solution_summary: The author shares source code for their contribution to a team solution. The brief description credits teammates with next-click features using specific sorting and weights-of-evidence features. The author reports that their best single-model leaderboard score improved from 0.9815 to 0.9828 over ten days, but gives no detailed modeling or validation pipeline.

The solution combined two pipelines in which 2.5D Faster R-CNN detectors supplied region features to DeiT-Small transformers. Training on all anatomical planes addressed unreliable image-orientation metadata, while inference used the plane requiring the least interpolation. The detector variants used ResNet-50 with three slices and ConvNeXtV2-Tiny with five slices, followed by transformer aggregation into location and aneurysm-presence predictions. Weighted averaging achieved a private score of 0.80592, improving over either individual transformer pipeline.

solution_title: 5th Place Solution: Diversity and Bug - Both Are All You Need
solution_summary: The solution blends distilled HGNetV2 and EfficientNet CNNs with ProtoSSM and a distilled SED baseline. Training combines competition focal recordings and labeled soundscapes, with focal-only validation guiding model selection. Distillation provided the largest gains, followed by augmentation and architecture changes. Shifted-window inference, temporal smoothing, and file-level scaling improved predictions, while multiplicative frequency augmentation in the dB domain unexpectedly added more than 0.01 in partial testing.

The solution combined seven XGBoost binary classifiers, each predicting whether the ordinal response exceeded a different threshold, and summed their probabilities. Features included product dummy variables, medical keyword counts, and target-derived keyword summaries. Iterative boundary optimization maximized kappa, including separate boundaries for subsets defined by selected binary variables. Repeated and nested cross-validation guided calibration evaluation, and some solutions were combined using median predictions. The highest private score reported was 0.68002, although that submission was not selected for the final pair.

solution_title: [2nd place] My approach - LightGBM quantile regression
solution_summary: The author trained LightGBM models to predict each bandit's original threshold and selected actions greedily using decay-adjusted predictions. The strongest variant switched between the 60th percentile prediction before step 750 and the 65th percentile afterward, achieving a reported score of 1521.1. Training used 20,000–30,000 selected competition episodes, with features capturing rewards, decay-adjusted hit rates, opponent actions, recency, and relative ranks. Local evaluation used win rate and cumulative chosen-threshold differences, with the latter providing a more stable comparison than rewards. Reinforcement learning and quantile regression below the median were unsuccessful.

The solution repeatedly ran LKH from the best available arrangement, perturbing permutation assignments between three strings. It initialized from the standard permutation sequence, swapped selected one-cycles, removed redundant non-mandatory permutations, and introduced wildcards. Thousands of runs produced a score of 2431 before progress stalled. Adding wildcard support to LKH MinMax CTSP and running it overnight improved the score to 2430.
compute: Thousands of LKH runs, followed by an overnight LKH MinMax CTSP run.

solution_summary: The team's best single model combined text representations, image quality features, aggregate features, and Ridge-derived features. Text inputs included SVD features, TF-IDF over descriptions and titles, and title counts. NIMA supplied image quality features, and the reported public leaderboard score was around 2210 as written in the post. The underlying final estimator and exact ensemble composition were not specified.

solution_title: A solution that I hope will earn a silver medal (currently in 29th place)
solution_summary: The team extended the public Relicbound bot with five rule-based modifications. Ships intensified relic searches when scoring indicated undiscovered rewards, accumulated energy while harvesting, and used SAP attacks to disrupt opponents. A coordinated attack near the end of the game targeted opposing harvest areas. Board-change prediction improved routing, while score-based occupancy estimates enabled attacks on unseen opponents.

solution_title: 81st Place Solution for Bengali.Ai Speech Recognition.
solution_summary: The approach fine-tuned Wav2Vec2 using the normalized Bengali Common Voice 13 dataset. Training ran for 15 epochs with a learning rate of 1e-4. Optuna optimized decoding parameters, selecting alpha 0.3802723523729998, beta 0.053996879617918436, and a beam width of 1024. The reported public scores were 0.432 and 0.435, with both submissions scoring 0.518 on the private evaluation.

solution_title: Kaggle's The Hunt for Prohibited Content Competition
solution_summary: The solution used logistic regression in Vowpal Wabbit with text features, raw advertisement fields, and feature interactions. Combining ranked predictions from the full-data model and a model trained on proven blocked and unblocked advertisements improved performance. Log loss consistently outperformed the other tested losses, while combining models using different losses did not help. The implementation included grid search, sample weighting, and bootstrap bagging, and achieved a score of 0.98527.

solution_title: AdaBoost, SSD: object detection for lions counting
solution_summary: The approach progressed from AdaBoost detectors to a VGG-based Single Shot Multibox Detector, ultimately using large image tiles. Square training boxes were constructed around annotated dots, and resizing plus tiling improved pup detection. Attempts to combine multiscale features, learn image scale, and add a counting regression objective were unsuccessful. Stacking provided a further improvement of about 1.5 leaderboard points.
compute: AdaBoost evaluation: about one hour per model on CPU; full-image SSD testing: about one hour on GPU; tiled approach: about eight hours on GPU.

solution_summary: The solution used a U-Net with an EfficientB3 encoder, trained on resized overlapping TIFF tiles and additional hand-labeled data. Five folds were balanced by example count, and global Dice was used to evaluate models. Cross-entropy training followed by Lovasz softmax fine-tuning and Adam with SAM improved performance and stability. Center-crop stitching was the largest reported inference improvement, while model ensembles did not improve results and submissions mostly used a single model.

solution_title: [Updated] Solution sharing: Private LB 0.695 in 12 mins
solution_summary: The post shares a notebook reproducing a submission that scored above 0.69. Its main described technique is GPU-based CSV reading and label encoding with RAPIDS. The author reports a 40-fold speedup compared with pandas on CPU, but does not describe the predictive model or validation setup.

solution_summary: The post announces a promised benchmark script for the competition. It claims the script can exceed 0.80 on the public leaderboard and that modifications improve its performance. The provided text contains no model or pipeline details.

The pipeline used an unchanged public retrieval implementation followed by a fine-tuned Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct reranker. Fine-tuning presented shuffled candidate misconceptions containing the correct option and the retriever's top eight choices. The final predictions combined one fine-tuned-model inference run with multiple runs of a public AWQ model. This improved public/private scores from 0.503/0.464 to 0.529/0.493, although slow inference limited further experiments.
