The solution ensembled YOLO-V4 detectors trained on individual radiologists and on merged annotations from all radiologists. A specialized detector trained on selected annotators and two disease classes supplied replacement predictions for aortic enlargement. Classifier-based post-processing substantially improved the detector ensemble. The final reported scores were 0.348 public and 0.305 private.

The author formulated wellbore prediction as two-dimensional alignment using a ConvNeXt-backed U-Net and probability-map losses. Engineered gamma-ray features, calibrated typewell signals, particle-filter outputs and spatial-neighbor estimates supplied complementary information. Strong geological and signal augmentations improved robustness, while spatial-neighbor features were retained based on local validation despite worse public results. A reliability-dependent weighted ensemble achieved CV RMSE 4.627 and private RMSE 5.639.

solution_title: 42nd place submission | jumped 880 places = lucky seed?
solution_summary: The solution primarily used BERTweet, following the author's previously shared notebook and retaining seed 777. It substituted RoBERTa predictions whenever BERTweet encountered an unknown token. BERTweet was preferred because its performance varied less across folds, although both models had similar CV and public scores. The substitution increased the reported private score from 0.718 to 0.719, with final public score 0.712 and CV 0.709.

The post announces that Team Algorithm's papers and slides are available on an external website. It invites comments from readers. No solution methods or implementation details appear in the post itself.

The team's best single model was RoBERTa-Large with an attention head, improved through layer-wise learning rate decay and layer reinitialization. It used five folds and five training epochs with a maximum sequence length of 256, achieving scores of 0.467 on the public leaderboard and 0.468 on the private leaderboard. The final solution combined two shared notebook models with their own best model using weights of 0.35, 0.35, and 0.30. This ensemble achieved 0.457 on both leaderboards.

The author's contribution combined a basic tabular approach with features extracted from fMRI component maps. Predicting four domain targets from out-of-fold age predictions and then modeling their residuals with FNC and loading features improved the leaderboard score by 0.0002. Regional fMRI summary statistics fed into LightGBM were useful in blends for domain2_var2. Out-of-fold imputation improved cross-validation without improving the leaderboard, while t-SNE and UMAP exploration did not produce a clear benefit.

solution_title: [2nd Efficiency Solution] In a few words
solution_summary: The author used DAIGT V2 and modified essays with a fixed topic prefix, separator tokens, and a padding suffix. A classification ensemble with weights of 0.08, 0.46, and 0.46 was combined with a regression model using 28 engineered features. The final predictions weighted the classification ensemble at 0.4 and the regressor at 0.6, achieving a reported public leaderboard score of 0.917. Transformers, ridge methods, alternative vectorizations, and heavier ensembles failed to improve the result despite some strong validation scores.

The solution ensembles five 3D U-Nets with pretrained ResNet3D encoders and pixel-shuffle decoders. Encoder regularization, auxiliary segmentation heads, EMA, and heavy augmentation improve generalization. Training first fits the decoder on simulated data with the encoder frozen, then fine-tunes all parameters on competition data. Overlapping inference with central-patch predictions improves scores, and final postprocessing corrections for mask and coordinate errors produced the author's best submissions.

The solution used coordinate-independent crystal geometry features with XGBoost. It constructed 80 radial-distribution features and 80 angular-distribution features for nearby atoms. Predicted formation energy became an additional input for band-gap prediction, producing a local CV score of 0.049 and public score of 0.0515. Direct density functional theory calculations were insufficiently accurate under the available CPU budget.
compute: A few minutes of CPU time per crystal for the unsuccessful density functional theory approach.

solution_title: Andrew Newell and Lewis Griffin on winning the ICDAR 2011 Competition
solution_summary: The method represented handwriting with multiscale oriented Basic Image Feature column histograms. Root-normalized histograms were expressed as deviations from the training mean and classified with Euclidean nearest neighbours. Test-set distance analysis and assignment constraints helped handle potentially unknown authors. A final reassignment using an unused author's second-nearest match eliminated the public error, while both later entries achieved zero final error.

The author's best submission came from a deliberately simple baseline. It used regression to impute missing training values and Optuna to optimize hyperparameters before prediction. The author accidentally omitted imputation on the test set and emphasized the risks of overfitting the public leaderboard.

The team obtained public test labels through leaderboard probing and incorporated them into training. Most models used YOLO or Faster R-CNN detections to create crops, followed by bagged image classifiers with ResNet50 and VGG16 backbones. Hill climbing selected an ensemble using two-fold validation split between the public training and test sets. The ensemble also included a custom model and a U-Net-based model, while only one model used the additional training data.

The final submission used separate default-parameter Ridge regression models for each target pair, with logarithmic returns as the only feature. Additional features and more complex nonlinear or time-series approaches did not consistently improve the baseline. Rolling backtests showed strong variation across market regimes, and combining Ridge with mean predictions reduced its upside without compensating for its lows. An unintended one-day lag in inference features worsened retrospective performance.
compute: Training <5 seconds; inference <5 seconds.

solution_summary: The author's best-performing agent came from a few modifications to the example agent. They also implemented Q-learning, but that agent performed poorly and may have contained bugs. A strategy-based attempt exposed a delayed-reward problem because kore totals change only after ships return. DQN and strategy-based reinforcement learning were suggested as directions for further work.

The solution ensembled U-Nets with squeeze-and-excitation blocks and several encoder families on ash-color images. Progressive training increased image resolution, followed by a final stage that removed flip and transpose augmentations while retaining affine or perspective transforms. This staged augmentation strategy improved validation from 0.6756 to 0.6838. Training used Dice loss and the provided train/validation split, with no test-time augmentation.

solution_title: Part of 3rd Place Sol: Multi-label Classifier-based PP
solution_summary: This component postprocessed detector predictions using image-level classifier probabilities. The final approach combined three EfficientNet-B4 multilabel classifiers trained with radiologist-agreement soft targets and different image sizes or aspect-ratio handling. Class-specific thresholds determined when classifier scores multiplied detector box confidences. This improved the public score to 0.348, but its private score of 0.305 matched the simpler class14-only multiplication approach.

solution_title: Silver medal in three days of work
solution_summary: The solution used tabular features and a simple neural network trained with pinball loss at quantiles 0.2, 0.5, and 0.8. Patient-grouped three-fold validation used only the last three measurements per patient and initial Percent values to better match test conditions. Features included initial FVC and Percent, a sex–smoking-status interaction, and group statistics, with selection driven by validation performance. Image features, linear regression, LightGBM, and ensembles of those alternatives did not improve the results.

solution_title: PB 68th solution and all code(No hack)
solution_summary: The author shares their team's competition code and ideas. The 2–2.5D models start with BCE plus Dice loss and later switch to Dice alone, while randomly zeroing depth channels improved the score by about 0.01. A native-resolution patch transformer then corrected residuals, followed by a physical-reference drift corrector based on measured versus typewell GR agreement. The solution trained a neural network from scratch using 96 days of player history, dense embedding layers, residual blocks, and a GRU with hidden size 128. Randomly masking up to 32 recent days of historical targets simulated the missing-target interval encountered during evaluation. The final predictions averaged the six checkpoints with the lowest validation losses and were clipped to 0–100; alternative sequence architectures and normalization layers did not improve results.

solution_summary: The author built a low-variance ensemble of 95 EfficientNet models spanning B0–B7, ImageNet and Noisy Student initialization, and image sizes from 256 to 1024. solution_title: Heuristics for bit, cryptarithm and equations
solution_summary: The author extended a baseline puzzle-reasoning solution with symbolic search and heuristics for bit manipulation, cryptarithms, and equation puzzles. Bit manipulation used a compact three-argument function basis and candidate filtering, but excessive brute-force reasoning prevented effective deployment. Cryptarithms used operation restrictions, modular constraints, and constrained branching, although a late training attempt appeared to overfit. The practical improvement came mainly from equation operator-inference rules, which added roughly 50 solved tasks.

solution_title: Silver with a one-line Notify prompt
solution_summary: The final approach used a single short Notify message that induced an email tool call and triggered the CONFUSED_DEPUTY rule. Candidates used distinct recipients and were retained only after the tool call actually succeeded. The author measured replay latency and tailored prompts to the two models to fit hundreds of successful candidates within the time budget. Each successful candidate earned six raw points, while additional turns and bundled requests reduced efficiency or reliability.

solution_title: Multi-agent RL Silver solution by 3Comets, 14th place
solution_summary: The final approach used multi-agent PPO with shared actor parameters, individual agent observations, and a critic that could see both teams without fog. Manually calculating relic fragment locations and switching to full-map 47×47 egocentric observations produced a major improvement after unsuccessful recurrent-memory experiments. The final network used convolutions with residual connections, basic action masking, and sampled actions. Training the latest submission took 15 days on one RTX 4090, while reward design and agent coordination remained limitations.
compute: Latest submission: 15 days on one RTX 4090, about 30 million update steps and over 1 billion environment steps; all experiments cost about USD 500 on vast.ai.

solution_summary: The solution added 400 uniqueness-based features to the 200 raw variables, using real test samples when determining which values were unique. It trained LightGBM and a custom neural network with shared feature processing and attention-like weighted pooling. Both models used class-conditioned shuffling augmentation and confident test pseudo-labels, with stratified ten-fold validation and multiple seeds. The neural network reached 0.92546 private AUC, while LightGBM reached 0.92332; their final blend weighted the neural network 2.1 to 1.

The solution used disease-specific point detectors to locate regions of interest, followed by classification of those regions. Separate disease classifiers and a combined multimodal classifier used 2.5D CNNs, GRUs, and attention heads with ResNet50 and SE-ResNeXt50 backbones. Random ROI jitter improved robustness to localization errors, while severe-category oversampling addressed class imbalance. Final predictions used weighted model averaging and probability scaling by 1.3.

The solution used iterative noisy-student-style self-training, first ensembling image models to pseudo-label external pet images and then retraining with the expanded data. A second pseudo-labeling round modestly improved CV and allowed inference with only two test-time augmentations. The final ensemble combined Swin, EfficientNet, ViT, NFNet, and ConvNeXt models from different training rounds. SVR ensembling improved CV and later proved stronger on the private leaderboard, but was excluded because its public leaderboard performance had dropped.

solution_title: 86-th(bronze) writeup - solution description and lessons learned.
solution_summary: The final submission voted across five public-leaderboard-selected submissions, each itself combining five folds of EfficientNet-B4 U-Net or FPN models. Training used BCE or BCE-Dice loss, reflective geometric augmentation, RAdam, and separate encoder and decoder learning-rate schedules. Voting required four of five masks to be nonempty and at least two positive votes per pixel. Single models exceeded 0.66 public score, while TTA generally helped private performance and pseudo labeling did not work.

The solution estimated path shape using a generalized linear distance model and magnetic-field directions, then aligned Wi-Fi location predictions to that shape. Per-path simulated annealing tuned Wi-Fi hyperparameters and model weights. Wall-aware path refinement and probabilistic waypoint transitions produced a final snapped trajectory through repeated forward and backward passes. Predicted test positions were subsequently fed back into the Wi-Fi model and training data.
compute: Per-path optimization ran for several weeks; hardware unspecified.

solution_summary: The final system used an ImageNet-pretrained EfficientNet-B3 adapted to six-channel images, AdaCos metric learning, and metadata embeddings. Training combined image and color augmentation with late-stage CutMix and interpolation of metadata embeddings. A staged freezing and fine-tuning schedule used AdamW and repeated one-cycle schedules. Inference extracted embeddings with three test-time augmentations and used FAISS cosine similarity search; several domain adaptation and embedding clustering approaches did not improve the basic setup.

solution_title: 13th Place Team (a story from a Kaggle newbie's view)
solution_summary: The team combined diverse image-to-molecule models predicting InChI, SMILES, and SELFIES representations. Their main contribution was a merge pipeline that first selected chemically valid predictions, recovered additional valid molecules from epoch-specific inference, and then resolved competing valid outputs through voting and minimum distance. Model diversity, including Transformers and CNN–recurrent architectures, substantially strengthened the merged predictions. The merged leaderboard score eventually reached 0.62; pseudo-labeling improved individual models but did not improve the merged score.

solution_title: 13-th place solution [Knowledge Distillation helps a lot]
solution_summary: The solution trained an OpenCLIP ViT-H backbone with a projection head and ArcFace loss on several image datasets. Two-thirds of the transformer blocks were frozen, while the remaining blocks and projection head used different learning rates. Relational knowledge distillation compressed 256-dimensional embeddings to 64 dimensions and outperformed adaptive average pooling. The distilled model scored 0.663 publicly and 0.666 privately, exceeding direct training of a 64-dimensional projection.

The image model used an EVA02-small backbone, GeM pooling, and an MLP for tabular inputs, concatenating image and tabular representations. An auxiliary cosine embedding loss targeted 1024-dimensional embeddings from multilingual-e5-large, while negative downsampling preserved examples with high false-positive rates. The combined image-model changes achieved a reported leaderboard score of 0.161. The tabular pipeline incorporated image predictions and features from another notebook, retuned hyperparameters, and ensembled three seeds.

A single 3D U-Net predicted segmentation masks, and connected components converted them into localized detections. Seven-fold validation held out one sample at a time and evaluated all held-out predictions together. Larger patches, interior-only loss and prediction assignment, balanced patch sampling, and tailored augmentation improved validation. The reported CV score was 0.7781, with public and private scores of 0.72782 and 0.71783.

solution_title: 9th place solution (a lot of LGBMs blended)
solution_summary: The solution trained many default LightGBM regressors across different historical window lengths and forecast horizons. Inputs and targets were normalized by each region's historical maximum, and recent training dates received exponentially greater weight. Predictions were aggregated using their minimum, maximum, and mean, then transformed into quantile forecasts using coefficients optimized on the last 30 days of validation data. A horizon-dependent deviation factor adjusted forecast uncertainty for later dates.

The author reviews experiments with multiple ensemble strategies, including combinations of neural networks and gradient-boosted trees. Similar CV and public leaderboard results often produced substantially different private scores, preventing a clear choice of ensemble complexity or model mix. Some strong private submissions were neither the best CV nor the best public submissions. The post also highlights distillation, columnwise temporal modeling, and TabNet ensembles learned from other competitors, without claiming to have used them.

The author combined BEiT-large and two Swin-large models in an optimized weighted ensemble. All models used ten folds, mixup, binary cross-entropy with logits, gradient accumulation, and test-time augmentation. Adding an SVR head improved the high-resolution Swin model, while including BEiT improved diversity beyond a Swin-only ensemble. The final ensemble achieved CV 17.121 and private leaderboard RMSE 16.936.

The solution uses a modified RetinaNet with an SE-ResNeXt101 backbone on 512 by 512 images. Smaller anchors, auxiliary whole-image classification, loss computation on images without boxes, and classification dropout improved detection and training behavior. Predictions from four stratified folds and nearby checkpoints are averaged before thresholds and NMS. A percentile-based adjustment shrinks predicted boxes to approximate the test labeling process, and training takes about 12 epochs at one hour per epoch on a 1080 Ti.

solution_summary: The solution trained several image-captioning architectures, generated diverse InChI candidates with beam search, and reranked those candidates. solution_title: [4255th solution] From Spectral Filters to a Learned Policy
solution_summary: The approach predicts Q = TVT + depth and recovers TVT by subtracting observed depth, using well geometry as evidence about formation structure. Development progressed from spectral transfer functions to spline coefficient prediction with an error critic, then PPO-based sequential path generation. The final version selects between actor and conservative base paths using out-of-fold performance, shrinks predictions toward the last observation, and weights fold predictions by inverse squared validation RMSE. Reported performance improved from 15.565 to 12.016 private RMSE across the four versions.

The solution used a single XGBoost model trained on May through December data. Product ownership lags and customer characteristics from the following month provided the main features, alongside total product counts. Income gaps were filled using provincial averages, categorical variables were one-hot encoded, and selected low-impact categories were grouped together. The author evaluated the model with five-fold cross-validation and multiclass log loss.

solution_title: simple trick to silver for any open source code!
solution_summary: The approach adjusts image and text matching thresholds according to the number of initial matches. It tightens the threshold when multiple matches exist, retaining the original matches if tightening leaves too few. For singleton results, it relaxes the threshold and returns at most two matches. The author reports public and private scores of 0.744 and 0.732 after applying this trick to open-source pipelines.

The final system weighted TF-IDF predictions at 0.85 and DeBERTa predictions at 0.15. TF-IDF used vocabulary derived from the test set, while DeBERTa trained on a broad balanced corpus of human text and LLM continuations. Semantic filtering diversified the source corpus, and paired random truncation prevented text length from becoming a label shortcut. Several alternatives, including style fine-tuning, spelling-based methods, and direct Mistral classification, were unsuccessful or abandoned.

solution_title: 7th place solution 🥇 : The very simple method !
solution_summary: The author adapted an existing NCAA baseline that used seed information, team averages, an EOL ratio, and GLM-based team strength. solution_summary: The approach used LightGBM with Tweedie loss, training 24 models across six time-series folds and four weekly forecast blocks. Validation used 250 weeks of training and four weeks of validation, with level-12 aggregation weights in the gradients and WRMSSE-based early stopping. Calendar, price, rolling-sales, and nearby-event features supported the forecasts, while identifying out-of-stock zeros provided the largest reported validation gain. The team used simulated annealing over unrestricted word permutations for sentence IDs 1–4, with simple traveling-salesman-style neighbor moves. solution_summary: The solution combined spatial-domain and DCT-domain CNNs through a second-level fully connected network trained on their bottleneck features. The spatial model preserved higher resolution and used squeeze-and-excitation attention, while the DCT model processed one-hot-encoded frequency coefficients. Layer normalization, Softplus activations, gated messages, and separate prediction heads for coupling types improved the architecture. Angle-aware edge-to-edge convolutions produced the strongest individual model, improving performance at a substantial speed cost. Adding model checkpoints expanded the stacking inputs to 50 predictions and improved the reported leaderboard score from -3.13 to -3.15.
compute: 1 GTX 1080 Ti for 2 months; RTX 2080 Ti allocations of 1 month and 3 months; 1 rented V100 for 2 months and 4 rented V100s for 2 weeks.

solution_summary: The final pipeline combined pretrained LoFTR, SuperGlue, and DKM matches, followed by MAGSAC++ estimation. Model-specific resizing and fixed keypoint budgets were central, with DKM particularly sensitive to image dimensions. Changes were assessed using both local training-data validation and the public leaderboard. An alternative keypoint allocation achieved a private score of 0.822, although its weaker local and public results made selection difficult.

The team trained Ridge, LightGBM, and RoBERTa models on earlier Jigsaw data, Ruddit, and a Jigsaw regression dataset. Features included TF-IDF, reduced sparse text representations, embeddings, and word and character counts. Validation used the supplied validation data after removing overlapping training sentences. Predictions were min-max scaled and combined with weights optimized on CV, producing an ensemble score of 0.7048.
external_data: ["Jigsaw Toxic Comment Classification Challenge", "Ruddit Jigsaw dataset", "Jigsaw regression data"]

solution_title: Kaggle Melbourne University AES/MathWorks/NIH Seizure Prediction challenge - Winning Solution
solution_summary: The team combined 11 subject-specific EEG models by averaging ranked predictions with equal weights. Models used short-window spectral, statistical, correlation, and information-theoretic features with XGBoost, nearest neighbors, linear SVM, and generalized linear classifiers. Window predictions were aggregated into ten-minute probabilities using maxima or means depending on the model group. Validation preserved one-hour sequences through two complementary fold schemes, and the released ensemble reported a private score of 0.80856 with a noted reproducibility difference from the competition submission.
compute: Alex/Gilberto's four models took less than half a day including feature extraction; Feng's four models took less than five hours on an 8 GB RAM MacBook Pro.

solution_summary: The solution used asynchronous agents to optimize individual ONNX programs, supported by a persistent version registry and a shared catalogue of optimization idioms. Local evaluation and grouped leaderboard probes identified correct models before submission assembly. The final selection balanced model scores against total runtime rather than choosing every task's highest-scoring version. The submission achieved a local score of 8,142.02 and contained many single-node programs, particularly Einsum graphs.
compute: Runtime constrained final model selection; some Einsum programs required hours on one CPU.

solution_summary: The solution combined a slice-screening group, a 2.5D segmentation group, and a 3D segmentation group. EfficientNet U-Nets identified empty slices, while EfficientNet U-Nets and ConvNeXt UPerNets segmented positive slices alongside volumetric SegResNets. Training used model-specific slice selection, segmentation losses, geometric augmentation, and a second cosine-annealed stage for 3D models. Final predictions merged 3D and 2.5D logits with weights of 0.4 and 0.6 before thresholding.

The author used different imputation approaches for different column groups. The final F_4 approach used a dense neural network in Keras and TensorFlow, while F_1 and F_3 combined linear models with descriptive statistics. Earlier experiments included mean and median imputation, iterative imputation, and boosted tree models. Public notebooks about missing-value counts and neural imputation helped guide development.

The solution represented each molecule relative to a source atom using normalized coordinates and atom-type and coupling-type embeddings, without graph features. Its final Atomic Transformer stacked encoder layers without positional encoding and projected atom outputs to scalar couplings. Fourteen models with varying widths and depths formed an ensemble scoring -3.22349 on the private leaderboard, while the best single model scored -3.16234. The input representation was central, and dropout, auxiliary multitask learning, rotation-based TTA, and deeper decoders did not help.

solution_title: 4978th Place Solution - everything was known from the beginning🤣
solution_summary: The post describes overwriting predictions with values of 0.0 and 1.0. The author reports success in cross-validation and on the public leaderboard, followed by failure on the private leaderboard. No underlying model or rule for deciding which predictions to overwrite is provided.

solution_title: 8th Place Solution: Clova Vision, NAVER/LINE Corp.
solution_summary: The team clustered unlabeled test and index images into virtual classes and filtered noisy images to construct several training sets. Its final representation concatenated four normalized CNN descriptors with different backbones, pooling methods, losses, and training data. A sampled stage-two validation set guided feature ensemble selection. Database augmentation, query expansion, PCA whitening to 1024 dimensions, and DELF-assisted diffusion improved retrieval, with database augmentation and query expansion providing the largest reported gain.

solution_title: Story behind the 32nd place (top 1%) with 2 submissions
solution_summary: The author manually engineered 1,003 features from all available tables using the column descriptions and domain understanding. LightGBM models were tuned with five-fold random cross-validation, followed by many runs with different seeds and splits, mostly using ten folds. Final submissions used either an average of the top 30 runs or ridge stacking of the top 60 runs. Ridge stacking achieved a reported private score of 0.80043.

solution_title: Code sharing (60th position on private leaderboard)
solution_summary: The solution combined XGBoost and random forest classifiers trained on either all available data or recent data only. Weighted voting gave greater influence to the recent-data classifiers to account for the temporal boundary between training and testing. Categorical variables were one-hot encoded, session activity was represented by frequency counts, and rare categories were grouped into an other category. Cross-validation with a simplified NDCG score guided tuning and evaluation.

solution_title: 1st Place Solution — Five-Model Ensemble with Length-Adaptive Allocation
solution_summary: The solution allocated five RNA structure predictions across template-based modeling, Boltz2, RNAPro, DRFold2, and Protenix according to sequence length. Structural diversity was central because evaluation selected the best of five predictions. Template matching anchored medium and long sequences, while short sequences relied primarily on learned structure predictors. Geometric template corrections, confidence-based candidate selection, and chunked Protenix inference supported the pipeline, which achieved a final private score of 0.49669.

The team stacked diverse speech models using multiple audio representations, CNN and RNN architectures, and speaker-grouped out-of-fold predictions. A second layer of tree models and neural networks fed a weighted geometric mean whose weights were learned under nonnegative, sum-to-one constraints. Dedicated silence detection replaced an earlier confidence-and-power heuristic, while a synthetic double-word model handled unfamiliar words. Validation correlated poorly with the public leaderboard, so final submission selection relied on public results and alternative blends.
compute: XGBoost took approximately 8 hours for ten folds on GPU or 14 hours on CPU; LightGBM took 15 minutes on CPU.

solution_summary: The solution ensembled EfficientNet and RegNet backbones in a multiple instance learning architecture with attention pooling over eight large image tiles, ignoring the other class. Tissue-focused tiling and magnification-matched TMA crops supported efficient processing of large slides. Training used heavy augmentation, stochastic weight averaging, some synthetic TMAs, and label cleaning that removed about 5% of images and relabeled eight. External ovarian histopathology slides supplemented training, while light test-time augmentation supported inference.
compute: 3 CPU cores for multiprocessing during tiling; 20–30 training epochs per model.
external_data: ["Ovarian Carcinoma Histopathology Dataset (SFU)", "UBC ovarian cancer competition supplemental masks"]

solution_summary: The final submission used a single DeBERTa-base model trained for six epochs on one fold. Alongside the six original targets, the authors trained on 12 auxiliary targets describing vocabulary, readability, parts of speech, and grammar errors. These scores were normalized to the range 1–5 to help the model learn intermediate signals of essay quality. Hyperparameters were explored using a public baseline notebook as a reference.

The solution trained a U-Net on false-color satellite imagery with a pretrained ResNet50 encoder. Upscaling to 384 × 384 and then downscaling to 256 × 256 with bilinear interpolation helped refine boundary annotations. Moving from a scratch U-Net through a pretrained ResNet26 encoder to ResNet50 improved the reported Dice score to 0.64985 public and 0.64455 private. PyTorch Lightning supported multi-GPU training, while temporal LSTMConv modeling and an extra input convolution did not improve results.
compute: Multiple GPUs; count and type unspecified.

solution_summary: The solution trained 70 LightGBM models, one for each store and department combination, using a Tweedie objective. Training used data from 2014 onward and weighted samples by recent dollar sales. Demand lags, rolling statistics, price features, and leakage-free rolling target encodings supplied the main predictors. Temporal validation guided forecasting choices for each segment and permutation importance removed unhelpful variables.

The author tested graph, language, descriptor, and fingerprint approaches for polymer property prediction. Graph predictors and edge-prediction graph encoders worked well, while ChemBERTa features and adding unlabelled data did not help. XGBoost was the strongest tested regressor, and feature selection mattered because many generated features were unhelpful. Training on the initially released data gave the best results, with a reported best leaderboard score of 0.093.

solution_title: 32nd place solution - what worked for me
solution_summary: The author used species-specific frequency crops and losses designed for sparse audio labels. Training progressed through three BCE pseudo-labeling stages and two additional stages with a soft-label-compatible ranking loss. Positive-only feature pooling, audio augmentation, and full-spectrogram inference were also used. An EfficientNet-B0 fold-zero ensemble across three seeds achieved 0.927 publicly, while five-fold ensembling worsened the score; the author expressed uncertainty about individual improvements.

solution_title: Thank you all! First time competition, silver medal! My blending nn+tabnet+resnet
solution_summary: The final solution blended a neural network, TabNet, and ResNet. The neural network achieved a public score of 0.01832, while ResNet achieved 0.01861. TabNet was adapted from a shared notebook and included without an independently measured submission score because the author had exhausted submissions.

solution_title: From Cell Segmentation to Ancient Scrolls: WNet3D + nnUNet (LB 113, 0.582)
solution_summary: The pipeline trained WNet3D without labels to extract three structural feature maps, concatenated them with raw CT, and segmented surfaces with nnUNet ResEncUNetXL. The best result averaged two models using different WNet checkpoints and ground-truth versions, including manually cleaned labels and a boundary-aware loss. Sliding-window predictions with mirror augmentation were followed by hysteresis thresholding, z-closing, and small-component removal. The best private score was 0.582; tuned postprocessing and a TransUNet blend did not improve the approach, and the preprocessing benefit lacked a controlled leaderboard ablation.
compute: Initially 1×P100; later parallel inference on Kaggle 2×T4 GPUs. WNet checkpoints trained for 20 epochs with patch size 64 and 100 epochs with patch size 128.

solution_summary: The solution combined diverse CNN predictions from JPEG images with specialist weather, land, and single-class models. Five-fold out-of-fold predictions and 32-view test-time augmentation supplied inputs to second-level tree and neural classifiers. Spatial context came from averaged predictions for neighboring images and panoramas. The full pipeline required about a week on six GPUs.

solution_title: Climbing 1,649 Places by Ignoring the Leaderboard
solution_summary: The final pipeline combined a leak-stripped classical baseline with diverse neural models in a nonnegative ten-column stack. It modeled TVT plus Z, added an explicit pivot-anchored drift column, and applied uncertainty-modulated drift correction and boundary fading. Whole-well grouped and spatial validation governed every submission decision and rejected several apparent gains. Retraining twelve generative-model seeds on all 773 wells helped achieve public RMSE 6.579 and private RMSE 8.147.
compute: Final models retrained in the last 12 hours; final inference fit a 9-hour budget, while a 60-checkpoint version timed out.

solution_title: 19th Place Solution for the "ICR - Identifying Age-Related Conditions" Competition
solution_summary: The solution undersampled training data, filled missing values with zero, ordinal-encoded the categorical column, and min-max scaled other columns. The author compared several model families and ensembles using k-fold cross-validation with balanced log loss. The final ensemble combined XGBoost, CatBoost, HGBoost, LightGBM, Random Forest, and GBM models. The post does not report numerical validation or leaderboard scores.

This post reflects on mistakes made during participation rather than describing a reproducible solution. The author reports entering late, implementing an initial idea quickly, and making subsequent submissions mostly through hyperparameter changes. They emphasize insufficient dataset exploration and excessive commitment to one approach as lessons for future competitions.

The pipeline extracted DOI candidates from PDF documents using regular expressions and filtered them against the Data Citation Corpus. An LLM classified retained DOIs, while accession IDs were extracted with regular expressions and classified as primary or secondary. Corpus matching was more reliable than LLM-based DOI filtering. Additional LLM filtering of accession IDs did not improve performance over direct classification.

solution_title: 2nd Place - Weighted Box Fusion and Post Process
solution_summary: The solution combined ten long-sequence token-classification models, with 27 model-fold predictions used in the final submission. Predictions were averaged across folds within each model, processed with span-repair and discourse-specific rules, and combined using weighted boxes fusion. Post-processing improved cross-validation by approximately 0.008, while the fusion ensemble raised CV from roughly 0.700 for individual models to 0.741. Memory-saving training settings supported large models, and checkpoints were selected using the competition metric with post-processing included.
compute: V100 32GB and A100 40GB GPUs; approximately 4 hours per fold on one GPU for 3–5 epochs; final inference took 8 hours 30 minutes for 27 model-fold predictions.

solution_summary: The post describes selected findings from a final graph neural network ensemble and its feature engineering. Vienna RNA and its PERL scripts generated features including entropy and mountain plots, which helped private leaderboard performance despite some public score declines. An ensemble including an unscaled RNN performed worse, while WaveNet was the weakest individual model despite feature engineering and tuning. Full details of the final submission were left for a teammate to explain.

The final submission combined two 20-second EfficientNetV2-B3 sound-event detectors with a Perch-derived embedding and sequence branch, achieving private score 0.95531. The main detector learned from a taxon-specific blended teacher, with pseudo-label sharpening restricted to sonotypes and forced soundscape/audio mixup. Perch embeddings supported MLP probes, site/hour priors and sequence corrections, contributing much more weight for non-bird classes. Histogram matching and taxon-dependent blending aligned complementary branches, while OpenVINO and ONNX inference kept the ensemble within the CPU runtime budget. Small soundscape validation sets served mainly as sanity checks, with final selection also considering public scores, diversity and runtime.

solution_summary: The solution fine-tuned a pretrained Xception classifier with generalized mean pooling and sigmoid outputs using landmark and non-landmark images. It used a confidence-sensitive BCE modification and voting over 22 inference crops. A second stage matched Google DELF features against up to 32 reference images from the predicted category and geometrically verified the matches. Combining neural-network and DELF confidence increased public/private GAP from 0.145/0.149 to 0.211/0.192.

Hyperparameter tuning and increasing cross-validation from five folds to 15 or 20 folds improved scores. Predictions were blended exclusively with the harmonic mean, which the author considered helpful for generalization.

The solution combined word embeddings, classical text similarities, and extensive graph features derived from the combined training and test question pairs. Its strongest individual models incorporated text sequences and engineered features into neural networks, while tree models added diversity. A four-layer stack combined roughly 300 first-layer models and 150 second-layer models through ridge and lasso models, followed by a 55/45 blend. Rescaling predictions according to question-frequency groups improved log loss by about 0.001 over the public rescaling method.

The main submission stacked 43 models from six families using fixed L1 logistic regression on ranked predictions. Its strongest gains came from generator-aware GLM features, TabPFN, more extensive cross-validation refits, and supervised GPT-2 row classifiers. The workflow combined inexpensive declared screens with stricter finalist checks and independent audits, although member selection and some GPT-2 epoch choices remained outside fully nested validation. The final stack achieved nested CV 0.9467709 and private AUC 0.94581; a selected public-blend hedge performed slightly worse.

solution_summary: The author curated a general mutant training dataset and combined structural features, physics-based energy scores, and protein language-model embeddings in LightGBM and TabNet models. solution_title: RLIAYN's approach - Online deep reinforcement learning
solution_summary: The team trained a compact fully convolutional ResNet agent with PPO, a handcrafted dense reward, and KL distillation from earlier models. Normalized observations, invalid-action masking, and prioritized fictitious self-play were central to making training work. A separate behavior-cloned policy controlled city tiles, while transfer behavior used fixed rules to limit the action space. Inference averaged logits across eight map symmetries, and slow environment simulation remained the main training bottleneck.
compute: RTX2080Ti GPU and i9-9900k CPU; around 300 environment steps/second; training runs exceeded four full days without reaching a plateau.

solution_summary: The team aligned sentence-level translation pairs, cleaned dictionary data, and fine-tuned ByT5-base and ByT5-large. Additional fine-tuning on examples with high BLEU–chrF++ geometric-mean scores improved their models, although standalone performance remained below stronger public notebooks. Their final approach incorporated three public Akkadian ByT5 models and minimum Bayes risk decoding using the official competition metric. solution_title: 89th place: division reselection transferred to Private, our Public-picked chass
solution_summary: The solution extends a public cell-tracking pipeline containing temporal 3D U-Net detectors, an edge transformer and integer linear programming. Its main additions are an MLP coordinate correction head and logistic-regression division reselection trained with labels derived from the official metric. Small gains came from pruning unlikely annotated nodes and widening temporal smoothing for z coordinates. Final submissions scored 0.928 and 0.927 privately, while a rejected third-detector variant reached 0.935, exposing unreliable public-score-based selection.

The solution used high-pass filtering and discrete wavelet denoising before training bidirectional LSTM models with attention, including a variant that concatenated additional features. Adversarial validation guided preprocessing and feature removal to reduce train–test distribution differences. Eight predictions from stratified four- or five-fold models with different features and seeds were combined by hard voting. The author selected a conservative ensemble because validation and leaderboard scores were unstable, obtaining a private score of 0.688.

The solution blended DART LightGBM, standard LightGBM, and CatBoost using squared ranks, with a separate DART model for customers with at most two statements. Extensive customer-level aggregation generated about 7,000 features, which were reduced through several feature-selection procedures to roughly 2,900 for the best single model. Training included independently transformed histories ending at each customer's last two statements, while validation evaluated only the latest history using aligned customer-level folds and a separate holdout. Large minimum leaf sizes were crucial for matching local validation to leaderboard behavior, and the best single model achieved a public score around 0.801.

solution_summary: The team describes using multiple backbones with stacking and median ensembling to improve robustness. solution_title: #60: Data augmentation explained: Generating more stars
solution_summary: The approach augmented stellar observations to simulate dimmer stars in the test distribution. It scaled signals downward and injected additional noise to preserve the expected relationship between brightness and shot-noise variance. The implementation supported downscaling only, which matched the stated test conditions. This augmentation helped tune predicted sigma values.

solution_title: 75th Place Solution for the DEFCON31 Competition
solution_summary: The author describes challenge-specific methods used to obtain 22 flags in an AI capture-the-flag competition. These included inspecting classification errors, clustering and visualizing hidden structure, counting image pixels, and constructing small white-box adversarial perturbations. Other challenges were solved through prompt injection, XML injection, iterative word guessing, image thresholding, and Python object-construction behavior. Several challenges remained unsolved, and matching the server's MobileNet weights was essential for the adversarial-image tasks.

The team combined CNNs trained on three CT image representations: multiple intensity windows, cropped windowed images, and cropped adjacent-slice RGB images. They removed patients shared between training and test data and used patient-level folds with balanced positive and negative patient sampling. A described training pipeline used AdamW, backbone freezing followed by full fine-tuning, geometric augmentation, and horizontal-flip inference. Metadata-based H2O post-processing improved most models, and the processed predictions were stacked.

solution_title: Provisional 8th Place Solution - Monai x EfficientNets x LGBM
solution_summary: The pipeline combines image-level EfficientNet predictions with exam-level volumetric predictions using tree-based stacking. Fold-specific probability calibration and LightGBM over neighboring slices substantially improve image-level predictions, reducing cross-validation log loss from 0.12 to 0.105. Exam-level models use positive exams and aggregate image probabilities into statistical features. Final postprocessing enforces prediction consistency and estimates the indeterminate target without a dedicated model.

The pipeline detected helmets with YOLOv5l, tracked detections bidirectionally, classified teams, and mapped helmets to player coordinates. Optical-flow prediction and interpolation reduced missed detections, while MobileNet-v2 features clustered helmets into two teams. A Hungarian assignment incorporated spatial distance and team mismatch penalties. XGBoost estimated frame-level mapping reliability, which was accumulated over tracks to assign player identities and resolve conflicts.

The solution ensembled multiple ARC solvers and applied filters targeting their recurring output errors, including redundant lines and incorrect shapes. It exploited stable task ordering across submissions to identify which tasks existing algorithms solved, then tested additional algorithms for complementary coverage. Binary search helped locate newly solved tasks so other tasks could remain assigned to the strongest solver. The authors emphasized rejecting incorrect attempts as easier than directly selecting the correct answer.

solution_title: Efficient Bird Species Detection Using Distilled Sound Event Detection Ensembles
solution_summary: The pipeline uses five publicly available distilled sound event detection models on overlapping audio windows. It combines clip logits with maximum-pooled frame logits, averages probabilities across folds, and smooths predictions over time. Maximum pooling across overlapping windows produces timestamp-level outputs. Validation studies and runtime measurements were still planned, so no numerical performance evidence was reported.

solution_title: 25th Place Solution - Documenting 12 Days of Grinding/Suffering
solution_summary: The author built 400 independent static ONNX solvers and optimized each for memory and parameter cost rather than training a general model. The strongest recurring ideas were writing large tensors directly to the output, using signed evidence, compact internal representations, and cropping before processing. A reproducible solver factory promoted candidates only after correctness checks, generated holdouts, and strictly lower measured cost. The final score improved from 7,187.29 to 7,910.92 over twelve days.

The team retrained public ConvNeXt and CAFormer models for waveform inversion. ConvNeXt achieved validation MAE 22.01, while CAFormer achieved 23.13. They averaged the two models and used a public CAFormer model for additional validation and tuning. They also applied median ensembling and combined that result with a public 25.6 solution.

solution_summary: The solution ensembled multiple object detectors using weighted boxes fusion and tuned suppression thresholds. Investigating radiologist-specific validation exposed annotation-style differences, leading to box adjustments and fine-tuning on rare radiologists. Subsequent class-specific RetinaNet fine-tuning incorporated NIH boxes, balanced radiologist/class sampling, revised validation, and high-resolution models. The selected leaderboard-oriented submission scored 0.365 publicly and 0.307 privately, illustrating substantial selection uncertainty.

solution_title: 162d Place Solution for the AI Village Capture the Flag @ DEFCON31
solution_summary: The author describes task-specific approaches to an AI capture-the-flag competition, with some solutions reconstructed after a notebook was damaged. Methods included brute-force probing, UMAP visualization, pixel-intensity counting, OCR prompt injection, and Word2Vec similarity searches. Other challenges involved manipulating LLM prompts, packaging Python code in a pickle payload, and filtering image values to reveal hidden text. Several approaches recovered flags, although exact prompts and procedures were sometimes lost.

The author submitted a two-model ensemble of ViT-B/16 and EfficientNet-B4, plus a second ensemble adding DeiT-B/16 with weights of 0.5, 0.3, and 0.2. Training used bi-tempered logistic loss and augmentations, with CutMix applied to EfficientNet-B4; inference used 384-pixel images and test-time augmentation. The second submission fine-tuned the EfficientNet classifier on merged Cassava 2019 and 2020 data while freezing other layers, although training on 2020 data alone generally worked better. The two submissions reported PB/LB scores of 0.9019/0.9030 and 0.9002/0.9039, respectively.

The guesser first checked for Agent Alpha and then used either probability-balanced keyword search or entropy-minimizing natural questions. Keyword priors combined word count, frequency, and GPT-4o mini estimates of whether a term denotes a thing. Natural-question selection used a large keyword-question probability table averaged across three language models. The answerer routed general questions to Llama 3 and letter-counting or mathematical questions to DeepSeek-Math, while biased keyword priors improved guesser reward over uniform probabilities.

solution_title: 31st place solution - single fold 512x512 UNet EfficientNetB4
solution_summary: The solution used a U-Net with an EfficientNetB4 encoder on CLAHE-enhanced images resized to 512×512. Training combined BCE and Dice loss, mild augmentation, gradient accumulation, cosine learning-rate cycles, and stochastic weight averaging. Validation used a single stratified holdout. Horizontal-flip inference augmentation and two-stage thresholding suppressed false positives before producing segmentation masks.

solution_title: 1st Place Solution: Multi-Iterative Noisy Student Is All You Need
solution_summary: The solution used CNN sound-event detection models on 20-second mel-spectrogram inputs and iteratively trained students using pseudolabeled soundscapes. Equal-weight mixing of labeled audio and pseudolabeled audio, stochastic depth, confidence-based sampling, and power-transformed pseudolabels enabled effective self-training. A dedicated Amphibia/Insecta model used extra species from Xeno-Canto, and the final ensemble combined models from different training iterations. Inference averaged overlapping framewise predictions and applied smoothing and delta-shift augmentation; the excerpt reports substantial gains from longer chunks and self-training but provides no final ensemble score.
external_data: ["Xeno-Canto target-species recordings", "Xeno-Canto extra Amphibia and Insecta species"]

solution_title: S3E20 | 94th Private with RF Ensemble based on clustering
solution_summary: The solution used seven geographic reference coordinates as features and combined four models. The coordinates represented two zero-emission locations, one maximum-emission location, and four K-means cluster locations associated with emissions. Satellite measurements were excluded. Post-processing corrected prediction issues and scaled predictions by a factor of 1.15.

solution_title: 15th | How to train deberta & NLP tricks
solution_summary: The team formulated the task as token classification, combining discourse segments within each essay and classifying their first discourse-type tokens with DeBERTa models. Training stability benefited from small learning rates, layerwise learning-rate decay, warmup, and adversarial weight perturbation. Masked-language-model pretraining on FB2021 and FB2022 improved stability and accuracy, with dropout disabled for those pretrained weights. They also used soft-label pseudo-labeling on FB2021; alternative pooling methods and several additional training approaches did not work.

The solution was a rules-based agent that sequentially handled defense, attacks, expansion, mining, and spawning. It anticipated attacks on shipyards and calculated required reinforcements, spawning locally or sending ships from nearby yards. Offensive rules included shipyard captures, fleet interception, and sacrificial adjacent attacks. Mining selected routes for kore per turn while avoiding enemy fleet paths, and expansion and spawning depended on resource surplus and relative fleet size.

The solution used a global, two-level XGBoost pipeline with 430 engineered features instead of local grid models. Nearest-neighbor counts first reduced the candidate places to 100, and averaged model predictions narrowed them to 20. Spatial neighbor statistics, historical temporal densities, accuracy groups, and robust deviations supplied most of the features. A second layer of 30 models combined 100 base learners, with predictions averaged to rank places.

solution_title: 1st Place - Kaggle Agent - Self Evolving Prompts
solution_summary: The author describes evolving agent prompts through competition between agents rather than writing final prompts directly. Agents accumulate useful experience in their conversation contexts during four-hour campaigns scored by total ONNX leaderboard gain. Human mentorship and self-review shape these contexts, and the strongest agent is promoted to guide others and document reusable practices.

solution_summary: The team blended diverse recurrent models with BERT and GPT-2 models, combining language-model fine-tuning with custom bias-aware losses. Recurrent models used different embeddings, tokenizers, and losses, while BERT variants covered base and large sizes with cased and uncased inputs. Identity-dependent sample weights, annotation counts, and auxiliary toxicity targets shaped training, and length-based batching improved inference efficiency. Averaging the teammates' predictions brought substantial gains, with the final blend retaining about 25% LSTM-based predictions because adding too much BERT reduced performance.

solution_summary: The solution used BigQuery for most feature engineering and LightGBM for prediction. Days 7 and 8 supplied training data, while day 9 determined the boosting round before retraining on training and validation combined. Models trained with different seeds were ensembled.
