The resulting score was much lower than expected, which the author attributed to sensitivity to differences in the test data. The post links to the implementation but provides no downstream model or validation details.

The solution stacked diverse regressors trained on loading, connectivity, atlas-derived, and graph-based brain features. Feature preparation included connectivity transformations, PCA whitening, robust scaling, and iterative imputation of missing targets. Base models included linear and RBF SVR, LassoLars, LightGBM, and a small 2D CNN, with Bayesian hyperparameter searches. A final LassoLars model combined 31 model outputs after robust scaling, using five-fold tuning and a separate holdout evaluation.

solution_title: Public 4th Place / Private 15th Place Solution - Konwinski Prize
solution_summary: The team adapted a public notebook into a patch-generation pipeline using an AWQ-quantized DeepSeek-R1-distilled Qwen model. It chose representative candidate patches by minimum total edit distance and aggressively skipped issues using statement length, file-content count, and time limits. Public leaderboard feedback guided tuning because the supplied training set was tiny and external examples differed in distribution. The best reported public score was +0.056243 with four correct patches and no incorrect patches.
compute: Global inference time limits of 8 hours for Public LB and 23 hours for Private LB.

solution_summary: The solution prioritized a diverse ensemble and CV after feature engineering produced little improvement and individual-model leaderboard correlation proved unstable. More than 2,000 tree models and ten MLPs were trained with varied hyperparameters under five-fold CV. Repeated sequential hill climbing reduced the prediction library to 79 candidates, followed by quadratic programming that retained 68. Seven MLPs contributed disproportionately to the final ensemble, which achieved 0.0588017 CV and 0.05846 privately.
compute: GPU used for CatBoost and ten MLPs; more than 2,000 tree models trained.

solution_summary: The solution used separate models and label transformations for consumption and production. It incorporated online training and blended models across seeds. The author reported disappointing final performance and suspected either label transformation or online training, but had not established the cause.

solution_title: Exploring the combination of search and learn for the ARC25 challenge
solution_summary: The strongest submitted approach made minor adaptations to the previous year's transduction method with test-time training. Most research instead explored deep-learning-guided program synthesis with hindsight relabeling in a search-and-learn loop. That experimental system outperformed pure search for an equal prediction budget, but remained incomplete and solved none of the private ARC-AGI-2 test tasks.

solution_title: "Single" LSTM model with Magic Features. 0.1093 LB.
solution_summary: The shared single model used four LSTM layers followed by dense and output layers with skip connections. Handcrafted aggregation features were the main ingredient, together with reversed sequence training that also exposed features from the original order. Additional transformations handled inspiratory u_in values and the sign of pressure targets. After standard postprocessing, the model scored 0.1093 publicly and 0.1133 privately.

The final agent used a rule-based evaluator and lightweight search with an original Mega Gardevoir deck. It mapped opposing archetypes onto six target board plans, scoring actions by progress toward the selected plan and switching when observations contradicted it. Improvements were screened through calibrated opponent bots, board-formation metrics, and real ladder comparisons, with replay diagnostics used to detect regressions. The final 1,000 ladder games produced a 57.1% win rate across 28 archetypes; endgame DFS and a learned self-play system were withdrawn after weaker results.

The team created 772 handcrafted features and retained 411 through manual and correlation-based selection, including removal of temporally unstable features. Ten diverse tree models were stacked with RidgeClassifier, calibrated, and averaged across five random seeds. Validation used five stratified group folds grouped by WEEK_NUM. A final year-dependent downward score correction used the maximum payment year, while the calibrated stack achieved a reported local CV AUC of 0.859322.

The final approach trained XGBoost with a custom multiclass-style MAP ranking objective using every row where a product was added. Key features included exponentially weighted product histories, relative income measures, calendar variables, and lagged customer information. Simple sums of model scores and a payroll-to-pension score rule provided additional gains. Using more training data drove major improvements, while attempted customer-record cleaning hurt performance and reliable local validation remained unresolved.
compute: 15-inch MacBook Pro with 16 GB RAM and 2.5 GHz Core i7; occasional EC2 X1 instances during the final two weeks.

solution_title: Part of 21st place solutions: Methods driven by biological information
solution_summary: The author links a notebook exploring ideas inspired by biology and bioinformatics. They report that selecting important genes and binarizing multiome data were the only approaches that worked for their best model. The post gives no model architecture, validation details, or numerical results.

The final approach used EfficientNet-B4 with black-border cropping, heavy augmentation, and five-fold test-time augmentation. It pretrained on selectively sampled older competition data before fine-tuning on the new data. Sampling favored severe classes in the older data to counter the new dataset's class imbalance while retaining all new examples. The model scored 0.920 on the final leaderboard; classification formulations, ResNet variants, Ben's preprocessing, and label smoothing were unsuccessful.

The solution used soft-constraint simulated annealing, increasing overlap penalties while testing fixed container sizes. Dimer lattice potentials encouraged ordered configurations, and a variable-box polishing stage removed residual overlaps. Parallel tournament selection and repeated basin hopping refined candidates, including seeds obtained by adding or removing particles from neighboring configurations. Maintaining three seed lineages improved diversity, and incorporating public configurations further reduced the final score to 69.106266.
compute: Maximum: 2× GCP C4A with 72 cores each and 2× OCI Ampere A1 with 80 cores each; total cost under $2,000.

solution_summary: The author's contribution first trained a CWT-based image classifier and then replaced its transform with a multilayer 1D convolution frontend. Training continued for 20 epochs before five epochs of fine-tuning on all data. Waveform shifts, channel removal, and negative-example channel swaps provided augmentation, and ten parameter variants were ensembled. That ensemble reached 0.8803 private AUC; a broader ensemble reached 0.8816 but was not selected for the final submission.
compute: TPU; staged training of 5 epochs, 20 epochs, and 5 full-data fine-tuning epochs.

solution_summary: The solution used a single-fold ResNeSt50 model adapted from a public kernel. Unlabeled audio intervals from example_test_audio and BIRDCLEF 2020 served as noise and as an additional nocall class. Three mel spectrograms with different window sizes were stacked to form the model's three input channels, although this choice was not compared against duplicated channels. Inference used a threshold of 0.5, and local validation on random clips agreed with the private leaderboard.

The solution used deep U-Net-style networks to predict nuclei masks and touching borders, combining complementary target definitions to improve separation and mask coverage. Heavy microscopy-specific augmentation and cross-entropy plus soft Dice losses supported training on a small dataset. Averaged masks underwent watershed processing, followed by LightGBM models that selected candidate separations and removed poor instances using predicted IoU. External microscopy datasets and flip/rotation test-time augmentation were also included.

The solution extracted three-hop subgraphs around configurable nodes and removed duplicate configurations. Separate models for each subtype used three SAGEConv layers with normalization and residual additions from the initial node embedding. Listwise loss converged faster and performed better than pairwise loss in the author's experiments. Using the provided training and validation splits, the approach achieved public and private scores of 0.684 and 0.688.

The pipeline filtered and downsampled transit signals, smoothed across wavelengths, and extracted and flipped the transit portion. It optimized a baseline and molecular concentrations against the observed signal using molecular spectra from ExoMol. Post-processing blended the first wavelength prediction with the remaining wavelengths, while wavelength-specific uncertainty estimates came from training RMSE and were clipped around their mean.

solution_title: 2nd Place | Single LightGBM and Target Encoding
solution_summary: The solution used a single LightGBM architecture with extensive target encoding and engineered numerical features. Target encodings covered combinations of one through six columns, with additional descriptive statistics over the encoded features. The processed dataset contained 1,552 features and 794,868 rows, and careful memory management enabled CPU training. The author trained on all data with five different seeds, with training taking about four hours.
compute: Kaggle CPUs; about 4 hours training; five seeds trained on all data.

solution_summary: The solution trains GPU CatBoost ranking models to predict accuracy_group, averaging five folds into a model blend. About 1,000 features capture accumulated events, accuracy histories, timestamps, and numeric event-data aggregates. Repeated truncated validation and feature selection address overfitting, while optimized thresholds convert predictions into ordinal groups. The final submission blends three feature-set variants and achieves a private score of 0.552.
compute: GPU training; hardware model and runtime unspecified.

solution_title: Less is More: Lessons from the Complexity Trap
solution_summary: The author compared a default CatBoost baseline against a tuned boosting ensemble and a multi-seed ensemble. The baseline used 1,000 iterations without feature engineering or external data and achieved the best reported private ROC-AUC, 0.95513. Interaction features, Optuna tuning, and NNLS blending produced only negligible validation and public-score gains. The post does not explicitly identify which experiment was selected for the final submission.
external_data: ["Original heart disease dataset, 271 rows (discussed but not used)"]

solution_summary: The solution concatenated image, TF-IDF, and Indonesian DistilBERT title embeddings into a 21,208-dimensional representation. Image models used ResNet backbones with GeM pooling and CosFace, while title models used ArcFace supervision. Matching used brute-force cosine nearest-neighbor search in Faiss on fp16 embeddings, enhanced with alpha query expansion and database-side augmentation. Five-fold validation grouped products by label_group, and final matching used a 0.59 similarity threshold with a nearest-neighbor fallback for unmatched products. Combining all three modalities with retrieval augmentation achieved 0.761 private and 0.775 public scores.

solution_title: Entropy-Weighted Majority Voting with gpt-oss-120b for AIMO3
solution_summary: The system serves gpt-oss-120b through vLLM and generates eight independent, Python-assisted reasoning attempts per problem. It selects answers through entropy-weighted voting and stops remaining attempts when five agree. Persistent Jupyter kernels, model-weight preloading, and adaptive problem budgets reduce overhead within the single-GPU runtime limit. The reported public score peaked at 43/50, while experiments with more attempts suffered from KV-cache pressure, time-budget collapse, and concurrency bugs.
compute: Single NVIDIA H100 85GB GPU; five-hour wall-clock limit; model startup reduced to approximately 130 seconds.

solution_title: 9th Place Solution: Own Detectors + Public Tracker + Restored Divisions
solution_summary: The final pipeline mixes two frozen public detection-and-linking checkpoints with six custom subvoxel nucleus detectors and a linker trained on their features. Coordinate rounding and correct offset handling deliver substantial gains, while DIVCARRY restores valid division edges lost by the public pipeline. Validation accounts for contamination of the local holdout by public checkpoints, and the final pair includes a second post-processing family for diversity. The selected pipeline achieved 0.967 publicly and 0.949 privately.
compute: Custom members increased runtime to about 1.24× the public pipeline; repair time limit raised from 7.5 to 9.2 hours.

solution_title: 220th place (silver): gold-batch fine-tuning on top of a public ensemble
solution_summary: The solution combined public 2.5D readers with fine-tuned CoAtNet weight soups, custom 3D models, and lateral-compartment specialists. MRI series were routed to fixed slots, cropped in physical coordinates, and canonicalized by mirroring left knees. Explicit sampling of radiologist-labelled studies at a 50% probability was a central fine-tuning choice. A fixed per-finding rank blend achieved 0.960 public and 0.944 private AUC.
models_pretrained: ["nartaa CoAtNet 384/224 public checkpoints", "heliosli compact 2.5D reader", "nartaa ConvNeXt-S all-data reader"]

solution_summary: The author used Ridge predictions as a base_score feature for CatBoost, with one-hot encoding for lower-cardinality inputs. CatBoost relied too heavily on this feature, so Gaussian noise was added to its training values. This improved CV to 0.955735 and also slightly improved the reported public and private scores. Applying the same operation to other models did not help.

The post reflects on unexpected public and private score differences and asks whether pseudo-labeling, iterative techniques, and submission averaging contributed to overfitting. It does not describe a reproducible final pipeline. The author congratulates the winners and saves several public notebooks for future reference.

solution_title: Detoxify Baseline ended up in the silver zone!
solution_summary: The post reports a Detoxify model achieving a private leaderboard score of 0.80857. It links a notebook describing offline use of the model. No additional training, feature engineering, or ensemble details are provided.

The author combined frequency encoding, out-of-fold target encoding, and quantile binning with several tabular models. XGBoost, CatBoost, LightGBM, and RealMLP variants used different feature subsets to diversify predictions. Rank-based hill climbing selected blend weights from approximately 10–15 models. The final ensemble achieved 0.95574 CV and 0.95532 on the private leaderboard, with CV-to-leaderboard alignment identified as a major concern.

The solution extended two public BERT pipelines with large models, concatenated representations from the last eight layers, and combined cased and uncased embeddings. Ten-fold cross-validation and candidate–pronoun product features improved results, alongside tuning the neural prediction heads. Four architecture variants were combined using LightGBM and Lasso, with LightGBM achieving CV 0.3059 and leaderboard loss 0.2047. Fine-tuning, label correction, ELMo, and a Siamese network did not work in the author's experiments.

The solution ensembled NFNet/CaiT and EfficientNetV2m pipelines for study classification, with NIH pretraining improving validation and leaderboard performance. Diversity came from preprocessing, architectures, augmentations, and training with BCE or CE loss; a segmentation auxiliary head was used in the EfficientNet pipeline. Image-level none predictions combined three sources, while opacity detection ensembled YOLOv5, YOLOX, and EfficientDet D5. The final ensemble achieved 0.636 CV, 0.645 public leaderboard, and 0.634 private leaderboard scores.
models_pretrained: ["NFNet: eca_nfnet_l1, eca_nfnet_l2, dm_nfnet_f2, dm_nfnet_f3", "CaiT cait_xs24_384", "EfficientNetV2m", "YOLOv5 with resnet52, resnet101, yolov5m, yolov5x, eca_nfnet_l0 backbones", "YOLOX with yolox-m and yolox-d backbones", "EfficientDet D5"]
external_data: ["NIH dataset", "Unspecified external training data for pipeline 2"]

solution_summary: The team's component used detected backfin images to train two EfficientNet-B7 embedding models at 512×512 resolution, one with ArcFace and the other with CurricularFace and a BN neck. Training covered three folds of a random ten-fold split and included test-set pseudo-labels from an ensemble. Individually normalized backfin and body embeddings were concatenated for nearest-neighbor retrieval, with Bayesian optimization used to tune embedding weights and new_id replacement applied afterward. The embedding ensemble achieved about 0.930 local cross-validation performance.
compute: Kaggle TPU resources; trained three folds of a random ten-fold split.

solution_title: 5th Place Solution | Imputation Without Any Imputers
solution_summary: The author imputed nearly all features except x_e_out using relationships found in the original dataset, with closest-value matching when synthetic noise prevented exact matches. Engineered features described cylinder geometry and combinations intended to cancel physical units. Models used different feature subsets and estimators, with ridge regression fitting ensemble weights including an intercept and negative coefficients. Original data supplemented training but was excluded from validation, while Optuna tuned gradient boosting models.

The solution trains a single CatBoost model on the competition training data combined with the original training data, removing duplicate rows and identifier columns. Product ID is retained as a categorical feature, which the author identifies as a major improvement. Optuna and Wandb support hyperparameter sweeps, and a fast 80/20 validation split determines the iteration count for full-data training. CPU training was more accurate than GPU training, and the final results were 0.98125 locally and 0.98426 on the private leaderboard.
compute: CPU training; hardware model and training time unspecified.

solution_title: Read the Scorer, Not the Model: Engineering for the Guardrail You Can't See
solution_summary: The solution analyzed the competition guardrails and focused on confused-deputy findings expected to survive both content and provenance defenses. A local harness using the competition models measured whether candidates fired and how much replay time they consumed. Incremental budget-aware filling and model-specific template selection raised the specialist's public score from 10.815 to 20.775. The author retained separate confused-deputy and exfiltration specialists; the former transferred unchanged to private evaluation, while every exfiltration submission scored zero.
compute: Measured gpt-oss candidate latency of 1.2 seconds with injection versus 4.3 seconds plain; Gemma measured 1.45 seconds plain versus 1.9 seconds injected.

solution_summary: The final ensemble combined EfficientNet, SE-ResNeXt, ResNeSt, and a GeM-equipped EfficientNet using hard voting. Training used sixteen 512×512 tiles from the middle resolution layer, with tissue distributed evenly across tiles and scale changes providing augmentation. Synchronized batch normalization was particularly important for larger models. O2U-Net noise filtering was excluded because it did not help the public leaderboard, although retrospective private results improved for Radboud data.

The team extended a public DeepSeek-math notebook with asynchronous vLLM inference to increase the number of sampled solutions. They generated both code and text answers, then asked the model to solve a multiple-choice question containing the five most frequent candidates and combined that result with original response counts. Parsing fixes and explicit code-error feedback improved robustness. AIME83-86 was chosen for validation, while a problem-type classifier and automatic code-formatting ideas were not adopted.

The selected submission uses L2-regularized logistic regression to stack clipped probability logits from 99 diverse base models, averaging test predictions over five seeds. Tree ensembles and MLPs supplied strong standalone predictions, while weaker sequence, graph, kernel, and factorization models contributed complementary rankings. Adding original F1-strategy data was the most reliable feature-development gain, and the final predictions received no post-processing. The stack achieved 0.95536 OOF AUC; a post-deadline rank blend of stronger candidates reached 0.95505 private AUC.

solution_title: rm -rf * Six Days Before Deadline — Then... Climbed Back to the Edge of Gold
solution_summary: The author built an automated search system in which coding agents competed to improve ONNX solutions across 400 tasks. Agents shared incumbent solutions and notes, while an advisor challenged premature claims of optimality with simple questions. Human-written task rules encouraged architectural rewrites, and validation gates screened indexing errors, duplicates, and runtime failures. The system generated 330,924 candidates over three weeks and achieved a final score of 7994.76, with additional validated improvements left unsubmitted.
compute: 21-day campaign; 64 concurrent coding agents at peak; remote compute VM with unspecified hardware.

solution_title: [3rd place] All Medalists Who BC'd on Our Records MUST Vote!
solution_summary: The solution used a 10.4M-parameter Transformer policy initialized through behavior cloning from strong teams' public replays and improved with self-play PPO. Stable learning required critic pre-warming, per-decision probability-ratio clipping, and a separate antisymmetric critic, with terminal win/loss as the reward. League training and promotion gates selected stronger generations, while paired games on verified fast engines guided decisions. Inference rules repaired ineffective actions and handled late-game melon purchases, increasing the reported gen70 win rate from 74.2% to 87.8%.
compute: Up to 23 A100s; 20.1B training positions across about 21M games and 1,883 generations; final run about 360M steps.

solution_title: 10th Place Solution for the Stanford Ribonanza RNA Folding Competition
solution_summary: The solution combined symmetric 1D convolution and transformer layers without positional encoding, training both sequence-only models and models with CapR and per-nucleotide BPP summaries. A custom uncertainty-aware MAE loss weighted prediction errors using a normal-distribution potential derived from measurement uncertainty, improving convergence and smoothness. Sigmoid output constraints and one-hot nucleotide inputs also helped. The final mixed ensemble favored sequence-only predictions with 5:3 weights to reduce dependence on structural features whose generalization the author distrusted.

solution_title: 27th solution, Swin transformer. Simple and Lucky.
solution_summary: The solution used a pretrained Swin Large model with 384-pixel inputs trained across ten folds. Image features were concatenated with a learned 256-dimensional representation of 12 auxiliary features before a linear prediction head. Training used four epochs per fold, AdamW, cosine scheduling, gradient clipping and BCEWithLogitsLoss. The reported scores were 16.98523 privately and 17.83676 publicly, and the author did not ensemble the model with a separately trained efficient model.

solution_title: LB 58th/PB 152th Place solution. Mainly about "Bert replication[SingleLB.847]"
solution_summary: The final submission used static weighted blending of four sensor-sequence models, including a BERT replication and several recurrent architectures. The strongest single model improved through IMU time stretching, copying gesture tails, and removing two subjects with abnormal device wearing. It used 10-fold stratified group validation and achieved an overall out-of-fold HF1 of about 0.8397 and a public leaderboard score of 0.847. The post focuses on these improvements rather than detailing every model in the ensemble.

The author trained RoBERTa and DeBERTa models on Jigsaw2018, Jigsaw2019, and Ruddit data. For the two Jigsaw datasets, their multi-label probabilities became inputs to linear severity models fitted on competition validation data, with weights optimized by genetic algorithms. Model selection emphasized validation performance because the public leaderboard appeared misleading. The final weighted rank average combined 15 models and achieved a private score of 0.8139.

The author shares a single XLM-R model trained with pseudo-labels and knowledge distillation. It scored 0.9475 on the leaderboard and 0.9487 after applying another competitor's hardcoded multipliers. The team struggled to ensemble effectively and felt that heavy reliance on pseudo-labels, compounded by distillation, made blending harder.

solution_title: Credit where credit's due: Joe Malicki on placing third in 'Give Me Some Credit'
solution_summary: The final solution averaged gradient boosted trees trained with a 50/50 class balance and random forests trained with a 10/90 balance. Domain knowledge drove features involving debt, disposable income, age, debt-to-income thresholds, and round income amounts. Unusual delinquency codes and debt-to-income values for missing-income records were important data observations. Logistic regression stacking on a small holdout underperformed selecting the best models, and private test results agreed more closely with local evaluations than with public scores.

solution_title: 7th Place Solution — Way Too Many Models, One Simple Stack
solution_summary: The primary solution combined 556 verified local and public prediction streams using six cross-fitted, regularized logistic regressions on rank-normalized predictions. Fixed ten-fold validation and outer-fold ensemble fitting guarded against optimistic blend evaluation. Exact-value target encoding captured synthetic-generator artifacts, while model diversity and negative residual corrections supplied smaller gains. The strict primary achieved 0.97087888 OOF AUC, while a separately selected Gaussian-copula hedge achieved the better private score of 0.97112.
compute: GPU used to refit the final clean 556-stream C-bag.
external_data: ["Public OOF/test prediction streams", "Public hedge blend components"]

solution_summary: This repository overview identifies the author's landmark retrieval competition solution but provides little methodological detail in the text. Its download scripts are forked from anokas's image-downloader kernel. It also includes scripts for DELF extraction and verification. No training setup or quantitative retrieval results are described.

solution_title: Building an Automation factory with different AI models
solution_summary: The author used several AI assistants to understand transformation rules, implement experiments, and review failures. The main technical observation was that changing internal representations mattered more than reducing graph node counts. Public solutions served as starting points for further optimization, but the post provides no detailed final pipeline or numerical results.

The team selected an early AutoGluon submission that also succeeded in the AutoML Grand Prix portion of the competition. Their third submission tied their fourth submission on the private leaderboard while being substantially simpler. The selected approach avoided the post-hoc ensembling described in their original writeup. The post suggests that improving the best default configuration was difficult, potentially because the synthetic data was already largely solved apart from injected noise.

The team optimized a public TF-IDF ensemble for runtime using the DAIGT v2 training dataset. They removed LightGBM and multinomial naive Bayes, reduced n-grams from lengths 3–5 to 3–4, and cut CatBoost training to ten iterations with Bayesian parameter tuning. These changes reduced runtime from over two hours to eight minutes while retaining public AUC above 0.956. Adding an unsupervised clustering blend improved the public score by roughly 0.0015 but hurt the private score, and code cleanup saved another twenty seconds.
compute: Runtime reduced from over 2 hours to 8 minutes; clustering added 60 seconds and code cleanup saved roughly 20 seconds.

solution_summary: The post explains a scorecard for tracking leaderboard movement and comparing teams over time. It defines score differences, distance to the leader, movement indicators, and a simple extrapolation of future leaderboard scores. It also links to notebooks analyzing top submissions and daily predictions.

The pipeline combined template-based modeling, DRfold2 predictions for short RNA, and Protenix diffusion predictions. Sequence identity determined whether three of the five prediction slots were reserved for templates, while Kabsch RMSD and farthest point sampling selected structurally diverse alternatives. Long sequences were processed in overlapping chunks, aligned and blended before applying physical constraints. The best private and public scores were 0.447 and 0.433.
compute: Kaggle T4 GPU with 16GB VRAM; DRfold2 time limit of 2 hours

solution_summary: The final approach used Chemprop directed message-passing networks with selected external polymer data, standardized targets, and auxiliary RadonPy prediction tasks. Rare elements were mapped to more common analogues, and exhaustive dimerization was retained despite mixed validation results. Hyperparameter search and averaging nine models across data splits and weight initializations produced public/private scores of 0.062/0.088. Post-competition experiments corrected a training–inference cyclization mismatch and explored a Tg Fahrenheit transformation, yielding further improvements.

The final solution blended modified versions of three public kernels, with SchNet receiving by far the largest weight. The main SchNet changes were separate models for each coupling type and increased batch sizes, often using 16 samples. Under time constraints, the author stopped generating out-of-fold predictions and guided later blending decisions using leaderboard scores. The best individual SchNet scored -1.971, while the final blend scored -2.21819 on the private leaderboard.
compute: Eight SchNet models, each taking 6–8 hours for 60–90 epochs on Kaggle GPUs; 99% of computing used Kaggle Kernels.

solution_summary: The final approach ensembled large pretrained language models with an attention head and an SVR component. Ensemble-generated pseudo-labels on cleaned external summaries and Wikipedia abstracts provided the largest improvement. Selecting three useful pseudo-labeled datasets and adding model and fold diversity helped achieve a public score of 0.450. Iterative pseudo-labeling, classification, added noise, and interval mean matching did not improve the final approach.
compute: Approximately 2–3 hours per model; up to 6 Colab accounts; 8GB RAM laptop
external_data: ["CMU book summaries", "Movie summaries", "Mark Wijkhuizen's Wikipedia abstracts"]

solution_title: Unselected top scored simple Kmeans solution
solution_summary: The author describes a simple k-means clustering approach. Toxicity severity was scored using Euclidean distance from the non-toxic cluster centroid. The approach achieved 0.818 on the private leaderboard, with no further pipeline details provided.

The proposed pipeline encodes categorical variables, removes features with low mutual information, and denoises inputs with a denoising autoencoder. It then splits the data for validation, tunes gradient boosting models with Optuna, and combines them using VotingRegressor. The author suspects information leakage because preprocessing precedes the validation split and asks for feedback. No performance results are reported.

The best solution ensembled seven full-data-trained DeBERTa models to increase model diversity within the inference budget. Models varied in pretrained checkpoint, input construction, pooling, freezing, layerwise training settings, and auxiliary loss. Increasing inference sequence lengths improved cross-validation and public scores, though its private benefit was limited. A simple mean ensemble selected with hill climbing achieved CV 0.46394 and private score 0.45515, while GBDT postprocessing was excluded from the best submission.

solution_title: 5th place solution: Llama 2 70B meets Sparse & Dense Retrievals from Own parsed wikipedia dataset
solution_summary: The solution combined BM25 and two dense Wikipedia retrievers with fine-tuned Mistral 7B and Llama-2 70B models. Custom Wikipedia parsing preserved numeric and mathematical content, while held-out question sets guided development. Quantized layer-by-layer inference and shared-prefix choice-order augmentation made the large model practical within notebook limits. A confidence-based three-stage pipeline achieved 0.926 private and 0.928 public scores.
compute: Kaggle notebook inference used approximately 6GB GPU memory; Wikipedia indexing took several hours, and 200 multithreaded searches took approximately 2 minutes.

solution_summary: The final retrieval system concatenated 512-dimensional descriptors from four models into a 2048-dimensional representation. It combined three GeM CNN models with a DELG model, trained on the clean training set with strong image augmentation. CosFace, focal loss, label smoothing, and warm-up cosine scheduling supported training, while validation used global average precision on sampled index images. The ensemble achieved public and private scores of 0.36644 and 0.32878, with an inference kernel runtime of 8 hours 20 minutes.
compute: Inference kernel runtime: 8 hours 20 minutes

solution_title: 45th Place | What I have learnt through TPS- Sep 2021
solution_summary: The approach addressed missing values with mean imputation and standardized the features, saving the processed data to avoid repeated work. Stratified cross-validation worked best, with two folds used for quick screening and ten folds for stronger candidates. LightGBM, XGBoost, and CatBoost predictions were ensembled using weighted averages and powered submissions. GPU availability and slow CPU runs influenced the experimentation workflow.
compute: GPU resources ran out twice; CPU runs were slow, and Google Colab was also tried.

solution_summary: The solution handled TMA images with center cropping and used a thumbnail segmentation model to locate a cancerous region in each WSI. Sixteen classifiers from four architecture families predicted six sigmoid scores, including a non-cancerous class, and their outputs were combined by median averaging. Regenerating thumbnails for slides containing multiple adjacent slices significantly improved performance. A single classifier paired with the segmentation model scored 0.49 publicly and 0.55 privately, and no external data was used.
compute: 2x T4 GPUs, with models divided between GPUs for memory efficiency.

solution_title: [40th place] Boltzmann Ensemble: A solution from statistical thermodynamics
solution_summary: The author combined shared notebook predictions using exponentially decaying weights based on public leaderboard error. Each model received weight exp(b*(S-x)), so stronger models contributed more, with b as the single meaningful tuning parameter. The best value of b changed substantially during the competition. The approach offered simple weight tuning but did not account for model correlation or allow negative weights.

The submitted solution was a single U-Net with a timm-resnest26d backbone, using 512×512 ash-color images and only the target frame. It used five folds, included validation data in training, and applied a 0.3 output threshold. An ensemble-code mistake prevented the intended multi-model blend from being submitted; the single model scored 0.688 in CV and 0.66321 privately. A corrected ensemble would have scored 0.67366 privately, while nine-channel temporal inputs did not work.

solution_title: 1st place solution: Bayesian Inference, of course
solution_summary: The solution converted raw sensor frames into wavelength-dependent signals, then used an iterative Bayesian model to estimate transit depths and uncertainties. Its prior combined physical transit modeling, polynomial drift, Gaussian noise, and a transit-spectrum representation using both Gaussian processes and PCA. Grid search and BFGS initialized the nonlinear inference, with fallback fits for suspicious signals. A 12-parameter post-hoc calibration was essential, with removing it reducing the private score by 0.152.
compute: Final submission used 8 Bayesian solver iterations; released code uses 4 to fit training and inference within the 9-hour submission limit, costing 0.001 score.

solution_title: Metamorphic contract tests for authorization in tool-using agents
solution_summary: The author built a deterministic, model-free contract audit of the public guardrail and scoring predicates in SDK 3.1.2. Its 174 schema-valid cases test field selection, authorization semantics, provenance windows, and path normalization. The audit found 27 authorization-semantic false negatives, while distinguishing reachable failures from cases blocked before scoring. Pinned sources and canonical JSON support reproducible regression testing, but the study does not demonstrate improved attack-search performance.
compute: CPU-only, internet-disabled validation run; no model or tool handler invoked.

solution_title: 113th place solution - some notes from the kaggle freshman
solution_summary: The solution used EfficientNet-B5 with 456 by 456 images and five-class classification. Preprocessing cropped gray borders, replicated the green channel, and applied CLAHE, followed by geometric and color augmentation. One model trained from scratch on 2019 data, while another pretrained on 2019 data plus non-normal 2015 examples before fine-tuning on 2019 data. Five-view test-time augmentation and averaging the two models improved the reported leaderboard score from 0.808 and 0.798 individually to 0.817.

The solution combined EfficientNet-b3 cell classifiers with an EfficientNet-b7 image classifier, HPA segmentation, and Gridify and Gapmask inference. Gaussian-noise label smoothing, mixup, public training data, and deep supervision substantially improved the cell models. Inference used eight-way test-time augmentation, prediction filtering, and a 0.7/0.3 blend of cell and image predictions, with blending adding about 0.04 mAP. The final configuration using the original HPA Segmentator achieved 0.5771 public and 0.5499 private scores.

Several models benefited from SQuAD 2.0 fine-tuning before training on chaii, MLQA, and XQuAD. A non-zero Jaccard percentage criterion stabilized checkpoint selection, while punctuation and year-extraction rules corrected answer spans. The two final submissions scored 0.767 and 0.777 privately, and a subsequently identified combination scored 0.784.

solution_summary: The solution ensembles a custom-tokenizer TF-IDF approach with LightGBM using DeBERTa-v3-base predictions and handcrafted text features. It uses DAIGT-v2 data, with readability, sentence, paragraph, punctuation, part-of-speech, and vocabulary statistics. Test-only tokenizer training, a roughly 120,000-token vocabulary, spelling correction, log-loss optimization, and post-processing helped. Mean-pooled DeBERTa features and train-plus-test tokenizer training did not help, while LightAutoML frequently exceeded submission time limits.

The solution used drift-removed, Kalman-filtered signals and discarded approximately 4% of training data as excessively noisy. WaveNet models were trained with macro-F1 early stopping and rollback to earlier weights. A Monte Carlo-inspired ensemble normally rounded the median prediction. For the group with the highest average number of open channels, it instead selected the maximum prediction to compensate for systematic underprediction.

For the first three weeks, the author manually forecast daily log increments for each location and applied daily decay to reflect slowing growth. The final week used XGBoost to predict next-day log increments from lagged and difference features for cases and fatalities, plus continent. Training emphasized recent observations, excluded the earliest data, and rounded features, while validation used the last seven days. The final forecasts applied a smaller daily decay, and adjustments based on news about testing expansion had previously proved unhelpful.

solution_title: 288th / 4,020 (top 7%): what 22 leaderboard probes taught us about this metric

Metric audits and experiments showed that train-movie validation was in-sample for the public models and that small public-score differences were unreliable guides to private performance.

solution_title: 96th Place Solution for the ICR - Identifying Age-Related Conditions Competition
solution_summary: The final approach used CatBoost with ten stratified folds and averaged predictions from one model per fold. It applied no postprocessing and did not use special splitting based on the Greek metadata. Small changes to a public baseline's splits and hyperparameters improved cross-validation and public scores slightly, but worsened the private score slightly. A separate neural network experiment optimized a custom implementation of the competition metric that the author believed was incorrect.

The solution used log-mel spectrograms with a previous year's architecture modified to use EfficientNet B0, B1, and B2 backbones. Its most stable training recipe pretrained on the first 15 seconds of earlier BirdCLEF recordings, excluding classes present in 2024, then trained the final models on the first 5 seconds of 2024 recordings. The pipeline included Mixup V2, while heavy augmentation improved cross-validation but hurt leaderboard performance. The best single B2 model scored 0.68 public and 0.67 private, and the final six-model ensemble scored 0.70 public and 0.67 private before postprocessing, which provided a slight further improvement.

Balanced sampling, minority-class upsampling, and author-grouped validation supported training, although small validation gains correlated poorly with public scores. solution_title: From Production Optimization to Competitive Farming: My Kaggriculture Solution
solution_summary: The agent combined a replay-derived production schedule with bounded crop and livestock substitutions and forecast-guided selling. A small gradient-boosted model predicted rival sales, while rules preserved production reserves, feasible procurement, and worker execution. Optimizing terminal cash difference exposed market-timing gains that production totals alone missed. Livestock selection added 1,770 mean cash difference across 18 recorded-opponent scenarios, and an online snapshot reported 57.84% wins over 925 completed games.

The final solution averaged four neural models: two shallow MLP variants, a residual-style multihead network with cluster embeddings, and TabNet. Preprocessing combined quantile transforms, PCA, statistical features, clustering, and feature selection, with recursive selection based on MLP permutation importance providing a substantial CV improvement. Training used multilabel-stratified folds, seed and split bagging, label smoothing, and nonscored-target pretraining for one MLP. Pseudo-labeling gave a small improvement, while drug-group validation and several augmentation approaches were unsuccessful.

The final system retained an unchanged MXFP4 gpt-oss-120b model and the public-consensus inference recipe. Eight parallel Harmony rollouts used stateful Python kernels, stopped when four answers agreed, and selected answers through entropy-weighted voting. It scored 42/50 publicly and 39.5/50 privately. The main contribution was a reproducibility package and negative-results study: none of sixteen tested departures produced a detectable improvement.

solution_title: #7 Private #3 Public approach| Simple ensemble with post-processing
solution_summary: The solution combined LightGBM, CatBoost, random forest, and gradient boosting models trained on varied feature subsets. solution_title: 302th place solution - Ensemble of three models

TabM contributed valuable diversity despite weaker standalone validation performance, while XGBoost received greater ensemble weight. XGBoost used target means, counts, categorical frequencies, missing-value filling, and a log1p target transformation. CatBoost was excluded because prediction-distribution diagnostics showed substantial redundancy with XGBoost.

solution_title: Mapping Matter with Matlab: Sergey Yurgenson on finishing second in Mapping Dark Matter
solution_summary: The author centered galaxy and star images and computed principal components separately for their image stacks. Principal-component amplitudes served as compact inputs to neural networks, while some components also helped refine object centers. An earlier approach using modified quadruple moments and fitting produced unsatisfactory results.

The team combined two separate pipelines in a weighted ensemble, mixing neural networks trained with pairwise ranking loss and tree or linear models. Both pipelines used race-based sample weights, engineered categorical and cyclic year features, and survival target transformations. One pipeline used stratified cross-validation, while the other trained on the entire training set without cross-validation. Predictions were scaled before blending, and improvements in cross-validation often conflicted with leaderboard results.

The solution classified square animal crops from MegaDetector using three ImageNet-pretrained CNNs and a geographic and seasonal prior. Location-grouped validation guided ensemble weights, while motion detection removed static false detections. Sequence predictions used majority species voting and the maximum number of valid detections in a frame. A late experiment combining full-image and crop predictions improved both public and private scores.

solution_title: My brief overview of my solution
solution_summary: The solution combines image classifiers trained at several input resolutions, including a dilated ResNet-34. Dark-channel-prior haze removal was especially useful across multiple labels. Predictions were combined using separate ridge regressions for all 17 labels and voting, with the best submission voting across nine models. Simulated public/private splits showed meaningful score variation, motivating model selection based on cross-validation and stable ensembles.

The solution used a cascade of three text normalization layers. A contextual statistical lookup handled sufficiently confident transformations, while regular expressions processed structured formats such as dates, numbers, and URLs. Several LightGBM models resolved ambiguous alternatives left by the first two layers. Limited development time led to missed cases and simplistic local validation, with some decisions based on a public leaderboard covering only 1% of the data.

solution_title: PUBLIC LB 24th SOLUTION by team Electrium Z
solution_summary: The team combined weather interpolation, extensive temporal and weather features, and targeted outlier removal with a diverse collection of models. They trained both joint models with meter downsampling and separate models for each meter, finding three-fold validation more useful for leaderboard performance than larger fold counts. Their main ensemble used Bayesian optimization to learn nonnegative weights separately for each meter against public leaked labels, which also replaced predictions at the leaked sites. They prepared an alternative average of strong submissions, giving extra weight to submissions with better out-of-fold performance on sites outside the leak.

The solution combined 12 logistic regression models using different subsets and averaging periods of weather variables. Species, geographic blocks, and a trap-level duplicate-row leakage feature supplemented the weather features. Limiting each model's weather variables reduced overfitting, and the ensemble scored 0.811 privately and 0.823 publicly. Fitting year-specific linear weights using the public test set improved these scores to 0.833 and 0.842.

The solution combined predictions from Mistral 7B variants and Gemma-7b-1.1-it trained on different datasets. Different opening verbs encouraged prediction diversity, and outputs were concatenated into a single recovered prompt. Appending a specially constructed suffix exploited sentence-embedding behavior associated with the token lucrarea, reportedly adding up to 0.05 to the score. Individual models stayed below 0.65, while the final diverse predictions and suffix reached about 0.71.

The solution used Dlib metric learning with a ResNet variant producing 128-dimensional embeddings from grayscale whale images. Model-derived heatmaps guided fluke cropping and PCA alignment, with training first on original images and then on crops. Mirrored whales became separate classes, playground competition data expanded training, and semi-automatic cleaning reduced label noise. Predictions ranked enrollment images by Euclidean embedding distance with a threshold for new whales, and the final ensemble concatenated embeddings from nine ResNet models. The author reported a best single-model score of 0.938, a final public score of 0.953, and a private score of 0.948.

The solution blended two-, three-, and four-hidden-layer neural networks with TabNet and DeepInsight models. Denoising-autoencoder features were concatenated with original inputs, while rank Gaussian transformation, statistical features, TabNet-specific PCA, and smoothing loss also helped. Rare-target weighted-loss models were blended with ordinary-loss models because weighting improved validation but did not improve the public score. The final submission scored 0.01608 privately and 0.01820 publicly, with a CV score of 0.01550 excluding control vehicles.

solution_title: 12th place - Disjunctions of bigrams, trigrams only

An Aho-Corasick automaton produced phrase counts and ranks, while query weights interpolated rank-based and uniform relevance assumptions. Hyphens joined phrase words to reduce token usage, and bitsets accelerated candidate selection. Phrase-only queries limited coverage and description searches were expensive; Bayesian tuning was also hindered by noisy evaluations and weak validation indexes.

solution_title: An Analysis of Evaluation Predicates in a Tool-Using Agent Security Competition
solution_summary: The authors crafted prompt templates targeting sentinel-based exfiltration and email-based confused deputy scoring after inspecting the evaluation SDK. Their selected exfiltration submission scored 102.42 public but zero private, while the selected email submission scored 13.385 public and 13.37 private. The final solution extended a tabular LightGBM pipeline with patient-grouped numerical normalization and categorical occurrence counts. Feature removal, image PCA features, RGB statistics, alternative imbalance treatments, and a second-stage probability-feature model did not provide useful improvements.

solution_title: 1st place - I think it was genetic programming
solution_summary: The author combined tree models and tabular neural networks, including tuned TabM models, Keras factorization machines, and TensorFlow embedding networks. Neural-network stacking became the preferred ensembling method, with 11 genetic-programming features contributing a small additional gain at the ensemble stage. CatBoost then refined a Keras ensemble through its baseline mechanism, improving public and private scores by about 0.00002. A final hill-climbing ensemble combined four previous ensembles, while many alternative networks and automatically generated models added little useful diversity.
compute: Neural-network ensembling took 1–2 hours for 40–50 models; Optuna ensemble searches took 4–10 hours; Lasso 10x10 repeated K-fold took about 2 minutes.

solution_summary: The author built a nested ensemble of seven XGBoost models and reported a private AUC of 0.828314. The component pipelines used Tomek links, edited nearest neighbors, undersampling, and one feature-elimination variant. XGBoost configurations used depths of four or five, 300–600 rounds, and learning rates around 0.0202. The final prediction averaged an ensemble of all seven models with an ensemble containing models one, three, and four.

The solution first classified temporal image sequences for contrail presence, then segmented only images whose classification probability exceeded 0.2. Segmentation used a weighted ensemble of five 2D U-Net models with different encoders and losses, with weights optimized on validation data. Human mask soft labels, pseudo-label pretraining on other time steps, geographic fold construction, and test-time augmentation contributed to the approach. Reported scores were 0.694 CV, 0.706 public, and 0.699 private.

The solution used a 2.5D pipeline combining segmentation and classification with U-Net models using Pyramid Vision Transformer V2 and MaxViT encoders. Rescaled CT volumes were sampled into 14 frames per epoch, with body and organ masks restricting the input to relevant regions. Pretraining on 2D masks improved convergence, and six classification heads were trained with metric-weighted cross-entropy. Transformers outperformed convolutional models, especially for extravasation, while the ensemble with scaling achieved a CV score of 0.3530 and an LB score of 0.39.

solution_title: 11th place solution: batch normalization and 2D post-filtering
solution_summary: The solution averaged pre-softmax heatmaps from 32 UNet models using a mixture of ResNet architectures and random seeds. Batch normalization improved training stability and consistency across inference windows, while a recall-oriented loss combined cross-entropy and Tversky terms. Connected components produced particle candidates, with a small 2D classifier filtering false positives for two protein classes. Large elongated ribosome components were split with K-means to recover multiple nearby particles, although limited training data made cross-validation comparisons inconclusive.
compute: 32 models, each trained for 2200 epochs; hardware and elapsed time unspecified.

solution_title: How to get a top 1% scoring solution with no ensembles
solution_summary: The author used a single EfficientNet-B3 image model, removing black borders while preserving image aspect ratios. Replacing cross-entropy with MSE and increasing resolution from 120×120 to 728×728 substantially improved validation performance. A small neural network combined information from the left and right eyes, producing public and private scores of 0.84613 and 0.83880. Balanced loading, class weights, and heavy augmentation did not improve results.

solution_title: 369th place solution YOLO part with PB0.840 notebook
solution_summary: The solution used YOLOv8l and YOLO11l on resized tomogram slices, combining competition data with an external flagellar-motor dataset. Training improvements included broader target-slice coverage, flip augmentation, larger images and batches, and checkpoint selection by distribution focal loss. Slice detections from multiple models were grouped with depth-first search and averaged to obtain motor coordinates. Multiprocessing, FP16 prediction, threaded image loading, and random slice skipping reduced inference time, with the eight-model ensemble taking about three hours and scoring 0.840 on the public leaderboard; the team's highest reported public score was 0.851.
compute: Four inference processes, two sharing each T4 GPU; about 1h40m for one model after acceleration and about 3 hours for the eight-model ensemble.

solution_title: 107th solution. Our first time to kaggle!
solution_summary: The solution combined three Swin-based prediction branches. The first incorporated metadata through linear layers and an SVR, while the second combined image-only Swin models with ridge regression. The third used FastAi test-time augmentation with a Swin Large 224 model. Final predictions weighted the three branches by 0.3, 0.3, and 0.4.

The final solution combined eleven GRU models: five using at most 128 pulses per event and six using at most 160. Increasing GRU depth and width helped, as did increasing the classification resolution to 64 bins with a 4096-unit output head. Converting data to TFRecords enabled efficient TPU training on almost all available data. Training used a batch size of 4096 and stepwise learning-rate reductions, while GNN combinations and alternative prediction targets were not retained.
compute: Kaggle TPU VM and Colab Pro TPUs; 8–12 epochs per 12-hour Colab Pro session, depending on model and data size.

solution_summary: The post announces the team's post-mortem and links to its GitHub writeup. It says the linked material covers bot implementation and lessons from the team's first competition. The provided post contains no concrete implementation methods or results.

solution_title: A simple approach based on baseline notebooks (6th place solution)
solution_summary: The solution adapted the baseline pipeline by stacking three neighboring grayscale frames as input channels to EfficientNet models. High-resolution inputs, four-class binary cross-entropy, augmentation, and checkpoint averaging strengthened the classifiers. Final submissions used three-model ensembles with horizontal-flip augmentation, including a variant combining temporal strides of one, two, and three. Inference on alternate frames with linear interpolation and image prefetching helped meet runtime constraints.
compute: 20 training epochs; GPU inference with image prefetching.

solution_title: Santa 2025 Competition Silver 126th Solution: Hybrid Optimization Pipeline
solution_summary: The solution combined SAGA parameter optimization with Spyrrow strip packing and geometric refinement. Genetic search followed by denser local parameter searches handled broader exploration, while repeated strip-packing runs targeted small groups. Rotation, inward compression, local perturbations, and ring rearrangement tightened layouts, with conflict-based repair removing overlaps. Only group-level score improvements were merged, and historical best layouts provided recovery baselines.

solution_title: Easter egg(whats my ip)+ my rabbit holes [9 solves]
solution_summary: The author described manual approaches to several language-model capture-the-flag challenges. Semantle was solved by iteratively exploring semantic associations, while flag extraction used variations of a prompt asking for characters from the model's first sentence. Counting 2 was solved through manual brute force. Attempts involving DNS records and address redirection failed, and their significance remained unresolved.

solution_title: 39th solution utilizing Pr(is_test|X) by adversarial validation
solution_summary: The solution combined a conservative prediction built around adversarial validation with an aggressive ensemble built through cross-validation and rank averaging. Adding t-SNE features enabled a train-versus-test classifier to reach 0.89 ROC-AUC despite original features failing to separate the datasets. Its test-membership probabilities guided validation splits, model and feature selection, sample weights, and per-example blending weights. Semi-supervised learning helped in validation but was not used to generate test predictions.

The solution used the provided baseline helmet boxes without training a custom detector. It estimated camera position and rotation by matching projected tracking coordinates to detection point clouds and refining the alignment with an ICP-like procedure. Sensor-based tracking included removal of unmatched detections and isolation of the main player cluster. Bounding-box IoU tracking used a threshold of 0.35.

Separate LightGBM models predicted production and consumption using four target formulations involving lagged targets, daily averages, and baseline predictions. Simple consumption and generation baseline models were retrained daily, while the LightGBM models remained fixed. The final weighted blend combined target variants, ten seeds, and two hyperparameter settings for 160 models. The author considered this large ensemble and frequent baseline retraining less promising in hindsight than allocating time to LightGBM retraining.

The solution used B5, B6, and B7 encoders with global average pooling, batch normalization, multi-sample dropout, and separate ArcFace heads for individuals and species. Training used four body and fin crop datasets, frozen batch normalization, and Lookahead with Adam. After 40 initial epochs, the models trained for another 10 epochs using 12,157 pseudo-labels selected through model agreement and a confidence-gap requirement. Inference used larger images than training.

The solution combined two fine-tuned Luke–RoBERTa models with three pretrained Detoxify models spanning previous Jigsaw datasets. It prioritized validation results, using leak-free grouped cross-validation for fine-tuning and a separate host-derived pair set for evaluating Detoxify outputs. Weighted combinations reduced multiple toxicity labels to scalar scores, followed by a rank-based final ensemble and randomized tie breaking. The final ensemble achieved a private score of 0.81282, while attempts to incorporate Ruddit and hate-speech data were unsuccessful.

solution_summary: The main model was a molecular message-passing network inspired by neural message passing papers. It updated both node representations and the adjacency matrix at each step. Skip connections enabled deeper networks, although going beyond seven layers brought no improvement. The solution used 4/5-fold cross-validation and some stacking, with implementation in TensorFlow 2.0.

The author combined two LightGBM models with a simple forecasting baseline based on the latest increment without decay. One LightGBM model used standard regression and the other used Poisson regression. Their predictions were averaged equally, then blended with the baseline using weights specified in the linked notebook. The post reports no evaluation scores.

solution_title: 37th Place Solution(And Let's talk about CV and private score)
solution_summary: The author ensembled five EfficientNet models spanning B0, B1, B2, B3, and B5. Images received circle cropping and Fast.ai transformations including flips, rotation, zoom, and lighting changes. Models were first trained with 2015 data using 2019 data for validation, then fine-tuned for 15 epochs on an 80:20 stratified split of the 2019 data. Validation-loss checkpoint selection and a fixed split guided comparisons without cross-validation or test-time augmentation. The ensemble achieved validation kappa of 0.932 and private kappa of 0.926.

The solution combined three U-Net variants with equal voting: background prediction followed by inversion, direct car segmentation, and separate top/bottom segmentation. The background model was strongest individually, scoring 0.9970 and handling difficult edges and wheel regions well. Contour-based antenna localization followed by Canny edge processing improved continuity, although its estimated score contribution was only about 0.00004. Training used Keras with a TensorFlow backend, primarily on four GTX 1080 Ti GPUs.
compute: Primarily 4× GTX 1080 Ti GPUs, with watercooling installed to prevent thermal throttling.

solution_summary: The post provides brief reproduction instructions for the author's competition solution. A training script generates features, and a prediction script creates the submission file. Feature generation takes a few hours, but the supplied text does not explain the models or feature definitions.

solution_title: 3rd place solution & become GM!! (updated with code)
solution_summary: The solution applies CT windowing and concatenates neighboring slices from the same series to exploit continuity in hemorrhage labels. It also trains models to predict multiple slice targets and combines slice context at the stacking stage. Additional components include external CQ500 data, black-border cropping, generalized mean pooling, and stage-two retraining. The final model scored 0.045 privately, while an unselected user-stacking-only model scored 0.043.

The pipeline combined screen-time accounting features, behavioral ratios, and smoothed out-of-fold target encodings with tree-based models. A 177-member multi-seed stack was combined with an anchor stream through percentile-rank averaging, with the selected submission weighting the stack at 1% and the anchor at 99%. Stratified validation guided selection, and adversarial validation produced an AUC of 0.5654. High-confidence pseudo-labeling provided a small experimental gain, while a CPU-limited TabNet trial was much weaker; the final private score was 0.97101.
compute: Free/local resources; CPU-constrained TabNet trial

solution_summary: The solution emphasized diversity across six language models, training methods, prompts, and classification label spaces. It combined 37-class models that separated answer correctness from misconception prediction with conventional 65-class models, using LoRA, QLoRA, and full fine-tuning. Validation grouped normalized student explanations to reduce duplicate leakage, while ensemble selection relied on public leaderboard improvements after CV correlation weakened. Weighted probability averaging, targeted answer-rewriting augmentation, and question-specific misconception masking completed the pipeline.

solution_title: (2nd) Weakly supervised semantic segmentation + Synthetic data
solution_summary: The solution treated biomass prediction as density estimation using DINOv3 ViT-Large and ViT-Huge backbones with convolutional or DPT heads. It combined original data with pseudo-labeled synthetic images and zero-biomass bare-soil edits, while strong cropping, erasing, Mixup, and CutMix improved generalization. Models predicted clover, dead, and green biomass using Smooth L1 loss, with target-specific checkpoints addressing different convergence times. An ensemble with state-dependent scaling, WA dead-biomass suppression, and clipping achieved a 0.67558 private score, and FP16 with two T4 processes reduced inference to 27 minutes.

solution_summary: The author fine-tuned ai4bharat's Bengali IndicWav2Vec model using almost half the competition data plus CV13, totaling 497,574 samples. Training data was arranged into six stages based on WER and Mospred, although the benefit of this ordering was not established by ablation. The final submitted acoustic model scored 0.405 before a modified five-gram KenLM language model improved the leaderboard score to 0.385. DeepFilterNet denoising worsened results, while a subsequent punctuation-model experiment improved the leaderboard score to 0.359.

solution_title: [20th] A simple solution, attempts and thinking.
solution_summary: The final approach used Agent Alpha with a keyword pool expanded by deepseek-chat to 30,000 similar keywords. When Agent Alpha was unavailable, predefined questions were followed by a self-consistency chain-of-thought question generator. An earlier semantic binary search strategy suffered from inconsistent answers across models. The two submitted agents scored 1006 and 934.

solution_title: LB 141th/PB 515th Sol.AttentionPooling/FE expansion(Left + Right + Diff + Prod)
solution_summary: The author improved public biomass regression notebooks using attention pooling with Mamba fusion and a separate FiLM-based left/right feature-fusion model. Attention pooling emphasized useful image patches, while FiLM combined left and right features with their differences and products. EMA with decay 0.999 improved leaderboard performance for the Mamba model despite weaker cross-validation results, and affine augmentations were particularly useful. A public Google SigLIP feature model was also used, and multiplying dry-clover predictions by 0.8 yielded an approximately 0.01 leaderboard boost.
compute: Two weeks of participation.

solution_summary: The approach primarily transferred coordinates from known RNA structures through template-based modeling. It combined RibonanzaNet representation-based search and alignment with conventional blastn search and Smith–Waterman alignment. Chai-1 and Boltz-1 supplied structures when templates were unavailable or incomplete, and structural superposition patched missing regions. Ablations showed substantial contributions from both template search routes, while the dot-product representation variant achieved a private score of 0.56966.
compute: Approximately 160 seconds to search 3,991 cluster representatives for a 300-nt target, including target RibonanzaNet inference.

solution_summary: The solution combined one ResNet34 trained at 512×512 with three SEResNeXt50 models trained at 320×320. Six-channel images were normalized using non-black pixels and passed through a learned convolution to match ImageNet input channels. ImageNet fine-tuning used moderate augmentation and SGD with Nesterov momentum and cosine annealing for 70 epochs. The single higher-resolution ResNet34 outperformed the SEResNeXt50 ensemble, but all four models were retained and plate-based leakage was used in postprocessing.
compute: Single V100 server from FastGPU.net

solution_title: AMO: Agentic Math Orchestrator for Olympiad Mathematics
solution_summary: AMO wrapped frozen GPT-OSS-120B in an inference orchestration system with parallel Python-assisted solvers, asynchronous verification, and evidence-weighted answer selection. Scout agents and adaptive budgeting routed problems between standard solving and a diversity-preserving beam search, while resolver agents addressed conflicting answers. Persistent tool kernels, additional optimization libraries, and trajectory monitoring reduced wasted work and exposed recurring reasoning failures. The baseline reached a public score of 45 and the fully orchestrated version reached 41; the selected final pipeline solved 39/50 local benchmark problems with nine minutes remaining.
compute: Single H100 GPU; five-hour wall-clock budget for 50 problems.

solution_summary: The solution used seven-fold training on experimental data, percentile normalization, and voxel patches with hard particle masks. Training combined right-angle rotations, brightness and contrast changes, flips, and Dice loss, followed by an additional weighted fine-tuning epoch. Inference scanned overlapping volumes through the seven folds with different rotations. Cross-validation reached 0.808, while weighted fine-tuning changed the reported score pair from 0.741/0.733 to 0.740/0.735. Synthetic-data variants, alternative augmentations, pseudo-relabeling, and several postprocessing approaches did not work.

The solution used a play-level spatiotemporal Transformer to jointly predict player trajectories. Moving the input/output cut before and after the pass generated roughly 200,000 additional samples and was the most important augmentation. Basic relative geometry, velocities, temporal context, and a temporally weighted Huber loss supported training. The final prediction combined 48 models across week-based folds, random seeds, and different output horizons.

The solution fitted a differentiable physical transit model to calibrated, outlier-filtered, binned sensor data. It modeled wavelength-dependent planet radius, nonlinear limb darkening, transit timing, and polynomial drift using staged Levenberg-Marquardt optimization. Post-processing removed spectral artifacts, corrected high-impact-factor planets, and reduced radius variation with three-component PCA. Gradient boosting predicted scalar corrections to AIRS and FGS means and uncertainties, raising the reported scores to 0.581 public and 0.589 private.
compute: P100, FP64; typically 20–25 seconds fitting per planet

solution_summary: The author trained one COCO-initialized Mask R-CNN with a SpineNet-143 and FPN backbone plus an attribute classification head. Training used 1280×1280 images, focal loss for attributes, random scaling, and a mask-compatible AutoAugment policy. Attribute thresholds were tuned individually within categories to maximize F1. The final pipeline selected only one instance per image using a random forest that predicted the competition AP from 13 prediction features, improving private leaderboard score by about 0.065.

solution_title: 8th place solution: One trick to win the gold
solution_summary: The solution inferred patient and control groups from each person's minimum interval between visits. It discarded the abnormal five-month group and mapped three- and 36-month intervals to the six-month patient group, while treating 12-month intervals as controls. Separate piecewise time trends were optimized for SMAPE, with pooled coefficients used initially until visit history allowed group identification. The author reported public scores of 54.2–54.8 and private scores of 60.1–60.7 from identifying these groups.

solution_title: 51 Place Solution for the RSNA 2023 Abdominal Trauma Detection
solution_summary: The solution focused on solid-organ injury classification and retained mean-baseline predictions for bowel injury and extravasation. A low-resolution coronal 2D U-Net generated organ bounding boxes used to crop full-height CT scans into saved 3D arrays. A 2.5D EfficientNetV2-s classifier then processed the cropped volumes, with predictions averaged across series for each patient. The final approach used a four-fold ensemble, and segmentation training reportedly took less than an hour.
compute: 2D segmentation training took less than 1 hour at 256×256 resolution; hardware unspecified.

solution_summary: The final submission stacks 20 diverse tabular models, combining boosted trees, trained neural networks, a pretrained in-context model, and logistic regression. Astronomy features, synthetic-data artifacts, original SDSS information, and fold-safe encodings distinguish the base learners. The final upgrades fine-tuned TabICLv2 and added one-vs-rest CatBoost. These changes increased CV balanced accuracy from 0.97028 to 0.97045 and private leaderboard performance from 0.97024 to 0.97033.

solution_summary: The solution ensembles four LLM discriminators fine-tuned with LoRA for one epoch using 4-bit base weights. Conflicting labels are resolved by majority vote and duplicate examples are removed, while subreddit information is excluded from prompts to reduce shortcut learning. Models receive a rule and comment and produce violation scores from the next-token logit difference between Yes and No. Local stratified validation averaged over three random seeds guided development, and weighted prediction fusion combined the models. Dual-GPU scheduling and conservative batch sizes kept the final training and inference pipeline within an 11-hour runtime.
compute: Dual GPUs on Kaggle; final submission training and inference runtime of 11 hours.

solution_title: 10th place solution: U-Net with squeeze & excitation
solution_summary: The solution used a 1D U-Net with squeeze-and-excitation, five encoder/decoder pairs, and 10,240-sample context windows. Inputs combined unnormalized acceleration with normalized time and its sine transform, while several signal and time augmentations regularized training. Inference combined overlapping windows and left/right flips, then averaged predictions from two models trained with different seeds. Selecting those models using local validation and leaderboard scores reportedly improved the score by about 0.01–0.02; wavelet features and normalization were unhelpful.

solution_title: The Allen AI Science Challenge, Winner's Interview: 3rd place, Alejandro Mosquera
solution_summary: The solution framed science question answering as question-answer pair ranking using a three-class logistic regression model for two candidate answers and an Other class. Its 22 features combined knowledge-base retrieval scores, Word2Vec similarities, and question/answer heuristics, with corpus heuristics and embeddings carrying the greatest weight. A knowledge base built from Quizlet and CK-12 supported retrieval and embedding training, and additional Aristo datasets augmented supervision. Five-fold validation scores were around 0.59–0.61, and more complex neural models and ensembles did not outperform the linear model.
compute: Knowledge-base generation and indexing took about two hours on a normal computer; feature generation including Word2Vec took another two hours per dataset.

solution_summary: A ship/no-ship classifier filtered images before segmentation to reduce false positives on empty scenes. Segmentation models used ResNet34 and SE-ResNeXt50 encoders with body and contour outputs, trained only on images containing ships. Training combined ship-centered and random crops, extensive augmentation, and a Lovasz loss. Flip-time augmentation, watershed separation, and an average of four models formed the final prediction pipeline.

The solution averaged FPN and U-Net segmentation models with different encoders, applying them to images selected by a classifier. FPN with SE-ResNeXt50 was the strongest model, while lighter encoders contributed ensemble diversity. Basic augmentation, large crops or full-image fine-tuning, balanced sampling, and gradient accumulation supported training. Two rounds of pseudo-labeling substantially improved results, and postprocessing filled holes and removed small masks. Ten-fold validation correlated well with leaderboard performance.
compute: Multiple NVIDIA cards; models and count unspecified.

solution_summary: The solution used rule-based breast cropping, 1520x912 inputs, and EfficientNetV2S models with GeM pooling. Combining individual-breast and concatenated laterality inputs, two seeds, and vertical-flip inference improved robustness. VinDr-Mammo data labeled using model predictions improved cross-validation, and the chosen ensemble achieved CV 0.534. GPU preprocessing, early filtering of clear negatives, and FP32 TensorRT inference helped meet the nine-hour inference limit.
