solution_title: [33rd place] Key points of my solution
solution_summary: The approach constructs survival targets that distinguish observed events from censored patients at the same follow-up time. Observed-event targets use Kaplan-Meier survival probabilities, while censored targets use half that probability through a conditional event-time argument. Censored samples receive a uniform weight of 0.6 to reflect their uncertainty. Dynamic weighting based on follow-up time was tried but gave unsatisfactory results.

solution_title: RL training on a laptop (80th place)
solution_summary: A small entity Transformer was initialized by behavioral cloning from winning top-player replays, which supplied most of its strength. Separate 1v1 and free-for-all policies were then fine-tuned with self-play PPO, using a champion pool and teacher KL regularization to limit collapse. Inference sampled several actions and selected the value head's preferred action, switching to the 1v1 policy when only two players remained. A deterministic ship-count planner and opening launch guards supplemented the learned policy, with all training performed locally on an M-series MacBook.
compute: Local M-series MacBook; behavioral cloning under one hour, final PPO training about three days, approximately 80–160 samples/second.

solution_title: 4th Place Solution for the Child Mind Institute — Problematic Internet Use competition
solution_summary: The solution emphasized selective preprocessing and stacked CatBoost, LightGBM, and XGBoost models trained with five-fold validation. Important missing measurements were reconstructed using KNN, linear regression, logistic regression, or direct formulas, while less reliable columns often retained missing values. Related-variable interactions and sigmoid-weighted CGAS and SDS features supplemented the inputs, and optimized rounding thresholds converted direct SII predictions into classes. The ensemble achieved validation quadratic weighted kappa of 0.3912; TabNet and predicting PCIAT totals before mapping to SII were unsuccessful.

The author built an ensemble from two high-scoring public notebooks shortly before the deadline. The selected sources were the linked submit-only notebook and PyBoost notebook versions. The post provides the final ensemble notebook but does not describe weights, validation, or further modeling changes.

The solution followed a shared baseline and improved its time features and event post-processing. Replacing discrete hourly features with continuous seconds-of-day features improved cross-validation by about 0.01. Peak detection used a distance of 100 steps and a threshold of 0.005. Removing predictions whose surrounding features repeated on an adjacent day improved public and private scores by approximately 0.007 and 0.016.

The final model combined molecular message passing with Transformer-style blocks and three forms of multi-head attention. Geometry features, separate bond and scalar-coupling message paths, and auxiliary predictions of coupling contributions captured molecular structure. An eight-fold submission scored -3.039 on the private leaderboard, and including an earlier MPNN ensemble improved the score by about 0.05. Training used fastai with a one-cycle learning rate schedule, with the largest model requiring two V100 GPUs and roughly 1.5 days per fold.
compute: Final training on GCP using distributed training on 2 V100 GPUs; roughly 1.5 days per fold. Most earlier experiments used Kaggle kernels.

solution_summary: The author developed three prompt attacks intended to produce complementary disagreements among essay-scoring models. Each attack was prefixed with random common English words and used equally often in the final submission. Local tests covered three instruction-tuned models, two prompts and 20 essay topics per model, helping assess consistency despite weak public-leaderboard correlation. Smaller attack batches were explored only briefly.

The final system combined KNN regression, CLIP interrogator, and four fine-tuned image models with weights of 0.3, 0.1, and 0.6. Diverse prompt datasets were aggressively deduplicated and filtered before regenerating images with Stable Diffusion v2. Fine-tuning used token-length-based validation, partial layer freezing, horizontal flips, and MixUp. Normalizing model outputs before the fine-tuned ensemble improved its public score from 0.59314 to 0.59673.

The author filled missing values with zero and label-encoded categorical variables. Multiclass CatBoost models predicted the training-only Beta, Gamma, and Delta variables through a five-fold procedure, and these predictions became features for predicting Alpha. Alpha probabilities were converted to the binary target by summing B, D, and G for class 1 and using A for class 0. Validation used multilabel stratification based on the Greek variables.

solution_title: 627th Solution for CommonLit ESS competition- What doesn't kill you makes you stronger
solution_summary: The final approach returned to DeBERTa-v3-base combined with LightGBM after experiments with alternative transformer models. The author added SymSpell spell correction, separated preprocessing from the submission notebook, and used Optuna to tune LightGBM. MobileBERT performed poorly, and T5 could not run within the existing pipeline. The final changes achieved a public leaderboard score of 0.44 but did not transfer successfully to the private leaderboard.

The final solution blended an 80-model feedforward neural network ensemble, a LightGBM model, and an NLP regression model with weights of 0.6, 0.2, and 0.2. The neural networks predicted all genes from categorical compound and cell features, while LightGBM used gene expression from other cell types, donor counts, and LINCS data. Regularization, seed averaging, and cell-specific gene correlation aggregation improved robustness. The most consequential final adjustment shrank low-variance compound predictions toward zero and increased the magnitude of high-variance predictions, improving the regular ensemble's public/private scores from 0.560/0.743 to 0.558/0.733.

The solution ensembles EfficientNet sound event detection models trained with a custom soft AUC loss and semi-supervised learning. The loss supports soft labels and generalized better on the leaderboard than cross-entropy, despite weaker CV results. Together with semi-supervised learning, it raised a single EfficientNetV2-B0 model's leaderboard score from 0.850 to 0.901. The final ensemble contains 16 models diversified through spectrogram settings, audio sampling and augmentation.

solution_title: Private 20th | Public 25th Soluion - Simple model + Data augmentation
solution_summary: The solution ensembles vision-transformer models using either mean-pooled features or tile-level prediction heads, with FiLM conditioning. Tile-level heads and larger backbones were the most useful architectural choices, while random sliding tiling provided modest augmentation gains. Training first optimized FiLM and heads, then unfroze the backbone with a lower learning rate and a scaled Huber objective. Both selected ensembles scored 0.64 privately, below a single model that achieved 0.65.

The solution implemented Uber's multimodal trajectory-prediction approach with a raster backbone and a separate metadata branch. Training used temporally separated frames, capped agent sampling in crowded frames, and a multiple-trajectory loss, while validation used negative log likelihood. Cumulative sums converted network outputs into trajectories before transformation to world coordinates for loss calculation. Averaging seven checkpoint-based models improved the private score from 13.580 to 13.154 and the public score from 14.265 to 13.722.
compute: RTX-Titan-X; approximately one hour for the described 100,000-step interval with batches of 32.

solution_title: Anchor-Based Ensemble with Controlled Sidecar Corrections
solution_summary: The solution preserved a strong rank-optimized anchor predictor with a 96.95% ensemble weight and assigned 3.05% to a complementary pretrained audio model. Its primary branch fused prototype and sound-event-detection predictions, with taxonomy smoothing and prior-aware adjustments. Auxiliary sidecars supplied constrained rank corrections only when agreement and movement budgets permitted them. The final scores were 0.95044 publicly and 0.94221 privately.

The solution averaged eight image models and then blended their predictions with XGBoost models trained on metadata from the previous PetFinder competition. Image training used binary cross-entropy, with some species-specific models and fold-specific pseudo-labels to avoid leakage. Ten-fold validation kept duplicate images together, and images were cropped to resemble website thumbnails. Metadata blending used AdoptionSpeed where available and separate mixture weights for previous training and test overlaps, improving CV from 17.0058 to 16.9042 and achieving private RMSE 16.89096.

solution_summary: The solution represented each tournament matchup as differences between season-level team profiles and trained jointly on men's and women's data. Features covered Elo, seeds, schedule strength, rankings, efficiency statistics, and recent form. Stratified group validation aligned better with leaderboard feedback, while a combined MSE-correlation loss slightly outperformed BCE. Training used multi-dropout and EMA, and the team also explored adversarial methods and tree-based stacking.

The final prediction averaged one LightGBM model and one neural network trained on largely the same feature space. Greedy feature elimination using LightGBM cross-validation removed all calc features and several additional variables. One-hot encoding categorical variables helped, and the neural network also needed one-hot encodings of selected low-cardinality numeric variables while retaining their originals. Regularization was emphasized, while autoencoder reconstruction error was discussed as a promising but insufficiently explored anomaly signal.

CutMix at probability 1.0 and an ensemble that propagated each detector's outputs separately through classification were particularly effective.

About 15 base models were stacked with additional meta-features, improving cross-validation loss from approximately 0.185 for the best single model to 0.157. The final ensemble mixed stacked and base predictions with weights of 0.75 and 0.25, improving leaderboard performance despite hurting cross-validation. Predictions were also adjusted according to question frequency to address systematic differences between validation and leaderboard data.

The author built neural models using PCA-reduced inputs, selected original features, metadata, and neighborhood or donor/day aggregates. Validation explicitly tested generalization across days and donors, alongside a relaxed split that allowed more training data. Linear regression combined out-of-fold predictions after balancing donor/day groups, and the relaxed-split ensemble performed best among the selected submissions. PCA denoising and validation discipline mattered more than pseudo-labeling or transformer experiments, which were unsuccessful.

solution_title: Detecting Hard Problems by Answer Diversity
solution_summary: The solver ran gpt-oss-120B with parallel Python-enabled attempts and used answer diversity to detect difficult problems during inference. It selected answers by plurality on the default path and median-capped logprob weighting when more than four distinct answers appeared without a 40% vote share. A fine-tuned problem classifier supplied category-specific mathematical hints at confidence of at least 0.90. The public score increased from 36/50 to 39/50 after adding routed hints, although concurrent changes and missing paired ablations prevent clean attribution.

solution_summary: The solution generated patent-search token pairs from CPC codes, titles, abstracts, and detailed descriptions associated with each target row. It retained pairs that discriminated target patents from other test patents and the broader patent collection. Pairs sharing tokens were merged to reduce query token counts. Calculating all patent metadata resolved the author's validation difficulties, and the linked notebook reported a leaderboard score of 0.83.

The author's best submission used Sentence-BERT embeddings as inputs to an SVR model, achieving a leaderboard score of 0.612. A separate experiment augmented competition texts with CBT training data and fine-tuned forward and backward AWD-LSTM language models using ULMFiT. Regression heads from these models were ensembled to pseudo-label CBT texts, which supported another training iteration. Both approaches were considered robust, but time constraints prevented further pseudo-labeling cycles.

The team built transformer models with concatenated CLS embeddings and separate question and answer modeling. Host and category embeddings, statistical features, and text cleaning improved performance. Resetting predictions to 0 and 1 reportedly added at least 0.05 on the leaderboard. Combining models improved validation and leaderboard scores by about 0.02; an unselected weighted blend achieved a private score of 0.42787.

The solution combined neural networks with fixed and trainable frontends, with architecture choices providing the largest gains. Bandpass filtering and selected waveform augmentations helped, whereas whitening did not. Retraining with soft pseudo-labels improved AUC by about 0.001, with a further benefit from label smoothing. Cross-validated ridge stacking and greedy model selection produced a 20-model ensemble with 0.88283 CV AUC and 0.8829 private leaderboard AUC.

The final solution combined predictions from numerous public notebooks through a manually tuned cascade of weighted blends, including negative weights. Each stage was adjusted using public leaderboard feedback, with little original feature engineering or model development. Final predictions were scaled, shifted slightly toward zero, and clipped, achieving 0.41521 public and 0.42192 private scores. A separate stacking submission used five-fold grouped cross-validation and achieved 0.42711 privately, performing worse than the leaderboard-tuned cascade.

solution_title: Avito Duplicate Ads Detection, Winners' Interview: 1st Place Team, Devil Team | Stanislav Semenov & Dmitrii Tsybulevskii

solution_title: 8th place solution: matched filter and CNN
solution_summary: The team combined a PyFstat matched-filter search with CNNs trained for stationary and non-stationary noise. High-confidence matched-filter detections supplied approximately 1,700 positive pseudo-labels, while synthetic mixtures expanded the small training set. The final scoring rule placed matched-filter detections above the remaining samples, which were ordered using CNN scores. Matched filtering alone achieved AUC 0.8406 on 600 training samples but only 0.764 privately and 0.760 publicly, motivating the combination.

The solution combined pretrained EfficientNet-B7 Noisy Student and ViT Base16 models using only competition data. Five-fold stratified validation and out-of-fold accuracy guided selection, with bi-tempered logistic loss, label smoothing, and model-specific augmentation. Standard four-pass test-time augmentation stabilized predictions. An equally weighted blend outperformed the individual models and the tested weighted blend, reaching 0.901 CV accuracy and 0.900 private leaderboard accuracy.

solution_title: 135th place - Adding item amount check and Prefix Tree+Binning based text processing
solution_summary: The approach combined RAPIDS nearest-neighbor search on TF-IDF text features with an EfficientNet and NFNet image ensemble using ArcFace. Text processing repaired split words, normalized similar misspellings, and cleaned strings. Quantity detection helped reject products with matching names but different sizes or quantities. Identical titles or perceptual hashes added matches, while Jaccard filtering refined text matches.

The author's best solution used XGBoost. They tried several XGBoost configurations and found no improvement from adding other model libraries. The post links to the implementation but provides no further pipeline or validation details.

The solution used stratified cross-validation and an ensemble of nine tree-based classifiers and regressors. Its components included a decision tree, random forests, XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost. Optuna optimized the coefficients used to blend predictions. Two notebook versions achieved private scores of 0.77044 and 0.77126, and the author reported selecting the wrong version.

The post describes a reproducible submission formed by averaging seven model checkpoints. That submission is reported to score 84.698 on the private evaluation, although it is not the team's best submission. The authors also provide their LOUPE TensorFlow toolbox implementing learnable pooling modules and gated variants. Further architectural details are deferred to the linked paper.

The author engineered 11,226 features and investigated predicting normalized earthquake-cycle position rather than time to failure directly. A CNN operating on binned waveform statistics estimated cycle position and helped infer the earthquake-interval distribution of the test data. Final LightGBM models excluded short-interval training segments and used selected segments to resemble the inferred test distribution. The four-segment submission achieved a private score of 2.41465.

Four path-dependent penalty constraints prevented tours that would require costly or impossible arm movements. solution_title: 17th Place Solution: Gradient-Boosted Tracking + Metric-Labelled Graph Edits

Adaptive detection scale addressed nucleus-size differences, while division rules, drift-aware smoothing, and metric-trained graph edits improved tracking. solution_summary: The team trained LightGBM and XGBoost multiclass log-loss models with varied features, weights, and parameters. Features included up to five months of lags and summary statistics over those lags. A greedy ensemble selected additional predictions by lowest Pearson correlation and slightly outperformed broadly merging many predictions. The shared code produced a public score of 0.0306377, while missing-month imputation, historical backfilling, and older lags did not help.

The team combined five absolute-position predictors and three motion-delta predictors using weighted averages and uncertainty-aware cost minimization. Validation used 548 training paths selected to match seven observed test-set conditions. Corrected maps supported iterative corridor snapping, followed by discrete optimization over nearby grids with penalties for position, motion, and path plausibility. Discrete optimization was the decisive improvement, producing final CV and leaderboard scores of 2.523 and 1.392 without using leakage.

The solution used a two-stage virtual-geosteering pipeline combining physics trackers, spatial geometry, and learned tracker-confidence estimates. A LightGBM classifier produced five error-bin probabilities that informed an ensemble of 24 LightGBM variants and three deep sequence models. Target and loss diversification, optimized blending, and stratified well-level validation addressed heterogeneous trajectories. Robust polynomial refinement and an uncertainty-dependent fallback to particle-filter predictions constrained implausible outputs.

The solution combined XLM-RoBERTa, RemBERT, and MuRIL question-answering models trained with competition data, MLQA, and SQuAD. Models shared a document stride of 135 and maximum length of 400, with selected fold models used for inference. This voting pipeline increased the public score from 0.792 to 0.811.

solution_title: 🎅 Generating a 2428 solution in 100 lines of code
solution_summary: The post thanks the organizers and community and congratulates participants. It links to a notebook describing the team's journey to a 2428 solution. The post itself provides no implementation details.

The solution combined four XGBoost models and two GRU models sharing roughly 600 features. It used capacity-normalized targets, including a residual relative to a two-day lag, and validated on a chronological holdout after the first 500 days. Monthly retraining incorporated newly available observations and improved test performance. The combined models achieved a reported test score of 52.3090 with three updates, while neural models contributed about 0.9 improvement.

The pipeline first segmented sagittal images to assign vertebral levels, then segmented axial slices to crop bone regions. A 2.5D EfficientNet-B5 classified fractures using slice labels inferred from bounding-box annotations and fracture-free patients. Pseudo-labeling raised slice-level AUC from 0.916 to above 0.94. A bidirectional GRU with attention and convolution combined extracted slice features into study-level predictions, while ensembles did not improve leaderboard results.

solution_title: Part of 8th Place Solution - Macro DSL
solution_summary: The team's overall submission combined three approaches, and this post explains the author's domain-specific-language contribution. The DSL used larger macro-like commands to make program composition manageable with a simple search. Its initial split-filter-combine operations targeted tasks where panels or objects are selected or combined into a smaller output. The author subsequently extended the approach to other task types, accepting reduced generality to obtain a feasible competition solution.

Eight-way test-time augmentation generated activation summaries that fed per-label XGBoost stacking models. Label-specific thresholds were optimized per fold with smoothing, and fold votes determined label inclusion. The final submission averaged second-level soft predictions and achieved 0.9345 CV and 0.93206 private score.

solution_summary: The agent combined behavior cloning from strong public players with PPO refinement of the later game. A small transformer consumed game-state tokens, recent history, and a fixed reference action tape, then emitted atomic unit commands and market orders. The submitted agent used a frozen imitation policy through day 11 and switched to PPO on day 12, with greedy inference throughout. Cached openings, GPU simulation, and accelerated distributed training made learning practical, while league-based greedy evaluation selected checkpoints.

solution_summary: The team built its approach around ConvNeXt and CaFormer backbones, drawing heavily on shared community work. Models were fine-tuned for 80–120 epochs. Final predictions used both weighted-mean and median ensemble strategies. The author reported almost no difference between public and private leaderboard results.

The author developed a diverse Ridge ensemble and a second submission based on a neural network augmented with model predictions. The better final submission added SVR, LightGBM, CatBoost outlier-classifier and XGBoost predictions as numerical neural-network features. Fold-specific median target encoding and leakage-controlled cross-validation supported the modeling pipeline. The neural ensemble scored 72468 in cross-validation and performed better on the leaderboard than the Ridge ensemble despite the latter's stronger validation score.

The author trained NASNetLarge from scratch on 224×224 images using only two training archives. Labels appearing fewer than 50 times were removed, leaving 3,862 categories. Albumentations transformations and four-way test-time augmentation supported training and inference, while tuning the prediction threshold to 0.049 raised validation F2 to 0.68. Blending NASNet, Xception, and VGG-16 helped stage 1, but the stage 2 solution used NASNet alone.

The authors trained a small transformer and a bidirectional GRU to predict three-dimensional unit direction vectors, optimizing mean angular error directly. solution_title: 23 flags with elegant solutions especially to Cluster 3 and Semantle

For Cluster 3, tuned t-SNE parameters automatically recovered the ordering of scattered tokens. For Semantle, gradient descent with buffer replay searched for words and reportedly completed the challenge in roughly a dozen or more guesses. The author shared training, inference, and tile-generation code, and reported that an older experiment scored 0.912 publicly and 0.948 privately but was missed in submission selection.

Multilabel CutMix and mosaic combine disease labels by union, with healthy tissue contributing no disease label. ResNet50 and ResNeXt50 models use extensive augmentation, test-time flips and center crops, and late class balancing. Training also uses label smoothing, warmup, cosine annealing, and AdamW; a proposed LeafGAN extension remained unfinished.

solution_title: 27th Place Solution - Listening to the Pantanal
solution_summary: The solution combined four CNN sound-event-detection streams with a Perch/ProtoSSM branch, prioritizing complementary predictions under a CPU runtime limit. Students learned from hard labels, Perch embedding targets, and frozen CNN teacher outputs, with selective pseudo-labeling used only in one branch. OpenVINO and ONNX deployment, shared audio preprocessing, temporal smoothing, and weighted percentile-rank fusion enabled the ensemble to fit nearly within the full 90-minute budget.

solution_summary: The author developed diverse forecasting models using reservation-derived expected visitors, rolling averages, competitor counts, and holiday indicators. Experiments used both expanding chronological validation and random five-fold validation, with some models predicting residuals relative to rolling averages. A one-hidden-layer neural network combined models, but the ultimately successful submission averaged the SurpriseMe! submission with the best single public-leaderboard model. That single model used random five-fold validation and features calculated from all training data, including future observations.

solution_title: 29th LB And  LB 0.94376 for single Bert-Base
solution_summary: The solution combined six LSTMs, three GPT-2 models, and three BERT models, assigning 80% of the ensemble weight to BERT and reporting a score of 0.94599. Training used identity-aware sample weights and a loss combining weighted binary cross-entropy for the main target with unweighted binary cross-entropy for additional outputs. solution_summary: The solution trained nine SE-ResNeXt classifiers with different input sizes and aspect ratios to accommodate varied image shapes. solution_title: just for fun - half of a general solution
solution_summary: The author proposes recovering hidden target values by probing the competition's average absolute error score. Changing one prediction between its minimum and maximum possible values isolates that target's contribution, allowing its value to be calculated from the score difference. Reusing the previous score and deriving the last target from the remaining error reduces the proposed requirement to N score evaluations for N targets. The post does not explain how to recover all 10,000 targets within the stated limit of 5,000 submissions or report an implemented result.

solution_title: 3rd Place Solution (convert the COVID affected 2020 week8-week32's emission)
solution_summary: The author identified weeks 8–32 of 2020 as COVID-related emission outliers using monthly year-over-year comparisons. They rescaled emissions in that period using ratios of weekly averages from affected and unaffected data. Training used only weeks up to 48 and the three complete features latitude, longitude, and week number. Final predictions were multiplied by 1.07 and corrected for a reported longitude-specific bug; the ensemble's composition is not described.

The solution trained 280 LightGBM models, with a separate model for each store and forecast day. Features included sales lags, time-ordered target encodings, binary sales predictions, and distances from event dates, while recursive features were excluded. Store-specific WRMSSE guided hyperparameter tuning and the choice of Tweedie or asymmetric objectives using two temporal validation windows. Final models used all days through 1941, trained for 300 rounds without early stopping, and ensembled predictions from iterations 100, 200, and 300.

solution_summary: The solution combined UniverseNet, Faster R-CNN, and YOLOv5 detectors with ResNet34 classifiers for filtering and adjusting box probabilities. Pseudo-labeling 31,000 NIH images added a small ensemble gain, while custom box voting accounted for confidence, overlap, and distinct supporting models. More than 30 GBMs were explored, with categorical handling and hyperparameters tuned across XGBoost, CatBoost, and LightGBM. Four repetitions with different random seeds and OOF predictions were used to assess robustness.

The full ablation reaches 40.8 private score, while reranking and stronger-model decoding ensembles provided no useful gains.

solution_summary: The reported approach combined XGBoost with ICA, PCA, truncated SVD, and Gaussian and sparse random projections. solution_summary: The team ensembled a CatBoost model with a Transformer for sequential answer prediction. CatBoost used 183 features describing question difficulty, user ability, recent behavior, timing, and learned question and tag representations. solution_summary: The author started from Dominic Breuker's solution and repeatedly replaced groups of bags with randomly constructed bags of the same type, retaining changes that improved the leaderboard score. They modeled overweight-bag counts probabilistically to estimate the benefit of different replacement strategies. A mixed-integer program allocated the available improvement moves across bag types. The final score was 37212, close to the model's projection of 37232 from a starting score of 36719. Sampling half a billion solutions helped estimate the prior distribution, though the author questioned its usefulness.

The author used an ImageNet-pretrained DenseNet with a temporal attention head for bird-call classification. The prose names DenseNet201, while the supplied implementation instantiates DenseNet161. Training used binary cross-entropy, five-fold cross-validation, Adam, cosine warm restarts, and stochastic weight averaging. Gamma adjustment, frequency spectrogram augmentation, and MixUp were used, while numerous alternatives including ResNet, denoising, and threshold optimization did not work.

A DenseNet121 classified five attributes from object crops, while individual XGBoost models predicted common relationships using bounding-box geometry. Rare relationships used empirical priors, and final scores multiplied object detection probabilities by attribute or relationship probabilities. Flipped-image inference and retaining low-confidence detections improved detection performance, and the full pipeline ran in under 24 hours on an i7 with one GPU.

solution_title: A jungle of models, "sophisticated" overfitting, and suboptimal selections: How I rose to #1, and fell to #299
solution_summary: The author explored ensembles of hundreds of out-of-fold prediction sets, comparing linear stacking, hill climbing, differential evolution, and AutoML ensembles. Lasso also served as a selector for downstream ensemble methods, while smaller combinations were investigated to limit overfitting. The final choices were the highest public-scoring submission and a five-OOF combination, which scored 0.96847 and 0.96833 privately. Extensive public and cross-validation tuning proved unreliable, although a retrospective negative-weight hill-climbing experiment performed better on a smaller model collection.

The team reconstructed user identities from D features and consistent transaction attributes, then used those identities for features, leaderboard probing, and prediction overrides. Adversarial validation created a restricted feature branch, while probe-derived pseudo-labels supported full-data LightGBM training and bagging. Their final blend combined models with different feature sets and applied identity-based post-processing. It achieved 0.9586 public and 0.9363 private AUC.

The approach emphasized forecasting features informed by energy-domain knowledge. Exponentially weighted air-temperature averages over daily, weekly, and monthly spans substantially improved the model. The author also added a linear time trend and holiday indicators and replicated CPMP's two-phase training and prediction procedure. The writeup identifies cleaning non-electricity meters and modeling different time subsets as opportunities that were not explored.

solution_title: Kaggle Homesite contest 3rd Place solution (New Model Army part)
solution_summary: The solution generated multiple transformed datasets and trained diverse classifiers to create out-of-fold prediction features. Shared fold assignments kept model comparisons consistent and prevented leakage during stacking. A further stacking stage removed linear combinations of metafeatures and trained neural-network, XGBoost, ranger, hill-climbing, and glmnet models. A handcrafted hill-climbing ensemble produced the final blend, with full replication requiring substantial memory and more than ten days of computation.

solution_summary: The pipeline first detected objects and cropped their bounding boxes, then classified the cropped images. Its best single model was an ImageNet-pretrained EfficientNet-B0. Training combined conventional augmentation with CLAHE, grayscale, cutout, mixup, and label smoothing. This configuration achieved a private leaderboard F1 of 0.224.

The solution followed the host pipeline of global descriptors, local matching, and reconstruction, with efficiency improvements in each stage. Global descriptors combined models previously trained for Google Landmark 2021. Detector-based matching favored SuperPoint and SuperGlue, with keypoints and matches ensembled and deduplicated. Lighter COLMAP settings reduced reconstruction time while preserving accuracy.

solution_title: 85th Place - Physics-Aware LightGBM with Test-Time Calibration
solution_summary: The solution generated multiple geological TVT trajectory candidates and trained LightGBM to combine them with engineered well, GR, typewell and spatial features. Candidate agreement and uncertainty helped the model assess which physical hypotheses to trust, while validation grouped samples by well. Structural post-processing reduced noise and unrealistic drift, and masked-prefix calibration estimated conservative well-specific bias corrections at inference. A robust physics consensus provided an additional constraint; geological features and priors contributed more than extensive model tuning.

The final solution ensembled 18 transformer models across DeBERTa, Longformer, and Funnel variants with a maximum sequence length of 1600. Training used Fast Gradient Method for robustness and exponential moving averages to smooth training. Post-processing merged selected discourse spans, filtered Lead and Concluding predictions, extended span boundaries, and scaled token probabilities using factors found by genetic search. Optuna tuned post-processing hyperparameters, and DeBERTa-xlarge achieved the strongest reported individual CV score of 0.7092.

solution_title: 8th place private solution - a single SMILES-based transformer model is all we need. And a proper benchmarking
solution_summary: The final solution used SMILES-only multitarget transformers, with separate training and averaging for shared and unseen building blocks. Fine-tuned MolFormer and a compact custom RoBERTa were the strongest models. For unseen blocks, similarity-aware and block-exclusive five-fold splits supported validation, while balanced training sampling retained a realistic class imbalance in validation. Shared-block models trained on nearly all 98 million molecules, and extensive experiments favored SMILES transformers over graph models and descriptor-based alternatives.

The pipeline used candidate blocking, transformer pair matching, and custom cluster merging. Blocking combined geographic coordinates, character TF-IDF names, category embeddings, and exact attribute matches to obtain about 12 candidates per record. A single mDeBERTa-v3-base model was fine-tuned on all training data with distance and country tokens and FGM adversarial training. Average-linkage-style post-processing requested missing pair predictions as needed and used raw logits, with an expected improvement of roughly 0.025 over predictions without post-processing.
compute: Google Colab V100 with high memory; 40 hours per epoch, 160 hours total

solution_summary: The model combined three pointwise convolution layers with four pre-layer-normalized transformer encoders and dense layers. It used 17 features, emphasizing player geometry relative to the rusher's movement direction; polar-angle features improved the score by about 0.0003. Cross-validation and adversarial validation guided feature removal, and the final submission included models selected under both grouped and temporal validation. Additional techniques included noise and positional augmentation, 20-pass test-time augmentation, snapshot ensembling, and downsampling 2017 data.

The final submission was a weighted average of two CatBoost models, two PerpetualBooster models, and one LightGBM model. Ensemble weights were found by hill climbing on out-of-fold predictions from non-stratified 10-fold cross-validation. Feature treatments included categorical representations of continuous values, binning, count encoding, target encoding, and a rounding transformer that mapped unseen values to the nearest observed value. A fastai neural network received no ensemble weight, while attempts to use k-nearest neighbors for continuous target encoding produced substantially worse results.

The approach extracted ORB descriptors from every image across the FLAIR, T1w, T1Gd, and T2 modalities and pooled them by patient. MiniBatchKMeans built a visual vocabulary from the training descriptors, and each patient was represented by a normalized visual-word histogram. A default SVC with probability estimation learned from these histograms and generated test predictions. Predictions were weakly separated, with private leaderboard scores around 0.60 and later submissions scoring 0.58 and 0.59.

solution_title: 78th Place Solution: Neural Stochastic Path Generator
solution_summary: A neural stochastic controlled differential equation generated candidate TVT paths using observed feature changes, correlated noise, and a frozen per-well offset network. Training used positive-word assignment inspired by YOLOX, random token masking, and one-cycle scheduling with late-epoch weight averaging. The final DeBERTa-large and DeBERTa-xlarge ensemble used non-maximum suppression and achieved a private score of 0.732.

solution_title: 3rd Place Solution — A Pure Global Feature Approach
solution_summary: The solution learned global image embeddings using Sub-center ArcFace with class-size-dependent dynamic margins. Models were pretrained on the full GLDv2 dataset and fine-tuned on images from the competition's landmark classes with progressively larger resolutions. Inference combined powered cosine similarities from five nearest neighbors with powered ArcFace-head scores. Ensembles concatenated model embeddings and averaged head logits, reaching a private score of 0.6344 with nine models.

The solution minimized perplexity through local permutation search using word relocation, phrase relocation, and phrase swaps, with neighborhood sizes adapted to each problem. Search history and recorded local minima supported backtracking, while scrambling and other kicks moved the search into new basins. Pinning the last word helped problem 3 improve from 197.5 to 191.5, and combining solutions from related problems helped escape a plateau on problem 5 before a custom kick reached 28.5. Simulated annealing, phrase-based decomposition, branch and bound, and random-permutation bandit approaches were unsuccessful.

Contrastive learning, auxiliary tasks, multiple temporal windows, and varied channel montages supported model quality and ensemble diversity. The final submission manually weighted heads from multiple models, with soft classification providing a useful balance between regression and hard species assignment.

solution_summary: The solution used a single DeBERTa-v3-small model to rank markdown cells against segments of ordered code cells. Each segment contained 16 code cells, with a maximum input length of 384, balancing context retention against sequence length. Separate heads predicted segment membership and within-segment position, while a third head learned cell continuity. Adaptive cell truncation retained more information within the token budget.

The final CPU pipeline combined frozen Perch v2 features with logistic regression, spatial Mamba, spatial attention, and temporal SSM heads, plus a pseudo-trained ConvNeXtV2 spectrogram model. Shared Perch inference and fold-safe pseudo-label generation were central to efficiency and validation discipline. Conservative family-level blending and file-level scaling produced a public score around 0.922. solution_summary: The final system was a weighted blend of sparse text classifiers, LightGBM, readability rankings, DeBERTa-v3-large, and a QLoRA-trained Mistral model. Sparse models used TF-IDF with test tokenization and spelling correction, while LightGBM selected its top 10,000 features in a two-stage pipeline. Training drew from several versions of essay datasets, with source-weighted sampling for LightGBM. Several alternative reward, ranking, token-level, and probability-based methods failed or were removed, and reliable CV-to-leaderboard correlation remained unresolved.

The solution combined topography-guided ConvNeXt regression, U-Net and Squeezeformer predictions, and particle-filter tracking through ridge-fitted ensemble weights. The strongest component rendered gamma-ray residuals and topographic uncertainty as images, then predicted control-point corrections to an initial physical TVT path. Large-scale staged synthetic pretraining, multi-trajectory prediction, and real-well fine-tuning were central to its accuracy. Vertical-flip inference and quarter-point re-anchoring improved validation, and the full ensemble reached an OOF RMSE of 4.998 despite uneven private-set generalization across components.

solution_summary: The solution combined a detection model covering all six targets with specialist models for opacity, none, and study-level predictions. EfficientDet-D5 represented each study-level label with a full-image bounding box, while the none score was computed from the top three opacity box scores. The five-fold detector achieved public/private leaderboard scores of 0.622/0.618. The best configuration used 36 tiles of 256×256 pixels and an EfficientNet B2 model. Training data were filtered using averaged predictions from a five-fold ensemble, with removal of 39 samples whose prediction-label difference exceeded three giving the best cross-validation result. Transpose and vertical and horizontal flips worked best at both tile and assembled-image levels, and the same transformations were used for test-time augmentation. Adam with gradual warmup and cosine annealing outperformed the other tested optimizer and scheduler combinations.

Feature engineering was minimal, while survival-target transformations, event-dependent target separation, and shuffled 10-fold validation were central choices. The author manually tuned ensemble weights, including negative weights, and submitted versions with and without classifier-based prediction masking. The unmasked final blend scored 0.693 on the private leaderboard, slightly above the masked version's 0.692.

solution_summary: The pipeline used separate ImageNet-pretrained EfficientNet B4 models for image and exam predictions, followed by models that incorporated neighboring slices. Metric analysis enabled image-model training on positive exams only, while the exam model focused on central slices. A random forest refined image predictions, and GRU and 1D CNN models predicted exam targets from sequences of pooled CNN embeddings. These stages improved the leaderboard loss from 0.215 to 0.183 and cross-validation loss from 0.235 to 0.203. Adding location information from class activation maps did not improve results.

solution_title: #19 Solution | AutoGluon + TF + LightGBM + XGBoost + Calibration
solution_summary: The author trained AutoGluon, LightGBM, XGBoost, and TensorFlow models, comparing three preprocessing options with 10-fold cross-validation. The final ensemble combined the best AutoGluon model with an AutoGluon combination of the other model ensembles, reaching 0.98527 CV. The team generated weekly recommendation candidates using popularity, purchase history, collaborative filtering, and color alternatives, then ranked them with LightGBM. Customer, article, and collaborative filtering features were especially important for late improvements. Training used selected candidate examples and a forward weekly validation split. Cold-start and sales-channel post-processing preceded a six-model blend that improved the leaderboard score by about 0.001.

It first averages neural-network and SVM predictions by identifier, then sequentially blends three more submissions with fixed weights. The final solution stacked 28 models with logistic regression, transforming their predictions into logits before fitting the combiner. An earlier submission combined nine diverse models, while a broader experiment combined 32 models from accumulated OOF predictions. Removing models with identical fold scores slightly improved CV and public leaderboard scores, although the unfiltered ensemble performed best privately. solution_title: 5th-Place writeup (with Better Compression Algorithm and Seed Cracking)
solution_summary: The team built handwritten Python solutions and reduced their size through intensive code golf and custom compression tooling. Their strongest compression improvements combined dynamic programming for Huffman code lengths, automatic variable renaming, and genetic optimization of source names and deflate payloads. They also recovered test-generation seeds and used regeneration for one particularly difficult task. Their compressor improved the score by about 700 points over native zlib, while early AI-generated and DSL-based solutions were ultimately replaced.

The solution used Feature Pyramid Network detectors with ResNeXt backbones, including variants with modulated deformable convolutions. Class-balanced image sampling and long single-GPU training were central to the pipeline. Parent-class boxes were added after inference, and eight models were combined with carefully tuned class-wise NMS and overlap-based score addition. Ensembling improved the private score from 0.56369 to 0.60231.

solution_summary: The solution combined repeated-trip matching with supervised driver signature models built from GPS-derived telematics features. Trip matching ensembled Douglas–Peucker runs at different sensitivities, while the telematics stream combined six models using random forests, gradient boosting, and logistic regression across three feature sets. Model choices were guided by leaderboard performance, and ensemble weights were chosen manually with individual performance in mind. Combining trip matching with telematics improved private AUC from 0.91375 to 0.97398.

The team stacked many base models built from diverse feature sets contributed by different members. A consistent cross-validation approach was central, with model decisions guided by agreement between validation and public leaderboard scores. They removed Scirpus’ features because their validation gains did not carry over to the leaderboard. Recurrent models on the time-series data were considered but never run.

Non-target features used all available data, including future listening behavior, while target-derived features used historical records. Training used the last 35% of records and a second shifted window; six windows improved validation by 0.005, but only two were used for test predictions. The final blend combined eight predictions from both model families, both windows, and variants with and without matrix-factorization features.

The author trained an MLP to imitate WeKick agents from scraped episode replays and sampled actions stochastically. Player-centered spatial features and extensive rules helped the policy handle states poorly covered by demonstrations. Rules governed sprinting, special game modes, boundaries, and distant-ball defense, while doubling logits sharpened action probabilities. Two agents reached approximately 1,300 scores on the final day, with hard built-in AI replacing easy AI for local evaluation.

solution_title: [0.67] 742nd Place Solution - Single Transformers Model Comparison Between Data Aggregation and None
solution_summary: The author compared a Llama sequence model with a Gated Tab Transformer using aggregated session features. The sequence approach grouped event rows by session, encoded categorical values as integers, and filled missing numerical values with zero. Despite five-fold stratified validation and experiments with alternative classifiers, the sequence model achieved only 0.621 privately. The Gated Tab Transformer performed substantially better, reaching a private score of 0.67; shorter sequences also worked better in submission experiments.

The solution extended an autoencoder-pretrained graph neural network with LSTM, GRU, and WaveNet layers for ensemble diversity. Training and inference used original sequences, reversed sequences, Arnie-generated structures, and reversed augmented samples. Additional base-pair probability features, graph adjacency matrices, and predicted 3D atomic distances improved predictions. Limited early pseudo-labeling accelerated convergence, and the final approach blended more than 20 models, although the author reported substantial sensitivity to evaluation conditions.

The solution combined silence-trimmed log mel-spectrograms with PCA-reduced spectral and temporal statistics. A modified MobileNetV2 extracted spectrogram features, which were joined with the additional features before dense classification layers. Ten stratified folds used staged training, variable-length inputs, random erasing, and mixup. Geometric averaging across folds and repeated crops at six lengths produced a MAP@3 score of 0.943289.

The solution blended slightly modified CNN14 audio models using standardized spectrograms with 128 mel bins. Recordings were resampled to 32 kHz, divided into 10-second chunks, and augmented by adding bird recordings, noise, and animal sounds. Four-fold validation attempted to separate recordings by author and creation information, with checkpoints selected using XC and BirdCLEF validation. The initial blend achieved 0.649 on the private leaderboard; later species-specific threshold adjustments improved public results without changing the private score.

Popularity weighting improved recall, while ranking features emphasized customer–item interactions, purchase timing, and category statistics. The author combined fine-tuned Qwen and Llama models with DeBERTaV3 and a bge-base-en nearest-neighbor classifier. Training data incorporated labeled positive and negative examples, with duplicate rule/body pairs removed. Models used test-time training, and cross-validation guided ensemble weights. Two submissions prioritized either CV or leaderboard performance; the best leaderboard ensemble included Qwen2.5-7B, Llama3.2-1B, bge-base-en, and seed-ensembled DeBERTaV3.

The author develops player evaluation metrics from tracking data while excluding ball information to reduce dependence on quarterback accuracy. Receiver scores combine separation, endpoint execution, route efficiency and consistency, while defender scores combine coverage tightness, pursuit angle, discipline and consistency. Experiments with artificial ball-location noise showed substantially greater degradation for the ball-dependent model. The analysis covers 14,108 plays and reports that player execution retained 76% of its level on wild throws.

The team trained separate survival-related regressors and classifiers using boosted trees, AutoGluon and PRL neural networks. Regressors targeting eight outcomes were combined through multi-task Elastic Net, while classifier probabilities drove race-specific prediction adjustments optimized with Optuna. The solution combined spatiotemporal graph convolutions and Transformers to jointly classify all 16 mouse agent-target pairs. Videos were standardized to 30 FPS and lab-normalized coordinates, with motion and inter-mouse features as inputs. Training transitioned from mixed cross-entropy and macro soft F1 to pure soft F1, with invalid behavior combinations masked. The final ensemble averaged probabilities from pairwise and non-pairwise models using different keypoints and sequence lengths, with horizontal-flip inference augmentation.

The submission used a simple Gaussian process classifier. Leave-one-out cross-validation suggested promising performance. Its public score of 0.70536 discouraged further tuning, but the model ultimately performed well on the private leaderboard.

The final solution averages XGBoost and LightGBM predictions across 20 seeds per model. Its main improvement came from frequency-based features computed on training data combined with non-fake test rows, replacing values with NaN according to frequency thresholds. The best single model used 601 features, including original columns, two transformed feature sets, and a null count. Five-fold stratified validation, positive-row duplication, and augmentation supported a final public score of 0.924.

Final processing restricted predictions to valid combinations, smoothed them over action-dependent windows, selected one action per frame, and merged consecutive frames into intervals.

solution_title: 3rd Place Solution - From Base to Stacking: A Multilevel Ensembling Approach
solution_summary: The solution combined TabM, residual TabM, XGBoost, LightGBM, and an MLP through a multilevel ensemble. Base models used target-stratified seven-fold validation with varied random seeds, which modestly improved out-of-fold scores. A neural stacker fed a YDF model alongside original features, and their predictions were blended equally. Merging this blend with the best public submission improved the reported public score from 0.05564 to 0.05563.

solution_title: Homesite Quote Conversion, Winners' Write-Up, 1st Place: KazAnova | Faron | clobber
solution_summary: The team built a three-meta-layer ensemble using approximately 125 selected models from a pool of about 500. Diverse categorical representations, date features, engineered interactions, and feature subset selection drove both model strength and diversity. Neural networks were the strongest stackers, alongside XGBoost and logistic regression. Careful stratified cross-validation and checks across fold seeds helped control overfitting, yielding a private AUC of 0.97024.

The final approach used EfficientDet5 and EfficientDet7 trained on 512×512 and 1024×1024 images. Training combined bounding-box cleaning, extensive online augmentation, stratified five-fold splits, and source-based splits for some fine-tuning. The team manually adjusted training, used early stopping, and changed augmentation distributions over time. Earlier Faster R-CNN and YOLOv5 experiments were superseded, with YOLOv5 removed after it was prohibited.

solution_title: 2nd place solution - pure Bayesian Inference, no deep learning
solution_summary: The solution uses Bayesian inference with Gaussian process priors to separate transit depth, stellar spectrum, drift, and detector noise. A custom iterative solver estimates posterior transit depths and uncertainties, with KISS-GP reducing the cost of spectral drift modeling. A rough fit across test planets supplies one uncentered PCA component for a second fitting pass. Invalid-pixel interpolation and adaptive temporal binning support preprocessing, while final depth and uncertainty scaling correct systematic errors.
The post thanks Kaggle and fellow competitors. It links to an external account of the author's experience. The provided text contains no solution details.

solution_title: I Solved Every Single Puzzle — And It Still Wasn't   Enough
solution_summary: Deterministic solvers recovered and verified rules for all 9,500 training puzzles, supporting a complete verbose reasoning dataset. The final training pool combined shared reasoning traces with solver-generated traces for missing puzzles and corrections to 66 bit puzzles. A one-epoch LoRA run used gentle category weighting to focus capacity on harder puzzles. Deep models, XGBoost, LightGBM, and linear regression were combined through multilayer stacking. solution_title: 6th place solution: spectrograms, wavelets, convnets, unets, and transformers
solution_summary: The final ensemble combined spectrogram, wavelet, and 1D convolutional models and reported scores of 0.369/0.462. Spectrogram models used CNNs with U-Net upsampling and transformers, while wavelet models used ResNet backbones and complemented the spectrogram models across event classes. Subject-grouped nested validation, local attention bias, waveform augmentation, and frequency filtering helped handle noisy data. Class-specific ensemble weights were optimized with GP_minimize while accounting for an outlier subject.

The post shares a feature-engineering notebook and its generated features for the ELO competition. The features focus on city, subsector, merchant, and merchant-category identifiers. The author states that target information was not used as in mean encoding. Processing exceeded the notebook runtime allowance and was run on a personal computer.

solution_title: 3rd solution | based on 90% multi AutoML solutions

solution_title: Public 531st -> Private 10th: The Complete Solution Code
solution_summary: The approach forecasts county-level microbusiness density with CatBoost and five separate models for different future horizons. Features combine technical indicators with external economic and demographic data, using only three months of history. Optuna minimizes SMAPE, and cross-validation is used to assess generalization.

The team combined a two-class classifier with an ensemble of several object detectors. The detector set included multi-head VFNetX, YOLOv5l, CenterNet2 DLA, and PAA with NFNet. Training used oversampling, light augmentation, and insertion of cropped abnormality boxes into healthy backgrounds. Weighted boxes fusion with IoU 0.3 prepared boxes, while a modified version handled post-processing.

The author engineered two datasets and trained a separate stacking ensemble on each. Both stacks used out-of-fold predictions and logistic regression as the second-level model. Their final prediction averaged the two stacks. The author attributed the main advantage to feature engineering and prioritized 10-fold cross-validation over public leaderboard feedback.

The solution ensembles U-Net segmentation models with four timm backbones and tunes each model's threshold on out-of-fold validation predictions. Training used no image augmentation, while the MaxViT models used stochastic weight averaging over their final five epochs. Experiments initially used small models and images before scaling up during the final week. Several alternative losses, architectures, and postprocessing approaches offered insufficient gains or were too expensive to pursue.

The final ensemble combined 29 token classifiers across six model families, including four DeBERTa variants, Funnel Transformer, and ELECTRA. Training used masked language modeling, with different losses and adversarial training methods for different backbones; DeBERTa models also used limited pseudo-labeling. Cross-validation guided ensemble weights, while selected clinical features received separate thresholds. Span-boundary postprocessing and threshold tuning improved the predictions.

solution_summary: The team built a two-level stack using LightGBM, XGBoost, and random forests across five feature datasets. Twelve first-level predictions fed second-level XGBoost and random forest models, blended with weights of 30% and 70%. Extensive order, manufacturing-path, timestamp, duplicate, and numeric features drove performance, with five-fold validation used to monitor stability. solution_summary: The pipeline combined multilingual text embeddings with geographic coordinates to retrieve candidate location matches, then classified candidates using separate XGBoost models for each neighbor rank. Missing text was filled from nearby locations, and embeddings from multiple language models were concatenated and refined with weighted DBA/QE. Graph postprocessing using Dijkstra distances expanded match sets and reduced false negatives. Training the embedding models on all available training data improved results but contaminated downstream validation; the reported score progressed from 0.922 to 0.947.

solution_summary: The team stacked CT windows into three-channel images and trained models using patient-based and study-based splits. Their two-stage 2D pipeline combined CNN backbones with a second CNN operating on predictions from five neighboring slices. An additional end-to-end sequence model used a bidirectional LSTM to incorporate study context. They stacked model predictions with a multilayer perceptron and averaged the outputs from the two split strategies.

solution_title: 40th Place Solution - Improving prediction with FFT-based data cleaning
solution_summary: The solution cleaned timestamps and event boundaries, then generated FFT-cleaned sensor features at several thresholds. Seven models combined different feature extractors with a UNet and a one-dimensional decoder, using five-fold grouped validation. Increasing recurrent feature dimensions from 64 to 128 helped more consistently than FFT cleaning on the private leaderboard. A two-stage optimized ensemble achieved 0.79049 CV and 0.802 private score.

solution_title: Study Log: Reflecting on the Differences Between Top Solutions and My Approach
solution_summary: The author reflects on their prompt recovery approach and compares it with stronger solutions. They constructed a validation dataset by applying extraction rules to public data, obtaining reasonably good correlation with the leaderboard. They identify insufficient attention to mean prompts and the T5 metric as weaknesses. The post provides validation insights but does not describe a complete final modeling pipeline.

The solution used XGBoost with iterative feature engineering and forward feature selection. V columns were grouped by missing-value counts, then reduced using correlations and unique-value counts. Additional features included frequency encodings, user-level aggregations, and transaction-day offsets derived from D columns. Similar reduction of C and M columns hurt AUC and was rejected. Reported scores were 0.951265 for local cross-validation, 0.928873 on the private leaderboard, and 0.954825 on the public leaderboard.

solution_title: [8th Public / 18th Private] - Full Wikipedia Passage-level Retrieval
solution_summary: The pipeline retrieved passages directly from full-text Wikipedia, reranked sentence chunks, and supplied the resulting context to DeBERTa answer models. A compressed full-Wikipedia index was complemented by a more precise science-specific index. Training used diverse synthetic questions and deliberately weaker retrieved contexts, which improved leaderboard performance. The full retrieval index alone achieved 0.891 with a public model, while learned tree-based rerankers performed worse than embedding scores.

solution_title: 7th Place Solution for the Open Problems – Single-Cell Perturbations
solution_summary: The author first learned cell-type, compound, and gene embeddings using a deep tensor-factorization approach trained on long-form competition targets. A second three-layer fully connected network used these embeddings to predict the target, with batch normalization and dropout. Four-fold validation held out selected compounds within each cell type, and final predictions averaged the fold models. Features from prior biological knowledge and other large models did not help, so the final approach relied on the learned embeddings.

solution_title: 6th solution: Node-level Instance Norm + Residual  SageConv on 5-hop-neighbour Subgraph
solution_summary: The solution uses separate graph neural network approaches for layout and tile runtime prediction. For layout, it reduces large graphs to five-hop neighborhoods around configuration nodes and trains a four-layer residual SAGE model with pairwise ranking loss. Graph instance normalization and gradient accumulation make training manageable in GPU memory. For tile prediction, GAT performs better than SAGE, and listMLE better targets the top-five ranking objective.

solution_summary: The team combined TF-IDF logistic regression, recurrent neural networks, attention models, and models using engineered text statistics. Word and character models used varied normalization and embeddings, including GloVe and fastText, while seed averaging and ten-fold stacking added diversity. The final blend assigned 60% to the strongest stacked and blended solutions and approximately 20% each to two individual blends. Setting predictions for 1,240 non-English comments to zero provided a small improvement, yielding scores of 0.9881 publicly and 0.9880 privately.

solution_title: TEAM HITHERTO — From Productive-Region Localisation to Transfer Failure
solution_summary: Team Hitherto developed a controlled search process for locating productive tool-agent attack configurations using aggregate public scores. They varied prompt representations, candidate generators, ordering, traversal, pacing, allocation, and portfolio composition, then attempted configuration-level reproduction. Several productive public regions were reacquired, although candidate-level and predicate-level attribution remained unavailable. The team reported zero private yield, with the exact selected configuration unverified.

solution_title: A brief overview of 13th-place LB solution
solution_summary: The solution trained ontology-specific MLPs on normalized ESM2 embeddings, using both the original training annotations and updates from UniProt and QuickGO. Target terms were selected by frequency, and predictions were averaged across cross-validation folds and six MLPs. Post-processing applied taxonomic constraints, propagated child scores to parent terms, and filtered low-confidence rare terms. The final predictions were averaged with eligible external GO annotations.

solution_title: 181th Place Solution | ChatGPT please rest now
solution_summary: The solution used a repeatable task-specific loop to generate, optimize, validate, and merge compact ONNX graphs. Direct-output Einsum representations, quantized intermediate tensors, and removal or sharing of constants produced substantial cost reductions. Candidates had to pass cached examples, fresh ARC-GEN tests, static checks, runtime checks, and the exact pinned inference runtime. solution_title: 116th: six weeks with LLM coding agents, and why replays mattered more than RL
solution_summary: The final bot directly replayed ShunkiKyoya's recorded games, selecting compatible tapes through a prefix trie and a simulation-tuned routing table keyed by shop sequences. Order prioritization and a weed guard improved execution without changing the underlying farming plan. On fresh worlds against seven opponents, it achieved 1044 wins out of 1120 games, compared with 974.5 for the plain replay trie. Earlier boosted models, bandits, and behavior cloning followed by PPO failed to compete with strong public bots.

solution_title: 29th Place Solution for the AI Village Capture the Flag @ DEFCON31 Competition
solution_summary: The writeup describes methods used to solve several AI capture-the-flag challenges. Clustering tasks used KMeans inertia and two-dimensional t-SNE visualization, while semantic guessing tasks relied on searching common English words and arranging high-scoring terms. Other challenges were solved through unsafe pickle handling, OCR-mediated XML injection, prompt injection, and task-specific prompts. The account covers selected tasks and omits complete executable solutions because the endpoints were unavailable.

The solution followed a compact training-data approach, sampling customers across months to approximate the June 2015 product distribution and adjusting it for popularity trends. It used random-split cross-validation, product-history features, customer-level aggregates, and one-hot encoded categorical values. A post-processing rule enforced the relationship between pension and payroll products, while older product history informed customer scores. Two team members' solutions were combined, and attempts to exploit household relationships or unrestricted historical features did not improve results.

The approach used T2-weighted MRI images with blank slices removed, slice cropping, depth-64 SIZ processing, normalization, and zero centering. A 3D ResNet50 was trained with batch size 16, an initial learning rate of 0.01, and a learning-rate scheduler. Using a single validation fold, the author selected five models from each training cycle for the submission ensemble. The author reported that the model did not generalize.

The solution emphasized engineered rental-listing features and diverse encodings of manager identity. Nested cross-validation supported target-dependent statistics and a large stack built with XGB and StackNet. A final XGB stage used recursive feature elimination, followed by averaging five selected models and predictions across validation folds. Stacking improved the reported leaderboard loss from roughly 0.515 for the strongest single model to 0.50068.

solution_summary: The agent used four LightGBM predictors trained on the latest 50 matches to predict either player's next move from two or three recent matches. Each predictor supported winning, drawing, and losing responses, yielding 12 strategies whose weights changed after each match. Confidence thresholds triggered random play for uncertain predictions, while a safety rule favored moves with low loss probability. The author repeatedly adjusted thresholds, weight updates, training history length, and LightGBM parameters.

The author combined ideas from public notebooks into a tabular modeling pipeline with interaction features, noise, hyperparameter tuning, and model ensembling. They used stratified cross-validation, progressively reduced regularization, and selected the best model in each fold. One submission achieved a private score of 0.84248 despite a less favorable public score of 0.84195. The writeup emphasizes uncertainty about which additions actually improved generalization.

solution_title: 11th Place Writeup - Transformers and Pseudo Label
solution_summary: The solution blended a hybrid regression network with a Conformer-based discrete-pressure classifier. The regression network combined convolutions, time-aware disentangled attention, and LSTMs, while the classifier added relative time distances to attention. Fine-tuning for individual resistance/compliance combinations and separate outputs for real and pseudo labels improved the models. Ensemble-generated test pseudo labels and a final blend of old and retrained models improved the public score from 0.1112 to 0.1074.

The team used a two-stage 2D pipeline that first segmented tumors and then classified MRI sequences using the original images and two predicted tumor masks. A UNet++ with a DenseNet121 backbone supplied masks to a bidirectional LSTM with an Eca NFNet L0 feature extractor. Tumor-based filtering, overlapping 35-slice chunks, patient-level prediction averaging, and zoom test-time augmentation helped stabilize predictions. The classifier achieved 0.685 validation AUC and 0.60696 private leaderboard AUC, while 3D models and external-data self-supervision did not improve results.

Topic texts incorporated ancestor titles, while reranking features captured embedding similarity, TF-IDF similarity, and topic-tree relationships. Embeddings were concatenated for retrieval, and reranker predictions were averaged before channel-specific thresholding and correlation-based post-processing. solution_title: Loss function and a short report (LB: 5)
solution_summary: The solution combined ten LSTM models, five BERT-Base models, and three GPT2 models using a shared sample-weighted loss. Sample weights summed each example's estimated influence across overall, subgroup, BPSN, and BNSP AUC terms. Inverse class-frequency contributions helped balance positive and negative examples within each metric component, although overlapping subgroups prevented exact balance. The overall reported score was approximately 0.94725.

solution_title: Brief summary of 13th place solution (hide the pain Harold)
solution_summary: The final solution combined one DistilBERT, two ALBERT-large models, and one BERT-large WWM model using a LightGBM candidate classifier. Model scores were supplemented with answer length and document-position features, while DistilBERT prescoring reduced inference work for the other models. Improvements included smoothing logits across neighboring windows, jointly scoring answer start/end pairs, and stochastic weight averaging. Validation used the official Natural Questions development set, where the best blend reached about 0.67, compared with about 0.68 on the leaderboard.

The solution blends two LightGBM models trained on closely related wavelet-derived feature sets. Its central post-processing step rescales predictions to a test-target mean estimated as 6.51 from a paper. Repeated nested validation guided feature selection and conservative, strongly regularized model settings. Statistical features were removed, while target normalization improved validation but hurt private leaderboard performance. The submitted models inadvertently used only about 60% of the training data.

solution_title: From nothing to something... a 103 LB jump!

Retrieval used a modified public notebook, expanded TF-IDF fitting, and a custom FAISS index built from page titles and two paragraphs. Predictions from parsed and cohere contexts were used when their ensemble confidence exceeded 0.41; otherwise, the same model's prediction using the custom six-million-page Wikipedia embeddings was selected. A more complex dynamic voting ensemble across four models and three contexts was tried but was not successfully developed further.

solution_title: Melbourne University AES/MathWorks/NIH Seizure Prediction 2016: 5-th place
solution_summary: The team split EEG recordings into unfiltered 30-second epochs and extracted kernel-derived, spectral-energy, and channel-spectrum correlation features. Patient-specific tree ensembles predicted each epoch, and their probabilities were averaged for each recording. Six-fold stratified validation without shuffling was essential to avoid leakage between neighboring epochs. A weighted ensemble of seven models achieved public/private AUCs of 0.81423/0.79363, although missing random seeds limited reproducibility.

The author tested a pure one-dimensional convolutional network after the competition by converting SE-ResNeXt50 from 2D to 1D operations. Inputs were normalized drawing sequences containing x, y, time, and pen-state channels, interpolated and clipped to length 224. Training for slightly more than a day achieved private/public scores of 0.939/0.940. The main benefit was speed, with 1,700–1,800 training samples per second on two 1080 Ti GPUs and over 3,000 inference samples per second on one GPU.

solution_title: 3rd solution - single TRANSFORMER model, link to kernel

Pretraining with 41,194 additional game-session labels and sequence-removal augmentation supported a best private score of 0.564.

solution_title: March Mania 2026: Top 8% (304th Place) – Bronze Medal Solution
solution_summary: The solution predicted point margins using a 60% GLM, 30% TabPFN, and 10% XGBoost ensemble built on 13 relative team features. Feature selection emphasized stable coefficients across seasons, with walk-forward validation providing realistic historical backtests. Separate modified sigmoid calibrations and probability clipping converted margins into men's and women's win probabilities. The submission achieved a Brier score of 0.1271382, prioritizing stability and interpretability over a larger feature space.

The solution used a single XGBoost classifier for men's and women's basketball win probabilities. Its central emphasis was possession-level efficiency features, including shooting, turnovers, rebounds, and corresponding opponent statistics. MinMax scaling and shuffled 10-fold cross-validation performed best among the tested preprocessing and validation choices. It used only competition data, made no manual prediction overrides, and reported a private score of 0.17619.

solution_title: 51st Place Solution - And Some of my Explorations and Learning
solution_summary: The final submission ensembled CatBoost, LightGBM, and a gradient boosted regressor using calendar, holiday, GDP, spline, and periodic features. Optuna tuning, stacking, and more elaborate ensembles produced strong validation scores, but the simpler ensemble performed better in leaderboard probing. Time series cross-validation did not fully track leaderboard performance. Deep learning was too slow, while Google Trends and additional spline or trigonometric features did not improve results.

solution_title: 2nd Place Solution  -  tmp's part ( code updated )
solution_summary: The solution blended complementary approaches, with the described CITEseq pipeline combining MLP and LightGBM models. Preprocessing combined count transformations, normalization, standardization, and day-based batch correction. Multiple decomposition features and features with stable target correlations across donor-day groups improved performance. Random five-fold validation tracked leaderboard results, while day-based splits provided an additional robustness check; the described Multiome feature experiments were excluded from the selected submission.

The solution combined six DeBERTa-v3-large models trained on the full dataset with different sequence lengths and slightly varied hyperparameters. It tokenized the supplied substrings, averaged subtoken probabilities, and reduced BIO targets to seven classes before restoring the format afterward.
