Name propagation, address newline corrections, and downscaling the O-class probability were important post-processing steps; augmentations did not improve the final submission.

solution_title: 10th Place Solution: Hierarchical Bayesian Model with 5 features
solution_summary: The solution used a hierarchical Bayesian regression model with five features to predict PCIAT total scores. It modeled age-category random effects and respected the target's lower bound of zero, while imputing missing features with training medians. Posterior means were converted to SII using thresholds optimized for training QWK. Seven-fold stratified validation and averaged, rounded test predictions produced reported scores of 0.441 CV, 0.447 public, and 0.473 private.

The solution used a modular library of rule-based strategies for factory placement, factory operation, and robot behavior. The latest placement strategy scored ice and ore separately and considered nearby rubble. Robot control combined spatial state matrices, environmental monitoring, and task allocation to manage mining, clearing, combat, charging, and collision avoidance. Searching for paths within cropped map windows proved unexpectedly useful.

solution_title: When the Public Score Lies: Guardrail Divergence & the Deputy Survivor
solution_summary: The team reverse-engineered replay scoring and measured real victim models to optimize scoring events per generation-second. Public performance reached 89.020 through output minimization, fixed-count candidate emission, and GPT-OSS-specific eight-hop posting, but exfiltration scored zero privately. A deliberately retained benign confused-deputy email portfolio produced the surviving private score of 18.375. The main missed opportunity was failing to apply the same throughput optimization effort to that surviving primitive.
compute: T4 GPU probe kernel; approximately 25 minutes per measurement cycle versus 12–16 hours for submission feedback.

solution_summary: The pipeline refined an existing grid-detection stage and focused on digitizing four cropped long ECG leads. ConvNeXt Large, an SNR-aware loss, and iterative grid alignment improved signal quality. Training and inference used three image resolutions and multiple model architectures. Extensive data generation, CycleGAN style transfer, and algebraic lead corrections did not help.

The solution modeled missing values separately for F1, F3, and F4 using an average of a TensorFlow neural network and a LightGBM/XGBoost regression combination. The number of missing values per row was a crucial feature, with its addition and other changes improving the reported score from 1.04555 to 0.94694. Public-test probing suggested that the public score mostly reflected F4, so model combinations were selected on that feature group before being applied to the others. Modeling every group slightly outperformed an alternative that mean-imputed F1 and F3.

The pipeline combined diverse image models with metadata, then fed their predictions into gradient-boosted tree stacks. Patient-aware validation balanced positives while limiting the influence of patients with many negative samples. Patient-and-location aggregate features and removal of zero-importance features improved performance, while restricting each stack to at most two CNN predictions worked best. An optimized weighted average of three stacking models, a metadata-only tree model, and a standalone CNN achieved CV 0.1793 and private leaderboard score 0.171.

solution_title: A simple post-processing for your solution
solution_summary: The authors apply selective rounding to model predictions as a post-processing step. Predictions within 0.2 of an integer are rounded, while other values remain unchanged; a tolerance of 0.3 is also suggested. They report that this adjustment helped improve their competition standing, without providing numerical scores or details of the underlying models.

solution_title: [8th Place Solution] Understanding Data Before Designing Methods
solution_summary: The solution processed TMA and WSI images separately while aligning their physical magnification scales. Mask-derived patches trained TMA classifiers and ArcFace retrieval models, with a classification ensemble resolving uncertain retrieval results. WSI predictions used multiresolution feature extractors followed by DTFD-MIL, with synthetic Other slides supporting outlier detection. TMA-trained features greatly accelerated MIL convergence, while PLIP validation results were poor and an additional high-resolution branch crashed.

The solution ensembles RoBERTa-large, DeBERTa-large, and ELECTRA-large architectures. A trained RoBERTa-large model generates pseudo-labels for 20,000 Wikipedia texts, which are used to train the different models before full fine-tuning on the competition training set. Differential learning rates are applied across transformer layers, while alternative hidden-state selections and pooling methods perform similarly. The ensemble reports private scores of 449–450; larger Wikipedia samples reduce performance, and feature engineering and reinitialization do not help.

solution_title: Label Denoising with Large Ensembles of Heterogeneous Neural Networks
solution_summary: The pipeline trained heterogeneous first-level neural networks using video-level and frame-level data. Their predictions were averaged across folds and merged into features for a second-level LightGBM model. LightGBM outputs supplied soft labels for subsequent TensorFlow ensemble models. Out-of-fold predictions from those models trained the final ensemble.
The post links to the team's model report hosted on GitHub. It invites comments and questions about that report. The provided post contains no technical description of the solution.

The solution blended LightGBM, XGBoost, and two neural networks, largely reusing the author's previous month's approach with parameter changes and categorical-feature handling. Optuna optimized blend weights using cross-validation out-of-fold predictions. The blend achieved 0.84228 private and 0.84157 public scores, improving on every individual model. Experiments with a denoising autoencoder were unsuccessful.

The solution combined XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost variants with target-specific categorical encoding and outlier removal. Optuna was used to optimize weighted ensembling, and the submitted blending approach used an arithmetic weighted mean. A geometric mean of five results achieved 0.88951 and handled outlier predictions better, but was not the selected approach. Neural networks generally performed poorly except on Other Faults.

The solution ensembles fine-tuned language models with support vector regression using pretrained embeddings. Embedding extraction varies pooling strategies and maximum input lengths across several transformer checkpoints. A very low layer-wise learning-rate decay factor combined with a high learning rate improved cross-validation and public leaderboard performance. The reported DeBERTa-v3-base example used AWP and achieved CV 0.44912, public score 0.436664, and private score 0.440466.

The team broke the ciphers and reconstructed preprocessing to match decoded text to possible classes. They narrowed ambiguous assignments using class occurrence counts, sampling without replacement, known training observations, and document difficulty consistency. Public submission scores and their ordering supplied constraints for evaluating candidate solutions locally. After manual reductions and an optimized C++ exhaustive search, they fixed a pipeline bug and obtained a perfect score.

solution_summary: The author trained protein classifiers with a custom F1 loss and combined them with teammates' BCE-trained models. Training used 512-by-512 RGBY images, HPA v18 external data, rare-class oversampling, and augmentation weighted by class frequency. The loss added BCE for classes absent from a batch and clamped negative-target probabilities to emphasize hard examples. A uniform threshold of 0.205 and replacement of poor-quality test images with similar better-quality images completed the approach; the latter improved the score by about 0.002. A five-fold SE-ResNeXt50 ensemble achieved private score 0.562 but was excluded from the final submission because of its weaker public score.

solution_title: 5th Place Solution - An ensemble of 53 OOFs
solution_summary: The author built a diverse ensemble dominated by XGBoost and LightGBM, with additional tree models, neural networks, and logistic regression. Diversity came from hyperparameter changes, different fold counts, and augmenting training with one to six copies of the original dataset. Treating numerical features as categorical, sometimes alongside their numerical representations or after binning, improved results. The selected submission scored 0.38502 on the private leaderboard, while the highest-CV alternative scored 0.38509.

The author improved a public notebook approach with stricter answer parsing, explicit time management, and sequential sampling. Rejecting malformed or invalid answers increased the public score from 14 to 19 without other changes. Sequential selection was more stable than Thompson sampling, and the final approach reached public scores around 19–20. The submission failed on the private evaluation.

solution_title: Prudential Life Insurance Assessment, Winner's Interview: 2nd place, Bogdan Zhurakovskyi
solution_summary: Linear regression gave the author's best results, with extensively tuned XGBoost achieving similar performance. The models were compared using kappa scores across 200 random train/test splits with a 30% test fraction. The main insight was that simple linear models can match or outperform more complex algorithms on this dataset. The writeup does not describe additional features or a final ensemble.

The solution stacked out-of-fold predictions from 35 models drawn from public notebooks and the author's own training runs. Its strength came from model diversity, since no individual model exceeded 0.97 on either leaderboard. The final submissions used single-level and two-level stacking, with a public GPU logistic regression stacker playing a key role. A ridge stacker augmented with three original features achieved the best retrospective private score of 0.97045, but was not selected.
compute: GPU logistic regression stacking; GPU type and runtime unspecified.

solution_summary: The author solved a collection of AI security puzzles through model inspection, targeted input manipulation, search, and challenge-specific exploits. Important breakthroughs included sorting tokens by embedding argmax, applying an inverse Fourier transform with careful scaling, and using pretrained MobileNet V2 with adapted attack code across three challenges. Character inference depended on flipped images and retaining progressively better candidates, while another challenge was solved by brute-forcing an API. Manual image edits and exploiting acceptance of negative demerits also succeeded, but CROP2 remained unsolved.

solution_summary: The solution convexly blended two independent pipelines built around particle filtering and multi-scale typewell matching, with LightGBM, CatBoost, and Ridge above them. Fold-safe development was the central safeguard against public leaderboard overfitting. The final scores were 7.764 public and 9.064 private, while oracle analysis suggested that further gains were limited by an inability to infer the direction of far-tail errors.

The author combined roughly 180 models, emphasizing weaker models whose errors differed from those of the strongest models. A Gaussian mixture Bayes classifier supplied useful diversity. Spatial features exploited preserved right ascension and declination through target encoding and HEALPix sky pixels. Converting redshift into three-dimensional spatial coordinates was unsuccessful because the synthetic data disrupted radial relationships.

solution_title: 7th Place Solution - How structured experiments saved my sanity
solution_summary: The author trained separate transformer agents from scratch with PPO self-play in a JAX recreation of the game. Timing-focused observations, an analytic shot planner, auxiliary future-state prediction, and early episode termination improved learning. Candidate targets were restricted to four high-logit targets plus four random targets to reduce planner cost. Historical opponent sampling rescued four-player training, while the two-player agent overfit to its own playstyle despite strong local evaluations.

solution_summary: The team combined EfficientNet B1 image classifiers, two study-level volumetric architectures, and a CNN with a Transformer head. solution_summary: The solution combined classification and segmentation in an asymmetric U-Net with a SE-ResNeXt50 backbone, attention, and hyper-columns. A second model used deep-stem, Mish activations, and filtered public-test pseudo-labels. solution_title: This is how you place 3rd without probing ...

solution_title: Top 100 Solution - Target Post-Processing Main Success Driver
solution_summary: The solution used a manually tuned LightGBM regressor to predict PCIAT total scores from tabular features and basic parquet statistics. It reduced missingness through related-feature consolidation and age-and-gender group median imputation, while dropping features with excessive missing values. Training records with missing or potentially unreliable targets were removed. Sorting regression predictions and assigning classes to match the training class distribution produced an approximately 0.04 leaderboard improvement.

solution_title: 3rd place solution: VQA/AES=0.81/0.64 Diffusion model + differentiable SVG optimization
solution_summary: The pipeline generated eight FLUX bitmap candidates per description, vectorized them with vtracer, and selected promising SVGs using SigLIP and short aesthetic optimization. The chosen SVG underwent 200 iterations of differentiable optimization over geometry and colors using aesthetic, embedding-similarity, and pixel losses. A differentiable approximation of evaluation preprocessing helped align refinement with the scoring process. Compression, size searches, and optional path pruning kept the final SVG within the 10KB limit.

solution_title: 302th Solution Writeup - Always trust your CV
solution_summary: The solution combined B4, B5, and B6 image models trained at different resolutions. MD5-based duplicate removal covered both original and external images, while validation used only the original training distribution and external data was added to each fold's training set. solution_summary: The solution combined a ResNet34 classifier with a voting ensemble of seven segmentation models using U-Net and FPN architectures. Segmentation training used an auxiliary classification head, Lovasz and binary cross-entropy losses, and progressively larger crops up to full resolution. Flip-based test-time augmentation and training augmentations, including simulated plate edges, supported the ensemble. The authors attributed weaker private results to low thresholds, pseudo-labeling, and limited validation coverage.

The solution fine-tuned CLIP image encoders to directly predict 384-dimensional prompt embeddings using about 400,000 examples. VizWiz captions were particularly important for leaderboard generalization, alongside regenerated SD2 images from Diffusion DB and smaller COCO and Lexica datasets. Linear probing before fine-tuning, EMA, and layer-wise learning-rate decay helped preserve pretrained representations. A diverse CLIP ensemble with weak augmentation and alternate generation seeds achieved a reported private score of 0.64814.

solution_title: Kaggle national datascience bowl 2017 2nd place code
solution_summary: The solution combined 3D convolutional nodule detectors and malignancy predictors with a U-Net that detected large suspicious tissue masses. solution_title: Congratulations, thanks and what worked (and what didn't) for me.
solution_summary: The final solution combined XGBoost and Keras neural networks through blending and stacking. Strong XGBoost results came from lower learning rates, much longer early stopping patience, and a fair objective constant of 0.4. solution_summary: The approach fine-tuned a Nemotron model with LoRA on carefully structured reasoning traces from original and synthetic problems. Trace design emphasized explicit local computation, consistent references, and uniform rules, with generation differences guiding repeated revisions. A bit-manipulation solver reduced complex cases to five templates and two anchor tables, achieving 99.4% exact match before model training. Category-specific operation priors and a rebalanced training mix provided additional gains, while final training reportedly reached 99% bit-manipulation solve rate after about eleven hours.

solution_summary: The team extended a popular Swin image model with supplied metadata and image dimensions, aspect ratios, and file size. These features improved cross-validation by about 0.3 and the leaderboard score by about 0.2, and the final submission used ten folds. They also used SVR ensemble heads with a search over the C parameter. A dual-output BCE and RMSE objective improved validation but was abandoned after weaker leaderboard results, despite later showing promise on the private leaderboard.

The model represented each assessment using its preceding 80 game sessions and up to 100 events per session. A hierarchical network used shared fully connected event layers followed by a session-level transformer, with tied accuracy-group embeddings improving QWK. Explicit blank categories worked better than transformer masking. Blending out-of-fold predictions with training targets improved the private score from 0.550 to 0.554, although it complicated validation and encouraged overfitting.

solution_title: 3rd place solution + my first Kaggle competition! 🎉
solution_summary: The author built an agent configuration that trained LightGBM, XGBoost, CatBoost, and a logistic regression baseline. Local configuration validation helped address failed submissions caused by schema errors.

solution_title: part of 4th place solution: GAPNet & dual loss ResNet

A second contribution used ResNet34 with an auxiliary segmentation loss derived from the green channel to regularize classification. solution_title: 24th Place Solution 🏅 - My second ever Kaggle competition 🔥
solution_summary: The solution ensembled XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost using ten-fold training. Geographic features included distances to large California cities and the coastline, PCA coordinates, rotated coordinates, and polar coordinates. Optuna was used for light tuning of XGBoost. Model decisions relied on a local 80/20 validation split that excluded the original dataset, which the author reports generalized well to the private leaderboard.

Five-fold validation used only original competition validation examples, with early stopping based on Jaccard score. A custom softmax normalized start and end logits across all context splits, making scores more comparable across models and raising the public score from 0.809 to 0.821. Custom punctuation handling and Tamil stemming provided additional improvements.

Its out-of-fold predictions supplied five additional channels to image classifiers trained at resolution 640. solution_summary: The team trained question-specific XGBoost models with five-fold validation, then retrained on all data using the selected iteration counts. Click aggregates and selected recap features helped, while neural-network blends and several spatial or embedding features did not. solution_title: 81st Place Solution for the Stanford Ribonanza RNA Folding Competition
solution_summary: The author replaced an initial 12-layer Transformer with repeated groups of three Conv1D blocks followed by a Transformer block. Training data were filtered to reads of at least 100, and selected unreliable reactivity targets were set to NaN and excluded from loss calculations. A final ensemble improved the public score to 0.14381 but worsened the private score to 0.18093 because it included a seed variant with poor generalization across sequence lengths. The author identified missing validation on test-like lengths as a major weakness.

The authors generated 20-question game demonstrations with GPT-4o and fine-tuned Llama 3.1 8B on successful games. Their guesser received a concise hint summarizing prior rounds, while the answerer answered each question without game history. On 108 held-out keywords, behavior cloning increased Llama's success rate from 5.56% to 24.07%, compared with GPT-4o's 23.15%. The resulting guesser remained sensitive to incorrect answers, and the answerer sometimes mishandled alphabetical questions.

solution_summary: The solution combined tabular regressors, voxel-based neural networks, and models trained on brain-parcellation signals. LightGBM and XGBoost used tabular inputs, voxel statistics, and selected neural hidden features. Prediction distributions were screened for train-test discrepancies, and cross-domain interactions fed linear SVM and LightGBM stacking models whose predictions were blended. Model diversity and removing noisy predictions mattered most, while several alternative stacking methods and pseudo-labeling failed.

The solution combined CNN, LSTM and GRU forecasts with LightGBM models. Validation reproduced the forecast horizon and weekly boundary while excluding future information across all series, then models were retrained on the latest data. Averaging ten random initializations and predictions from every epoch improved robustness. Adjusted promotion information improved the public score but performed poorly on the private leaderboard.

The author trained separate IMU-only and full-sensor classifiers using multibranch CNNs, phase-specific GRUs, and attention, mean, and max pooling. The full model additionally extracted spatial TOF features with a 2D CNN and fused TOF and THM sensors with a Performer. Physical sensor corrections, quaternion cleanup, model-specific augmentation, and ten-fold subject-grouped validation were central to the pipeline. Fold logits were averaged at inference, yielding CV scores of 0.842 for IMU-only and 0.898 for full data, with a private leaderboard score of 0.845.

solution_summary: The Tile pipeline used a four-block relational graph convolutional network with node opcodes defining relations and ListMLE as its ranking objective. For Layout datasets, the team used three GATv2 blocks and repeatedly concatenated configuration features so that information from the relatively few configured nodes would survive message passing. Configuration embeddings and one-hot vectors, together with a virtual node for graph representation, were central to this approach. Reported Layout Kendall-Tau CV scores ranged from approximately 0.3 to 0.94 across the four datasets.

The solution ensembled four Cascade Mask R-CNN models with ConvNeXt Tiny and ConvNeXt V2 Base backbones. Training used only the blood-vessel class, image augmentation, and two validation folds separated by whole-slide image. Inference combined six image scales, weighted boxes fusion, and hard voting over masks. The ensemble achieved a private score of 0.541 without dilation, while clipping masks to fused boxes was tested but omitted from the final submission.

The author created two small datasets covering rewrite-prompt recovery and original-text type classification. Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2 was supervised fine-tuned for each task, and combining rewrite-prompt predictions from three models produced a small improvement. Experiments with expanded text types, Mixtral-8x7B-Instruct-v0.1, and PPO did not work well. The post also acknowledges a shared mean prompt scoring 0.63 that the author could not improve.

The main solution equally averages one LightGBM model on raw features and five neural networks trained on denoising-autoencoder representations. It removes calc features, one-hot encodes categorical features, and applies RankGauss normalization for neural networks. Autoencoders learn from train and test features using swap noise, with hidden activations supplying supervised inputs. Five-fold validation guides modeling, and a second selected blend adds 32-bag variants and a lightly weighted public script for a small score increase from 0.2965 to 0.2969.

solution_summary: The post describes signal-offset correction rather than a complete modeling pipeline. Class-conditional signal averages exposed anomalous offsets in training batches 4 and 9, which were corrected with batch-specific additive shifts. For test data, KDE comparisons against corrected training data revealed a similar misalignment in group 4, addressed by adding 2.750 to its signal. The author identified this preprocessing idea as the most useful of their experiments but did not quantify its score improvement.

The approach scores candidate answers using positional distances between question and answer words in a corpus. For each word pair, it takes the 20th percentile of minimum within-document distances and converts it to an inverse square-root score. It aggregates pair scores by their median and selects the highest-scoring answer. Performance began to converge around 0.38–0.40 with more than 2,500 corpus pages, while memory usage was approximately 2–3 GB.
compute: Approximately 2–3 GB memory

solution_title: 69th solution of this competition without hacking metrics
solution_summary: The team ensembled LightGBM and CatBoost using 610 and 535 selected features respectively. Retaining highly sparse features, converting dates to day offsets, and reducing high-cardinality string values improved performance. Main complexity parameters were set manually, with Optuna tuning the remaining parameters. The reported best private score was 0.524 without a date hack and 0.591 with it; the adopted similarity-based date inference did not deliver the expected improvement.

The solution generated recommendation candidates with four recall models and ranked them with LightGBM LambdaRank. A gated two-tower mixture-of-experts model supplied candidates, embedding similarities, and demographic-based recommendations for users without purchase history. Text and image clusters provided additional product features, including for cold-start items. Its outputs passed through softplus, were normalized into probabilities, and were cumulatively summed for direct CRPS optimization. solution_title: [24th Place Solution] A Population-Based Reinforcement Learning Ecosystem
solution_summary: The solution bootstrapped a small Transformer policy from LightGBM imitation teachers and then improved it with population-based PPO and GAE. Teachers trained on a small replay collection generated tens of thousands of games for policy and value distillation. A roughly one-million-parameter Transformer represented board state and legal actions as tokens, supporting sequential choices through a pointer head. Fast C++ inference enabled extensive match collection and evaluation, while matchup-specific experts and human feedback guided policy and deck development.

solution_summary: The solution removed 13 bad images, resized inputs to 320 by 512, and trained augmented U-Net segmentation models. Seven model variants used different encoders, CBAM attention, and either hypercolumns or feature pyramid attention, with five folds per variant. Training combined BCE and Lovasz hinge losses with deep supervision, Adam, and cosine warm restarts. Averaging 35 models, flip-based test-time augmentation, and cross-validated mask thresholds produced public and private scores of 0.67698 and 0.66713.

The pipeline corrects image orientation, retrieves candidate pairs with DINOv2, and extracts ALIKE features from cropped image patches. LightGlue matching and tuned RANSAC filtering provide correspondences for COLMAP reconstruction with a Simple-Radial camera model. Geometric consistency and keypoint refinement are the main improvements over public baselines. solution_summary: The author trained several MMDetection detector families using five folds, primarily at 1024×1024 resolution. The central strategy was to pretrain on all data and then fine-tune on rare radiologists while preserving fold assignments and retaining a controlled number of empty images. Augmentation, mixed precision where supported, and cosine annealing with warm-up supported training. Higher-resolution GFL variants and class-balanced sampling were explored, with sampling providing no improvement and the 2048-resolution variants scoring worse privately than their 1024 counterparts.

The author built 135 sets of out-of-fold and test predictions using XGBoost and LightGBM. The final prediction averaged logistic-regression stacking with a hill-climbing ensemble of those predictions. Treating every feature as categorical and adding the original data improved performance, along with selected XGBoost settings. CatBoost was excluded, feature engineering was unhelpful, and additional predictions sometimes worsened hill-climbing performance.

solution_summary: The approach modifies CenterNet to detect helmet impacts from sequences of 15 consecutive video frames, using an EfficientB5 feature extractor and separate detection heads for individual frames. Training emphasizes impact-containing frames and combines independently computed losses for impact and non-impact helmets with a weighted sum. Video augmentation supports the temporal input pipeline. Post-processing links nearby detections with IOU-Tracker, retains the middle box of each trajectory, and applies a confidence threshold that varies over the course of the video.

The author used a single XGBoost model after disappointing results from ensembles in previous competitions. Validation followed a community-proposed cross-validation approach, whose details were not included. Most engineered features based on V1–V28 were unhelpful, while one linked feature slightly improved cross-validation.

The solution combined five XLM-RoBERTa-large, five MuRIL, and four RemBERT question-answering models through hard voting. SQuAD2 fine-tuning preceded competition training, with seed diversity for XLM-RoBERTa and fold diversity for the other architectures. Linear warm-up and early stopping supported training, while additional Tamil datasets and hyperparameter tuning improved the public score. The final reported public/private scores were 0.808/0.770, and several alternative ensemble and augmentation approaches did not help.

solution_title: 1st Place Winning Solution - Hungry for Gold
solution_summary: The final solution was a weighted blend of seven models spanning multistage neural stacking, TabNet, simple neural networks, a residual network, and DeepInsight CNNs. Blend weights reflected leaderboard performance and prediction diversity, while an alternative blend optimized out-of-fold weights with Optuna and SLSQP. Feature engineering included dimensionality reduction, quantile transforms, clustering, and gene and cell summary statistics; label smoothing and multiple seeds helped regularization and stability. DeepInsight CNNs added useful diversity and improved private log loss by about 0.00008, with the final blend reaching 0.01599.

The author reduced the arm configuration problem to a point-space traveling salesman problem by restricting the arm's degrees of freedom. They modified the standard configuration near the start and return paths and computed transition costs between configurations for LKH. The resulting tour was rotated to the desired starting point, converted back into configurations, and cleaned of duplicates. The restrictions simplified optimization but limited efficient movement between quadrants.

The solution used a two-stage U-Net teacher–student pipeline to combine catheter segmentation with classification. A teacher learned five-channel masks and eleven classification targets from annotated images, then supplied soft masks for student training on the full labeled dataset. Validation used five-fold GroupKFold separately for annotated and unannotated images. A hillclimb ensemble with identity and horizontal-flip inference achieved 0.968 public and 0.972 private scores.

solution_summary: The solution averaged two DeBERTa-v3-large configurations, each trained on four prompt-grouped folds, for eight inference checkpoints. The configurations differed in input formatting and pooling, using summary-only mean pooling or GeM pooling over the question and summary. Restricting pooling to the relevant text was the largest source of improvement, and individual model CV scores were 0.482 and 0.492. Cross-attention variants, separate backbone passes, layer changes, longer inputs, and ensembles with other backbones did not yield significant improvements.

Radboud U-Nets used segmentation supervision and random-density tile selection, which brought a reported 0.01 improvement and helped stabilize the ensemble; segmentation was unsuccessful for Karolinska.

solution_title: 2nd Private LB/ 3rd Public LB Solution - Transformer
solution_summary: The solution corrected year-specific measurement differences and engineered 36 player and spatial features. A transformer with two encoder and two decoder layers relied on many attention heads. Validation always trained on 2017 data and held out week-grouped portions of 2018. Alternating learning rates and snapshot ensembling improved performance within the CPU training limit.
compute: Four-hour CPU training allowance; final full-data training repeated for 11000 seconds and 9000 seconds in safe mode.

solution_summary: The solution stacked diverse neural networks and LightGBM models, then equally blended LightGBM and XGBoost stackers. Its neural network combined categorical embeddings, numerical features, character TF-IDF, and recurrent-convolutional text features. Public-kernel features, image descriptors, user duplicate counts, and consecutive-item price differences helped. More folds and seed bagging improved performance; the best individual neural network and LightGBM scored 0.2194 and 0.2196.

Every categorical feature was count-encoded using combined training and test data. LightGBM models were trained with five-fold cross-validation, and their predictions were averaged. The submission achieved public and private scores of 0.68406 and 0.66474, respectively. The author reported no special submission-selection validation strategy and estimated about ten hours for the complete pipeline.
compute: About 10 hours for data processing, training, and prediction

solution_summary: The team emphasized fewer models and greater variation in data. They trained using a referenced 60k dataset, set maximum sequence length to 640, and froze embeddings and 18 layers. Attempts to improve document retrieval through Sentence Transformer changes or BM25 were unsuccessful, as were additional answer-prediction data and paid custom data. Expanding retrieval sources was constrained by a stated requirement for more than 200GB RAM.

solution_summary: The final approach predicted each UPDRS score using an optimized month trend adjusted by protein-dependent constant shifts. A protein was selected using its average correlation with the four targets, and separate shifts were optimized within protein quantile ranges. Missing values were forward-filled, predictions were rounded, and validation grouped patients to avoid leakage. The final reported score was 69.7, compared with 69.8 for an earlier Random Forest and trend hybrid.

The author built two LightGBM classifiers per question using complementary summaries of gameplay events. One feature set captured elapsed time by room and level, while the other measured relative frequencies of fqid groups. Question-specific ensemble weights were selected using a small portion of the training data, with an emphasis on efficient execution. The selected submissions achieved a highest private score of 0.689 with roughly half a minute of code execution and four to six minutes of scoring; an unselected submission reached 0.693 in about nine minutes overall.
compute: About 30 seconds of code execution and 4–6 minutes of scoring; another submission took about 9 minutes total.

solution_summary: The team extracted DOI candidates with regular expressions and validated them against the competition corpus and dataset prefixes derived from DataCite metadata. An LLM re-extracted uncertain DOI candidates from their original context, while DOI classification used semantics in the main text and author overlap in references. Accession IDs passed through regex extraction and contextual rules before LLM classification. The authors suspected these rules caused overfitting and regretted rejecting a simpler pure-LLM alternative.

solution_title: how a newbie got to public 19th place
solution_summary: The author extended a shared neural-network baseline with separate branches for game context, players, wind, and ranked spatial features. Direction normalization, mirrored training examples, and mirrored test prediction averaging improved robustness. Dropout, batch normalization, early stopping, and greater weight on 2018 data controlled overfitting and season differences. The safe submission trained on 2017–2018 data and reached a reported score of 0.01200 after the fourth rerun, while the aggressive submission deteriorated and was suspected to have fallen back to prior predictions.

The described 2.5D pipeline first classified whether targets were present and then controlled segmentation with those predictions. It stacked three slices at stride two and used U-Net segmentation with EfficientNet B4-B7 backbones. Classification learned from empty and positive images, while segmentation trained only on images containing masks with a weighted BCE-Dice loss. Model fusion and horizontal-flip inference augmentation brought the pure 2.5D approach to approximately 0.889 on the public leaderboard.

The solution combined an optimized constant prompt with output from Mistral 7B Instruct using a fixed response prefix. The constant prompt was built by greedily appending tokenizer vocabulary items that improved mean embedding similarity, with repeated uses of the Romanian word “lucrarea” proving useful. Validation subsets were selected to reproduce observed leaderboard scores, and differences between Torch and KerasHub ST5 implementations informed prompt length choices. Constant prompts alone achieved scores around 0.69, while Mistral performed slightly better than Gemma 1.1 in validation.
compute: P100 GPU job mentioned for greedy prompt search; no runtime stated.

solution_summary: The team used pre-release AutoGluon with an experimental 2024 zeroshot hyperparameter portfolio. Second-level stackers received only model predictions, while numeric target values were used to stratify cross-validation folds and reduce outlier-driven distribution shifts. Additional data and text feature generation were excluded after validation showed no convincing benefit. Extensive cross-validation supported selecting their first submission despite its weak public score of 72221.55.

The team built a five-stage instance segmentation pipeline centered on ResNeSt200 Mask R-CNN models. Cleaned LIVECell SH-SY5Y data, higher image resolution, and backbone fine-tuning strengthened the initial models. Two rounds of pseudo labeling used mask-overlap clustering and pixel voting, followed by an ensemble of models from both rounds. A CatBoost false-positive filter using 130 instance features raised the reported leaderboard score to 0.341.
compute: Training batch size of 2; hardware and runtime unstated.

solution_summary: The solution used MMDetection Mask R-CNN models with Hybrid Task Cascade, with the final submission combining r101 and x101 models. Training began at lower resolutions and continued from checkpoints at 1024 × 1600, using SGD and learning-rate reductions. The best submission used the last two checkpoints from each model with three-scale and mirror test-time augmentation. Frozen batch normalization performed better than an attempted SyncBN setup, and accidental inclusion of validation data in training led the author to use leaderboard feedback for validation.
compute: Initially two machines with 3×1080Ti each; two additional devboxes became available for the weekend. r101 trained for 18 epochs and x101 for 9 epochs.

solution_title: Score! Xavier Conort on coming second in 'Give Me Some Credit'
solution_summary: The solution combined diverse models, with the best ensemble excluding SVMs. Its most important engineered feature estimated the likelihood of delinquency exceeding 90 days. A weighted GBM was the strongest individual model, scoring 0.86877 on the private set. Adding weaker but complementary models improved the overall result.

The solution combines three supervised feature sets with structure, sequence, and protein-interaction kNN label transfer. Each supervised set blends a hierarchy-aware neural network, logistic regression, and PyBoost using protein-language-model embeddings, taxonomy, non-experimental annotations, and optionally literature embeddings. Validation balances multilabel distributions while keeping identical sequences together. A NaN-aware weighted ensemble and GO hierarchy, taxonomic, known-label, and score filters produce the final predictions.

solution_summary: The final system averages two EfficientNetV2-S variants and a MaxViT model, with auxiliary supervision used in two models. Large mammograms, rule-based ROI extraction, VOI LUT, strong regularization and controlled class proportions in each batch were central to performance. Patient-grouped cross-validation selected thresholds, while inference used models trained on all data and averaged the top three predictions per prediction ID. The ensemble achieved local pF1 of 0.482 and private pF1 of 0.49.

The author investigated lower bounds for unrestricted wildcards using symmetric traveling-salesman formulations solved with Concorde and QSopt. An approximately 8,000-node model reached a bound of 2425.21, with a target of proving 2428. A smaller model was inadequate because it could not preserve the 2440 non-wildcard solution, while a larger model was proposed as a costly fallback. The post also describes earlier use of S5 subgroup structure and vertex-cover software to construct a 2428 solution, and proposes symmetry-aware cuts.

solution_summary: The solution combined pretrained QuadTreeAttention LoFTR and SuperPoint/SuperGlue without competition-specific training or fine-tuning. Three inference scales per model substantially improved matching, and the combined result reached 0.845 on the private leaderboard. Scale-specific confidence thresholds, aspect-preserving padding, and removal of out-of-image correspondences controlled match quality. FP16 reduced memory use, while standard MAGSAC++ was retained for accuracy after faster alternatives and a two-stage variant were tested.

solution_summary: The author reports using L1-regularized logistic regression, with a best single-model score of 0.38. They also report best scores of 0.40 for k-nearest neighbors and 0.41 for an SVM. The post provides no feature, validation, or ensemble details and asks others to share their methods.

The solution averages predictions from two nodule-based pipelines trained using LUNA data. One uses U-Nets in three anatomical directions, extracts measurements from the largest detected nodules, and classifies them with XGBoost. The other trains a 3D VGG derivative on nodule cubes and aggregates convolutional features across overlapping scan chunks for another XGBoost classifier. Using eleven-slice inputs improved the U-Net Dice score from 0.50 to 0.75, while strong LUNA performance did not always transfer to the competition data.

solution_summary: The author improved a shared baseline by switching from EfficientNet B3 to B4, using rectangular CutMix, and gradually decreasing the learning rate. Predictions were adjusted by inverse class frequencies, with the weights raised to the power of 1.2 for the final adjustment. The final approach trained on all available training data and blended two runs with different seeds. Learning-rate changes and class-frequency adjustment each added about 0.007 on the public leaderboard, within a budget of 60 TPU hours.

solution_summary: The solution centered on value-frequency features computed jointly over training data and genuine test rows. Identifying and excluding artificial test rows from these calculations stabilized validation and leaderboard performance, with additional frequency thresholds and mean-centered features bringing a single model to about 0.923. The final submission combined models trained on shared ten-fold splits using logistic-regression stacking and simple blending, selected by cross-validation.

solution_title: The last 2 hours: a solo bronze from a two-tier agent swarm
solution_summary: The author reduced the cost of already-correct ONNX networks using an autonomous agent swarm operating on a corpus seeded from a public solution. Read-only theorist agents identified optimization opportunities, while task-specific workers applied shared compilation tricks and redesigned expensive networks. Candidates were banked only after exactness, fresh-input generalization, independent-runtime scoring, and submission-safety checks. The final two-hour surge increased the public score from 7394 to 7430.00, banking 163 improvements with no reported regressions.
compute: One Mac Studio with 16 cores; approximately 1,000 concurrent agent sessions and 2,056 processes at peak; final surge lasted about two hours; approximately $220 in account costs.

solution_summary: The author built 24 models with varied feature sets, emphasizing prediction diversity and deliberate column removal. Ensemble construction used ROC AUC rather than leaderboard scores. A hill-climbing procedure selected positive and negative model weights, including small contributions from weak standalone models. The reported ensemble ROC AUC reached 0.92821, compared with 0.92781 for the best individual model.

The solution improved public approaches by smoothing the input signals with sliding-window averages and smoothing the estimated transit depths across wavelength bands. Savitzky–Golay filtering reduced fluctuations in the bandwise depth predictions. A linear regression model predicted uncertainty using the relationship between planetary uncertainty and variation across band depths. The reported correlation supporting this relationship was approximately 0.701.

The code fits a separate six-component Gaussian mixture for each of 512 magic-value groups, using combined training and test data. It selects high-variance features and appends a heavily weighted target coordinate, with test targets initialized to 0.5. Five perturbed initializations are tried, and the model with the highest lower bound supplies clusters that are labeled by training-class majority. Submission predictions depend on a per-group positive-count check, with small random noise added when that check passes.

The solution generated candidates using co-visitation matrices and reranked them with LightGBM, adding CatBoost for orders. Features combined session recency, interaction counts, viewing duration, item popularity, conversion rates, co-visitation weights, and Word2Vec similarities. Orders predictions were averaged across models trained on separately truncated session datasets, but this improved little over a single LightGBM model, and expanding the candidate pool from 50 to 75 brought little benefit. Final cross-validation scores were 54.54% for clicks, 42.08% for carts, and 65.80% for orders.
compute: Ran entirely on Kaggle using multiple notebooks; some notebooks took 4–6 hours.

solution_summary: The final system ensembled 65 CNN models covering 13 model configurations and five folds. Architecture diversity improved local and leaderboard scores, and models were selected using local inference results. Training used primary and secondary bird labels, BCEWithLogits loss, mixup, and cosine annealing. Six-second inference clips and a fixed prediction threshold of 0.2 were selected, while clip-length ensembles and several conventional augmentations did not improve results.

The solution combined five EfficientNet and EfficientNetV2 models using weights learned through ridge regression. Models used stratified five-fold validation, mixup, extensive augmentation, and flip-based test-time augmentation. Three-channel inputs and larger image sizes were particularly useful, with a six-channel model retained for ensemble diversity. Several alternatives were unsuccessful, including classifier stacking, logistic-regression weighting, and pseudo-labeling, which overfit.

The team used nnU-Net with a custom 3D encoder and 2D decoder, weighting depth features with squeeze-and-excitation blocks before aggregation. Fragment-specific normalization and intensity-based selection of 32 slices supported large training patches. They combined selected folds from two training configurations and used eight-way test-time augmentation. Both submitted post-processing approaches improved public results but did not generalize, with threshold and component filtering reducing final Dice by 0.002.

solution_title: 74th place: knee-centred views, LLM labels, and OAI-trained readers
solution_summary: The pipeline retained all slices from five MRI series and combined full-field images with detector-positioned local views in a multiple-instance reader. Report-derived labels were refined using rank-preserving OOF pseudo-labels, selected multimodal LLM reads and independent OAI image models. ConvNeXt-S and EfficientNetV2-S members were averaged, with one final submission additionally incorporating OAI readers at inference. Independent validation sets guided member selection, and the best private submission achieved 0.949 AUC.

Training relies primarily on synthetic ECGs with precise pixel labels, mixed with competition data for adaptation. A cross-row refinement model and a BiLSTM model provide complementary predictions, combined with weights of 0.6 and 0.4 respectively. solution_summary: The final pipeline ensembled five YOLOv5x detection folds and used a separate binary classifier to filter normal images. Annotation preparation fused boxes, removed suspicious annotations, and corrected some calcification boxes using RetinaNet predictions. The classifier used four EfficientNet-B5 noisy-student folds, followed by removal of highly inconsistent examples and retraining. Switching from RetinaNet to YOLOv5 substantially improved detection, while label smoothing, VFNet, and EfficientDet were unsuccessful. The custom classifier improved the private score from 0.271 to 0.272.

solution_title: 6th place:  Micro-inputs, Lots of Data + Distance Order to Ensemble!
solution_summary: The author's contribution used ResNeSt50 models with compact 128- and 196-pixel rasters and five condensed input channels. Training on multiple chopped versions of the full dataset, promoting scene diversity, and undersampling crowded scenes were central to improving data coverage and performance. The two models reached scores of 11.9 and 11.15 after 68.8 million and 71.4 million samples, respectively. The ensemble aligned trajectory modes by distance traveled before averaging, with validation-optimized weights incorporating distance and confidence.

The post provides incomplete code for an MLP and its graph-data loading pipeline. The loader joins node features and opcodes along graph edges and associates them with configuration features. It constructs normalized rank targets from the labels. Missing code tokens prevent reconstruction of the full architecture, and no validation results are reported.

solution_title: A kaggle newbie's 🥈23rd solution:  Just follow-up excellent public works & ideas
solution_summary: The solution used two external essay datasets with selected prompts excluded, supplemented by pseudo-labeled test examples. A tokenizer trained on test text produced TF-IDF features capped at five million, which fed a diverse ensemble of linear, probabilistic, and boosting classifiers. The final pipeline also included test-text correction and a referenced postprocessing method. Adding DistilRoBERTa increased the public score from 0.962 to 0.965; a submission without correction achieved 0.923 on the private leaderboard.

solution_title: My best solution only using manager_id
solution_summary: The author combined four XGBoost models linearly. Features included listing metadata, description length, creation times, room counts, and grouped property statistics. Manager-level statistics captured class rates and class-specific averages of price, bedrooms, and bathrooms. The solution trained a shared model for both defog and tdcs data. DeBERTa or vision transformer encoders fed an LSTM or GRU, typically with two to four encoder layers and one recurrent layer. Inputs used patches of size 7–13 and sequences of 192–384 patches. Heavy sequence augmentation was a central part of training.

solution_title: 317th Place Solution for the LLM Science Exam
solution_summary: The final system used Platypus2-70B-Instruct with Wikipedia retrieval and layer-by-layer weight loading. Questions and answer options were embedded with all-MiniLM-L6-v2 to retrieve five similar Wikipedia texts, which were included in the prompt. Answer probabilities were ranked to produce three options, achieving reported accuracy of 0.888. Earlier experiments included fine-tuned BERT, DeBERTa with sentence retrieval, and Longformer with paragraph retrieval.

solution_summary: The solution ensembled five 1D U-Net variants combining WaveNet, bidirectional GRU, and a small ViT component. Subject-wise scaling and overlapping daily sequences supplied sensor values, differences, and cyclic time features, with five-fold GroupKFold validation. Joint segmentation and event detection used segmentation outputs to inform the event head, with negative downsampling and extensive skip connections. Weighted probability averaging, smoothing, peak detection, and time-of-day filtering produced a private score of 0.786.

solution_title: 52nd Place Solution — Physics Bank + Typed Crossformer
solution_summary: The solution generated a bank of 65 candidate trajectories and context channels using physics, alignment, surface, and geometry methods. A Typed Crossformer distinguished candidate families, contextual evidence, and protected trajectory anchors to predict changes from the last known TVT. Frequency-aware fusion and bounded physical corrections produced a stable parent prediction, followed by a 10% residual correction between two differently regularized Typed models. Well-level cross-validation and conservative corrections were central to reliable transfer, with the final model achieving 6.1150 OOF RMSE and 7.087 private RMSE.

solution_summary: The solution combined many tabular models and ensembles, with LAMA DenseLight working best as the ensembler. Strong individual models included tuned CatBoost and XGBoost, xLearn FFM, and Keras FM. Thirteen genetic-programming features improved scores by 0.0025–0.003 when added to raw data and still added about 0.0001 after count and target encoding. Adding more models eventually improved CV slightly without improving the public leaderboard.

The team trained ImageNet-pretrained SE-ResNeXt50, DPN-92, and SE-ResNeXt101 models using both simplified and raw drawings. Strokes were stored in individual binary files to accelerate random access and experimentation. Larger image resolutions improved results, while three-channel stroke timing and stroke-count encodings raised the public score to about 0.951. Batch sizes increased across snapshots to as many as 10,000; the post leaves details of the final 0.953 phase to a teammate.

solution_summary: The solution equally blended a public tabular model with a MaxViT image model, emphasizing prevention of overfitting under extreme class imbalance. Its most effective method was training first on historical ISIC data and then on ISIC2024 alone. The image pipeline used patient-grouped stratified validation, extensive augmentation, post-augmentation standardization, and six-channel RGB plus HSV input. Test-time augmentation improved the private result despite little change in local or public scores, while oversampling and auxiliary loss did not work.
compute: RTX4070 Ti Super throughout the competition; also tried vast.ai and runpod.io near the end.

solution_summary: The team combined spectrogram-based 2D models, raw-EEG 1D models, and hybrid models using a geometric mean of predictions; the detailed writeup covers the Japanese team's components. These components used CWT spectrograms with EfficientNet and hybrid networks that converted raw EEG into image-shaped CNN features. Two-stage training, pseudo labels for sparsely annotated samples, and adjustments to the Other class improved leaderboard scores. The best Japanese spectrogram-only single model scored 0.264 publicly and 0.313 privately, while the best hybrid scored 0.266 and 0.331.

The team treated ion-channel prediction as a parameter-optimization problem using a single highly customized hidden Markov model. They corrected drift and signal scale, removed periodic noise, and decomposed higher-channel categories into combinations of lower-channel processes. Modified forward-backward passes exchanged information and were blended across several preprocessing variants. Batch-specific unsupervised thresholding matched estimated label distributions, and the optimized model reached 0.94584 on the private leaderboard.

The pipeline pretrained models on identities expanded through horizontal and vertical flips, then trained branches for seen graphemes, unseen graphemes, and ArcFace embeddings. Encoder heads used GeM or average pooling, normalization, and fully connected layers, with a separate convolutional stacking head. Training combined CutMix and geometric augmentation with pc-softmax, negative log-likelihood, SGD, cosine annealing, and stochastic weight averaging. ArcFace inference compared train and test embeddings using cosine similarity and a threshold derived from validation embeddings.

The solution mainly used EfficientNet B0–B5 image models, including models that concatenated patient metadata with CNN features. Effective choices included BCEWithLogitsLoss, progressive learning, warmup, AutoAugment, CutMix, random resized crops, and snapshot ensembles. Predictions were combined through several ensemble strategies, with weights searched on cross-validation. Models trained at resolution 384 also performed better when evaluated at 456 and 512, and combining these predictions improved results.
compute: Used public TPU notebooks.

solution_summary: The solution stacked more than 30 EfficientNet models trained with different image sizes using an ExtraTreesClassifier. Five-fold validation used logloss because it was more stable than AUC, and EfficientNet B5 at 512 pixels was the strongest model-size combination. External-data pretraining followed by fine-tuning on 2020 data, checkpoint averaging, and extensive test-time augmentation improved performance. Statistics across repeated predictions supplied stacking features, producing a reported validation AUC of 0.9536 and leaderboard AUC of 0.9457.

solution_summary: The author used CatBoost with handcrafted text features for the efficiency track, emphasizing writing errors, readability, prompt overlap, and early-summary characteristics. Optuna tuned separate content and wording models, while GroupKFold with five seeds supported validation and the public leaderboard sometimes informed feature decisions. Regex, word lists, and NumPy vectorization reduced feature extraction overhead. Reported CV, public, and private scores were 0.52, 0.452, and 0.504; inference compilation alternatives were rejected because compilation costs outweighed their speed gains.

solution_title: Godday's Solution that didn't Appear in Public Notebooks.
solution_summary: The team used a GRU to forecast trends and XGBoost to predict residual information, adding both outputs for the final forecast. GRU validation used five rolling windows, while XGBoost used three group-based validation runs. They also shifted forecast origins to test longer horizons against the January leaderboard. The residual model improved both local and leaderboard results, with the fifth-month leaderboard score decreasing from 3.4 to 2.5.

The solution adapted Agentless into a pipeline that localized relevant files, generated reproduction tests, created patches, and verified them before submission. Qwen2.5-Coder-32B served through vLLM provided structured outputs, with execution feedback driving test and patch retries. Carefully selected few-shot test examples and selective skipping of uncertain patches were central to performance. Evaluation used SWE-Bench-Verified, while exhaustive unit testing and extra tests generated after patching were discarded because they hurt efficiency or reliability.

solution_title: 26th Solution - 3D UNet + CCL with Morphological Post Processing + Custom Loss Function
solution_summary: The solution used MONAI 3D UNets trained on small spherical particle labels and reconstructed predictions from overlapping volumes. Tversky-loss variants, rotation and flip augmentation, and model/TTA aggregation formed the core ensemble. Thresholding and morphological dilation before connected-component labeling improved detection, with Optuna tuning particle-specific settings. Validation used one held-out tomogram, and a custom object-recall loss model was retained for ensemble diversity despite no clear standalone leaderboard gain.

The author focused on events with hits confined to a single detector string, typically involving three or four sensors. Their modeling attempts performed worse than a copied EDA+PCA notebook baseline. The post reports an unsuccessful exploration and asks whether others found effective methods for these events.

The team combined a five-fold 3D EfficientNet approach with an end-to-end 2D model containing four different CNN branches. Training used volumetric or Keras augmentation, while the 2D pipeline randomly exchanged MRI modalities between branches. Bayesian optimization selected linear ensemble weights, and test-time augmentation improved the reported component scores. The final ensemble scored 0.68340 publicly and 0.52730 privately, reflecting a substantial generalization gap.

solution_summary: Across four competition weeks, the team used a custom growth model with a growth rate reduced by an accelerating decay. Earlier fatality forecasts combined lagged case predictions with country-specific fatality rates, while the final week modeled fatality curves directly. The final submissions blended their model with public solutions using different weights, generally favoring their own forecasts and using them exclusively for Chinese locations. More optimistic assumptions performed better overall, while short-term growth tuning produced overly pessimistic forecasts in the second week.

solution_title: Top #3 score solution writeup - Predict the Introverts from the Extroverts
solution_summary: The final submission blended tree-based models, an MLP, and logistic regression with weights of 50%, 45%, and 5%. Predictions were converted to labels using a 40% probability threshold. The author spent only a few hours and made four submissions, relying on a shared notebook.

solution_summary: The author built a Keras graph convolutional network using atom identities, bond information, distances, angles, and dihedral features. Six graph convolution layers updated atom representations before transferring information to edges for coupling prediction. Auxiliary predictions of charges and shielding eigenvalues fed back into the network, while predicted magnetic contributions were summed for the final target. A single run scored about -2.6 after 27 hours, and averaging roughly ten runs produced a final score of -2.9.

solution_summary: The final solution equally averaged four models: two EfficientNet-B5 models, a Vision Transformer, and an SE-ResNeXt50. Different training pipelines provided useful diversity, with eight-way test-time augmentation applied to all models except SE-ResNeXt50. The author's models used combined 2019 and 2020 data, duplicate removal, stratified five-fold validation, extensive augmentation, and bi-tempered loss. Pseudo-labeling and self-distillation improved validation but hurt leaderboard performance and were excluded from the author's final models.
