solution_title: Took a gamble.  Didn't pay off.  1122th place.  😕
solution_summary: The author trained independent XGBoost models for each protein using fingerprint representations, emphasizing 2D pharmacophores to improve generalization to unfamiliar chemistry. Validation included stratified random splits and splits with no building blocks shared between training and validation; the latter performed worse but still appeared promising. A 1145-bit building-block presence fingerprint improved both public and private leaderboard performance when its predictions were used only for shared building blocks. The author also explored per-building-block pharmacophores and concatenated similarity vectors, but the overall competition outcome was disappointing despite encouraging cross-validation.

The final submission combined LightGBM with a neural network and trained on all available data. Validation used the last three months of training data, and useful features included time-of-day indicators, month-boundary indicators, and wind magnitude. Although the neural network scored worse individually, it substantially improved the ensemble. The team modeled both the target and its difference from the value 48 hours earlier, retained a submission without refitting, and found capacity-normalized targets ineffective.

The team averaged 12 fold models across three architectures using equal weights. They used multilabel-stratified folds and image sizes of 128×128, original resolution, and 300×300. Training combined CutMix, Mixup or Cutout, label smoothing, Adam, and plateau-based learning-rate reduction over 100 or 150 epochs. The first architecture produced 186 outputs split into three softmax groups. The reported score changed from 0.9784 on public evaluation to 0.9507 on private evaluation.

The team combined several language-model pipelines trained to classify misconceptions through assigned answer-token logits. Synthetic explanations, filtered misconception candidates, and additional prompt context improved selected models, while distillation and label smoothing addressed label noise. Correct-answer status was identified separately and added during post-processing. The pipelines used Gemma, Qwen, and a distilled DeepSeek model, with one two-model ensemble reaching 0.948 on the private leaderboard.

solution_title: How to take the ArcFace Baseline from private lb: 0.470 (public: 0.522) to 0.804 (public: 0.834)
solution_summary: The author improved a public embedding solution from 0.470 to 0.804 on the private leaderboard using EfficientNet B5 with noisy-student pretraining. The model combined concatenated average and maximum pooling with species classification and a metric head using multi-sample dropout and Elastic Margin Loss. Training used the entire dataset without validation, 12,157 pseudo labels, diverse crop sources, and image augmentations. Inference averaged embeddings across crops and horizontal flips before KNN retrieval.
compute: Trained on GCP; hardware unspecified.

solution_summary: The solution trained multiple U-Nets, mainly with MobileNet encoders, using different RGB composites and image scales. Augmentation and staged training with BCE/Dice followed by Lovasz loss were important. A second U-Net stacked the first-stage probabilities and improved the score by 0.006 over simple averaging. Threshold tuning, tiny-mask removal, and hole filling completed the pipeline.

The solution binned each signal to 187 points and normalized each wavelength by its mean before averaging wavelengths. A five-segment, degree-two fit estimated transit breakpoints and mean transit depth. Uncertainty came from the standard deviation of 100 estimates using random subsets of 50 wavelengths. A deep feedforward network predicted the spectrum relative to its mean, increasing the score from 0.62 to 0.65, although mean estimation remained the main limitation.

The team created roughly 500k samples using several LLMs and publicly available source texts. RoBERTa models predicted T5 prompt embeddings, enabling cosine-similarity retrieval, while Mistral generated additional candidate prompts. They improved outputs by evaluating permutations of concatenated candidates against the predicted embedding. Experiments with end-token suffixes led to the replacement token “lucrarea,” while deliberate overfitting to the public prompts was rejected.

solution_summary: The solution built on public code and averaged predictions across folds before detecting event peaks. It removed predictions from repeating dummy-signal periods identified using daily signal means and variances. Several feature transformations, tuning changes, event-filtering rules, and local-time correction were unsuccessful. Unsupervised segmentation features could not be developed within the notebook time available.

solution_title: Knowing Is Not Enough: We Predicted the Private Board, Optimized the Wrong One
solution_summary: The selected final generated simple sentinel-post candidates and tuned their count to maximize public replay throughput. A compliant mock agent, controlled ablations, and simulated stricter guardrails helped characterize scoring and transfer. The authors correctly predicted that payload inspection would block their exfiltration channel, but still selected it over a transferable email-deputy probe. The selected submission scored 56.96 publicly and zero privately.

The solution used robust weighted least squares, Kalman smoothing, and RTKLIB for GNSS position estimation. Routes were manually labeled Highway, Tree, or Downtown using Google Earth Pro, and Optuna tuned satellite-selection criteria separately for each environment. For non-highway routes moving below one meter per second, position covariance was tripled before Kalman smoothing, improving the reported private score from 1.904 to 1.863. After the competition, annotation-independent post-processing achieved a private score of 1.784.

The solution started with an LKH tour and refined it using a custom penalty-aware Lin–Kernighan search. Cumulative sums accelerated penalty calculations, while non-sequential moves, restricted candidate sets, and relaxed gain constraints enabled increasingly high-order moves. Localized tour kicks followed by reoptimization and GPX2 recombination provided further gains. The reported score improved from 1516321 after the initial TSP stage to 1514014 after the final stage.
compute: Intel i5-3470 with 4 cores for most of the competition; later Azure F64s v2 low-priority instance with 64 cores.

solution_summary: The final blend combined a Transformer, TabNet, and neural networks using different feature sets. Handcrafted book and trade features replaced a slow RNN feature extractor with almost no performance loss, while the Transformer captured relationships across stocks. Nearest-neighbor time buckets supplied averaged stock features, improving reported CV from 0.211 to approximately 0.198 and public leaderboard performance from approximately 0.200 to 0.189. Validation grouped by time_id, and changes were retained when both CV and leaderboard checks supported them.

The solution ensembled five submissions using preprocessing from two public kernels. Two models used three GRU layers with 400 or 410 units, while two others used three dense layers with 500 or 400 units; context features were concatenated between layers. These networks produced nine linear outputs and trained with quantile losses, Adam, dropout, and plateau-based learning-rate reduction. A public quantile-regression baseline supplied the fifth model.

The solution combines several transformer regressors using ridge regression and LightGBM, with manual features contributing through LightGBM. Five-fold validation without shuffling was chosen to approximate generalization across text sources. Dropout remained active during inference, and predictions were averaged across random seeds. Averaging the ridge and LightGBM outputs achieved a private score of 0.448, although the author questioned the improvement because the public score worsened.

solution_title: Pushing the Limits of General-Purpose LLMs with a Judge-based TIR Loop
solution_summary: The solution used Qwen3.5-35B-A3B in a Python-driven, multi-turn tool-integrated reasoning pipeline without fine-tuning. A planner proposed computational steps, a comparative judge selected one candidate, and execution feedback guided subsequent reasoning. Dynamic time allocation, context summarization, syntax repair, and role-specific sampling helped manage limited compute. The public score was 14/50, and the experiments exposed confirmation bias in zero-shot process judges and weaknesses in borrowing time under sequential benchmark ordering.
compute: Single NVIDIA H100 GPU; five-hour budget for 50 problems; approximately 30GB model weights.

solution_summary: The author used the challenge dataset and trained models through MLJAR's automatic training workflow. The post links to project results and a video showing how the project was created. It provides no model, feature, validation, or ensemble details.

The approach aligned training windows with the previous year's season and removed recent median levels to make year-to-year values comparable. It combined robust Huber regression, custom-objective XGBoost, and a feedforward neural network using median-based traffic features. An XGBoost residual stack incorporated out-of-fold Huber and neural predictions, reaching a stage 1 public score of 41.4 versus 41.8 for the neural network alone. Page-grouped validation, outlier removal, and robust losses were central, while stage 2 performance was still uncertain when the post was written.
compute: GTX 1080 Ti; neural training ran for 200 epochs, with 10 epochs taking a few seconds per model. Custom-objective XGBoost training took 12 hours.

solution_title: [93th place solution] BPP as embedding layer
solution_summary: The solution constructed contextual nucleotide embeddings from base-pair probabilities, distance-derived matrices, and an identity matrix. A learned convolution combined five relationship channels, and the resulting scores mixed nucleotide embeddings before positional encoding and a transformer. This aimed to capture information associated with pseudoknots without representing them explicitly. Across four fold models, learned weights consistently favored base-pair probabilities and self-identity while penalizing distance; an earlier custom self-attention approach failed.

The solution used a DSL-like collection of Python converters and mergers to transform grids through object representations. More than 100 converters and ten mergers handled operations such as object identification, recoloring, rotation, movement, and composition. A shared context carried information inferred from training examples, including output-only colors and output shape. An earlier CNN image-generation approach failed because training data were too scarce.

The authors provide an extensible end-to-end toxic comment classification starter with fastText–GRU and GloVe–LSTM pipelines. Their ensemble workflow tunes a second-level model using held-out validation predictions and then applies it to test predictions. The ensemble notebook reports a leaderboard score above 0.986, while the supplied fastText–GRU configuration is described as reaching 0.9852.
compute: Cloud configuration uses gcp-gpu-medium; gcp-large is recommended for ensembling, with second-level training estimated at less than an hour after parameter selection.

solution_summary: The final predictor averaged four public notebook models with weights of 0.60, 0.20, 0.15, and 0.05. An ensemble site classifier identified scans likely to originate from site 2, enabling corrections for apparent underprediction of age and domain2_var1. The correction assumed equal target means across sites and adjusted predictions according to site probability. Postprocessing improved the final public score from 0.1588 to 0.1583, with a smaller reported private improvement of 0.00025.

The approach used semantic segmentation followed by simple regression to estimate sea lion counts. The author removed the fully connected layer from ResNet-34 and used its 7×7 bottom feature surface for segmentation. The post linked the implementation but provided no numerical results or training details.

solution_title: Quick 3rd place solution (no pp) + source code
solution_summary: The solution combined a character-level GRU-head model with a token model using a beam-search-like span decoder. Its model mix included RoBERTa base, RoBERTa large, and BART large, with diversity emphasized. The token decoder conditioned end predictions on three candidate start states and ranked the resulting nine spans by probability products. Fuzzy label matching and freeze-unfreeze training supported the pipeline; each main approach scored about 0.728 on the public leaderboard.

The solution used a diverse ensemble of LightGBM, GradientBoostingRegressor, random forests, and linear regression. Model and ensemble decisions were driven by ordinary KFold cross-validation rather than the small public leaderboard. Nonlinear feature engineering and iterative feature removal were especially important for linear regression. Target encoding AgeInDays also helped some tree models, while LightGBM hyperparameters were tuned manually after Optuna results proved sensitive to fold seeds.

The solution combined EfficientNet-b5 classifiers operating on RGB, YUV, and Lab images with a modified EfficientNet-b2 processing engineered DCT coefficients. Training used flips, right-angle rotations, CutMix for color models, and SGD with cosine annealing. An MLP fused normalized pooled features because simple averaging did not combine the weaker DCT model effectively. A final LightGBM stacker used MLP predictions and t-SNE CNN features, reaching 0.9405 validation and 0.931 private scores.
compute: Color models: 4 cycles of 50 epochs; DCT model: 50 epochs, 1 cycle.

solution_summary: The pipeline standardized DICOM volumes, located a coarse vessel ROI, and refined vessel masks with two complementary nnU-Net models. A vessel-pretrained classifier used region-masked pooling and a location-aware transformer to predict anatomical labels and overall aneurysm presence. Backbone pretraining and heavily weighted auxiliary aneurysm localization were central to performance. Four-fold averaging and flip augmentation produced a reported full-resolution score of 0.916.
compute: Single RTX 4090 training: fine segmentation 14 h, classifier 6 h at reduced resolution or 12 h at full resolution. Inference measured on two T4 GPUs.

solution_summary: The solution divided the spatial domain into grids and trained local models on the resulting subsets. It augmented grid borders and periodic time boundaries, then explored feature subsets and grid resolutions. The final version blended KNN, XGBoost, and random-forest probabilities with tuned mixture weights. The author reported a score around 0.60078 for the improved pipeline.

The final approach regressed sea lion counts from whole images using a fully connected network and averaged the two best models. An earlier Tiramisu segmentation model predicted six classes around annotated dots but was biased toward background. Larger segmentation masks with Dice loss detected plausible regions of interest, although the subsequent regression overfit. TensorFlow object detection and U-Net segmentation remained unimplemented ideas.

The team ensembled BERT, DistilBERT, and XLNet models trained separately on questions and answers. They used five-fold GroupKFold validation and concatenated hidden states for prediction. Rank averaging improved the score by 0.002, followed by threshold adjustments for highly imbalanced targets. Several alternatives failed to help, including BART/T5 encoders, stochastic weight averaging, separate head training, statistical features, BERT with USE, GloVe, and LSTM.

The post compares differing predictions across nine submission files sharing a public score of 0.976518. It lists thirteen row IDs with assigned Extrovert or Introvert labels. A private score as high as 0.970850 is reported, but no training pipeline or rule for selecting the listed labels is explained.

solution_title: 41st Place Solution for the Child Mind Institute - Detect Sleep States Competition
solution_summary: The solution combined ten U-Net models using five backbones and two training-validation splits. Inference used overlapping windows with half-window hops to reduce false detections near segment edges, followed by non-maximum suppression. A custom ensemble inspired by Weighted Boxes Fusion combined predictions within each fold and then across folds, and predictions in periodic padding intervals were removed. The full pipeline achieved a private leaderboard score of 0.802, with ablations showing benefits from overlapping inference and padding removal.

The team combined Qwen3 sequence classifiers with Qwen2.5 causal language models fine-tuned using LoRA. Prompts included all answer choices, and question-specific misconception hints or restricted candidate labels improved accuracy. Multi-task learning, R-Drop, adversarial weight perturbation, and exponential moving averages improved classifier generalization. Confidence-based staged inference reserved larger models for difficult samples, while float16 inference and reduced padding enabled a larger ensemble within the time limit.
compute: Kaggle T4 inference environment; 9-hour inference limit. Full-test 72B inference took about 3 hours, reduced to about 1 hour through selective inference and CPU offloading.

solution_summary: The solution fine-tuned a LAION-2B-pretrained CLIP visual encoder for 22 epochs on a custom mixture of landmark, product, food, car, furniture, and storefront datasets. A single 64-dimensional fully connected projection layer was trained using ArcFaceMarginLayer and outperformed deeper projection heads. Increasing inference image size from 224 to 240 improved the score by approximately 0.003–0.004. Strong augmentation, contrastive learning, alternative pooling and margin layers, and several dataset expansions were unsuccessful.

solution_summary: The solution stacked predictions from RoBERTa, ELECTRA, MPNet, and Longformer models together with sentence embeddings. Polynomial kernel PCA reduced the embeddings to two dimensions, which gave the best cross-validation result. The final stack averaged Ridge and ARDRegression predictions, while LightGBM was rejected because its strong validation score did not translate to the public leaderboard. Some transformer models used reinitialized layers, and pseudo-labeling and data augmentation did not work.

The solution used list-wise ranking with separate pretrained sentence embeddings for each notebook cell, augmented by eight structural features. A notebook-level transformer predicted cell ranks alongside auxiliary ordering targets. Training used L1 loss on ranks scaled by notebook length, giving longer notebooks greater influence. Preprocessing included translation, and roughly 50,000 additional notebooks improved the reported score by 0.01.

solution_summary: The solution combined four-class study classifiers, binary opacity classifiers, and YOLOv5 detectors. Classification models used auxiliary segmentation heads, diverse image sizes, and horizontal-flip inference augmentation; some also used padding removal and percentile clipping. Classification predictions were combined using power ensembling, while binary predictions lightly calibrated detection scores. One submission scored 0.619, and several external-data and pseudo-labeling experiments failed to improve the overall blend.

solution_summary: The team trained diverse audio classifiers on overlapping three-second chunks represented as mel-spectrograms. Manually collected labels were the main improvement, followed by pseudo-labeling that raised the reported score from about 0.950 to 0.96x. Training used waveform and spectrogram augmentation, four folds, and validation-based checkpoint selection. The final ensemble contained more than 80 models.

The approach adapted a BirdCLEF 2018 sound event detection model by replacing its predictor with a pretrained PANN CNN. Training used 30-second snippets from the official data plus xeno-canto crawls, with binary cross-entropy covering foreground and background species. Augmentation randomized stereo downmixing and added bird-free noise from two external datasets. Inference first selected recording-level species using 20-second windows, then localized those species in 5-second windows with a lower threshold.

solution_title: 94th solution, with 4G RAM and GPU 740M .  Extract ResNet feature using Keras
solution_summary: The author extracted features with a pretrained ResNet50 and trained XGBoost on those features, reporting a score of 0.95030. Limited memory constrained experiments with VGG19 and merging feature sets. Dimensionality reduction reportedly improved the score by 0.003, while ensembling was suggested as another improvement.

solution_summary: The approach clustered each class before Gaussian mixture modeling, using three clusters per class. StandardScaler stabilized covariance calculations, while two-fold training supplied regularization by fitting each model on half the available samples. The author combined 42 models of the same type to improve robustness and retained default regularization parameters. Model-specific tuning was unsuccessful, and comparisons between rank and probability averaging gave mixed results.

The solution used feature trimming based on a randomly generated dummy feature. Features whose importance fell below that dummy feature were removed. The author reported little improvement after three attempts and did not implement the more advanced methods considered.

The solution combined image-retrieval shortlists, MASt3R matching, and COLMAP reconstruction. It supplemented MASt3R semi-dense correspondences with ALIKED and SuperPoint keypoints, improving matching coverage and scores. Engineering optimizations and parallel execution across two T4 GPUs allowed more image pairs within the runtime budget. The best submission scored 52.64 publicly and 56.00 privately, while pre-clustering was omitted from the final pipeline.
compute: Two Kaggle T4 GPUs, processing scene subsets in parallel.

solution_summary: The solution used LightGBM with 19 calendar, building, weather, and aggregate features. Validation followed chronological splits, while leaked test-period data supported training, evaluation, fusion tuning, and submitted results. Feature engineering included group counts, energy aggregates, cosine wind direction, and log transformations. Memory reduction and aggressive filtering of unreliable sites and anomalous readings were central practical measures, although removing zero readings increased overfitting.

The author trained toxicity models using data from the first Jigsaw competition and selected models against a filtered version of the competition validation data. Filtering removed pairs with close toxicity scores, low toxicity scores, or similar meanings, reducing the evaluation set to roughly half its original size. The final ensemble combined RoBERTa and TF-IDF with ridge regression at weights of 0.892 and 0.108. Training used five folds and ten epochs without learning-rate changes or a scheduler.

The final pipeline fed predictions from eight bagged LightGBM models into an FTRL model. It used 38 engineered features across roughly 100 million records, with chunked construction and manual array conversion to fit memory limits. Bagging increased cross-validation from 0.791 to 0.792, while standalone FTRL was weak. Adding LightGBM predictions to FTRL improved the leaderboard score from 0.792 to 0.793.

solution_summary: The author trained AutoGluon with best_quality presets separately on each training split of a manual 20-fold cross-validation loop. Test predictions were averaged across the resulting models, and final submissions were selected using average validation scores. This added an outer ensemble around AutoGluon's internal ensembling and stacking and reportedly improved cross-validation performance. Training took approximately 20 hours.
compute: Approximately 20 hours total training, about one hour per fold.

solution_summary: The approach perturbed convolutional weights around their original values, then trained on the retain set for four epochs to restore useful knowledge. Training used SGD and a custom cross-entropy-based loss that heavily favored class 0, with another light weight perturbation before the final epoch. An earlier research approach worked in the starting kit but encountered compilation problems in the competition. The submitted algorithm took about six hours and obtained a final validation score of 0.0885.

solution_title: Kaggle "The Allen AI Science Challenge" competition

Custom search functions produce most retrieval features, while PyLucene supplies seven additional feature sets. The pipeline prepares and caches features before cross-validation, full-data training, and prediction. Reported training cross-validation results are 0.83054 AUC and 0.616 accuracy, but the model family is not specified.

solution_summary: The solution used a transformer embedding retriever followed by a transformer sentence-pair classification ranker, with XGBoost for ranker stacking. Retriever pretraining combined masked language modeling and supervised SimCSE contrastive learning over three rounds, refreshing hard negatives from earlier checkpoints. Five pretrained models generated mean-pooled embeddings for cosine-similarity retrieval of the top 100 contents per topic. Validation used five stratified group folds by topic ID, and the final ensemble used eight models across two folds, achieving public and private scores of 0.717 and 0.745.

The author developed two image-matching pipelines based on previous prize-eligible solutions and validated them on diverse historical datasets. The AffNetHardNet8 and AdaLAM pipeline combined several detectors at different image resolutions and benefited from higher RANSAC thresholds. The best-scoring pipeline used ALIKED, DISK, and SIFT alongside LightGlue, NetVLAD retrieval, PixSfM, and rotation matching, with ALIKED detection and resizing settings tuned through validation. Scene-specific combinations were tested but were not selected because their behavior on unknown private scenes was uncertain.

The submission supplied two template-based structures, two Protenix predictions, and one RNAPro prediction for every target. A LightGBM model ranked templates using RNA, description, protein, DNA, ligand, and chain-composition similarities. Neural inference incorporated associated molecules while limiting their size, MSA depth, and diffusion work to meet runtime constraints. Long sequences were split into overlapping chains and chunks, then reconstructed with Kabsch alignment. RNAPro and Protenix ran concurrently on two T4 GPUs.
compute: Two T4 GPUs; RNAPro and Protenix inference run in parallel

solution_summary: The solution used a three-layer ensemble built from over 200 diverse out-of-fold prediction sets generated with AutoGluon and custom models. Four second-layer models combined XGBoost and neural networks with confident test pseudo-labels, either appended as training rows or converted into nearest-neighbor features. Feature interactions, target and frequency encoding, and averaging across folds and seeds supported the base-model diversity. A hill-climb weighted blend of the four second-layer models achieved CV 0.977594 and private leaderboard score 0.97790.
compute: Kaggle Notebook environment with a 12-hour runtime limit; feature-combination search repeated about five times, with memory and disk-space constraints.

solution_title: 72nd place solution(ensemble of LightGBM and Sequential NN)
solution_summary: The solution combined LightGBM DART models using customer-level aggregates with GRU and transformer sequence models. Tree features included aggregate combinations and recent differences, while neural inputs used one-hot categories, missingness indicators, and linear interpolation. Although neural models scored below the tree models individually, combining them improved the public score from 0.799 to 0.800. Logistic regression or MLP stacking performed particularly well, and the final submission scored 0.80011 locally and 0.80780 on the private leaderboard.

The author trained two groups of heterogeneous language models in Kaggle kernels and distilled them into BERT students. A five-fold group including BERT, XLNet, GPT2, and LSTM was compressed into BERT large cased, while a four-fold transformer group was compressed into BERT large uncased. Final inference averaged folds and blended the two student groups across nine runs. The resulting blend achieved approximately 0.946 on the leaderboard.

solution_title: [Private 47th / Public 55th] Stable local cv & public leaderboard using stacking with linear models and forward selection
solution_summary: The team stacked diverse transformer predictions with readability measurements using Ridge regression, linear SVR, and ElasticNet, then blended the three outputs. Five-fold validation stratified on binned targets guided model selection and produced out-of-fold features. Readability features, attention heads, learning-rate scheduling, and target perturbation helped handle the small dataset and noisy labels. Forward feature selection improved ensemble diversity and performance, while additional pretraining did not help.

The final system combines four Helsinki translation pipelines and four byT5 pipelines, using extracted external translations and gold-quality data. Each model generates four beam-search candidates, and weighted Minimum Bayes Risk decoding selects a translation from the pooled candidates after normalization and deduplication. The ensemble completed inference in under 33 minutes across two GPUs. Multitask training improved stability, but final adaptation to competition data erased much of the benefit from earlier training, and Qwen experiments were excluded because of uncertainty and inference runtime constraints.

solution_summary: The team combined complementary candidate generators with LightGBM ranking models. One pipeline filtered roughly 600 popular items to 130 candidates before adding purchase history, while the other generated diverse candidates using grouped popularity, image similarity, co-occurrence, and graph walks. Rich customer, article, interaction, repurchase, and similarity features supported the ranking stage. Combining candidates improved the reported score from 0.0355 to 0.0362, and the ensemble reached 0.0368.

The author contributed modified Puzzle-CAM models trained on RGBY images to a broader team ensemble. A Siamese CNN learned image labels and consistent activation maps, with external data and balanced sampling supporting training. Inference combined cell-mask intersections with full-image activation maps and predictions from individual cell crops. Only SE-ResNeXt50 variants entered the author's final ensemble, and a faster segmentation pipeline traded a small score loss for roughly sixfold acceleration. Averaging variants reached public scores around 0.52–0.53.

solution_summary: The author built a chart-reading pipeline combining chart classification, text detection and recognition, object detection, and segmentation. Geometric filtering and label-to-tick matching converted detected chart elements into numerical values, with specialized handling for each chart type. Training used only competition data, reserving half of the extracted data for validation before retraining on all data. The reported best validation score was 0.871, while the best public and private scores were 0.86 and 0.69.

The solution used UNet with a ResNet34 backbone and an auxiliary branch for empty-mask classification. Training combined mask BCE, Dice loss, and empty-mask BCE, while gradually reducing the proportion of non-empty samples to match the dataset. It trained on random 512×512 crops and inferred at 768×768, with validation-selected rules suppressing empty or small predicted masks. The final ensemble averaged four selected checkpoints across eight folds and used horizontal-flip test-time augmentation.

solution_title: Why does postprocessing work? 2nd place magic
solution_summary: The team inspected most buildings individually and removed anomalous readings, particularly zeros, making data cleaning central to its approach. Removing these readings raised the mean prediction, and downward multiplicative correction improved results. A controlled experiment introduced artificial zero readings into an otherwise clean building to examine the interaction between cleaning and prediction scaling. Removing the artificial training outliers improved CV from 1.16 to 0.17, while subsequent scaling by 0.92 improved the experimental leaderboard score from 1.19 to 1.14.

The solution combined feature-engineered CatBoost and XGBoost classifiers with multi-label transformer–LSTM sequence models. Validation used five-fold GroupKFold by session, and 11,343 additional complete sessions extracted from raw data particularly benefited neural models. Game-specific timing, movement, task, and previous-prediction features supported tree models, with null-importance feature selection for level-group and combined classifiers. Separate logistic regression stacks for tree and neural models were blended at a 6:4 ratio, producing CV 0.7046 and a private score of 0.704.

The solution used a fixed validation set of 663 images drawn from usask_1 and portions of other sources. Its main described contribution was a custom augmentation pipeline with cropping, padding, resizing, color transfer, background-image Mixup, and rotation with pseudo-labels. Standard flips and right-angle rotations supplemented these augmentations. For the SPIKE dataset, weighted boxes fusion combined pseudo-labels with supplied ground-truth boxes; the text does not specify the detector architecture or numerical results.

The solution combined three models implemented in R and Python, mainly using LightGBM and XGBoost with different features. One component was a stacking regressor containing ten regression models. Models were tuned and validated using the current dataset and previous competitions. Submission variants used different amounts of extreme-probability clipping, and one shifted predictions toward models ranked more highly by historical validation.

solution_title: Solution Arhitecture Pipeline for Bronze Medal
solution_summary: The pipeline began with tuned EfficientNet B2, B3, and B4 models using ImageNet or noisy-student initialization. Weighted out-of-fold predictions with eight test-time augmentations identified noisy training labels and reliable examples from the previous year's competition. Models trained on original, cleaned, and extended datasets then supplied twelve predictions to a bagged, two-layer stacking system. Bagging generalized better on the leaderboard than boosting despite boosting's stronger validation accuracy.

solution_summary: The solution combined several transformer backbones and input text arrangements with LightGBM, CatBoost, and XGBoost models. solution_title: Model Capability Dominates: Why Prompt Diversity Fails
solution_summary: The baseline used quantized GPT-OSS-120B with eight samples, temperature 1.0, and entropy-weighted voting. Repeated experiments found that prompt diversity and smaller alternative models did not reliably improve this baseline, whose public mean was 39.3/50 across 21 runs. The final submission added a code re-execution verifier and scored 41/50 publicly and 40.5/50 privately, although external testing found no robust benefit from any tested verifier. The main diagnosed limitation was selection loss: correct generated candidates often lost the vote by a single agreeing attempt.

Ridge scaled more reliably than hill climbing or genetic algorithms as the ensemble grew. Additional diversity came from neural networks, boosted trees, and classification models trained as one-hot target regression. solution_summary: The team modeled filtered raw gravitational-wave signals with multi-kernel Conv1D networks, later using separate encoders for each detector and ResNet34 to fuse their features. Synthetic pretraining followed by brief fine-tuning on the original data mattered more than mixing synthetic and real samples. Predicting signal parameters during pretraining added a small improvement, while augmentation hurt the strongest synthetic-pretrained models. The strongest described model reached 0.8858 public leaderboard score; segmentation, denoising autoencoders and hard-example mining did not improve the approach.

The final system blended three Perch-v2-based audio classifiers, with nearly all weight assigned to the strongest Perch MLP model. solution_title: 1st Place Solution - From Embeddings to Matches
solution_summary: The solution trained separate image and text encoders with ArcFace and combined their normalized embeddings for product matching. Its main improvement came from three-stage Iterative Neighborhood Blending, which refined embeddings using similarity-weighted neighbors before searching for matches again. Final predictions united refined combined matches with image-only and text-only matches, using tuned distance thresholds and a relaxed rule for the second match. Embedding retrieval and refinement mattered more than further encoder improvements, and the reported public leaderboard score reached 0.793.

The solution combined ResNet50, InceptionV3, and InceptionResNetV2 trained from scratch at different image resolutions. Diversity came from architecture, image size, and augmentation schedules, while tuning on the tuning set addressed differences in label distributions. Predictions on original and mirrored test images were combined using a weighted average. Tuning substantially improved all three models, with the strongest reported Stage 1 score reaching 0.550.

solution_title: 38th Place - ZoneMix - A domain specific augmentation
solution_summary: The solution introduced ZoneMix, a rule-based augmentation that extracts grapheme components from spatial zones and resizes them onto other characters. Direct training was too noisy, so separate models targeted grapheme roots and difficult consonants, with synthetic consonants formed by combining existing components. The final system used ZoneMix models for roots with fewer than five combinations and consonants 3 and 6, retaining an older ensemble for the remaining predictions. Experiments emphasized generalization to unseen graphemes, and cropped preprocessing failed while simple resized inputs and several augmentation choices performed better.

The solution merged 45 DBSCAN variants built with different helix features, radius samples, and z shifts. Tracks were then divided by curvature consistency and merged in order of decreasing quality using overlap heuristics. Training-derived radius samples and diverse unrolling functions improved track coverage, while quality-aware merging added about 0.03–0.04 over merging everything together.

solution_summary: The author searched word permutations using a genetic algorithm with Edge Assembly Crossover, initialized and refined with simulated annealing. Gemma parent logits guided edge reconstruction toward lower estimated perplexity, while selection penalties maintained population diversity. Longer cases used structured initial permutations with stop words first and alphabetically ordered groups. Simulated annealing supplied the final solutions for cases 0–2, and nearly all alternative crossover methods were ineffective.

solution_title: 5th place solution: Stack-sliding and Differential Evolution
solution_summary: The solution used a physics-based stack-slide search to align frequency-modulated signals and sum their power across short Fourier transforms. Differential evolution searched source position and frequency derivative, with combined power from both detectors substantially improving performance. Normalization and glitch isolation supported the search, and a logistic transformation converted maximum power into predictions. An optimized Julia implementation processed the test set in about 10 hours, while earlier Transformer and CNN approaches were unsuccessful.

solution_summary: The team evaluated fingerprints, polyBERT embeddings, and Mordred descriptors with AutoGluon, then combined models using five-fold out-of-fold weighted averaging. Mordred performed best overall, while embeddings were strongest for Rg, and additional fingerprint types improved the fingerprint model. The better final notebook blended Mordred, fingerprint, and embedding models, with TgSS used only for Mordred training. It scored 0.090 privately, and the author reports 0.069 on both leaderboard splits with a C-to-F transformation, concluding that distribution shift mattered more than featurization.

The solution corrected an existing polynomial-fit baseline with a neural network rather than predicting the output directly, improving the metric by approximately 0.1. It used channel-wise normalization, a ViT backbone, and a weighted combination of scaled MSE and Gaussian log-likelihood loss. A sample-quality feature improved the metric by about 0.015, while synthetic data, alternative prefilters, and manual corrections were unsuccessful. The final submission combined the best and last checkpoints from ten folds, totaling 20 models and approximately two hours of inference.

Graph reconstruction achieved 95% exact validation InChI predictions, but occasional broken molecules required a direct-string model as a fallback. solution_summary: The solution used seven Linear-Tree models to limit model flexibility in a noisy financial setting. Stocks were ranked by the mean model prediction divided by prediction dispersion to penalize uncertainty. Features combined technical indicators, financial changes, disclosure timing, and chart or sector similarities, while training excluded returns spanning earnings disclosures and validation used CPCV.

The system used unfine-tuned GPT-OSS 120B with parallel Python-assisted reasoning threads coordinated through a shared Blackboard. Sharing recent tool inputs and outputs helped threads reuse computational discoveries, while sharing reasoning text encouraged harmful answer copying. Each thread forked after its first answer so both branches could verify or revise it, and final selection used majority voting with entropy-based tie-breaking. Adaptive sandbox execution limits and problem budgets managed the inference deadline. The reported peak public score was 46, typical scores were approximately 40–42, and the private score was 41.5.

solution_summary: The solution retrieved 25 candidate misconceptions with a fine-tuned Qwen2.5-14B model and reranked them individually with Qwen2.5-32B binary classification scores. Both models used competition examples and GPT-4o-generated synthetic data, with validation emphasizing unseen misconceptions. Iterative hard-negative mining strengthened retrieval, while cached shared context reduced reranking runtime. The reranker reached OOD validation MAP@25 of 0.571 and private leaderboard MAP@25 of 0.558, with the complete notebook running in approximately seven hours.

solution_summary: The author describes a segmentation test model using an ImageNet-pretrained SE-ResNeXt50 encoder with hypercolumns, attention gates, dilated convolutions, and deep supervision. Removing unusual masks left 3,884 training images and produced a strong private-set improvement despite weaker public results. Five-fold validation with the best checkpoint from each fold achieved 0.8875 CV. The best submitted variant used the full dataset and three unspecified post-processing rules.

The pipeline clustered DINOv2 image embeddings after t-SNE reduction, using confidence scores to decide how strongly clustering should guide reconstruction. ALIKED and LightGlue supplied local correspondences across multiple image resolutions and keypoint-guided crops, followed by custom RANSAC verification. PyCOLMAP reconstruction used deterministic initialization with fallback image pairs. Low-confidence scenes were handled through iterative reconstruction, followed by merging and overlap removal, with runtime around six hours.

solution_title: 21th place solution, puzzlingly shaking from public LB 3th
solution_summary: The solution combined RoBERTa-Large models predicting answer types and long/short spans with ALBERT-xxlarge short-span models, all pretrained by the team on SQuAD. Answer-type rules, null-answer score adjustments, and selection among candidate span pairs materially improved predictions. The ensemble first voted on long answers and then used the selected long-answer candidates for short-answer prediction. It achieved 67.569% development F1, 71% public F1, and 67% private F1, leaving an unexplained public-to-private drop.

The solution used an ensemble of DeBERTa variants that read whole essays and predict effectiveness for marked discourse spans. Prior Feedback competition weights and iterative soft pseudo-labeling on about 11,000 additional essays were central to training. XGBoost stacking incorporated model probabilities, token probability statistics, neighboring discourse predictions, and essay-level aggregates, improving scores by about 0.004. The best private score was 0.553, with 0.554 for the best selected submission.

solution_summary: The final solution rank-averaged image classification and sound-event-detection models. The strongest image approach trained EfficientNets on annotated time-frequency patches cropped from log-mel spectrograms, with randomized temporal cropping. Eight image models were stacked and achieved a reported public score of 0.942. The SED component combined 11 models with different encoders, augmentations, supervision, and training stages, reaching 0.901 public and 0.911 private.

The solution trained many diverse base models using a shared shuffled ten-fold stratified validation split. Linear discriminant analysis stackers gave more consistent agreement between local validation and the public leaderboard than logistic regression or Gaussian naive Bayes stackers. Out-of-fold predictions from the four strongest stackers were combined using hill-climbing ensemble weights, reaching 0.38247 publicly and 0.38385 privately. Treating every feature as categorical and adding repeated copies of the original dataset helped, while feature engineering did not.

solution_title: Top 3%: Feeding wrong predictions from initial model to training set - Boosted the Scores
solution_summary: The approach combined a TensorFlow neural network, LightGBM, and CatBoost after feature selection, transformations, imputation, scaling, and outlier removal. The neural network and LightGBM used randomly undersampled data, while CatBoost used custom class weights on 80% of the training data. Each model's probabilities were mapped to near-binary values using a selected threshold, then averaged for submission. The authors also duplicated misclassified rows 30 times and reran training, reporting an improvement without a readable numerical score.

The solution used ten-fold RoBERTa span extraction, supplemented by models trained on cleaned target spans and models that restored character-level label noise. Separate RoBERTa models predicted which examples needed noise and how far to shift their span boundaries. Majority voting combined the pseudo-labeled, cleaned, and noise-restored predictions, achieving a private Jaccard score of 0.718. Pseudo-labeling improved the public score but slightly hurt private performance, while noise restoration delivered only a small overall gain.

The author interpreted the eight API outputs as character-position classes and probed the model with single-pixel perturbations. The resulting importance maps clearly revealed five positions, while three positions resisted direct inversion. Recognizing that repeated or visually similar characters could cause class preference resolved the ambiguity. Overlaying the clear character images onto the unresolved positions revealed the static key, "letmeout".

solution_title: 27th Solution - What Worked and What Didn't for Me...
solution_summary: The final solution combined transformer models trained with MarginRankingLoss and a custom attention output head, using low learning rates for their backbones. The author prioritized a shared cross-validation strategy over unstable leaderboard feedback and added toxicity pairs derived from Measuring Hate Speech for ensemble diversity. Final predictions were a weighted sum of model rankings across RoBERTa, DistilBERT, DeBERTa-v3, BERT, and BART variants. Models generally converged before completing the first epoch, while TF-IDF, word embeddings, toxic-domain MLM pretraining, and Electra approaches were unsuccessful.

The note describes ImageNet-pretrained CNN experiments using roughly 23,000 drawings per class, typically rendered at 128×128. Inputs encoded stroke order, country code and highlighted endpoint strokes. Training used Adam and six cosine learning-rate cycles, with SE-ResNeXt50 obtaining the highest reported score of 0.930. Horizontal-flip TTA helped weaker models but hurt models already scoring at least 0.920, and several further improvements remained proposals.

Aggressive probabilities, including 99% first-round win probabilities for seeds one through three, were credited as a major contributor, with substantial year-to-year volatility acknowledged.

solution_title: Private score 0.81148. What could've been the 5th place solution (Single model)
solution_summary: The author fine-tuned BERTweet Large for pointwise toxicity-ranking regression, achieving a private leaderboard score of 0.81148. Training used the original Jigsaw competition data, retaining toxic examples and sampling non-toxic examples, with inverse-frequency weighting of the six toxicity labels. Validation pairs were converted into regression targets using a Bradley–Terry model. Text cleaning removed IP addresses, converted emojis and Unicode, and limited repeated characters or words.

The best agent used imitation learning with a U-Net trained on roughly 1,000 winning episodes from a strong team. Training explicitly included idle center actions, limited sampling to four actions per turn, and undersampled the dominant idle class. Test-time augmentation was retained for robustness, and ONNX Runtime accelerated inference. PPO reinforcement learning and value-guided MCTS were explored extensively but did not outperform the imitation-learning solution.

The recovered prompt concatenated an optimized generic mean prompt, a Mistral-generated component, and a rule-based component. The mean prompt was searched token by token against a mean embedding, using competition scoring and random candidates for diversity. Mistral used few-shot prompting and chain-of-thought, while rules extracted dialogue participants and style keywords from rewritten text. The mean prompt scored about 0.67 privately, and the two additional components each reportedly added roughly 0.005–0.01.

solution_title: 16th place solution: Data augmentation and fixes + Evaluation across different models.
solution_summary: The author trained XLMR, Muril-Large, and Rembert from SQuAD2 QA checkpoints using Chaii and several external Indic QA datasets. Important preparation steps included realigning answer starts and sampling Chaii contexts to maintain a 1:2 relevant-to-irrelevant ratio. The selected pipeline used Rembert for passage selection and other models for answer extraction, but this reduced the score from the best three-fold Rembert result of 0.778 to 0.757. A separate LightGBM ranker combining three model outputs also performed well on the private leaderboard.

solution_title: 14th place solution: data and metric comprehension
solution_summary: The team reconstructed mosaics from training masks and extracted overlapping training windows, placing strong emphasis on local validation and the competition metric. A ResNet34 U-Net performed segmentation, while a separate ResNet34 classifier filtered predicted ships near the end of inference. Training used a one-cycle schedule, frozen then unfrozen stages, mixed precision, and geometric and brightness augmentations. solution_title: Flavour of Physics Winner's Interview: 3rd place, Josef Slavicek
solution_summary: The original solution blended a neural network with XGBoost trained on normalized, decorrelated inputs. An estimated particle mass supplied another feature, while exponentiating the XGBoost predictions before blending enabled stronger contributions without failing agreement and correlation checks. solution_summary: The solution combined EfficientDetD7 and YOLOv5x opacity detectors with separate study-level and box-presence classifiers. Yeo-Johnson transformation and robust scaling preceded LightGBM importance-based selection of 20 features. Coordinate-aware decoding, RGB skip connections, PixelShuffle upsampling, and weighted pixel classification preserve thin waveform details. Segment-specific degradation augmentation and training on the entire dataset improved performance, while horizontal-flip inference and Einthoven correction provided additional gains. It calculated a fundamental matrix from the merged matches and passed it directly to PyColmap reconstruction, bypassing exhaustive matching. It relied on ten-fold stratified cross-validation, adding the original stroke dataset while restricting validation to synthetic samples. Category replacements, recursive feature elimination, and selected interaction features improved the models. The approach combined CatBoost, LightGBM, and a LightAutoML Denselight network using aggregated tabular features. The solution forecasts microbusiness density with simple multiplicative trends estimated for counties, states, and groups defined by active-business quantiles. Recent six-month performance determines clipped growth factors for one- and two-month horizons. Forecasts start from the best public submission and cover optimistic and pessimistic trend scenarios, with a May seasonal adjustment. Validation favors different persistence or trend rules for counties with low active-business counts and finds complex gradient boosting less stable.

solution_title: fast.ai, a viable time series solution

It marked text sequences shared with the original passage using braces around overlaps of at least three tokens, supplying copying information with little added sequence length. solution_summary: The solution used a large multilayer ensemble with minimal feature engineering and base models trained on different target transformations. A repository of 98 models supplied diverse tree, neural-network, and AutoML predictions. solution_title: 21st Place Solution -> Binary Classification with a Bank Dataset Competition
solution_summary: The solution used a large stacking classifier built from roughly seventy models, including neural networks, boosted trees, decision trees, and logistic regression. A Keras neural network extracted features for downstream models and substantially improved cross-validation scores. Additional engineered features helped particular model families. Careful validation that avoided preprocessing leakage guided submission selection, and the submission with the highest validation score performed best privately.

The solution trained XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost regressors on four feature subsets and stacked their out-of-fold predictions with RidgeCV. Features described essay structure, writing bursts, key presses, word lengths, stylistic errors, punctuation, and tokenizer n-grams. solution_summary: The approach extracted and cached 256-pixel tissue tiles from fourfold downsampled slides, then sampled 26 crops per image. A shared-weight siamese network used a semi-weakly pretrained ResNet18 and averaged crop outputs before a binned prediction head. Random crop selection, flips, rotations, and rectangular occlusion helped generalization, while color augmentation offered little benefit. A single 70/30 split yielded a validation score of 0.8504, with reported public and private scores of 0.8503 and 0.8966.

solution_title: Kaggle Otto Group Product Classification Challenge

solution_summary: The final approach averaged five-fold DeiT-base-384 and EfficientNet-B4 models, including models trained with additional 2019 cassava data. Handling label noise was central: the author removed a small fraction of confidently identified noisy samples, used a modified OUSM loss, and applied strong augmentation with mixup and CutMix. solution_title: The Great Shakeup: 92.2 public to 0.0 private, and why my hedge survived
solution_summary: The author selected two specialist submissions to hedge against changes in the private guardrail: pure marker exfiltration and nearly pure confused-deputy attacks. Marker exfiltration fell from 92.245 public to 0.000 private, while the confused-deputy submission retained 9.820 private from 10.445 public. The best-of-two scoring rule made diversification across submissions central to the strategy. Restricting the confused-deputy engine to whitelisted domains proved overly cautious, since a broader variant scored 10.755 privately.

The solution trained LightGBM on categorical identifiers, calendar features, cyclical encodings, and a binary year-parity feature. Training excluded February through June 2020, and an explicit adjustment removed Argentina's declining annual sales trend. Predictions were multiplied by coefficients borrowed from a community notebook. A second submission stopped applying those coefficients after May, but performed poorly on private data despite a much better public score.

The team treated temporal localization as classification of five-frame video segments. Transformer and bidirectional GRU sequence models used whole-video context, while NeXtVLAD models used only the segment frames. An EM-like pretraining process generated segment labels from video-labeled training data, retrained models on those labels, and fine-tuned on segment annotations. Two EM iterations were run, and tested multiple-instance learning approaches did not outperform this process.

The solution combined fine-tuned language models, models further trained with pseudo-labeled Feedback Prize 1 essays, and RAPIDS SVR models on language-model embeddings. Fold-specific pseudo-labeling and duplicate removal controlled leakage, and pseudo-labeling produced a substantial improvement. Target-specific ensemble weights were optimized with Nelder–Mead and shared across folds, yielding local CV of 0.4436. Final predictions averaged the five-fold models with models trained on all data; the author reported good CV–leaderboard correlation despite a validation implementation bug.

solution_title: 59th Place Solution for the Home Credit - Credit Risk Model Stability Competition
solution_summary: The final solution combined six models: the author's CatBoost, LightGBM, XGBoost, and LightAutoML components, plus a teammate's CatBoost and LightGBM. The two contributors engineered features independently, and one final ensemble gave CatBoost the largest weight. Counting category occurrences in previous-application data improved the leaderboard score by 0.013. Additional features used riskassesment_302T and the number of months associated with previous loans, with the former adding 0.001.

solution_title: Delta x,y CNN + MLP network from 5th place solution
solution_summary: The solution predicts waypoint-to-waypoint displacement using a CNN over IMU signals combined with a large neural network for contextual path features. Inputs include site and floor embeddings, device calibration information, movement timing, nearby waypoints, and wall geometry. Gaussian noise, alternating losses and optimizers, site-specific fine-tuning, and averaging roughly a dozen networks improved accuracy. The multisite model achieved below 1.0 m MAE averaged across displacement coordinates, with some fine-tuned sites reaching 0.6–0.7 m.

The pipeline extracted slice features with EfficientNet B0 and B2, then classified exams and slices using a sequence-level 1D CNN. Trainable CT windows and metric-weighted binary cross-entropy adapted training to the competition, while mixed precision reduced resource use. Predictions were averaged across five folds and both backbones, followed by minimal corrections for label consistency. The combined submission scored 0.156 privately, and the reported total cross-validation BCE was 0.201473.

solution_summary: The team optimized tree packings using Spyrrow/Sparrow initialization, simulated annealing, and a memetic algorithm. For large configurations, they represented a dense lattice block as a single concave-hull polygon so Spyrrow could arrange free trees around it before restoring the lattice. Aspect-ratio perturbations helped escape local minima, and adding or removing trees transferred strong layouts between neighboring problem sizes. Their two best layouts achieved scores of 0.328x.

The author divided the location task into spatial cells and tuned models on a small geographic subset using a temporal holdout. The final ensemble summed probabilities from 13 models spanning nearest neighbors, tree ensembles, naive Bayes, and several kernel density implementations. Diversity across model families and cell configurations, followed by greedy ensemble selection, was central to the approach. Optimizing ensemble weights produced only negligible improvement, so the final combination was unweighted.

solution_summary: The team trained four-layer bidirectional LSTMs using a small set of unnormalized raw, cumulative, logarithmic, and difference features. They improved learning by adding similar training breaths and their known pressures as input features, together with auxiliary regression and classification targets. Inference ensembled predictions from five neighbor choices, and the final training used full data with more than 30 seeds. Pseudo-label training with 14 models slightly improved the reported leaderboard score from 0.0999 to 0.0998.

The solution detected scientific panels before looking for reused content between blot or microscopy panels within a figure. Class and geometry filters plus ResNet-50 retrieval shortlisted pairs for RootSIFT matching with horizontal-flip checks and MAGSAC++ verification. Matched regions were grouped, projected into original image coordinates, filtered, and encoded as instance masks. Figures without multiple relevant panels were submitted as authentic because intra-panel detection was unfinished.

solution_summary: The author ensembled five pretrained language-model configurations using separate question and answer branches, with categorical embeddings in some models. Simple text cleanup and last-hidden-state CLS representations supported the models, while validation Spearman correlation guided early stopping. Mapping predictions to percentiles of unique training-label values produced the largest reported improvement. The final ensemble reached 0.438232 local CV and 0.41208 on the private leaderboard.

The author pooled data across subjects, which substantially improved leaderboard performance over subject-specific models despite their strong cross-validation results. Signals were resampled to 500 samples per second, and short windows from three segment positions were converted into log band-power features. Channels were selected and ordered by ictal-versus-interictal d-prime discrimination, yielding 192 features per segment. RBF SVMs with gamma 1.58 produced the required predictions, with one SVM per prediction task.

The solution computed engineered features and trained XGBoost to predict duplicate questions. Most features came from public competition kernels and discussions, with additional contributions from teammates. Some supplied feature CSVs were unavailable in the shared material, limiting reproducibility. The reported private leaderboard score was 0.14137.

The solution detected characters with a two-stage CenterNet pipeline using HourglassNet backbones, then classified cropped characters with three ResNet-based models. The second detection stage removed image margins using first-stage boxes, and both stages' boxes were ensembled. Classification incorporated bounding-box aspect ratio, horizontal-shift test-time augmentation, and a pseudo-labeled third model. Augmentation was essential for avoiding overfitting, and the final private leaderboard score was 0.900.

solution_summary: The final pipeline used a single ByT5-large model pretrained on external Akkadian-English material and fine-tuned on organizer data. solution_title: 2nd place solution to Facebook V competition on Kaggle

Mean transit estimates combined polynomial degrees, while wavelength-specific predictions used noise-adaptive smoothing and mean alignment. The solution fine-tuned BERT-large with a small custom output head and no additional statistical features. Offset-aware tokenization and truncation located the pronoun and candidate names, whose embeddings were combined through element-wise interactions and shared trainable projections. solution_summary: The final notebook combined three prompt attacks adapted from public notebooks and forum ideas without filtering. They exploited model sensitivity to option positions, direct instructions to award a grade of nine, and model-specific wording in an adapted add-it-up attack. solution_title: (16th place) Improve your imitation agent with rules
solution_summary: The team adapted sazuma's imitation agent by training a center action and removing its nighttime movement restriction. They added rules for city production, movement ordering, evacuation, transfers, and returning units to resources or cities. These rules achieved roughly a 90% win rate against the modified vanilla imitation agent with identical model parameters when no time limit was imposed. Frequent time-limit violations remained an unresolved weakness of the final bots.

The final approach used a frozen CLIP backbone with an ArcFace head to learn 64-dimensional image embeddings. Restricting training to 4,000 classes from Products10k and GLR worked best. Validation across multiple retrieval datasets had weak leaderboard correlation, although a Stanford Online Products furniture subset was relatively useful. Text-image contrastive training, UMAP, separate category spaces, CLIP fine-tuning, other pretrained backbones, and extra transformer layers did not improve the approach.
