solution_summary: The team used Codex and ChatGPT to rewrite task-specific ONNX programs, giving each run the current implementation, cost measurements, prior attempts, and related solutions. Large gains came from changing representations and transferring successful mechanisms across tasks, supported by persistent histories that prevented repeated failures. Candidates were rebuilt and checked locally before replacing existing solutions. Validation combined bundled examples, a consensus-filtered set of 2,000 generated examples per task, and separate unfiltered fresh examples to expose narrow rules and overfitting. Two reported architectural rewrites reduced costs by more than 95%, while Codex supplied roughly 70% of improvements in the final week.

The solution trained a custom byte-pair tokenizer and TF-IDF representation on the test texts, then combined three lightweight classifiers with voting. Carefully curated training data, especially DAIGT v2 and generated educational essays based on Kids Frontier articles, mattered most. GPT-3.5 generated 60,000 samples, of which 30,000 were used for training. The final CPU submission scored 0.947061 publicly and 0.91967 privately, with 17-minute inference.

solution_title: 26th place solution | Recursive Gated Convolutions + Lung Tiling
solution_summary: The team used pretrained ConvNext and HorNet backbones with UPerNet decoders, combining six weighted model families and a separate lung model. Most tissue images were resized to 768, while lung training used overlapping tiles and selected annotation styles. Strong color augmentation, morphological mask refinement, and adaptive probability thresholds were important parts of the pipeline. The ensemble achieved both public and private scores of 0.81.

The solution used two pipelines pairing 2.5D Faster R-CNN detectors with DeiT-Small transformers that aggregated region features into location and aneurysm-presence predictions. Resampling and training across anatomical planes addressed unreliable image orientation metadata. The detectors used different backbones, slice-channel counts, and bounding-box configurations, while transformer training used augmented cached region features and staged backbone unfreezing. A weighted ensemble achieved public and private scores of 0.82494 and 0.80592, outperforming the individual pipelines.

solution_title: 17th Place Solution - SpaCy 3 (EntityRuler) and NER CRF model
solution_summary: The approach filtered documents to sentences with dataset-related context, then generated candidate names using custom SpaCy rules and abbreviation matching. A LightGBM classifier resolved uncertain candidates using simple structural and geographical features. The team also developed BERT-CRF NER with casing-based masking, which improved cross-validation generalization to unseen names. Their best submission scored 0.451 on the private leaderboard without NER, but unreliable evaluation led them to select weaker submissions. Excluding acronyms was identified as a missed opportunity.

The solution blended three diverse tabular pipelines using LightGBM, CatBoost, and XGBoost, with predictions from different image backbones included as features. Patient-level contextual statistics, group aggregates, ranks, and different negative-sampling ratios provided diversity. Five-fold stratified grouped validation and repeated seed experiments guided feature retention, while image models used short training with class resampling and augmentation before resizing. Hill-climbing blend weights produced reported scores of 18.2 CV and 18.7 public LB.

solution_title: [20th Place] ByT5-base, span corruption, synth & soup
solution_summary: The solution used ByT5-base with extensive text normalization and approximately 80,000 translation pairs assembled through segmentation, extraction, and synthetic translation. Training progressed from Akkadian span corruption to mixed-quality supervised translation and finally fine-tuning on approximately 10,000 curated pairs. Weight averaging combined two training seeds with the gold-data model without increasing inference cost. Long-input splitting and domain-specific spelling corrections provided additional improvements.

solution_title: 9th place solution or how we spent last one and a half month
solution_summary: The team treated whale identification as face recognition, learning CosFace and ArcFace embeddings and ranking identities through cosine similarities to training images. Lightweight ResNet34, BNInception, and DenseNet121 models were trained at low resolution before higher-resolution training. Strong augmentation, weighted sampling, and distillation incorporated new_whale examples, while pseudo-labeled test images further improved training. A snapshot ensemble achieved 0.958, although combining models trained with pseudo-labels and distillation brought no further improvement.

solution_title: 44th solution: Add all the randomness or how to improve your ensemble when all your models suck
solution_summary: This post links to a notebook containing code and comments about reducing correlation between models. It refers to ideas from an earlier post but provides no concrete methods or pipeline details in the supplied text. The linked notebook's contents are not included.

The team iteratively blended multilingual XLM-RoBERTa, language-specific Transformers, and FastText bidirectional GRU classifiers. Soft pseudo-labels for all test samples were repeatedly refined, with models restarted from pretrained weights and pseudo-labels upsampled late in the competition. Weighted blending reduced training variability, while submission-history post-processing gave a further small improvement. Validation became noisy as validation data entered training, so development increasingly relied on the public leaderboard, reaching 0.9556.

solution_title: [Private LB 20th]How did I reach 0.82 from 0.68 on the public LB?
solution_summary: The author progressively improved organ segmentation from a tiled UNeXt model with a ResNeXt-50 backbone to untiled MiT-B2 and CoaT models. The best reported configuration used 1024×1024 images, organ-specific thresholds, cutout, varied initialization, stain tools, and lung-only pseudo-labels, reaching 0.82. Threshold selection and ensemble diversity were especially useful. Ordinary CutMix harmed training, while self-CutMix helped diversify ensemble members.

The solution combined neural networks and LightGBM models with roughly 30/70 weights. Single-feature LSTMs generated probability features for both model families, while the neural network incorporated a transformer pretrained to reconstruct missing values. Log transforms, removal of two distribution-shifted features, and pseudo-labeling improved the neural models. The pseudo-labeled network scored 0.799 on the public leaderboard, and the final ensemble also incorporated a public submission.
compute: Approximately 100–200 hours of overall work; hardware unspecified.

solution_summary: The author used private leaderboard probes to identify Confused Deputy events as the only reliably scalable scoring route. A customized Greedy Coordinate Gradient search preserved the required first-hop tool call while forcing Gemma to terminate immediately on the second hop, increasing replay throughput. BF16 proposal generation, ridge reranking, and sequential GGUF evaluation addressed quantization drift and cache dependence. Screening stable recipients and strengthening token margins increased the score from about 44.5 to 46.5; the corresponding GPT-OSS optimization did not transfer successfully.
compute: Rented NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000

solution_summary: The submission combined XLM-RoBERTa, MuRIL, and Hindi WECHSEL models trained with competition data plus MLQA and XQUAD. Reference markers were removed, and token logits were projected to characters, adjusted to favor complete token spans, and summed without weights. The automatically selected final submission used two full-data fits of each model; an alternative five-fold ensemble scored 0.787 publicly and 0.779 privately. Extra scraped Tamil examples helped the Tamil WECHSEL model, but it remained weaker than multilingual models.

The pipeline predicts women's NCAA matchup probabilities with LightGBM using detailed regular-season and tournament results. Features include season-level team statistics, tournament seed differences, and FiveThirtyEight rating differences. For each prediction season, training excludes that season's tournament games while retaining its regular-season games, then averages predictions from ten shuffled folds with early stopping. The notebook also generates a projected tournament bracket, but provides no numerical validation results.

The team trained a SAINT+ based encoder-decoder Transformer using only question interactions from train.csv. Inputs combined question and positional embeddings with discretized timing features, user question counts, correctness, and explanation indicators. Lectures did not improve validation, and early stopping based on unseen-user AUC worked poorly. Training took approximately 20 hours on one K80 GPU.
compute: One K80 GPU; approximately 20 hours training.

solution_summary: The solution calibrated signals using the host procedure with binning and hot-pixel handling omitted, then split transit regions using derivatives. It estimated transit depth by combining polynomial fitting with a local relative signal-drop calculation at multiple wavelength resolutions. Uncertainty was estimated from the standard deviation of four coarse wavelength-chunk depths. The final spectrum blended global and fine-grained estimates, increasing the fine-grained contribution as estimated uncertainty grew.

The solution linearly combined averaged XGBoost predictions with averaged Lasagne neural-network predictions. A final rule-based correction pushed predictions below the current minimum for several feature-defined groups. The rule ordering was based on training-set counts. Retrospective comparisons showed that the submitted corrections hurt performance, while a smaller set of corrections would have performed better.

solution_title: My solution - please learn from my mistakes
solution_summary: The author built 15 temporal training datasets and incorporated scraped Google Analytics demo activity to reduce the prediction gap. Features described visitor recency, activity duration, purchase frequency, and calendar effects. LightGBM and XGBoost predictions fed a neural network, followed by linear regression over all three models' out-of-fold predictions. A last-minute correction to a major feature severely worsened cross-validation, but the resulting pipeline was submitted because there was no time to rerun it.

The solution ensembled feature-extraction and fine-tuned image models with diverse architectures and resolutions. An EfficientNet-L2 feature extractor with ridge regression complemented heavily augmented EfficientNet, ViT, BEiT, and Swin models. The ensemble achieved CV 17.144, improving on individual model scores. Pet-centered cropping improved a standalone model but did not help the ensemble, while metadata features and previous competition data were unsuccessful.

The approach filtered features using variance and target correlation before fitting a six-cluster Gaussian mixture model. Its six probabilities and six additional probabilities from a QDA classifier formed the input to a final QDA classifier. Training ran for three iterations, with later iterations flipping labels for 90% of misclassified targets using previous out-of-fold predictions. Pseudo-labeling reduced the score and was excluded.

The approach exploited a public safety check that inspected destination URLs while allowing the benchmark's fake secret in request bodies. The author filled the submission with independently validated, single-action cases and tailored request formats to each target model. Longer conversations and multiple actions generally reduced throughput and reliability. The best public score was 113.850, while a separate private-board alternative targeted different authorization and provenance failures.

solution_title: 12th place solution: 8 CNN models ensemble with OpenVINO
solution_summary: The final solution combined eight CNN models using four backbones and two spectrogram configurations per backbone. Waveform and spectrogram augmentations improved individual models, including background noise, mixup, CutMix, and frequency masking. Converting PyTorch models through ONNX to OpenVINO reduced submission inference time by roughly 50%, enabling the larger ensemble. The best single model achieved a private leaderboard score of 0.72463.
compute: Approximately 15 minutes inference per model using the PyTorch–ONNX–OpenVINO workflow.

solution_summary: The pipeline detected rectangular image tiles, extracted SuperPoint features, and matched all tile pairs with LightGlue. Histogram heuristics excluded plots and diagrams, while DB50 text detection removed keypoints likely to create false matches. RANSAC affine verification identified coherent matching regions, which were converted into bounding-box masks and merged when overlapping. Grid-based tile splitting was abandoned because it reduced public leaderboard performance despite improving local validation.

solution_title: 19th place - 4 Body Parts Invariant Features with WaveNet + GRU
solution_summary: The solution used lab-specific models combining three WaveNet blocks, three GRU blocks, and an MLP, with separate models for individual and pair actions. Four body parts and invariant features were paired with Gaussian noise, minority-class upsampling, and hard negative mining. Inference used sliding windows with stride two, averaged five-fold and three-fold ensembles, and merged neighboring actions for the same mouse or pair.

solution_title: 3rd place solution: SED with attention on Mel frequency bands
solution_summary: The solution used ImageNet-pretrained EfficientNet encoders with a modified sound event detection head that attended over frequency bands. It trained on 659 bird and nocall classes using multiple audio sources, pseudo labels, and extensive augmentation, especially reverb to reduce recording-domain differences. Shared cached spectrograms and TorchScript models reduced inference cost, while a timer supported partial ensemble completion. The best ensemble averaged eight models and achieved a private score of 0.76365.
compute: CPU inference under a two-hour limit, with a timer stopping execution around 118 minutes.

solution_summary: The solution used a two-branch Conv1D network to process FGS1 and AIRS signals and predict wavelength-dependent mixture distributions. A 15-component Laplace mixture modeled both expected values and uncertainty, trained with wavelength-weighted negative log likelihood. Segmented transit features, inverted transit shapes, and multiple segment resolutions improved the representation. A small gating module and ensembles across distribution families, folds, and seeds provided further gains, with stable validation-to-private gaps below 0.01.
compute: About one hour of training per model

solution_title: 6th Place Solution for the CAFA 6 Protein Function Prediction
solution_summary: The solution ensembled four neural networks that fused protein sequence, structure, literature, taxonomy, and non-experimental GO annotation features. Transformer encoders represented taxonomy and term-evidence sequences, while separate ontology heads incorporated gated annotation logits. Development used temporal validation across GO annotation releases, and training weighted binary cross-entropy by information-accretion-derived label weights. Random feature dropping during training and inference supported a final average of 35 predictions.

solution_summary: The solution used a weighted ensemble of 1D CNNs selected through six-fold patient-based validation. Inputs included standardized accelerometer signals, high- and low-frequency components, spectrograms, and relative temporal position. Training used class-weighted cross entropy for tdcsfog and focal loss for defog. The ensemble scored 0.362 public and 0.305 private, while combined-dataset, auxiliary-head, and CNN-to-LightGBM variants did not improve accuracy.

The final approach used a Lasso blend of 57 models, including some AutoGluon ensembles. LightGBM and CatBoost were the strongest individual methods, each achieving a private leaderboard score of 0.86890, while the best AutoGluon ensemble reached 0.86893. The final blend improved the score slightly to 0.86902, with additions beyond roughly five models affecting only the fifth or sixth decimal place. Cross-validation scores correlated well with both public and private leaderboard scores.

The final submission blended a ten-model PyTorch average at weight 0.7 with a FastAI component at weight 0.3, using five-fold and eight-fold validation respectively. All models used pseudo-labeled images from the earlier PetFinder Adoption Speed competition. Diverse architectures, augmentation configurations, and separate cat and dog models improved the ensemble. Training used binary cross-entropy, and inference used center crops with and without horizontal flips; broader augmentation, metadata, MSE, and several alternative ensemble methods did not help.

The team combined several complementary transformer pipelines with tree models and retrained public approaches. Their models included summary-question regression, grouped span regression, retrieved sentence context, long-context modeling, and a dual encoder initialized from a long-context model. They prioritized training stability and diversity because cross-validation and leaderboard scores correlated poorly. Full-fit checkpoints helped, while LLM-generated synthetic data and target-wise LoRA models did not improve the final ensemble.
compute: Reported inference times: transformer/CatBoost pipeline 32 minutes; long-context model 205 minutes for 4 folds; dual encoder 39 minutes for 4 folds.

solution_summary: The solution uses an IBN-ResNet50 classifier with 1024×1024 inputs to address fine-grained visual similarity and field-related domain differences. Histogram equalization, ArcFace, architectural adjustments, mixup, CutMix, and adversarial weight perturbation improved performance. The team also used part of the FGVC8 training data, test-time augmentation, and pseudo-labeling, reporting a total score of approximately 0.957. Alternative architectures, model fusion, and loss variants did not improve results.

The team built unique-count features using training data and the non-synthetic portion of the test set. They combined neural networks with individually tuned LightGBM and XGBoost models trained on single features. Each retained model used four seeds, five bagging rounds, and eight-fold cross-validation. Their final blends assigned approximately 70% weight to neural networks and 30% to single-feature models, while CatBoost and other explored model types were excluded.

The solution adapted the U900 CAFA5 pipeline using mean-pooled ESM2 and ProtT5 protein embeddings with taxonomic features. Conditional and raw gradient-boosted, logistic, and neural predictions fed an ontology-aware GCN stacker together with electronic GO annotations. It merged CAFA5 training data and used OOF base predictions plus alternative inference configurations. ESM-IF experiments provided inconsistent gains, so the original ESM inference configuration remained the main submission, which scored 0.44640.
compute: Rented GPU for protein encoding; hardware and duration unspecified.

solution_title: 1st Place Removed Solution - All Faces Are Real Team
solution_summary: This statement primarily explains why one submission was disqualified, but also describes two ensemble approaches. The retained solution used competition data alone and an unweighted mean of 12 models, obtaining a private score of 0.44531. The disqualified submission combined six competition-data models with nine models trained using additional external data and scored 0.42320. Its external data comprised license-filtered Flickr face images and manually collected faces from CC-BY YouTube videos; the dispute concerned additional permissions from depicted individuals.
external_data: ["Resized FlickrFacesHQ dataset, filtered by license", "Face images manually collected from CC-BY YouTube videos"]

solution_summary: The solution used a CNN with squeeze-and-excitation blocks, five-fold validation, geometric augmentation, and fold prediction aggregation. Test-set pseudo-labeling was the most effective technique. Iterative training added correctly classified Dig-MNIST examples to limit the harm from its distribution differences. The final model trained on approximately 75,000 images achieved 0.9924 private accuracy, while an alternative without Dig-MNIST achieved 0.9916.
compute: About 4 hours per five-fold training set on RTX 2080 and i9-9900KF

solution_summary: The layout solution combined engineered graph features with a GPS-style GNN using SAGE convolutions, Linformer attention, and random-walk positional encodings. Graph pruning retained configurable nodes and their neighbors, while a late variant merged other connected nodes and achieved the best CV on xla:default. Training used pairwise hinge loss, Adam, cosine annealing, and collection-specific fine-tuning after joint training. The final submission used different pruning strategies by collection, while the tile dataset used a simpler five-layer SAGE GNN without extra features or positional encodings.

solution_title: 4th place solution - 🎖️ my first gold medal 🎖️ (+source code available!)
solution_summary: The solution ensembled DeBERTa token-tagging models with careful preservation of line breaks and offset-based subword labels. GPU beam search enforced more coherent BIO sequences, while entity-level ensembling combined models with different tokenizers by averaging overlapping span boundaries. Training used learning-rate warmup and decay, gradient clipping, checkpointing, and frequent selection with the competition metric. Both final selected ensembles achieved a reported private score of 0.735.
compute: A100 GPU; batch size 8.

solution_summary: The team reused its previous landmark pipeline with sub-center ArcFace and dynamic margins, newer architectures and improved reranking. The retrieval ensemble combined three transformers and four CNNs, with transformers providing stronger local retrieval scores. Training used progressive image sizes for CNNs, cosine scheduling and Adam or AdamW. Reranking softly boosted or penalized similarities according to confidence that an index image was positive or negative.
compute: Multi-GPU training with DistributedDataParallel.

solution_summary: The provided pipeline generates separate XGBoost and LightGBM submissions and a combined submission. Their public scores were 0.03061, 0.03059, and 0.03063 respectively, with the combination performing best. solution_summary: The selected submission changed the prediction threshold to 0.152 based on an expectation of more positive samples. A separate model trained on data rotated about 15 degrees around two or three axes achieved 0.492 privately but was not selected because its public score was weaker. Rotation improved the private score by about 0.04 over the baseline while reducing the public score by 0.074. The author did not implement local cross-validation and attributed the selection mistake to reliance on the public leaderboard.

This repository documents one team member's LightGBM pipeline for click-fraud prediction. It uses cached Feather datasets and engineered click counts, temporal differences, attribution ratios, and latent features. Multiple negatively downsampled datasets are generated with different seeds, and their prediction values are averaged in the illustrated configuration. Validation is filtered to click hours matching the submission test period, and early stopping controls training.

solution_title: 6th Place: Select Feature Combinations based on RMSE Scores
solution_summary: The final pipeline combined five regression model families and then corrected predictions using anomalous values and reliable feature-group means. Feature combinations were evaluated by validation RMSE to select useful target encodings, while original-source rows supplied additional labeled examples. Extracting the integer part of episode length was the most impactful engineered feature. A later published five-fold single-LightGBM implementation achieved a private score of 11.63.

The author trained a RoBERTa-base encoder with an MLP regression head on data from an earlier toxicity classification competition. Toxicity targets were formed by weighting original label features, and simplifying text cleaning improved the reported private score from 0.80826 to 0.81363. Predictions were averaged across five independently sampled training subsets. Adam, a decreasing learning-rate schedule, weight decay, dropout, and validation-loss early stopping supported generalization.

The solution first removed large signal noise using methods including linear regression, Gaussian mixture models, and FFT filters. A single WaveNet then processed cleaned signal and a baseline of open-channel predictions in sequences of length 4,000, training for 150 epochs. The baseline helped the network infer noise from the difference between signal and predicted channels, allowing it to model both channel patterns and noise patterns. The single model achieved private and public scores of 0.94541 and 0.94683, and even rounded signal values worked as a useful baseline.

The team built primarily bidirectional GRU classifiers using diverse pretrained FastText and GloVe embeddings. Back-translated comments augmented training and inference, while ensemble-generated pseudo-labels expanded training with test samples. A blend of arithmetic averaging and optimized LightGBM stacking reached a reported public score of 0.9890. Careful validation, translation grouping, and model selection across multiple metrics supported the ensemble's robustness.

solution_title: One week to Silver - LB 86 Approach
solution_summary: The solution blended Arboretum, XGBoost, and LightGBM using just over 100 features drawn from public baselines and custom purchase-history statistics. It combined product embedding components, customer segments, order streaks, lag features, and purchase-state skew. A broken out-of-fold pipeline led to validation on a fixed 25% holdout, and F1 expectation optimization converted predictions into final baskets. The final blend weighted Arboretum at 0.7 and the other models at 0.15 each; retraining with lower learning rates improved the private score by 0.0002.
compute: One intensive week of work, 50+ hours; hardware unspecified.

solution_title: Silver Medal Solution (that was not selected) :(
solution_summary: The author shares a team kernel and highlights its feature-generation work. The team did not select that submission, and attempts to build on it were unsuccessful. The post provides no specific features, model architecture, validation procedure, or scores.

The solution combined DeBERTa essay-level discourse models with a second stage of LightGBM and neural models. Processing all discourses in an essay together improved accuracy and efficiency, while auxiliary discourse-type prediction and token-classification variants supplied useful diversity. Predictions were adjusted to training class means and blended with optimized weights, with second-stage models adding about 0.003–0.005 improvement. Three rounds of leak-free pseudo labeling on data from the previous Feedback competition were another major component.

solution_summary: The solution used a YOLOv7 segmentation approach based on a public baseline, with input resolution adjusted to account for the segmentation head's quarter-resolution output. The author finished with fine-tuning on ds1 to avoid dilation. A higher-resolution experiment from 640 to 800 achieved the team's strongest individual model scores, reported as LB 0.473 and PB 0.563. Several alternatives, including repeated pseudo-labeling, YOLOv8, and U-Net refinement inside detected boxes, did not go well.

solution_title: The thrill of the chase: Tim Salimans on how he took home Deloitte/Fide chess comp
solution_summary: The author extended TrueSkill by shrinking player ratings toward recent opponents and weighting recent matches more heavily. Rolling out-of-sample predictions supported two post-processing stages using standard and locally weighted logistic regression. These stages incorporated player ratings, match counts, opponent-strength statistics, monthly predicted win rates, and random-forest predictions. Exploiting information in Swiss-system match schedules dramatically improved the score, while follow-up data also supported the model's usefulness without that information.

The best model used one-dimensional temporal convolutions over linear-frequency log magnitude spectrograms, followed by temporal max pooling and a classification head. Training used time and frequency masking, with oversampling proving the most useful class-imbalance treatment. Longer training clips, Wav2Vec 2.0 fine-tuning, and pretraining on all 152 classes did not improve the baseline. Models overfit despite validation-based checkpoint selection, while reducing the prediction threshold from 0.5 to 0.3 improved the reported score from 0.51 to 0.57.

solution_title: LLM-Guided Evolutionary Visual Transformation (0-Score but Interesting)
solution_summary: The system combined evolutionary search over grid-transformation programs with a multimodal DistilGPT2 proposer. A small CNN supplied visual embeddings, while successful evolutionary trajectories supplied task-specific fine-tuning examples. Search used elites, mutations, extensions, novelty filtering, and local improvement; inference selected the most frequently sampled program. The approach scored zero and appeared slow, with long programs and possible model distortion identified as concerns.

solution_summary: The pipeline generates physically plausible well trajectories, blends them into a parent curve, and applies a small learned residual correction. A frozen neural prior and LightGBM/CatBoost trajectory branch supply additional signals, while a multi-output Ridge decoder predicts 16 low-frequency DCT coefficients. Conservative shrinkage and physical correction caps limit damage when gamma-ray alignment selects the wrong geological layer. Nested well-grouped validation produced 6.275 pooled OOF RMSE versus 6.368 for the physical parent, with a public score of 5.766.
The post directs readers to a blog describing the author's approach. It also links to a GitHub repository containing source code. The supplied text contains no technical details of the solution.

solution_title: NeurIPS - Ariel Data Challenge 2024: Bronze Medal Solution( 113th)
solution_summary: The solution refined public notebooks into a signal-processing pipeline that calibrated, cropped, differenced, and binned the telescope readings. Gradient-based transit detection isolated the event, and Nelder-Mead optimization fitted a transit scaling factor against a polynomial signal model. Training-derived scales adjusted the predicted spectra and constant uncertainties, followed by rounding to six decimal places. Reported scores were 0.5543416 on the public leaderboard and 0.5743219 on the private leaderboard.

solution_title: 98th Place Solution for ICR Identifying Age-Related Conditions Competition
solution_summary: The approach first predicted training-only Greek variables and added their probabilities to the measurement features. A diverse ensemble of mostly underbagged models then predicted the target, with mean blending after excluding weak members. Greek preprocessing was fitted within cross-validation to prevent leakage, and the final validation scheme stratified on Alpha. The actual submission scored 0.14 publicly and 0.38 privately, illustrating the difficulty of reliable model selection on this dataset.

solution_title: First time Competition, 75th place solution silver region
solution_summary: The team addressed noisy cassava labels using label smoothing and knowledge distillation with EfficientNet-B4 and ResNeXt50 classifiers. Five-fold training, image augmentations, and eight-pass test-time augmentation supported the final inference approach. The distilled EfficientNet-B4 achieved 0.9034 private accuracy, while the distilled EfficientNet-B4 plus ResNeXt50 combination reached about 0.904 public and 0.90036 private accuracy. Taylor cross-entropy with smoothing was reported as the best loss, and NFNet was abandoned because time was insufficient.

solution_title: 17th place finish - description of my methodology
solution_summary: The author adapted Chessmetrics to basketball by iteratively estimating team strength from opponent ratings and margin-based game scores. Ratings used current-season games equally and were regularized with two hypothetical draws against a conference-strength estimate derived from current members' previous five years of ratings. Rating differences were converted to win probabilities with separately tuned intervals for men and women. Two submissions used regular-season versus tournament-based tuning, with the tournament-tuned version performing better.

The author trained an ensemble of eight transformer models for the six scoring targets. Multi-task learning added the minimum and maximum target values as auxiliary targets after comparing several aggregate targets by cross-validation. Training used four groups of layer-wise learning rates, mean pooling, and multilabel stratified cross-validation. Nelder-Mead optimized the final blend, and the author relied on cross-validation despite limited leaderboard improvement.

The post congratulates competitors and opens a solution-sharing discussion after preliminary standings became available. It highlights the substantial leaderboard shakeup. The author asks participants to explain their solutions, final submission choices, and cross-validation strategies.

solution_title: 275 Place Solution for the Optiver - Trading at the Close (Drop from silver on public to bronze on private)
solution_summary: The team blended LightGBM, CatBoost, and LSTM models for the time series prediction task. Their most important feature compared each stock's WAP with the mean WAP across stocks at the same date and time bucket, expressing the relative difference in basis points. They identified the absence of retraining during the online period as their main mistake, with performance deteriorating over that period.

solution_title: A noob's journey to the  258th(Top 20%) place.
solution_summary: The final submission blended MobileNet and SE-ResNeXt predictions, achieving a score of 0.922. MobileNet training repeatedly resumed from saved weights and progressed from 64×64 to 128×128 images using 30,000 examples per class. SE-ResNeXt was trained on all available images for one epoch and scored 0.919. An earlier CNN with bidirectional LSTMs achieved 0.85, while limited compute credits constrained further experimentation.

solution_summary: The solution combined four-class study classification with auxiliary segmentation masks derived from bounding boxes, alongside YOLOv5 image-level detection. Study models used pseudo-labels and additional RICORD and BIMCV data, with noisy BIMCV samples manually removed. The final study ensemble combined EfficientNet variants and a transformer across input sizes, with horizontal-flip inference augmentation. Pseudo-labeling increased the reported detector mAP@0.5 from 0.567 to 0.576, while additional inference augmentations and binary classification formulations did not work.

The solution exploited value-frequency leakage by computing counts over training data and the real test subset, excluding fake test rows. Synthetic samples preserved the pairing between each feature value and its count, with roughly 20-fold positive and two-fold negative augmentation. Neural networks receiving 200 value-count pairs outperformed LightGBM, while transformed features, pseudo-labeling, and neural-network stacking provided further gains. The neural networks reached about 0.924 public leaderboard performance, and stacking added around 0.001.

The original model decoded 1,292 unique labels and struggled with unseen character combinations. After the competition, the author compared a three-head model with separate models for root, vowel, and consonant components. Combining the original model for seen combinations with the component models for unseen combinations achieved public 0.9925 and private 0.9552. Adding unspecified postprocessing further improved the reported private score to 0.9704.
compute: Trained only on TPU.

solution_summary: The solution combined EfficientNet-B5 and EfficientNet-B4 with soft voting and rotational test-time augmentation. Strong augmentation used different cropping rules for complete and cropped eyeballs, unrestricted rotations, and pixel-level changes. Models were pretrained on 2015 data and trained with class weights, an ordinal categorical cross-entropy loss, and a decreasing Adam learning rate. A single model achieved about 0.87 validation kappa without TTA, and the final ensemble scored 81.6 on the public set and 92.0 on the private set.

The solution averaged groups of correlated Fvar columns and removed constant columns after exploring the combined training and test data. It split observations into three groups according to feature availability, then imputed and modeled each group separately to minimize imputation. The final prediction was a weighted blend of random forests, gradient boosting, support vector machines, and multivariate adaptive regression splines. Repeated two-fold cross-validation guided tuning, and subsequent models did not improve the blend.

solution_title: 24th Place Solution for the RSNA 2024 Lumbar Spine Degenerative Classification Competition
solution_summary: The solution first located diagnostic points using a TD-CNN for slice selection and a heatmap-trained U-Net for vertebral coordinates. DICOM affine transformations mapped coordinates between image stacks, and fixed physical-size crops standardized diagnosis inputs across varying pixel spacings. DenseNet121-based TD-CNNs classified conditions with weighted cross-entropy, followed by a master classifier that combined outputs within each spinal level. The team corrected mislabeled training coordinates and standardized right-side subarticular views by flipping them; 3D models and a single TD-CNN consuming all images did not work well.

The solution used a custom, strongly regularized iterative LS ensemble implemented from scratch in native C. Feature development used a leave-one-out environment and produced roughly 900–1500 features depending on the number of channels. Features described temporal energy, frequency-band energy, and relationships between channels, with nonlinear transformations added. Post-processing paired likely adjacent ten-minute segments and generally assigned the maximum of their scores.

The solution used LightGBM with 40 features. Most features were count encoded. It achieved a public score of 0.68563 and a private score of 0.66370. The shared kernel reduced the data from eight million to four million rows because of memory limits.

solution_title: SMILES😘 Data Science Competition: A Deep Dive
solution_summary: The post describes exploratory analysis of donor, dose, timepoint, control, and cell-type distributions. It introduces Morgan fingerprints and applies t-SNE and PCA for visualization, alongside RDKit molecule rendering. It also reports benchmarking several conventional and neural models using MAE, MSE, and R-squared. The author trained a separate graph neural network for each target and averaged predictions across five folds. Functional connectivity data became weighted symmetric adjacency matrices, while a pretrained MedicalNet 3D ResNet-10 supplied fixed component features. Node-wise implementation enabled independent edge parameters, and DropEdge provided essential regularization. The approach worked well for age prediction but was less effective for the other targets.

solution_title: A bronze for prompt engineering (Public: 20, Private: 24)
solution_summary: The author adapted a public DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B AWQ notebook with limited submission opportunities. The main change was to alternate expert mathematics prompts requesting detailed reasoning or Python code using SymPy. This prompting variant scored 20 publicly and 24 privately, while a separate configuration reached 26 publicly. An accidental switch to ordinary Qwen-14B performed substantially worse.

solution_title: Denoising Autoencoder- Unique solution for TPS-FEB2022
solution_summary: The author developed a denoising-autoencoder pipeline to address noisy data and perceived train-test drift. The approach emphasized exploring unfamiliar algorithms rather than extensive tuning. NLP techniques were also tried, although their implementation and outcome are unspecified. The author deliberately avoided post-processing and did not provide detailed architecture or training settings.

The pipeline combined three retrievers with six rerankers, taking the union of each retriever's top ten candidates. Separate topic and content encoders, short sequences, and large batches improved retrieval, reaching candidate recall of 0.853. Some rerankers were initialized through additional retriever training, and balanced sampling accelerated convergence. Simple averaging of reranker predictions achieved validation F2 of 0.6882 and a private score of 0.693.

The final solution used a weighted ensemble of 12 neural networks and eight gradient boosting models with several hundred historical features. LightGBM models predicted 17 product-addition classes, while Keras networks predicted the presence of 16 products using two hidden layers of 512 nodes. Models varied in training periods, feature sets, and random seeds. Postprocessing substituted selected products' predictions from alternative scoring months, removed already-owned products, and adjusted product scores and ensemble weights using public leaderboard feedback.

solution_title: 18th Place: Many OOFs, Neural Networks over GBDTs, and Greedy Features
solution_summary: The final solution stacked 140 diverse models with Ridge regression and relied more on feature diversity than extensive hyperparameter tuning. Useful features included discretized numerical categories, digit and modular transformations, bi- and tri-gram interactions, and target-encoded bitwise combinations. Linear ensembling consistently outperformed nonlinear stacking, while pseudo-labeling, autoencoders, and higher-order categorical interactions did not work. The author concluded that including weak out-of-fold predictions hurt the ensemble and that stronger prediction selection could have improved it.

solution_title: 122nd Solution for Google - American Sign Language Fingerspelling Recognition Competition
solution_summary: The solution improved a public Transformer and 1D-CNN baseline through frame feature engineering and augmentation. Preprocessing gathered lip, hand, and pose landmarks, filtered frames using hand information, and resized and normalized sequences. Augmentation included cropping, temporal resampling, horizontal reflection, affine transforms, and masking. The authors reported a 0.007 improvement over the baseline score of 0.699, while supplemental data and a late learning-rate increase did not improve the final approach.

solution_title: [Rank 283 private LB] PurgedCV + Stock clustering approach
solution_summary: The approach emphasized feature engineering and trained LightGBM models on five purged validation folds. Features combined imbalance, time, rolling statistics, order-book signals, and stock cluster, sector, and market-cap information. Inference averaged the five models, subtracted the prediction mean, and clipped the outputs. Mean subtraction performed better than the alternative zero_sum function.

The solution built on 213tubo's repository and ensembled U-Net models with MaxViT and NFNet encoders. The author manually inspected every series and corrected missing or misplaced event labels. Training used Mixup, SpecAugment, and sleep-label smoothing, while sliding inference discarded window ends. Post-processing removed predictions in repeated daily sensor patterns considered invalid, reducing false positives.

The author built a neural network combining text and categorical inputs with an optional image branch made of convolutional layers, reporting a final leaderboard score around 0.2180. CBOW word2vec, CNN and RNN text processing, attention, and extensive batch normalization were helpful. Adding images improved the score by about 0.0005, while smaller architecture changes provided further gains. Images were resized to 64×64 and preloaded as uint8 NumPy arrays to manage loading time and memory.
compute: Approximately 20 GB of memory for preloaded training images.

solution_summary: The post documents experimental changes rather than a complete fingerspelling pipeline. Increasing maximum sequence length and the expansion ratio, together with borrowed post-processing, raised the reported private score from 0.741 to 0.752. Longer training produced no further private-score gain. Normalization accelerated convergence without improving leaderboard performance, while reduced dropout, moving batch normalization, and spatial masking were unsuccessful.

solution_title: 43rd place: Every cloud has a silver lining
solution_summary: The author describes an ensemble inspired by two public notebooks and advocates combining CatBoost, LightGBM, and XGBoost. The notebook ensemble achieved the author's highest private score but was not selected as the final submission because of concerns about overfitting. The discussion favors weighted averaging over ranking predictions to preserve prediction magnitudes and consistency across racial groups. TabNet was considered but explicitly not used.
compute: GPU time was exhausted; hardware and runtime were not specified.

solution_summary: This post synthesizes several teams' approaches rather than presenting the author's own final pipeline. BERT-based models commonly combined information across layers and used separate learning rates for encoders and heads. Pseudo-labeling, auxiliary training on StackExchange data, and back-translation supplied additional supervision or augmented examples. Other recurring choices included separate question and answer models, custom pooling heads, and ensembles with varied text truncation.

solution_title: A model used in the 24th solution - pure linear algebra!
solution_summary: The author predicted gene differential expression by fitting linear transformations between cell lines using chemicals measured in both source and target cells. Full-rank SVD reduced the gene space from 18,211 dimensions to 614, allowing the transformations to be fitted and applied with lower memory requirements before reconstructing gene-level predictions. The final ensemble assigned 70% combined weight to this method and a neural autoencoder imitation, with 30% assigned to public Pyboost, neural-network, and Linear SVR approaches. The pure linear algebra model achieved the best private score, reported as 0.768 private and 0.582 public, with CD4+ T cells particularly useful for predicting B cells and NK cells for predicting Myeloid cells.
compute: The direct linear model required more than 20 GB of memory and could not run on the free Saturn Cloud tier used by the author.

solution_title: Next top GB model solution to The 2nd YouTube-8M Video Understanding Challenge
solution_summary: The repository provides a reproducible video-classification workflow covering training, evaluation, weight averaging, quantization, distillation, and graph ensembling. Its worked example trains a gated NetVLAD model on frame-level RGB and audio features. Quantized models can be combined into a weighted ensemble graph, and ensemble predictions can generate distillation datasets for subsequent training. Models were trained individually on a single GPU using TensorFlow 1.8.0.
compute: Single GPU per model; creating a distillation dataset requires approximately 1.4 TB of storage.

solution_summary: The final system ensembled five compact CLIP-style transformers with varied architectures, seeds, sequence lengths, and landmark features. Strong spatial and temporal augmentation, motion features, and simple video mean/std normalization supported training. Models were trained in PyTorch and manually transferred into TensorFlow implementations to reduce inference latency and accommodate a larger ensemble. The ensemble achieved public and private scores of 0.794 and 0.87, compared with 0.786 and 0.865 for the best single model.

The author assembled an ensemble from public language-model notebooks and borrowed disagreement handling. Inference probabilities were constrained by the misconception classes observed for each question and answer pair, which the author considered central to the result. DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-14B-bnb-4bit replaced Gemma after favorable validation and leaderboard results. Text augmentation had mixed effects, and augmented examples in local validation were identified as a source of misleading validation scores.
compute: Local GPU: 5070 Ti; GPU and time constraints limited experiments.

solution_title: 15th Place Solution: SD3.5M + Vtracer + select best from 3 image
solution_summary: The solution generated images with SD3.5M using a flat-illustration prompt suffix, then converted them with vtracer using binary-searched parameters. PaliGemma2 selected the best of three candidate images. The largest improvement came from splitting each description into three questions for evaluation.

The solution engineered card-level features from eight combinations of historical transactions, new transactions, and merchant information. Transaction aggregates, interval and interaction features, sequence embeddings, and transaction-level LightGBM predictions supplied diverse signals. Feature selection produced 12 feature sets for LightGBM and neural networks, whose predictions were stacked and averaged. Stacking and isotonic regression improved validation but hurt private results, while combining predictions with a non-outlier model delivered a small consistent gain.

The team replaced discourse text classification with transformer token classification to improve accuracy and inference speed. Models predicted discourse labels either by averaging token predictions or by using the first separator token, with weighted cross-entropy helping the averaging variant. The best public submission combined Nelder–Mead blending, LightGBM stacking, and XGBoost stacking in equal proportions. Pseudo-labeling with Feedback 2021 data and adversarial weight perturbation also improved reported validation loss.

The solution combined a probabilistic date interpolation model for groups seen in training with group-level predictive models. Each group was treated as a statistical observation, and within-group feature histograms supplied the model inputs. Predictions mixed logistic regression, k-nearest neighbors, and XGBoost-based public scripts. Leaderboard feedback formed a third component, although its use was not explained.

solution_title: 142nd Place Solution — Surface Least-Squares Field + Seed-Averaged Matching Bank
solution_summary: The solution combined a sequential GR/typewell matcher with small CNN correction models, a geological surface estimate, and a GR common-error correction. The largest improvement came from a sparse least-squares surface field injected through an uncertainty gate with a capped correction. Averaging repeated jackknife gate estimates reduced deployment variance, while grouped validation and statistical controls guided decisions despite noisy public scores. The final system achieved pooled offline RMSE of 6.85 and private RMSE of 7.906.

solution_title: Last Place Solution - The Worst Kaggle Solution Ever!!!
solution_summary: The post celebrates an intentionally poor competition result and links to the author's solution notebook. It describes the score as dramatically worse than other submissions. No methods or implementation details are provided in the post.

The author trained CatBoost models separately for galactic objects, extragalactic objects, and extragalactic objects with spectroscopic redshift, using roughly 1,000–2,000 features. Features included supernova template fits, light-curve timing and slope statistics, feets descriptors, Gaussian-process features, and distance-scaled shifted flux. Class-specific weights optimized on out-of-fold predictions combined CatBoost, LightGBM, and neural-network predictions. Class99 probability formulas developed through leaderboard probing produced a further 0.057 improvement, bringing the public score to 0.680.
compute: Gaussian-process feature extraction used 30 instances.

solution_summary: The solution ensembled CNNs trained on mel spectrograms of 30-second audio crops, splitting each crop into six segments for backbone processing and using five-second snippets at inference. Mixup, background noise, rating-based loss weights, and label smoothing helped address weak and noisy labels. Validation used training soundscapes with three silent recordings removed and bootstrap sampling to assess robustness. Predictions were averaged across models and seeds, refined using a binary bird detector and metadata, and converted to labels using percentile-based thresholds. Full-soundscape validation F1 approached 0.84, and the final inference kernel took approximately one hour.

solution_summary: The post announces the release of source code and a model description in a downloadable archive. It also links to a simplified executable script. The author reports a post-deadline private leaderboard score of 0.999594 but provides no technical description in the post itself.

solution_title: 25th Place - GBDT plus NN - Trust CV
solution_summary: The final solution equally combined CatBoost, XGBoost, and a multilayer perceptron with simple feature engineering. Model selection used cross-validation AUC as a smoother proxy for the competition's accuracy metric. The neural network treated every column as categorical strings, grouping rare values and explicitly representing missing values. The ensemble achieved CV accuracy 0.9406 and private leaderboard accuracy 0.9415; adding other models did not improve ensemble CV.

The team ensembled transformer sequence-labeling models, primarily DeBERTa variants alongside BART and Muppet, using overlapping chunks to handle long essays. Training combined small batches, cosine learning-rate decay, multisample dropout, token masking, and diverse loss functions or CRF decoding. Out-of-fold predictions guided span thresholds and ensemble pruning, while post-processing linked evidence and constrained Lead predictions. Averaging one-hot CRF outputs with other models' probabilities produced final submissions with private scores of 0.723 and 0.721.
compute: GPU of unspecified type; typically five training epochs

solution_title: Rank 2 approach - a century of component feature sets and deep ensemble
solution_summary: The solution combined extensive categorical feature engineering with a three-level ensemble of boosted trees, neural networks, and ridge regression. More than 1,600 features included categorical combinations, target encodings, and both numeric and string representations of weight capacity. Consistent shuffled 20-fold validation supported 65 boosted-tree models, 35 neural stackers, public artifacts, and a diversity classifier. The final 100-model combination achieved CV 38.62860836 and private score 38.62947; integer rounding produced a slightly weaker alternative.
compute: Colab TPU with over 200GB RAM for feature creation; A6000 Ada with 128GB RAM for XGBoost, A6000 with 128GB for LightGBM, two A6000 Ada with 256GB for CatBoost; Kaggle/Colab TPUs for neural stackers; local CPU for ridge; local 3090 with 128GB RAM for experiments.

solution_title: 65th-Place Simple Solution Without Using Data Leakage
solution_summary: The selected solution used tsfresh to extract and select features from time-series signals. These features captured statistics and signal characteristics such as extrema, standard deviation, approximate entropy, skewness, and peak counts. LightGBM produced probabilities for each surface class, and the highest-probability class became the prediction.

The solution combines sequence classifiers and causal language models for misconception classification. Text corrections and GPT-4o-generated question and label explanations enrich the inputs, while label processing restricts candidate misconceptions by question. Qwen2.5-14B classifiers and several 7B causal models are combined through weighted rank blending, with probability masking for unavailable categories. Selected ensembles scored 0.947 on the private leaderboard, while an unselected configuration reached 0.948.

solution_title: [7th Place] Reversing the Polarity of the Information Flow
solution_summary: The author generated prediction features through an original, reverse, and double-back training workflow built around public notebooks. A separate public model supplied pseudo-labels for the test set, allowing reversed models to predict the training set and create matching prediction features. Retraining with these features improved three of four double-back models. The final submission took the median of seventeen predictions, including four double-back models, and achieved private and public scores of 570.52851 and 574.77083.

The solution trained directly on supplied answer candidates, sampling one negative per document each epoch. Hard-negative sampling substantially improved on uniform sampling, and HTML tokens preserved document structure. Five uncased BERT and ALBERT models were ensembled through word-level span probabilities. Final threshold changes raised the reported score to 0.71 on both public and private leaderboards.

solution_title: Private LB 0.66758 solution: From single Network multi folds
solution_summary: The solution used an ImageNet-pretrained InceptionResNetV2 backbone with an FPN segmentation model at 384 × 512 resolution. Training used Lovasz loss, RAdam, and a learning rate of 1e-4, with Albumentations transformations. Predictions from four saved weights for each of four folds were averaged and refined using confidence and area thresholds. This setup outperformed the author's other networks and ensembles, achieving 0.66758 privately and 0.66654 publicly.

solution_title: 14th Place Solution with best single model only scored 0.461/0.463 on LB
solution_summary: The solution combined more than 20 models, roughly half trained on original labels and half using pseudo-labeled external public data. XLNet-large was the best model trained on original data, while RoBERTa-large was the best pseudo-label model. Training incorporated a second loss term targeting labels shifted by their standard deviations. A multilevel Lasso stack organized models by type and performance, and extensive statistical analysis guided submission selection; a separate 12-level stack achieved 0.448 on both public and private leaderboards.
compute: Final submission selection took almost 3 days.

solution_title: Phil Brierley on winning tourism forecasting part two
solution_summary: The solution combined seasonal naïve, damped Holt-Winters, ARIMA, and ETS forecasts to reduce the risk of extreme forecast failures. One ensemble used globally shared weights derived from holdout MASE, while another took the median of 13 forecasts generated from multiple training windows. The final forecast blended these two ensembles. For the second forecast year, algorithmic forecasts were replaced by approximately 1.04 times the first-year predictions, with that factor selected using the leaderboard.

The final pipeline stacked DeBERTaV3 base and large predictions with handcrafted features in LightGBM. DeBERTa received the source passage, prompt question, and student summary, while its prediction head pooled only summary tokens. Inference averaged the three models with the best cross-validation scores to fit runtime constraints. The final pipeline scored 0.433 on the public leaderboard and 0.463 on the private leaderboard despite a worse CV score than the standalone large model.

The solution geometrically averaged two 3D low-resolution models with different patch sizes and normalization settings. A 3D full-resolution cascade handled much of the subsequent refinement. Public five-step postprocessing supplied the remaining improvements. The author also changed the nnUNetV2 optimizer from SGD to Adam to reduce training computation.

The main predictor was LightGBM using hand-engineered features and metafeatures from text, image, and tabular neural networks. Relative-price aggregates, text statistics, missingness indicators, and activity-duration statistics supplemented predictions from BiGRUs, sparse TF-IDF networks, image models, and an autoencoder pipeline. Image checkpoint predictions and the sparse text network delivered particularly useful improvements. The final submission blended boosted trees trained on slightly different feature sets.

solution_title: [1st place solution] Last Query Transformer RNN
solution_summary: The solution modified Transformer attention so that only the final question served as the query against the full history. This reduced query-key computation to linear complexity and enabled histories of 1,728 interactions. The final submission ensembled five models using five input features with little manual feature engineering.

The solution combined diverse two-dimensional segmentation models using ensemble weights optimized with Optuna. Long multistage training, stochastic weight averaging, doubled image size, and selective test-time augmentation strengthened the models. Pseudo-labeling on additional time slices worked when batches balanced real and pseudo examples, pseudo examples received heavier augmentation, and mixup combined the two sources. The final ensemble achieved CV 0.7026 and private score 0.71059; direct temporal architectures and temporal post-processing did not improve the approach.

The final ensemble averaged four SeResNeXt and InceptionV4 models using global average pooling and an ordinal-style regression output. Models were pretrained on 2015 competition images, trained with additional retinal datasets, and refined using pseudo-labels with head-only fine-tuning. Simple cropping, square padding, and 512×512 resizing outperformed elaborate preprocessing, while heavy augmentation helped control overfitting. Inference used horizontal-flip augmentation, and simple prediction averaging worked better than stacking.
compute: 3×1080Ti GPUs; FP16 training

solution_title: 45th place solution (the most simple method to get seliver madel)
solution_summary: The approach combined a tabular model with a CNN. Helmet trajectory summary statistics and a video-derived step_rate feature improved the tabular model. Test-time augmentation improved the CNN, whose predictions were then added to the tabular model. The combined system achieved public and private scores of 0.724 and 0.728.

solution_title: 26th Place solution - Record the first kaggle competition ,failed to gold (unlucky)
solution_summary: The author first improved DeBERTa base models with adversarial training, attention heads, layer normalization, and grouped layerwise learning rates. An optimized ensemble then labeled earlier Feedback Prize essays for knowledge distillation before further five-fold fine-tuning on the competition data. The final ensemble combined four distilled models using Optuna-tuned weights. Distilled models reached CV scores around 0.438–0.440, although the author acknowledged leakage in the procedure and uncertainty in model selection.

solution_summary: The solution combined Swin models with one EfficientNet model. The author emphasized that keeping batch normalization in evaluation mode was the most important change for training EfficientNet, alongside freezing early layers and using dropout. All models used pseudo-labels from the earlier Petfinder competition. The single EfficientNet achieved CV/public/private scores of 17.3041/17.92043/17.1051, and model selection relied on CV.

The solution used two rounds of stacking over 30 gradient-boosted tree models spanning XGBoost, CatBoost, LightGBM, and different targets and settings. Kaplan, Nelson, and Rank Gauss target transformations were explored, with Rank Gauss preserving target uniqueness and slightly improving leaderboard scores. The final ensemble combined models trained on efs=1 cases with models trained on all data, then replaced predictions below a threshold with the all-data model predictions. This metric-aware ensemble reached 0.694 CV and 0.695 on the private leaderboard, while target encoding and UMAP/t-SNE features did not work.

The team trained diverse audio models using mel spectrograms, extensive audio augmentation, and mostly GPU-based processing. A two-stage procedure first identified high-probability bird segments from out-of-fold predictions, then trained additional models on those segments, improving the public score from 0.582 to 0.596. The final ensemble combined 8–10 models through a union of predictions with individually tuned thresholds, followed by a no-bird majority vote to reduce false positives. Their synthetic validation set correlated only weakly with the leaderboard, and public-leaderboard threshold tuning was acknowledged to overfit.
compute: Mostly GPU-based processing and augmentation; inference took around 1 hour 30 minutes with resampled audio cached in memory.

solution_summary: The author describes a solution based mainly on ensemble algorithms and fine tuning. Implementation details are delegated to a linked notebook. The post provides no numerical scores, validation design, or ensemble configuration.

The solution combined eleven model configurations through LightGBM stacking of four-fold models followed by a weighted ensemble that also incorporated public ten-fold models. The author's DeBERTa variants used pseudo-labels from earlier Feedback Prize data, predicted topic prefixes, concatenation of the last four hidden layers, and averaged dropout heads. A custom loss variant was useful, while masked-language-model pretraining and the harder loss variant did not improve results. The reported scores were 0.4426811 in cross-validation and 0.435906 on the private leaderboard.

The author predicted the fraction of an earthquake interval remaining, then rescaled predictions to time to failure. About 20 selected features captured histogram and peak statistics from filtered signals, and a feed-forward PyTorch network modeled them. Quake-separated 15-fold validation, overlapping signal windows, and extensive feature selection were central to the approach. Prediction scaling materially affected results; a later adjustment of the submission mean produced a score of 2.24127.

The final submission combined four to five LightGBM models with weighted blending. Reconstructed user identities supported aggregation features, pseudo-labeling, and prediction adjustments based on previous fraud labels. Validation mimicked the temporal test split, while a separate model used stronger regularization and user-grouped folds to improve predictions for unseen users. User-based postprocessing provided the main improvement, and blending the specialized model only for new users added about 0.001.

solution_title: From 400 Score to Top 13: Kaggriculture Bronze Medal Solution
solution_summary: The final agent combined deterministic farming routes with reactive controls for capital, worker execution and shared-market sales. It selected routes from the visible shop sequence and generally used a lean cattle-and-geese farm with a fixed carrot programme. Replay analysis and paired-seat tests against diverse opponents guided improvements, while replay-only behaviour cloning and several production-expansion ideas failed. The final policy achieved a rating of 2089.3, won 136 of 200 validation games against ten opponent families and completed full-game validation without hard action errors.

solution_title: Team CGILAB x H2O.ai (7th place) solution
solution_summary: The agent combined supervised imitation learning, an AlphaZero-like Monte Carlo tree search, and two hand-designed heuristics. Its network learned from 21,000 strong leaderboard episodes and predicted policies and values for all four players in one evaluation. Search used decoupled PUCT, omitted new food generation, and incorporated several runtime optimizations. Against three smart_rl opponents, the full system achieved a 77.50% first-place rate in 400-game evaluations; the planned reinforcement learning stage was unfinished.
compute: Approximately 50–150 MCTS simulations per second in Kaggle's contest environment.

A LightGBM model used 50 selected features, while AutoGluon used all features with its best-quality preset and a four-hour time limit. Averaging their predictions produced a reported private score of 0.90462. The author also applied a referenced postprocessing trick and added some public features, although the latter changed little.

solution_summary: The solution cleaned LaTeX and HTTPS content and split punctuation before modeling. It combined GloVe and a component named Params in a 0.64 to 0.36 ratio for embeddings. The final approach ensembled three models and tuned architecture parameters and AdamW weight decay. The brief post does not describe the model architectures or validation procedure.

The approach divided slides into adjacent 512-pixel patches and used supplied masks to identify tissue types for training. A two-stage EdgeNext system first detected malignant patches and then classified their cancer subtypes. Inference discarded completely dark or light patches and averaged predictions across malignant patches. Validation accuracy was approximately 75%, while the selected submission scored 0.44 on the private test set; multiple-instance learning, external data, and novelty detection did not improve the approach.

The deep learning contribution combined TimeFormer, which models three adjacent signals, with PlanetFormer, which models the full spectrum through TimeFormer embeddings. Zone supervision and zone-aware attention supplied temporal structure, while constrained polynomial and basis-function output heads reduced PlanetFormer's parameter count. Both models used filtered, centered signals, time-axis flipping, and a custom metric-oriented uncertainty loss. Their predictions were blended with weights of 0.15 and 0.85; PlanetFormer alone achieved an approximate public score of 0.48–0.49.

solution_title: [88th place solution] How a beginner just barely won a medal
solution_summary: The final solution combined seven YOLO models with one 3D U-Net. YOLO models were pretrained on synthetic data and fine-tuned at a lower learning rate using seven cross-validation splits. The YOLO ensemble retained particles detected by at least two models before combining them with U-Net predictions. The approach scored 0.730 publicly and 0.723 privately; relabeling false positives and adding lateral-view models did not improve results.

The solution used a modified ResNet34 segmentation model with scSE, hypercolumns, and ELU decoder activations. It trained with extensive geometric and photometric augmentation, depth-stratified five-fold validation, SGD, and repeated cosine learning-rate cycles. Predictions were averaged across later cycles and folds with horizontal-flip test-time augmentation and a 0.45 threshold. The ensemble achieved 0.888 private and 0.865 public scores without additional post-processing, taking about five days for training and inference on two 1080 Ti GPUs.
compute: 2x 1080 Ti GPUs; about 5 days for training and inference

solution_summary: The solution combined two-stage models built with XGBoost and scikit-learn with online logistic regression. The writeup provides dependencies and instructions for reproducing the pipeline but few modeling details. The best single model scored 0.0044595 on the private leaderboard, while the best ensemble improved this to 0.0043324.

The approach combined permutation-based feature selection, substantial pseudo-labeling, and moderated prediction post-processing. Pseudo-labeling experiments included repeating test examples with predicted targets, although a strong model using three copies was not selected. Scaling predictions with outlier probabilities above 0.50 improved the best final submission, while the author remained uncertain about which changes survived the leaderboard shake-up.

solution_title: Private 7th(Public 12th) solution&code with keras GCN library
solution_summary: The solution used a two-layer graph convolutional network with multiple outputs, custom layers combining graph attention and GraphConvSkip, and attention pooling after each graph layer. It used 115 features per player, with projected interactions over the next zero to two seconds providing substantial gains. Training combined binary cross entropy and MAE with intermediate auxiliary losses, Adam, and y-axis flips. Post-processing padded unreachable outcomes with zero or one, while distribution adjustment, additional time-shifted data, and test-time augmentation worsened results or did not work.

The solution used a single LightGBM regressor, with most effort devoted to feature engineering guided by feature importance. Decisions were evaluated with six overlapping walk-forward folds grouped by timestamp, including a one-week gap between training and validation. Numba accelerated feature generation, while careful memory management allowed training on the entire dataset. Regularization, augmentation, and feature neutralization did not improve cross-validation, so the final pipeline remained simple.
compute: 25 minutes for data import, feature generation, and training; approximately 50 timestamps/second for prediction. Submission limits were 9 hours and 16GB RAM.

solution_summary: The team combined geometric-mean ensembles of public submissions with a LightGBM solution and XLM-RoBERTa models. They split validation data by language and added external data covering three additional languages for second-stage fine-tuning. Language-specific fine-tuning and ensembling raised the reported public score from 0.9473 to 0.9500. Further external-data training was limited by exhausted TPU availability.

solution_summary: The solution pretrains mixture-based video classifiers on 2018 YouTube-8M data and fine-tunes them on 2019 segments. Its segment loss adds weak negative supervision from video-level annotations, and stochastic weight averaging combines checkpoints selected using a held-out split. Inference uses video-level predictions to constrain segment labels and reduce false positives. The final weighted ensemble combines several VLAD and DBOF models with three ResNetLike variants.

The final system averaged three EfficientNetB3 classifiers with five-fold ResNet50 models.
