solution_title: 1188th Place Solution for the AI Village Capture the Flag @DEFCON31 Competition
solution_summary: This post collects beginner resources on machine-learning cybersecurity and hints drawn from other participants' CTF solutions. The author reports completing only the demonstration challenge whose answer was provided by the host. It links to educational material and public solution notebooks, with short hints for individual challenges rather than an original competition pipeline.

The agent combined an AlphaZero-like policy/value network with Monte Carlo tree search. Training iterated between behavioral cloning from strong agents, reinforcement learning, evaluation, and episode collection. Floodfill and food features, improved value handling, and correct terminal-state treatment strengthened play. GPU-generated episodes with larger searches improved the leaderboard rating by approximately 20–30 points.
compute: GPUs used for enhanced MCTS search and episode generation; several months of iterations.

solution_summary: The solution ensembled five folds each of Longformer, Funnel Transformer, DeBERTa, and DeBERTa-v3 token classifiers. Line feeds became separator tokens, and training used token masking, multi-sample dropout, and label smoothing. Out-of-fold predictions guided discourse probability thresholds and minimum span lengths, with additional linking of evidence spans. Both simple and weighted averages were submitted; the weighted ensemble achieved a reported private score of 0.720. Grouping documents of similar word lengths accelerated inference.
compute: Single V100/A100 GPU on Google Colab Pro+; A100 used only for deberta-large.

solution_summary: The solution combined the competition data with the original data, retaining the latter despite a slight public-score decrease because it might improve generalization. Sleep values were converted to continuous numbers and obvious typos were corrected. Degree and profession categories were consolidated, invalid profession answers were marked missing, and a degree-type feature was added. Four model parameters were tuned with Optuna using eight-fold stratified cross-validation; the model family was not explicitly named.

The approach predicted a binned PCIAT total score and converted predictions with fixed thresholds after threshold optimization proved unstable. An ensemble generated pseudo-labels for unlabeled rows, which were combined with original labels to train final models. KMeans-derived activity features supported additional GBDT models in the ensemble. Adding logistic regression and decision-tree regression slightly improved CV and public results but reduced the reported private score from 4.81 to 4.77.

solution_title: Single Bert [1 epoch] to get silver medal
solution_summary: The approach uses pretrained HateBERT for regression. The reported score increases from 0.80077 after one epoch to 0.80345 after five epochs. The post links an inference notebook but provides no validation or ensemble details.

The final ensemble used five BERT and RoBERTa variants, each trained across five folds for five epochs. Predictions were aligned to each target's training label distribution, with this adjustment disabled for columns where it performed poorly. Within each fold, model predictions were averaged before alignment; fold predictions were then averaged and aligned again. This sequence addressed the distribution changes introduced by averaging while targeting Spearman correlation.

The solution averaged diverse neural networks using features largely drawn from public notebooks, with PCA the only reported feature-engineering improvement. A custom dense-layer alternative learned a gate between linear and nonlinear transformations. Pseudo-labeling substantially improved CV and leaderboard performance, including a workflow that pretrained on all targets before fine-tuning with pseudo labels. The ensemble used two validation schemes and achieved 0.01815 public and 0.01610 private leaderboard scores.

solution_title: Solo write-up: 2.5D attention-MIL ensemble — what helped, what didn't (own 0.928 / blend 0.942 private)
solution_summary: The author trained 2.5D ConvNeXt and MaxViT models using averaged public soft labels, fixed folds, and per-finding attention over slice stacks. Their own model ensemble achieved 0.947 public and 0.928 private AUC, while adding it at 10% rank weight to a public ensemble left the final scores unchanged at 0.958 and 0.942. Several experiments missed predefined improvement thresholds, including higher resolution, another seed, OAI data, and slice transformers. Hidden-run crashes motivated explicit numerical retries, per-case model fallbacks, and validated atomic submission writing.

solution_title: 1st place solution for the LEAP competition
solution_summary: The solution equally blended 13 modified Squeezeformer models trained on expanded low- and high-resolution data. MAE loss, confidence prediction, multiple normalized input representations and careful handling of extreme values were central components. Auxiliary spacetime supervision and masked targets complemented the architecture, while precision-aware output processing and the ptend correction completed inference. The ensemble achieved public/private scores of 0.79410/0.79123, although model and ensemble selection relied partly on the public leaderboard because local validation became less representative at scale.
compute: Training on Kaggle and Colab TPUs; inference on Kaggle P100 GPU; at least $200 in Colab compute units and probably under $300 total.

solution_summary: The solution blended breast-level CNN feature fusion with patient-level transformers that jointly processed four mammogram views. Shared preprocessing used DICOM windowing, breast cropping, and detail-preserving PIL resizing, with most augmentation performed before downsizing. Auxiliary supervision and staged backbone freezing helped train both model families. Seven single-seed full-data models formed the final ensemble, with its binary threshold selected from cross-validation.

The solution used an off-the-shelf Faster R-CNN Inception-ResNet-v2 detector and adapted a deep structural ranking network for visual relationship prediction. Precomputed bounding boxes supplied spatial features, allowing relationship training without repeatedly running the expensive detector. The author reformatted annotations and built subject-object-predicate conditional priors using boxable classes, later adding visual attributes. Word2vec embeddings and priors restricted to the original VRD classes did not work, while relationship training took about four hours on a 4 GB Quadro M2000M.
compute: Detection inference on 8 Nvidia K80 GPUs on GCP, costing about US$35; relationship-network training took about 4 hours on an Nvidia Quadro M2000M with 4 GB RAM.

solution_title: 23rd Place Solution: Supervised Contrastive Learning Meets Domain Generalization (with TF code)
solution_summary: The team built an audio-tagging pipeline centered on DenseNet121 and BCE loss, with supervised contrastive pretraining to reduce overfitting. Label-preserving time CutMix, MixStyle, class-balanced sampling and explicit negative supervision improved training. At inference, each class used a window size selected by cross-validation. A diverse ensemble, including weaker models chosen to complement uncertain predictions, achieved public 0.942 and private 0.943.

The solution combined dictionary text matching with a second-stage ELECTRA-based NER model. It expanded the matching dictionary by extracting headline-style phrases and filtering them using document frequency, curated words, and Jaccard similarity. The NER model used a BiLSTM and CRF, and its predictions were added only when sufficiently different from matching results. The combined submission scored 0.322 privately, while an alternative that also mined test documents reached 0.427.

The solution used a custom YOLO detector to extract dorsal fins and full bodies, then trained large image embedding models with separate heads for the two crop types. NFNet and EfficientNet backbones, large input sizes, and two rounds of pseudo-labeling drove substantial improvements. Four models were combined through embedding concatenation and then ensembled with teammates. Species-specific thresholds for recognizing new individuals produced the best reported score of 0.884.
compute: Many GPUs (or TPUs); separate fin/body heads increased training time by 1.5×.

solution_summary: The author trained a CatBoost Langevin model with depth 8 and very strong regularization. The stated purpose of the regularization was to prevent training from becoming stuck. CatBoost predictions were combined with a Keras solution using a modified, more sensitive Mish activation. The author cautioned that this activation often caused vanishing gradients.

The authors state that they used mixed-integer programming for the competition. They describe reaching an optimum but provide no formulation, solver, or validation details in this post. The substantive explanation is linked in an external blog article.

The author's best candidate used a common LightGBM approach supplemented with 11 additional features. These features consisted of statistical parameters and nearest-neighbor information computed in a separate kernel. The candidate scored 0.900 publicly and 0.90016 privately, but the author chose other submissions for final evaluation. The post emphasizes the consequences of overlooking this stronger simple model during submission selection.

solution_title: 12th Place Solution - Stacking with XGB and NN
solution_summary: The solution stacked 28 first-level models, mostly gradient-boosted trees and neural networks. Its strongest single model was LightGBM with a five-fold CV score of 0.9761. XGBoost and a small neural network served as nonlinear stackers, which performed better than linear alternatives such as Ridge. The final prediction was a simple average of the two stackers.

solution_title: Things I have tried and my final solution
solution_summary: The final solution used ResNet18 with 150×150 images and five history frames, enabling batches of 512 within 8 GB of VRAM. Large batches improved the multimodal trajectory model, which predicted three routes and their confidences. Training used Adam for 400,000 steps on the full dataset with a learning rate halved every 50,000 steps and took more than 15 days intermittently. A diversity loss and gradient accumulation were unsuccessful, and a substantial training-validation loss gap remained.
compute: 8 GB VRAM; 400,000 training steps over more than 15 days intermittently.

solution_title: A Noob's Story : Silver in very First Competition (My Magical Experience)
solution_summary: This post reflects on the author's first competition and learning NLP through community notebooks and discussions. It describes personal progress, teamwork, and gratitude toward community members. It does not describe a concrete competition solution or pipeline.

The agent extended a previous Kore Beta rule-based framework with prioritized defense, expansion, combat, and mining logic. Its main advantage came from irregular mining routes, with more than 80,000 routes precomputed and candidates pruned at runtime. A space-time net-power map balanced mining safety against missed opportunities. Mining rewards favored contested areas near enemy shipyards to preserve local resources and deny resources to opponents.
compute: About 30,000 routes evaluated across all shipyards within a 3-second step limit after caching and precomputation.

solution_summary: The submission averaged four models, including TabNet, drug-ID-based PyTorch models, and a two-head ResNet. Each model contributed 49 predictions that were averaged into its final output. Several feature extraction and selection approaches failed to help, including ResNet-derived features, autoencoder selection, and clustering/statistical features. NODE/CatBoost tuning, EfficientNet with Deep Insight Transform, and prediction clipping were also unsuccessful.

The solution predicted per-class Gaussian heatmaps using 3D segmentation models pretrained on simulated volumes and fine-tuned with four-fold experimental-data training. Weighted BCE with large positive weights and heavy augmentation encouraged high recall. The final ensemble combined three four-fold model soups using logit averaging, flip augmentation, and overlapping sliding windows. Gaussian smoothing, local-maxima detection, and weighted fusion produced particle coordinates, yielding a private score of 0.77708.

The team combined domain-pretrained BERT models with BART using linear blends. Question-title grouped validation and fold-specific pseudo-label generation prevented overly optimistic validation caused by similar external examples. Training improvements included multi-sample dropout, separate encoder and head learning rates, and learned combinations of CLS representations across layers. Distribution-based discretization improved individual-model scores by roughly 0.027–0.030, and the reported final private scores were 0.430–0.433.

solution_summary: The solution estimated rectification geometry at low resolution and applied scaled transformations to original high-resolution ECG images. It trained segmentation models on thin one-pixel masks at 4400 × 1700 resolution with aggressive augmentation and BCE, continuing training to obtain sharp waveforms. ConvNeXt V2 and HRNet predictions were converted into sub-pixel signals with parabolic interpolation and then combined by weighted averaging. Flip TTA, Lead II fusion, and a weighted Einthoven correction further refined the reconstructed signals.

The solution combined decomposition-based features with DANets and XGBoost, using different feature pipelines for Cite and Multi. Cite used PCA, NMF, factor analysis, ICA, and missing-value-aware PCA variants, while Multi used PCA and NMF with SVD-reduced outputs for XGBoost. Averaging and stacking neural and boosted-tree models improved results, and building proper cross-validation raised the reported Cite leaderboard score from 0.812 to 0.814. Several alternatives, including nonlinear autoencoders and nonlinear dimensionality reduction, were unsuccessful.
compute: GPU training for XGBoost after dimensionality reduction; hardware unspecified.

solution_summary: The writeup describes a PyTorch training and inference pipeline with a default of 50,000 examples per class. Training logs point to an SE-ResNeXt-101 model, and the workflow includes cleaning training and validation data using model logits. The final prediction workflow ensembles the five best training checkpoints, reportedly improving the score by 0.0005.

solution_title: Creativity and CV [golden medal level solution: private 0.813]
solution_summary: The approach converted six Jigsaw toxicity labels into scalar regression targets, optimizing their weights against Ruddit and OffenseEval reference scores through a TF-IDF ridge surrogate. A pretrained toxicity RoBERTa model then used MSE regression, progressive unfreezing, and a head combining CLS, maximum pooling, and average pooling. Two refined validation sets tracked private results better than the public leaderboard. The author ultimately submitted a worse single-score ensemble after forgetting to validate the alternative ensemble.

solution_title: 45 Place Solution for the Open Problems – Single-Cell Perturbations Competition
solution_summary: The final submission blended public kernel predictions with PyBoost predictions using different recipes for two index ranges. For the first 128 entries, two public kernel outputs were weighted 0.2 and 0.8; the remaining entries combined PyBoost and a public kernel. Multi-target CatBoost performed worse than constant predictions on submission. Ridge regression and ChemBert were also reported as unsuccessful.

solution_title: 48th → 407th Place: How It Failed, and What We Learned Along the Way
solution_summary: The author explored physics and gamma-ray alignment, trajectory tracking, and tabular residual corrections for wellbore prediction. H72 doubled a TabM residual correction over a bounded per-well Ridge baseline, while K161 combined trajectory tracking with Ridge and CatBoost residual learners. H72's local CV closely predicted its private RMSE, whereas K161's apparently stronger CV missed by more than three RMSE. The central lesson was that repeated adaptive reuse of fixed validation wells and public scores led model selection astray.

The solution stacked ridge regression and recurrent neural network predictions into a LightGBM model using two-fold training. Ridge models used name and description n-grams, including a variant trained on a transformed target, while the recurrent model was simplified to accelerate training. LightGBM worked best with unigram count features, and adding longer n-grams degraded its performance. Using different inputs for each model was central to ensemble diversity, with the full combination scoring 0.400x.

This team component combined extensive multimodal feature engineering with LightGBM and neural models. Text representations included reduced bag-of-words features and averaged pretrained embeddings, while image embeddings, grouped aggregates, categorical factorization and interactions supplied additional signals. Training time led to selecting the top 1,000 importance-ranked features from roughly 4,000. Rescuer-grouped validation was chosen to avoid optimistic scores from shared rescuers, and the reported LightGBM achieved about 0.462 CV and 0.470 public score.
compute: 7,200-second training-time constraint.

solution_summary: The final pipeline windowed mammograms, detected and cropped breast regions, and ensembled EfficientNet and NFNet image classifiers. Training combined positive BCE, negative focal loss, invasive-status supervision, and averaged standard and EMA weights. Flip augmentation at inference, LP pooling across images, and percentile thresholding produced target-level predictions. A simpler submission without the detector and using mean aggregation achieved a better private score, 0.50 versus 0.48 for the final submission.

The men's tournament submission combined predictions from the publicly available Salma–Moore–Raddar approach with betting-market probabilities. For settled first-round matchups, the author converted bookmaker odds to implied probabilities and normalized each pair to remove the bookmaker over-round. The odds-based approach outperformed the baseline in the first round and became the stronger submission. The author also explored aggressive extrapolation from baseline predictions and discussed the risks of extreme probabilities under the competition scoring rule.

solution_title: 🛡️ Top 63 / 2817 Solution: Surviving the Shake-up with Physics & Deep Stacking
solution_summary: The final solution stacked 19 public baseline models with seven custom models using a logistic regression meta-model. Custom features represented spherical coordinates trigonometrically, approximated cosmological distance, and compressed spectral bands with PCA. Diversity across boosting models, Extra Trees, and an MLP was intended to improve stability. The author rejected a Ridge Flip approach despite its strong public score; the final stack scored 0.97098 publicly and 0.97024 privately.

The author improved their public notebook using EfficientNet-B7 and DenseNet201 backbones. Cosine learning-rate decay and GridMask augmentation were reported as useful. Pseudo-labeling was said to help achieve a score above 0.98. Overfitting caused performance to decline from the public leaderboard result.

The author used cumulative gameplay histories to predict each question group, including question identity as a feature. Features combined elapsed-time aggregates, behavioral transition counts and probabilities from earlier question models. Their contribution ensembled nine boosted-tree models, with the strongest private single model being DART at 0.704. Inference took about 40 minutes, while inconsistent validation behavior made model weighting and submission selection difficult.
compute: Approximately 40 minutes for inference.

solution_title: #44 place solution using features based on LinearRegression
solution_summary: The author trained linear regression models on component features and supplied their predictions and diagnostic statistics to XGBoost. solution_title: March Machine Learning Mania 2016, Winner's Interview: 1st Place, Miguel Alomar
solution_summary: The author used regression described as logarithmic regression and random forests, with offensive and defensive efficiency as the central signals. Different degrees of efficiency adjustment and strength-of-schedule treatment were checked against past seasons. The final model trained only on 2016 data and correctly anticipated most first-round upsets. AdaBoost was tried but excluded after poor results, and training plus prediction took five minutes.

solution_summary: The main model was an EfficientNet-B7 trained in mixed precision at 1024 × 1024 resolution and evaluated at 1280 × 1280. Its input preserved the temporal order of all six segments and added a binary channel indicating on-target versus off-target periods. The author attributed its effectiveness to this representation, which preserved signal continuity and target-state information during aggressive random resized cropping. Mixup, horizontal and vertical flips, AdamW, OneCycle scheduling, and gradient clipping completed the reported training approach.

The author outlines a workflow covering exploratory analysis, preprocessing, a model baseline, outlier removal, and feature selection. Outlier handling and feature selection are highlighted as the main learning points. The post provides no model specifications or implementation details.

The approach pretrained a transformer to predict engineered tabular features before fine-tuning it on default labels, including test data during pretraining. Separate MLPs processed variable groups before concatenation and transformer encoding, with the latest node feeding a linear output layer. Pretraining used standardized feature targets, Huber loss, and masking of missing targets for roughly 200 epochs; supervised fine-tuning needed fewer than five epochs per fold. Pretraining improved public performance by about 0.002, and soft pseudo-labels from the best ensemble raised a single transformer's public/private scores to 0.800/0.808, although the author acknowledged leakage from not using nested cross-validation.
compute: Approximately 200 pretraining epochs and fewer than 5 fine-tuning epochs per fold.

solution_summary: The solution blended recurrent models with multiple BERT variants and GPT2. Transformer training used head-and-tail tokens, learning-rate decay, additional toxic-comment data, and negative downsampling. Optuna selected blend weights through repeated validation splits, producing public and private scores of 0.94705 and 0.94707.

solution_title: Parallel Sampling + Rule-based Prompt Generation (4th place)

solution_title: 106th Place Solution (A Simple Data Preprocessing Method)
solution_summary: The approach encodes prompt context by changing the case of summary sentences according to their word overlap with prompt sentences. High-overlap sentences become uppercase, intermediate-overlap sentences become title case, and the rest become lowercase. The reported setup uses DeBERTa-large-v3 with 512 input tokens and dropout of 0.007, alongside additional trigram and parenthesis preprocessing. Its tracker reports a four-fold result of 0.425, although the metric columns are not identified.

solution_title: 66th (LB 10th) solution: k-means for background noise reduction
solution_summary: The pipeline applied mammogram windowing, removed background noise with pixel-value k-means, and cropped breast regions before resizing images to 1536×960. Three EfficientNet V2 S models predicted cancer with auxiliary targets, and image predictions were combined by mean aggregation. Positive oversampling, weighted binary cross entropy, multi-sample dropout, and geometric and intensity augmentations supported training. Background suppression improved the leaderboard score from about 0.58 to 0.63 despite little change in cross-validation.

The author describes their contribution to a team solution, using separate binary classifiers for 18 questions and a five-fold XGBoost model that scored 0.702 in cross-validation and 0.701 on the private leaderboard. Features captured time between level groups, progression milestones, prior-question prediction probabilities, and aggregated gameplay behavior. Feature selection was evaluated separately within each fold and question to avoid leakage, but it was ultimately dropped after public performance worsened. Additional incomplete sessions reconstructed from raw logs improved cross-validation by about 0.002 without improving the private score.

solution_title: 345th Place Solution for the NVIDIA Nemotron Model Reasoning Challenge
solution_summary: The team fine-tuned Nemotron LoRA adapters through supervised learning, emphasizing trace consistency, balanced batches, and repeated adaptation. They normalized reasoning traces and generated targeted arithmetic examples, filtering subtraction puzzles with a rule-based solver. Category-level validation guided adapter selection, and their final reported revision reached 0.860 private accuracy.

The team combined CNN classifiers and sound-event detection models trained on expanded and cleaned bird audio data. Validation used a held-out portion of BirdCLEF 2023 while all BirdCLEF 2025 data supported training. Random audio sampling, audio mixing, focal BCE, checkpoint averaging, and pseudo-labeled soundscapes supported robustness. A 20-model ensemble reached a private score of 0.927, while the best result used six CNN and six SED models with rank-aware post-processing and ONNX inference.

Training used ten folds, image augmentation, and a frozen-then-unfrozen schedule with checkpoints selected by the competition metric. Extracted embeddings fed a stacked regression model using SVR, Ridge, and linear regression. Inference used YOLOv5-derived dog/cat features and 15 augmentations, with greater ensemble weight on stacked regression and the worst out-of-fold models removed.

solution_title: José P. González-Brenes and Matías Cortés on winning the RTA challenge
solution_summary: The final approach uses random forests trained only on the more recent dataset. Features describe time, date, weekday, neighboring routes' latest observations, and optionally recent travel-time trends. Two feature configurations are assigned to different route segments according to which worked better. Linear regression, recency-weighted regression, and autoregression were explored before settling on this approach.

The author generated approximately 6,000 features and selected several subsets using validation-set permutation importance. XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost models varied in preprocessing, features, hyperparameters, and seeds, and about 40 models were averaged. XGBoost was the strongest individual model, with single-model five-fold AMEX scores around 0.797. Feature engineering and selection consumed most of the effort, while several neural approaches, distillation, and stacking features did not help.

The solution used a compact DeepFinder-inspired volumetric network trained on randomly sampled 128-cubed patches from all seven volumes. Percentile-based normalization, spherical training labels, spatial and intensity augmentation, and regularized training supported the small architecture. Inference combined four seeds, overlapping patches, and flip and rotation augmentation, followed by connected-component filtering. It achieved public and private scores of 0.7798 and 0.7825; larger models overfit and a multicascade network did not improve results.

The author explored several WaveNet-based architectures for sensor-sequence classification and found that temporal 1D CNNs performed better than WaveNet. Experiments included multi-kernel dilated inception convolutions, a WaveNet–Transformer hybrid, and WaveNet combined with xLSTM and attention pooling. Another architecture split each sequence into equal transition and gesture segments, processing them with WaveNet and a temporal CNN respectively. The post describes architectural experiments without identifying the final submitted configuration or reporting numerical scores.

Team-level posterior distributions modeled field-goal attempts and percentages, with a league-level error term absorbing additional variance. Win probabilities came from 5000 posterior simulations per potential matchup. Overrides for high-seed versus low-seed tournament games helped the final score.

The solution combined five biomass regression pipelines built on DinoV3 and DinoV2 representations. It varied spatial coverage through patch grids, dense sliding windows, larger patches, and a multiple instance learning transformer. Frozen embeddings, robust regression loss, seed averaging, and removal of two noisy samples helped address limited training data. The weighted ensemble achieved a public R2 of 0.779, while conventional fine-tuning and aggressive test-time augmentation caused overfitting.

solution_summary: The solution first trained EfficientNet-B5 on labeled data, then repeatedly fine-tuned it on test data with pseudo-labels. Limited augmentation, strong stochastic depth and dropout, and mixup with logical-OR targets helped retain sensitivity to weak signals. Images were merged along time and resized to 512×512, with vertical-flip augmentation at inference. Repeated pseudo-label training raised Public LB from 0.800 to 0.813, and the final submission averaged five high-scoring submissions.

solution_title: Avito Duplicate Ads Detection, Winners' Interview: 2nd Place, Team TheQuants | Mikel, Peter, Marios, & Sonny
solution_summary: The team engineered 587 features describing text, images, location, prices, attributes, and connected groups of ad pairs. They trained diverse base models, including bagged XGBoost and neural networks, and combined 14 predictions through random forest and XGBoost meta-models with weighted rank averaging. Temporal feature screening helped control overfitting, although their final chronological holdout became unreliable during meta-modelling. Cluster-size features were particularly useful, and the final rank average achieved a reported leaderboard score of 0.95294.

The team trained sentence-level named entity recognition models with a joint objective for dataset presence and entity boundaries. They ensembled RoBERTa with SciBERT, Conll, and BioBERT pipelines, filtering test sentences with regular expressions to fit inference limits. Limiting publications per dataset stabilized validation. Postprocessing and dataset-name string matching improved public results but hurt private performance; the unselected ensemble achieved about 0.414 privately.

The author shared an agent-swapping augmentation for predicting game-playing strength. Agent1 and agent2 were swapped during both training and inference. A simple CatBoost model with five-fold cross-validation and almost no feature engineering achieved public and private scores of 0.427 and 0.432.

The pipeline generated SN_filter predictions and pseudo labels, following the author's earlier TReNDS methodology. XGBoost stacking combined model outputs, but pseudo-label-model out-of-fold predictions made stacking prone to overfitting. Adding Gaussian noise to both out-of-fold and test predictions resolved this issue. Cross-validation and leaderboard scores were reported to be strongly correlated, allowing relatively few submissions.

The solution combined four Swin Large models with SVR and Gaussian process regressors trained on normalized 1536-dimensional image embeddings. Selected neural models used focal loss and mixup, and all models used five-pass test-time augmentation for cross-validation. Ridge and CatBoost stacking incorporated metadata and YOLOv5 animal features, with their outputs blended at weights of 0.8 and 0.2. The author also reported that an earlier Swin Large 384 submission achieved a private score of 16.975.

The final submissions blended seven strong, diverse models. One blend optimized cross-validation performance, while the other selected weights using model correlations and leaderboard scores. CNN models contributed useful diversity and improved the blend. The team retained its existing validation scheme rather than adopting a drug_id split because of time constraints.

The team combined global and finding-specific local features from densely cached multiview MRI windows using CoAtNet and CAFormer models. Training targets blended multiple report-label sources, image-first Astra assessments, and calibrated OOF predictions through two self-distillation rounds. Their models used hierarchical attention or contextual window-logit aggregation, followed by frozen-backbone fine-tuning on larger bags with reset heads. Two selected ensembles achieved 0.957 private AUC, while an unselected combination reached 0.958.

The solution fine-tunes a pretrained 1.1-billion-parameter DINOv3 backbone on paired image halves, fusing their features with two local gated convolution blocks. It predicts Green, Dead, and Clover biomass directly and derives the remaining targets through mass balance. A SigLIP semantic-feature tree ensemble contributes 25% of most final predictions, while Clover uses only DINO. Regularization, grouped cross-validation, log-space Huber loss, and target-specific calibration supported a mean CV R2 of 0.83 and a private leaderboard score of 0.74.

solution_title: A Self supervised approach for detecting gravitational waves

Signals from different detectors served as alternative views of the same underlying event, with one network handling Hanford/Livingston and the other handling Virgo. After representation learning, the frozen networks produced embeddings from all three detectors, which were concatenated for a fully connected classifier trained on 10% of the training data. The experiment scored 0.851 on the leaderboard.

solution_title: 548th Place Solution for the RSNA 2023 Abdominal Trauma Detection Competition
solution_summary: The final approach combined an EfficientNet-B4 DICOM image model with a weighted baseline using organ-specific ensemble weights. An initially planned NII branch was removed because its contribution was negligible, while organ-specific image crops failed because of overlap and occlusion. The image model used binary cross-entropy, Adam, and three training epochs, with additional regularization and batch-normalization adjustments. Evaluation used an 80:20 holdout and an additional in-sample check, reporting out-of-sample F1 of 0.73 and accuracy of 67%.

The pipeline trained pairwise Huber regressors, LightGBM models, and shallow Extra Trees on technical indicators and engineered features. It retained seven experts according to how frequently each achieved the smallest training residual, then learned per-row expert probabilities with Extra Trees and Gaussian naive Bayes classifiers. Missingness indicators, temporal differences, and predictions from small linear regressions expanded the features. Final predictions combined the experts using the selector probabilities and were clipped to a fixed range.

Prediction optimization consumed more time than hypothesis sampling, while extensive additional runs changed little about final test performance. solution_summary: The author moved away from deep learning and explored genetic programming inspired by a public simulated annealing approach. A tree-based representation appeared most promising and produced good results. Its resource demands exceeded those of annealing, limiting further work.

The solution used two U-Nets: one localized sea lion centers and the other segmented sea lions by type using manually refined masks. Morphological operations combined the center predictions and outlines to separate touching animals and count them. Predictions at different scales were ensembled, particularly for pups, but image scale variation remained unresolved. The best ensemble scored 13.03/14.03 on private/public data, only slightly better than the best single model.

The solution used only AIRS-CH0 and derived critical preprocessing and fitting choices from the simulation code. It disabled hot-pixel processing, subtracted wavelength-dependent foreground and jointly fitted transit dips with a separable gain-drift model. Bootstrap uncertainty estimates supported Gaussian-process smoothing, which was blended with autoencoder and NMF reconstructions at weights 6:2:2. A separate uncertainty blend completed the predictions, yielding public/private scores of 0.7330321/0.7420624.

The solution inverted the ventilator's proportional–integral controller to recover pressure directly from u_in. It enumerated discrete controller parameters and candidate pressures, solved for the initial integral, and reconstructed the pressure sequence using an exponentially decaying integral. A strict discreteness check recovered exact pressure for about 30% of inspiratory observations, while piecewise-linear inputs and clipping prevented broader recovery. An earlier recurrent physics model scored around 0.5, and the author lacked a strong model for the remaining observations.
compute: C++ brute-force search took about 5 minutes for all test data; hardware unspecified.

solution_summary: The final approach used regularized linear regression to predict changes in a log-transformed target, with a separate model for each forecast horizon. Features captured current density and population, changes in density and active businesses, and three- and six-month summary statistics. solution_summary: The solution stacked Swin image predictions with tabular features in XGBoost, CatBoost, and LightGBM, then combined their outputs with weights selected from out-of-fold performance. Five patient-grouped folds were shared across both stages to prevent leakage, and correlation filtering reduced the tabular inputs to 116 features. The image classifier used partial layer freezing, augmentation, focal loss, and negative subsampling. Balanced sampling and Gaussian noise on image predictions helped the boosting models handle imbalance and avoid excessive reliance on the image classifier.

The solution alternated random word deletion and beam-search reinsertion with local optimization of word arrangements. Local moves included subsection shuffling, swaps, and word relocation, while duplicate arrangements were excluded. Search improved substantially by placing words that increase valid_length early and grouping function words before content words. For the longest sequence, splitting alphabetically sorted content words into two groups and removing “and” from the function-word group reduced its score to 28.529695, with a reported leaderboard score of 246.81784.
compute: About 3 hours to discover the optimal id3 solution when starting with magi; hardware unspecified.

solution_summary: The solution ensembled multiple DeBERTa models with RAPIDS SVR trained on extracted model features. Replacing newline characters with [BR] improved public and private scores, and target-stratified five-fold validation supported model evaluation. Target-specific ensemble weights were optimized with Nelder-Mead, while soft labeling, pseudo-labeling, and batch size two were useful. A Gaussian-process ensemble achieved the best private score among the described variants but was not selected because of its public score.

solution_title: Argument Order as an Attack Surface: measuring a held-out guardrail
solution_summary: The author developed sandbox attack submissions in two families: marker exfiltration through HTTP posts and confused-deputy email actions with clean bodies. Analysis of 49 submissions and a within-run model comparison showed that the public guardrail rewarded exfiltration that largely failed against the private defense. The final selection diversified across both mechanisms, preserving a private score of 20.130 when the exfiltration submission scored zero. The main finding was that optimizing the public proxy diverted effort away from the more transferable email family.

The team used complementary 2.5D CNN, 3D CNN, and video-transformer segmentation approaches with simple decoders. One branch predicted at 1/32 resolution to devote more resources to the encoder, while another predicted at 1/2 or 1/4 resolution. Strong regularization, mixed precision, and overlapping inference supported the models. Inference included flip augmentation, percentile thresholds, and discarding unreliable prediction edges; a 0.93 percentile threshold performed better than 0.90.

solution_title: 1st place: What happened to our team during the last 2 days?
solution_summary: Removing hot-pixel processing was the turning point, improving the public score by about 0.015 despite little change in training performance. This change also enabled two-stage gain-drift fitting, an autoencoder, and non-negative matrix factorization to improve leaderboard performance. Removing foreground processing with a 1.007 multiplier was tested but reduced scores. Final adjustments to sigma and other settings brought the public score to 0.7330321 and the private score to 0.7420624.

solution_title: Team 42’s solution and food for thought [LB: 0.623 late submission]
solution_summary: The team built a three-head U-Net that predicts semantic masks, contours, and cell markers, then separates instances with random-walker postprocessing. Border and centroid weighting, focal and IoU losses, external training images, and synthetic touching cells improved performance. Their competition ensemble averaged dilated and standard encoders, but unreliable validation and broken TTA hurt submission selection. After the competition, pretrained ResNet and corrected TTA produced a score of 0.623.

The author trained 40 base models spanning generalized linear models, random forests, gradient boosting, and deep neural networks. Each family was combined into a separate ensemble, while XGBoost combined all 40 base models. A final stack combined the XGBoost ensemble and the four family ensembles. The author submitted the wrong file and estimated that the intended approach would have scored about 0.55142.

The main approach searched physical signal parameters rather than training a neural network, scoring candidate wave trajectories by their observed power. GPU-batched random search used empirically chosen parameter distributions, interpolation between frequency bins, and noise masking followed by normalization. Scores from the two detectors were averaged, yielding public/private scores of 0.835/0.826. A late discovery of identical noise in nearby-frequency real samples further improved these to 0.855/0.849.
compute: NVIDIA V100; 3,276,800 search points in about 20 seconds per sample; approximately 3 GPU hours for training data and 2 GPU days for test data.

solution_title: Solution writeup, Efficiency leaderboard #24. My first kaggle competition, top 50!
solution_summary: The solution extracted frozen DeBERTa V3 xsmall features and trained a separate CatBoost or SVR regressor for each of six essay scores. Most targets used concatenated mean pooling, max pooling, and first-token representations from 12 hidden layers, while grammar used only mean pooling. Optuna and five-fold iterative stratification selected hyperparameters and the regressor for each target before fitting on all training data. A maximum sequence length of 400 balanced predictive quality against runtime; other transformer embeddings and ensembles did not improve results, and rounding predictions slightly hurt performance.

solution_title: A way to get silver medal without magic
solution_summary: The solution stacked QDA, Gaussian mixture, NuSVC, and label-spreading models with pseudo-labeling. The key correction was to generate predictions for pseudo-labeled test points through cross-validation, avoiding training and predicting on the same points. This made stacking improvements transfer from validation to the leaderboard. The linked implementation achieved a private score of 0.97248.

The author provides a solution file that generates a submission scoring 0.88691 on the private leaderboard. The workflow uses R scripts with separate directories for data, scripts, and submissions. The text describes setup but gives no model or feature details.

The solution uses glmnet in R with sparse features extracted from user and business information. It ensembles a model using all features with a model using only user and business identifiers. Post-processing combines the predicted review score with a user offset derived from user and review JSON files, and feature preparation also uses US Census name data. The released scripts produce a score of 1.23669, slightly better than the reported competition version's 1.23688.
compute: 2–3 GB memory; about one hour to run all scripts.
external_data: ["US Census name data: dist.all.last, dist.male.first, dist.female.first"]

solution_summary: The pipeline generated geographic and exact-match candidates, then classified pairs with LightGBM and XGBoost using text similarity and geographic features. Shallow models filtered the 200 nearest neighbors in chunks before more expensive final training. Repeated grouped splits produced ten models, and inference added inverse matches and graph-derived pairs. RAPIDS enabled efficient processing; the author reported 0.908 holdout CV for a single model and 0.935 leaderboard performance for the ensemble, attributing part of the gap to implicit leakage.
compute: GPU acceleration with RAPIDS; hardware model and runtime unspecified.

solution_summary: The solution combined LightGBM, XGBoost, and CatBoost using ten-fold stratified cross-validation and Optuna tuning for AUC. Within each fold, SciPy optimized the prediction blend weights by minimizing negative AUC, followed by shared post-processing code. The final cross-validation score was 0.90667, with relatively stable agreement between validation and leaderboard performance. Feature engineering and pseudo-labeling did not provide useful gains.

The author describes stacking random forest, generalized linear models, and XGBoost. They report a large difference between public and private leaderboard scores. The post links to implementation code but gives no validation or training details.

solution_title: 8th Place Solution for the CZII - CryoET Object Identification Competition + Code Released
solution_summary: The final system combined four model soups of complementary MONAI 3D U-Nets pretrained on synthetic tomograms. Training used small patches, while inference used substantially larger windows, Gaussian overlap reconstruction, and geometric test-time augmentation. Predictions were combined at the logits level and converted into particles using watershed segmentation and particle-specific thresholds. Synthetic pretraining and larger inference patches each improved the leaderboard score by roughly 0.01.
external_data: ["Six synthetic tomograms: TS_0, TS_1, TS_10, TS_11, TS_12, TS_13"]

solution_title: 7th Place Solution - Wavenet and Some Tricks
solution_summary: The main model was a modified WaveNet operating on three days of minute-level aggregates. Engineered motion and time features, tolerant event labels, two prediction heads, and hard-example mining supported training. Inference retained the middle day of sliding windows and used custom peak suppression and scoring. LightGBM stacking and an LSTM–Transformer ensemble each added about 0.001, while the final cross-validation score was around 0.826.
compute: RTX3090; 18 seconds per epoch for six epochs; submission took 30 minutes total.

solution_summary: The solution generated candidates using item-based and user-based collaborative filtering plus revisits, then reranked them with separate CatBoost models for orders, carts, and clicks. It created 226 features, including collaborative-filtering scores, visit counts, and recency statistics. Orders and carts used a second ranking stage restricted to the top 50 candidates, with target-specific negative sampling. Five seed and data-split variants were combined using weighted predicted rankings; candidate generation achieved 0.725 orders recall, and the best single model scored 0.602 on the leaderboard.
compute: Google Colab Pro+; GPU CatBoost training

solution_title: March Machine Learning Mania 2026: 5nd Place Solution
solution_summary: The solution modeled men's and women's basketball independently with chronological Elo updates and different game weights and K-factors. Predictions came directly from each team's final regular-season Elo through a logistic formula, without margin-of-victory adjustments. Evaluation used tournament Brier scores, and final probabilities received champion-specific modifications for UCLA and Michigan. The reported final Brier score was 0.1174602.

The author contributed a single sequence-to-sequence forecasting model that scored 0.499 on the public leaderboard. Separate encoders and decoders used roughly 30 dilated causal convolution layers, with a bidirectional LSTM supplying future promotion information. Raw sales, categorical embeddings, and engineered temporal features were combined with an explicit zero-probability output. Validation held out entire series and sampled evaluation periods across the final training year, while randomized promotion imputation improved the score by about 0.004.

solution_title: 4th Place Solution: ALIKED+LightGlue is all you need [Prize Eligible]
solution_summary: The solution processed transparent and non-transparent scenes separately before reconstructing camera geometry with COLMAP. Non-transparent matching used ALIKED-n16 features across four image orientations and LightGlue, while transparent scenes used foreground segmentation and full-resolution grid-based matching. Exhaustive image pairing and inclusion of test images omitted from submission.csv improved reconstruction coverage. Handling transparent objects and using all available images were the main gains, with the combined ablation reaching 0.197 private LB and 0.194 public LB.
compute: Two T4 GPUs; parallel CPU and GPU processing.

solution_title: Medium article, code and 15th place solution
solution_summary: The team trained many neural networks and blended their predictions. The post gives no architecture, preprocessing, or validation details. The author also mentions a repository containing a minimal example and a short post with ideas and examples.

The author released a Keras Mask R-CNN pipeline with ResNet50, ResNet101, and ResNet152 backbones. An ensemble of the three achieved 0.4670 on the public leaderboard and 0.4311 on the private leaderboard, but was omitted from the team's best submission because training finished too late. Uniform class sampling produced rapid improvements, and transferring decoder weights from ResNet152 accelerated ResNet101 training. Training also involved backbone freezing, learning-rate reduction, and gradient accumulation.
models_pretrained: ["Mask R-CNN with ResNet50, ResNet101, and ResNet152 backbones"]

solution_summary: The agent replayed coordinated production schedules extracted from public matches and selected among general, milk, and wool plans using the first two shops. Candidate schedules were compared within early-shop categories and checked on a separate replay set. Cash and planting safeguards protected the next hiring and production cycle. The focused variant scored 2345.5, while a broader variant scored 2325.3; switching between schedules without reconciling farm state remained a weakness.

The final ensemble combined FastText-LSTM-GRU, GPT2, and multiple cased and uncased BERT models, including a BERT model further pretrained on competition text. Subgroup negative examples received extra weight, and training jointly predicted toxicity and related labels. Sentence statistics were concatenated before the final layers, while dynamic batch sizes and gradient accumulation made large models practical on limited hardware. Many alternatives, including prior competition data, back-translation, XLNet, and focal loss, did not help.
models_pretrained: ["FastText embeddings", "GPT2", "BERT base uncased", "BERT base cased", "BERT large uncased", "BERT large cased", "XLNet"]
