solution_summary: The pipeline separated car detection and orientation estimation from depth prediction using two independent models. A modified CenterNet-style detector predicted image centers and local orientations, with four depth-range specialists using EfficientNet or SE-ResNeXt backbones. A dedicated FPN depth model used grayscale images and coordinates relative to the camera principal point, with distance-normalized regression loss. Camera intrinsics converted detected image positions and predicted depths into 3D coordinates, while averaging detector outputs across folds did not appear effective.

The post provides training and prediction instructions for a solution containing neural networks and gradient-boosted tree models. Training uses two stages so models can be tuned on the released stage-one data. The downloadable package includes training data and model weights, but the post gives little architectural or evaluation detail.

The solution generated arithmetic interactions between pairs and triples of features and selected them by Pearson correlation with loss. Its pipeline combined GBM classifiers with Gaussian process regression, support vector regression, and GBM regression, then linearly blended the regression predictions. It modeled log loss to address the target's long tail and shuffled the time-sorted training data for validation. The reported best private score was 0.44465, and Gaussian process regression required about 96 GB of RAM.
compute: About 96 GB RAM, primarily for Gaussian process regression.

solution_title: [CPU Only]６th Place Solution for "Linking Writing Processes to Writing Quality"
solution_summary: The solution reconstructed essays and built a compact set of 169 features, including character TF-IDF compressed with TruncatedSVD and typing behavior statistics. Repeated stratified cross-validation guided decisions, with the author prioritizing CV over public leaderboard scores. A diverse three-level ensemble combined tabular models, feature bagging, seed averaging, intermediate stacking models, and geometric mean blending. Predictions were clipped at a lower bound of 0.5, and all computation ran on CPU.
compute: CPU only; no GPU used.

solution_summary: The final submission combined a Nelder–Mead weighted blend and a Bayesian ridge stack built from eleven base models. These models included fine-tuned transformers and pretrained embeddings followed by SVR or XGBoost. Longer sequences, head-and-tail token handling, and freezing early transformer layers were particularly useful. Out-of-fold improvement guided ensemble additions, and the Bayesian ridge stack achieved a reported CV score of 0.4446.

solution_title: Virtual LB 130th: Mel spectrogram feature + class balance simple solution
solution_summary: The approach converted sliding windows of acoustic samples into 62,900 mel-spectrograms of size 128 by 128. It summarized each spectrogram using mean, standard deviation, and trend-like statistics to produce 384 features. The dataset was balanced through a stratified procedure that treated it as a labeled set. A simple LightGBM model used the resulting features; no score was reported.

solution_title: Place 70 solution  trust CV is all you need
solution_summary: The author emphasizes trusting cross-validation when selecting submissions for this synthetic Playground dataset. Their reasoning is that training and test distributions should be consistent because the data are machine generated. They report achieving 0.918 but submitting a result of 0.916, expecting the choice to generalize better to the private leaderboard. No model architecture or feature pipeline is described.

A modified ResNet10-based 3D CNN initialized predictions around target medians and achieved 0.1695 cross-validation without additional features. Its out-of-fold predictions were combined with loading and functional connectivity features in LightGBM, MLP, SVM, and ridge models. Feature-specific regularization and aggressive loading-feature duplication supported the second-stage models. Adversarial validation predictions supplied sample weights, narrowing the validation-to-leaderboard gap to 0.1562 versus 0.1566, although the author believed this adjustment mattered less on the private test set.

The solution combined image-level classifiers that assigned cell predictions through class activation maps with classifiers operating on individual cell crops. Two rounds of soft pseudo-label training, D4 test-time augmentation, and simple averaging linked these complementary approaches. Training used competition and public HPA data, while model selection relied heavily on public leaderboard feedback because local metrics correlated poorly. Area-based confidence scaling improved the final public score from 0.580 to 0.594, with a private score of 0.540.

solution_title: 5th place solution, maskrcnn, pseudo label and cellpose
solution_summary: The solution combined Mask R-CNN and Cellpose through staged training on LIVECell and competition data. Mask R-CNN generated pseudo-labels for the semi-supervised dataset, and its predictions were converted into flow and semantic segmentation representations. Cellpose was pretrained on LIVECell excluding shsy5y cells, then fine-tuned with additional channels and used for final prediction and post-processing with diameter set to 19. Deep Watershed variants and OmniPose did not work.

The author explored detecting the Other class using soft thresholding and anomaly detection on latent features from a subtype classifier. One-Class SVM and Isolation Forest experiments did not improve results. A convolutional autoencoder was also attempted to identify unfamiliar tissue through reconstruction error, but the approach was not finished or optimized. Evaluation remained a major difficulty, and the post asks others for successful ideas.

The author trained a graph convolutional network to classify compiler configurations by their runtime order. Node features and edges contributed to a handcrafted runtime estimate used to normalize configuration runtimes and construct ordered classes. The model produced configuration-by-class probabilities, and the top five classes were returned for the tiles dataset. Cross-config attention was identified afterward as a possible improvement.

The solution resized and padded images for an ImageNet-pretrained ResNet34 encoder with FPA attention and a convolution-plus-GAU decoder. Training used Lovasz loss, SGD, cosine annealing and extensive geometric and brightness augmentation. Depth channels and a revised stratification method improved the pipeline, with the latter reportedly adding 0.03. A transferred five-fold average ensemble reached 0.883 privately using a 0.45 threshold.

The author built separate men’s and women’s tournament models using competition data and engineered team ratings and summary statistics. Bidirectional stepwise regression selected variables, including multiple weight-of-evidence transformations of a relatively small set of underlying characteristics. Out-of-time evaluation guided development, while normalization appeared to add little for the women’s model. A simpler alternative without weight-of-evidence fields performed substantially worse.
compute: Moved execution from a local machine to Kaggle; hardware and runtime were not specified.

solution_title: 49 place solution - meh models, +0.04-0.05 private LB postprocessing
solution_summary: The author averaged six five-fold model configurations using EfficientNet-B2 and RexNet200 on PCEN and mel spectrograms. Normalizing prediction scales and using overlapping inference windows improved ensemble behavior and temporal coverage. Species-specific false-positive suppression and smooth geographic and temporal adjustments provided substantial additional gains. Conservative threshold selection worked well on private data, and the best submission scored 0.63/0.68 with postprocessing versus 0.59/0.62 without it.
compute: RTX 2060 Super; at most one five-fold training run per day with mixed precision; cached spectrograms approximately 150 GB each.

solution_title: 1st Place Solution ➡️ Distill is all you need🔥🔥🔥
solution_summary: The solution adapted Llama 3 70B, Qwen2 72B, and Gemma2 9B using LoRA or QLoRA after an initial training stage on UT data. Five-fold teacher predictions from the larger models supplied distillation targets for Gemma2 9B, which the author identified as the most important component. The fold-specific LoRA weights were averaged, and the resulting model was quantized to 8 bits with GPTQ. Submission inference used test-time augmentation with a sequence length of 2000, improving the reported leaderboard score from 0.882 to 0.876.

The author used a linked updated GOTO conversion solution as the basis of their submission. They added subjective tournament expectations favoring Duke, Florida, Auburn, and Houston for the Final Four, with Duke reaching the final. They also favored Connecticut and South Carolina reaching the final. The post attributes the result to these six gambles and luck, while linking a notebook for implementation details.

The post announces a packaged team solution available through a GitHub repository and a Docker image for prediction. It also links a downloadable example output for interactive browser viewing. It provides no substantive description of the modeling pipeline.

The solution used BERT question-answering models with unchanged text and experiments on negative sampling rates. Whole-word-masking BERT Large Uncased performed best, and its weights were combined with ordinary BERT Large before classifier-only fine-tuning and teacher-to-student distillation. Knowledge distillation was described as the key contribution, with further classifier-only tuning of the student. The student scored about 0.7118 on the development set and 0.7 on both public and private leaderboards; the attempted augmentation methods did not help.

solution_title: 1151 Place Solution for the Linking Writing Processes to Writing Quality Competition [275 efficiency leaderboard]
solution_summary: The author focused on engineered writing-process features and selected LightGBM and CatBoost for tuning after comparing four baseline regressors. Features described activity streaks, text structure, production rates, writing and revision time, and intervals between keystrokes, with selection based on correlation with essay scores. Optuna tuned hyperparameters, and shuffled 10-fold cross-validation guided model comparison. The reported public and private scores were 0.607 and 0.589; removing the lowest-scored essays and oversampling low scores did not help.

solution_title: 40th place solution | MLPs, ResNet, TabNet & Clustering
solution_summary: The final ensemble combined four MLPs, one ResNet, and one TabNet with weights of 0.5, 0.1, and 0.4 respectively. Training used multilabel-stratified ten-fold validation, five seeds per fold, label smoothing, low weight decay, and OneCycleLR. Changes were generally retained only when both CV and public leaderboard performance improved. One final submission additionally blended predictions with known drug labels using nearby t-SNE clusters, improving private loss from 0.01611 to 0.01609.

The team built a multi-stage state-space model with active and inactive states and Negative Binomial emissions for discrete demand. They simulated demand at level 12 and aggregated independent store trajectories through level 10, while modeling levels 1–9 individually. Hand-crafted seasonality and store-department event coefficients incorporated supply-chain knowledge. The approach produced explainable demand distributions and stable scores across years and periods, but did not model pricing effects or new SKUs.

The solution prioritized candidate recall, combining 21 retrieval methods with article embeddings and similarity search. Image, text, TF-IDF, and word2vec embeddings supported candidate generation and cosine-similarity features. A single LightGBM ranker used windowed article, customer, and interaction statistics, with reusable features cached to accelerate inference. Word2vec trained on all transactions improved both validation and leaderboard scores, but future information inflated local validation: MAP@12 was 0.0441 locally versus 0.0350 on the leaderboard.

solution_title: 9th Place Solution (Forget set-free Approach, 3rd on Public LB)
solution_summary: The approach alternated stochastic layer re-initialization with knowledge-preserving training using only the retain set. Two final variants each trained for five epochs, distributed over three or four forgetting-and-remembering cycles. Layer-wise selection, excluding fully connected and projection-shortcut layers, was more effective than element-wise selection. MSE performed best among the tested losses, and repeated cycles improved unlearning more effectively than increasing the re-initialization ratio.
compute: Submission constraint: 512 independent unlearning runs within 8 hours; each final algorithm uses 5 epochs.

solution_title: 28th place, A 0.0006x boosting trend feature and non-overfitting target encoding (attributed rates)
solution_summary: The post describes feature experiments that were omitted from the final submission after misleading public leaderboard feedback. Day-excluded target encoding reduced overfitting, and combining smoothed and unsmoothed encodings gave a small additional gain. Ratios of downloads on the previous two days captured trends and improved the private score from 0.9821 to nearly 0.9828. The author also reported useful count-ratio features and emphasized trusting local validation.

solution_title: 22th place solution / for English edition and 中文版本
solution_summary: The solution used Mask R-CNN with a Swin Transformer backbone and category-specific anchor sizes and aspect ratios. Models were pretrained using external data supplied by the competition. Training combined image augmentation, cosine annealing, and stochastic weight averaging, while inference used test-time augmentation. Four models handled classification and segmentation, followed by confidence and minimum-area filtering and index-ordered overlap removal.

The solution averaged predictions from WaveNet–GRU variants trained on overlapping time-series windows with subject-grouped validation. One variant initialized its convolutional backbone through next-value prediction on unlabeled sequences, while variants differed in validation filtering and checkpoint selection. Final inference used long segments, resampled tdcsfog signals, and converted models for CPU execution. A post-competition investigation found that the pretrained variant helped GPU inference despite hurting the submitted converted ensemble; a two-variant GPU ensemble scored 0.437 on the private leaderboard.
compute: RTX 3090: approximately 1–1.5 hours per pretraining epoch; final converted-model inference ran on CPU.

solution_title: 69th Place Solution for the AI Village Capture the Flag @ DEFCON31 Competition (22 Flags)
solution_summary: The author solved a collection of AI capture-the-flag tasks using data analysis, adversarial images, and iterative prompts. Pivot tables identified misclassified populations, while KMeans and manifold dimensionality reduction recovered clues from embeddings. Square Attack produced adversarial images, and pixel counting and intensity filtering solved image-based tasks. Other flags came from OCR XML injection, prompt refinement, unsafe pickle deserialization, and natural-language DNS updates.

solution_title: 3rd place solution - beam search and character head
solution_summary: The solution combined two diverse span extraction pipelines using RoBERTa-base, RoBERTa-large, and BART-large backbones, each trained with five seeds. One pipeline used refined tokenization and a conditional start/end decoder, while the other expanded token representations into character representations and applied GRU layers to predict character spans. Handling shifted labels caused by consecutive spaces was central to performance. Tweets with consecutive spaces used only the character model ensemble, while other tweets used substring search to maximize agreement with model predictions under Jaccard similarity. The combined ensemble achieved a private score of 0.733.

The solution used separate preprocessing and ensembles for Citeseq and Multiome. Citeseq combined four MLP models with two LightGBM models, using alternative preprocessing pipelines and out-of-fold predictions to select weights. Multiome used TF-IDF, log transformation, normalization, and PCA before ensembling four MLPs with different activation functions. Donor-based validation reached 0.896 for Citeseq and 0.670 for Multiome, while the combined submission scored 0.814 publicly and 0.772 privately.

The selected submission used IsolationForest to identify and remove anomalous rows, retaining 3,325 of 3,500 rows and achieving a private score of 1.01699. An alternative applied outlier detection separately to each column and then dropped rows containing missing values. That unselected submission retained 2,687 rows and achieved a better private score of 1.01535.

The solution jointly optimized GNSS observations and trajectory smoothing through a custom constrained solver implemented in TensorFlow. It combined pseudorange, Doppler, and ADR residuals with a piecewise-constant-jerk trajectory model, robust observation constraints, and uncertainty weighting. External base-station and satellite products supported relative positioning and atmospheric corrections, while an optimized timing offset addressed velocity discrepancies. The final submission took the median of multiple base-station solutions, with all optimization performed in double precision on CPU.
compute: CPU optimization using double-precision floating point; convergence described as slow.

solution_summary: The author adapted their small-dataset approach by computing nearest neighbors from similar queries within the same category and omitting category-specific normalization. When fewer than five items were available, they filled the recommendation list using category, query, and global popularity. A 10% validation holdout tracked leaderboard performance well, and the author reported no overfitting problems. The last submission scored 0.57142, and the final Python script ran in 21.5 minutes on a laptop.
compute: Final Python submission script: 21.5 minutes on a laptop.

solution_title: Non-technical write-up & on the importance of the Kaggle community
solution_summary: The team combined transformer outputs with a character-level LSTM for sentiment span extraction. Preserving spaces in this pipeline substantially improved performance, and the team later recognized that this exploited a pattern in the labels. They also used smoothed cross-entropy loss and selected ensembles that scored 0.734 on the public leaderboard. Later work improved cross-validation performance and robustness without surpassing their earlier public score of 0.735.

The author trained several ResNet, ResNeSt, and ResNeXt models and selected checkpoints and ensembles using F1 on train_soundscapes. Adding secondary labels with probability 0.3 helped, while other augmentation produced gains below 0.01 and EfficientNet B0–B5 did not work. Two ensemble candidates were chosen: one optimized for local F1 and another incorporating some randomness in model selection. Predictions were filtered using season and location, with H3 geographic segments derived from training metadata providing a reported 0.01 improvement.

The solution used false-color images and UNet models with strong backbones, training on all individual annotations. The central finding was a suspected half-pixel image-mask misalignment that made ordinary flips and rotations ineffective. Shifting images by half a pixel during training and inference corrected alignment and allowed normal augmentation. A custom mask-flipping alternative also worked, while other bands and 2.5D inputs were abandoned and successful small-model pseudo-labeling was not extended to larger models.

solution_title: My creativity paid off in this challenge, but nevertheless DAE is the goal and key.
solution_summary: The author fine-tuned a DAE implementation shared by another participant. Its predictions were ensembled with predictions from XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost, and an Octopus machine learning model. Combining these model scores was credited with improving the final result, although no ensemble weights, validation details, or numerical scores were provided.

The pipeline generated recommendation candidates through repurchases, related products, popularity, collaborative filtering, and tag-vector similarity. CatBoost YetiRank reranked candidates using static attributes, transaction aggregates, recency, interaction counts, similarity scores, and LightFM user embeddings. Four models trained with different history lengths and parameters were ensembled. The best single model achieved CV 0.03589 and private score 0.03391, although changing training duration sometimes reversed the validation and leaderboard trend.
compute: 224-core machine; up to 20 hours to train one model.

solution_summary: The solution built diverse customer-level datasets using pairwise feature differences, sequence aggregates, temporal changes, missingness features, and sequential encodings. It combined LightGBM DART, CatBoost, XGBoost, neural tabular models, and a public transformer model. Training TabNet on out-of-fold SHAP values from LightGBM made it useful for the ensemble and achieved a leaderboard score of 0.797. Five-fold validation, multiple seeds, and forward selection of ensemble weights supported the final blend; ordinary feature selection, sequential models, and alternative losses did not help.
compute: 12 GB GPU; NODE used batch size 64.

solution_summary: The solution uses U-Net segmentation models trained with Adam, adding batch normalization and ReLU to convolution blocks. Multiple pipelines vary image resolution, spectral channels, patch size, and class coverage, including a three-input network that combines imagery at different resolutions. Hard-negative mining supplies roughly one third of each epoch's samples, while flips and rotations augment training. Selected predictions are combined across epochs and pipelines, with morphological processing and water-class subtraction used for some masks. The author's solo public score was 0.50165, and further results came from combining predictions with ZFTurbo.

The approach combined diverse 3D ResNet, SEResNet, and DenseNet models with other team predictions through stacking. Individual 3D models were relatively weak, but their complementary predictions improved ensembles, including a weighted blend that achieved 0.1582 on the public leaderboard. Resizing volumes and normalizing them using site-specific statistics improved diversity and leaderboard performance. Float16 data accelerated experimentation, while selected important models used float32 for accuracy.
compute: One float16-data model took about 5–10 hours for five folds with ten epochs each; float32 took 2–3 times longer.

solution_summary: The solution blended several LSTM neural networks and XGBoost models trained with slightly different settings. Feature engineering supplied about 60 motion, geometry, and metadata features, while five shared body parts enabled joint training across laboratories. Lab embeddings and allowed-action masking supported the neural model, and XGBoost used feature selection, F1-based early stopping, and probability smoothing. Lab- and action-specific thresholds were tuned on out-of-fold predictions, with conflicting actions resolved by probability-to-threshold ratios.

The author built deep-supervised and multiclass segmentation models across seven random train-validation splits, using pretrained ResNet34 with scSE encoders. Model-specific padding or bilinear resizing produced 128×128 inputs, followed by varied geometric and photometric augmentation. Training used cosine learning-rate restarts, with object-context modules added to some folds. The final ensemble averaged sigmoid predictions from selected cycles and horizontal-flip inference, then applied a 0.5 pixel threshold. Larger encoders and alternative ensemble methods did not improve on this approach, while directly averaging raw Lovasz-trained outputs performed poorly.
compute: GTX 980m; Neptune.ml and Google Cloud Platform also used; fold training schedules ranged from 210 to 295 epochs.

solution_title: 86th - Bronze Medal - with Silver Gold Magic Explained
solution_summary: The competition submission combined EfficientNet models with a learned image-resizing module, larger input sizes, and five-fold ensembling. A final correction increased predictions for test images identified by a model trained on disagreements between two approaches, improving the leaderboard score to 0.779. Several attempts to exploit off-cadence images or test pseudo labels reduced performance. Post-competition experiments showed that strong mixup with a large EfficientNetB4 improved generalization, reaching public and private scores of 0.786 and 0.781.
compute: 4 NVIDIA V100 GPUs, running constantly for several days.

solution_summary: The repository describes a default-risk prediction pipeline using LightGBM with Gradient-based One-Side Sampling. This model contributed to a larger ensemble of 13 models combined through linear regression. The standalone model achieved a private ROC AUC of 0.8044, and the repository lists its dependencies and tested Python environments.

solution_title: 35th Place Solution- Magic PP - Site 2 correction
solution_summary: The team used tabular data and blended a public kernel with two three-level stacking ensembles. They adjusted features between acquisition sites using mean shifts and estimated site membership with an ensemble of classifiers. Ranked classifier outputs were converted into site probabilities to blend predictions under alternative site assumptions. Each main component scored 0.1585 on the public leaderboard, while the final blend reached 0.1584.

The team used coding agents and manual orchestration to optimize task-specific ONNX programs, merging independently developed candidates by verified score and then speed. Shared recipes, compact memory and per-task histories helped agents reuse discoveries and avoid repeated failures. The strongest improvements came from algebraic representations that minimized charged intermediate memory, often ending directly in Einsum. Runtime screening became essential: the locally best set scored 8041.20 but exceeded the time limit, while the submitted set scored 8038.62.

The final ensemble combined 14 two-stage XGBoost models with seven online models. The key choice was using the second half of training data for base learners and the first half for the meta learner. Base predictions came from random forests, SGDClassifier, online logistic regression, and XGBoost, with XGBoost providing the meta classifier. The best single model scored 0.0043835 publicly and 0.0044595 privately; several additional ensemble and structured prediction ideas did not help.

solution_title: 🏅 37st Place Solution: Self Prompt Tuning with DINOv3
solution_summary: The final model kept DINOv3 frozen and trained task tokens, prompt tokens, and target-specific regression heads using token embeddings plus pooled patch statistics. Target-informed initialization, Gram Schmidt orthogonalization, and an orthogonality loss maintained distinct token representations. Random multi-crop training averaged independent predictions, and full-data training used cross-validation training loss to determine duration. Inference combined tiled crops, geometric flip augmentation, and multiple checkpoints from one training run; reported leaderboard scores reached approximately 0.75.

The author pursued computational efficiency with an LSTM model operating on raw game events without manual feature engineering. Two LSTMs separately processed user interactions and conversations, using categorical embeddings and elapsed-time differences between consecutive actions. Optimizations improved five-fold cross-validation from 0.698 to 0.700 and the public leaderboard score from 0.701 to 0.703. All private leaderboard submissions scored below 0.69, an unexplained generalization drop.

The solution used a WaveNet-based neural network with random-forest probabilities as additional inputs. Signal cleaning and augmentation mattered more than model tuning, with signal flipping and random shifts improving generalization. Models trained on different synthetic datasets were compared using out-of-fold scores on the same original, non-synthetic data. One submission blended two models and achieved 0.94529 private, while another modified the seventh test batch using a separate reduced-signal model and channel restoration.

The solution combined three neural networks, XGBoost, yunbase version 21, and a collection of XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost models through weighted integration. Feature engineering and parameter tuning improved the neural network, while weighting difficult samples helped address challenging cases. The author reported neural network scores of 0.6837 CV, 0.688 public LB, and 0.691 private LB in the prose. Embeddings, attention, GNN modifications, and alternative losses did not improve performance, and additional combination features were ineffective for the tree models.

The pipeline combined a pretrained Bengali speech recognition model, a six-gram KenLM language model, and a punctuation restoration model. ASR training used several speech datasets, stronger augmentation for read speech, and removal of samples with the highest fitted word error rates. Chunked inference handled long recordings, while external Bengali text corpora supported language modeling. Punctuation restoration used an IndicBERTv2 backbone with an LSTM head and an ensemble of three models.

solution_summary: The solution used seven ImageNet-pretrained CNN regressors to predict multimodal trajectories and their confidences from rasterized scenes. Long training on the full dataset, suitable optimization parameters, and extensive raster caching mattered more than more elaborate prediction architectures. A Set Transformer combined candidate trajectories into three outputs by optimizing a confidence-weighted ensemble loss directly on validation or test predictions. Predictions from a 16-mode model contributed to this loss but were excluded from transformer inputs. Rasterization and caching improvements reduced CPU load by roughly sixfold, while the transformer ensemble improved loss by about 0.2 over numerical optimization.
compute: Each CNN trained about 5–7 days on one GPU: 2080 Ti or 3090 for larger models; cached full-dataset samples occupied around 1.3 TB.

solution_summary: The solution normalizes signals and averages over time to form 360 by 360 inputs, improving CV and leaderboard scores by about 0.02 over power spectrograms. Generating balanced synthetic samples with signal depth uniformly distributed between 10 and 100 was the most important improvement, supporting a single-model leaderboard score of 0.761. The ensemble primarily uses ConvNeXt-XLarge, with NFNet and EfficientNet variants, strong augmentation, and leaderboard-based weights. Validation keeps corresponding noise and signal pairs together, while segmentation-based alternatives were abandoned because training was unstable.

The solution emphasized cleaner training labels, manually selecting and relabeling ten-second segments from recordings with secondary labels. Its final rank ensemble combined four sound-event-detection models with a separately trained ProtoSSM plus MLP model. Perch v2 and BirdSet-based distillation, tuned mel spectrograms, checkpoint soups, and sampled pseudo-label data supported the neural models. Nighttime-aware mixup and rare-class oversampling addressed data distribution issues, and the additional ProtoSSM model reportedly improved the score by about 0.005.

The solution first constructed strong horizontal-photo subsequences and joined them using vertical photos. Remaining vertical photos were paired using a modified, vectorized method with penalties for selected slide sizes, adding about 60 points. The resulting slides were inserted and rearranged using the same subsequence-building procedure, followed by segment reversals to improve the score. The final score was 443363 against an estimated theoretical maximum of about 443400, with a runtime of roughly 40 minutes.
compute: Runtime approximately 40 minutes.

solution_title: 2nd place solution: SED + CNN with 7 models ensemble
solution_summary: The solution ensembled seven SED and CNN models trained on current and historical competition recordings plus additional xeno-canto data. Training combined extensive audio augmentation, label-based sampling weights, and pretraining on 834 species before fine-tuning on the 264 target species. Cross-entropy training generally preceded binary cross-entropy training, with varied clip lengths and mixup rates providing diversity. OpenVINO reduced inference time by about 40%, enabling the seven-model ensemble. Weighted raw-logit averaging achieved public/private scores of 0.84/0.76, outperforming the rank-based alternative.

solution_summary: The author selected two submissions to hedge between public-score throughput and survival against an unknown guardrail. The surviving submission used marker-free CONFUSED_DEPUTY candidates with two messages, exact email argument keys, and a clean final continuation request. Static SDK analysis and local checks guided predicate eligibility, message ordering, recipient choices, and scoring behavior. The public-optimized submission scored 136.250 publicly but zero privately, while the hedge scored 24.360 privately. Keeping a fixed recipient sacrificed distinct-cell bonuses, which the author identifies as a mistake.

solution_summary: The final approach fine-tuned LLaDA-8B for ARC and recursively refined grid predictions through soft masking and continuous token embeddings. It replaced one-dimensional positional encoding with a two-dimensional scheme and used a separate model to predict output shape. An earlier autoregressive approach used task-specific adaptation, speculative decoding, and augmentation-based candidate scoring before being superseded. The selected diffusion submission scored 21.67% publicly and 16.53% privately; another hyperparameter selection achieved 19.17% on both.

solution_summary: The final pipeline combined attention-head embeddings from nine fine-tuned transformers and trained a Gaussian process regressor on their concatenated out-of-fold representations. The regressor reduced overconfident predictions in the small-data setting and achieved public and private scores of 0.448. Transformer training used stratified five-fold validation, masked-language-model pretraining for selected models, stochastic weight averaging, and selective removal of transformer dropout. Pseudo-labeling improved an alternative submission to a private score of 0.446, but those models were excluded because their public scores were worse.

solution_title: 3rd Place Solution — Feature Engineering and Logistic Regression Stacking
solution_summary: The final solution stacked 115 prediction columns with L2-regularized logistic regression on clipped logit predictions. Diverse tree and neural models benefited from cross-fitted target encodings, income rounding, original-data statistics, and soft pseudo-labels. Income tokenizer groups and features from a source-trained DistilGPT-2 added useful diversity. The ensemble achieved 0.946717 CV and 0.94584 private AUC, although later stacking experiments reused historical OOF predictions and were not fully nested.

solution_summary: The pipeline reconstructed PDF text using font sizes, then extracted DOI links and accession identifiers from PDF structures and regular expressions. It filtered ambiguous identifiers with Qwen and DOI prefixes using metadata obtained through the DOI API. Classification contexts incorporated mention frequency, table references, and extracted author names. Separate Qwen models handled DOI and accession classification, while several context expansions, verifiers, and ensemble approaches were rejected after reducing public scores.

solution_title: 1st place solution [segmentation with partly U-NET and ensembling part]
solution_summary: The solution combined 3D segmentation networks with MONAI object detectors, training from scratch without external or simulated data. The segmentation approach used a partial U-Net with single-pixel targets on its penultimate feature map and strongly weighted cross-entropy. Seven experiment-based folds supported threshold calibration, while rank-based distribution matching made segmentation and detection feature maps compatible for blending. JIT or TensorRT export accelerated inference enough to support a larger ensemble.

solution_title: Linear Regression Is All you Need (9th solution week 4)
solution_summary: The submitted solution blended simple linear models for cases and fatalities, using log-space relationships to capture epidemic trends. Cases combined an autoregressive model with a model designed to capture curve flattening, with weights adapted to historical case counts. Fatalities combined regressions on lagged cases, past log fatalities, and past log cases. Time-based validation guided the approach, and a post-deadline change using more recent case information achieved a private score of 0.41840.

solution_title: 10th Place Solution: A Compass, Not a Map
solution_summary: The solution generated geological trajectory candidates using structural priors, particle filtering, and HMM inference, then combined them with neural stratigraphic-position estimates through a learned selector. A TCN and an additional U-Net corrected the resulting trajectory, with disagreement-dependent blending and a heel-anchored gain providing final improvements. Paired OOF evaluation across 773 wells supported a final CV score of 5.7189, while the selected submission scored 6.269 privately. A strong local gain from nearby-well anchoring was rejected after evidence of poor public transfer, although that rejected variant later scored better privately.

solution_title: 12th Place Solution: Linear Regression + XGBoost for Residuals
solution_summary: The solution modeled sales trends with linear regression and learned residual effects with XGBoost. Product-specific sine and cosine features captured annual cycles for most products and two-year cycles for Kaggle and Kaggle Tiers, with a logarithmic target transformation supporting the regression formulation. The model also represented relative GDP, store effects, weekends, and holidays. Imputing missing Kenya Holographic Goose sales was a major improvement, while inaccurate forecasts for 2018 and 2019 hurt private evaluation performance.

The team ensembled sound event detection models using SE-ResNeXt and EfficientNet backbones, with five folds per backbone and 30 epochs per run. Both primary and secondary labels were used, while the backbones saw different five-second audio segments and used different seeds. Audio and image augmentations, CutMix, Mixup, and cosine learning-rate schedules supported training. Focal loss with alpha 0.75 and gamma 5 delivered a major improvement and better validation-to-leaderboard agreement; the ensemble threshold was 0.25.
compute: Trained in Google Colab notebooks; five folds per backbone and 30 epochs per run.

solution_summary: The core pipeline used YOLOv9 to locate key points and extract patches, followed by a Siamese network for severity classification. Random patch pairs supplied similarity labels, and a custom cosine similarity loss trained the embeddings. Inference compared each patch against diverse reference images, averaged similarities by class, and normalized the scores into probabilities. The author also used an ensemble containing single-stage multitask models and a sagittal T2 volume approach.

The team ensembled RoBERTa and ELECTRA models with varied pooling heads, pretraining choices, and layer reinitialization. Differential learning rates, gradient accumulation, and reinitializing the last five layers helped fine-tuning. One submission used forward selection on out-of-fold predictions to combine 14 models, while another used leaderboard-based weights. Both achieved a private score of 0.458; external-data pretraining and embedding-based stacking were unsuccessful.
compute: Kaggle Kernels and Google Colab using seven accounts for experiments.

solution_summary: The solution combines a 1D U-Net with a GRU, using raw enmo, absolute angle changes, and contextual time and sensor flags. Event targets mix broad and narrow Gaussian heatmaps to balance training stability with accuracy at different tolerances. Training uses random 12-hour samples, binary cross entropy, AdamW, and stochastic weight averaging, while inference processes entire series. A 120-model ensemble feeds smoothing and candidate extraction designed to retain multiple possible events per night.
compute: Approximately 18 minutes for full test processing, including 45 seconds of model inference; 120-model ensemble completed within 120 minutes.

solution_summary: The solution filtered prediction features by their value ranges and Spearman correlation with the target. It applied isotonic calibration and trained with AutoGluon. Feature removal based on expected calibration error and experiments with FLAML did not work. The author emphasized trusting local cross-validation and the usefulness of calibration and stacking.

solution_title: 246th Place (Silver): Report Labels Are Not Expert Labels
solution_summary: The final pipeline rank-blended public Raptor, R6 and S6fall models with per-finding weights and flip augmentation. Its main original contribution subtracted cross-compartment OA ranks to reduce excessive coupling inherited from report-derived labels. Independent OAI expert reads supported the correction before submission, while leaderboard feedback guided its strength. Both final submissions achieved 0.944 private AUC, and none of the team's own trained models remained in the final blend.

solution_title: 13th Place Solution: Using Positive Examples from Other Rules as Negative Exampl
solution_summary: The approach trained on positive and negative examples from the public test set and augmented 30% of examples by assigning different rules and negative labels. The ensemble combined quantized Qwen3 models with DeBERTa models, withholding additional data from DeBERTa-small because it hurt ensemble performance. Qwen3-8B achieved a private score of 0.923. Experiments also explored reinforcement learning and synthetic rule-specific examples, with mixed results.

solution_summary: This post outlines the neural-network component of a broader solution containing four neural networks and several XGBoost models. Denoising autoencoders learned interactions among numerical, categorical, text, and image features using both training and test data. The learned encoder was then reused with a classification head, with image features also supplied directly to that head. Input-feature dropout helped control overfitting and encouraged reconstruction of missing information from other modalities.

The solution combined a full-data regression model with two specialist regressors trained on subsets defined by predicted outlier probability. A binary classifier split cards at probability 0.015, and its predictions together with full-regression predictions were central features for the high-probability model. Feature selection reduced thousands of candidates to about one hundred, including two-stage target encodings aggregated from transactions to cards with less weight on earlier month lags. The final prediction blended the specialist outputs with the full regression, while model decisions relied on local cross-validation.

solution_title: 1st Place Solution for the Vesuvius Challenge - Surface Detection Competition
solution_summary: The solution used weighted four-model nnU-Net ensembles trained with different patch sizes and fine-tuning schedules. It fused post-softmax probabilities and applied extensive geometric mask repair to remove small components, close holes, patch sheet gaps, and fill cavities. Post-processing raised the best ensemble's private score from 0.596 to 0.627. The authors also found that public-score-driven choices of probability fusion and thresholds were inferior on the private evaluation, while touching sheets remained unresolved.

The solution trained separate LightGBM models for pitchers, batters, and players without 2021 playing time, using role-specific performance features. Training and validation were restricted to in-season data and excluded 2020. Features described daily league activity, game popularity, season progress, and player performance at daily, season, and previous-season scales. Two chronological validation schemes supplied parameter sets for retraining, and final submissions blended their predictions with reciprocal 0.7/0.3 weights. Target lags were omitted because they reduced validation accuracy for pitcher and batter models.

The tracker combined flow-based 3D nucleus detection, pseudo-label refinement, learned linking and division models, and global integer linear programming. Biology-derived features and a learned per-node division cost produced the largest individual improvement, adding 0.035. Out-of-fold training and cross-embryo validation supported the stacked models, while track verification, smoothing, and gap bridging cleaned the output. The final public/private scores were 0.969/0.962, with the full pipeline running in about 30 minutes on two T4 GPUs.
compute: 2 × T4; approximately 30 minutes for four visible movies; gradient-boosted models run on CPU.

solution_title: Guardrail Archaeology: Reconstructing a Hidden Defense from Code and Commits
solution_summary: The author used public implementation details, release history, and controlled proxy tests to predict which attacks would transfer to the hidden guardrail. The selected attacks targeted conditional draft authorization and a mismatch between action-time authorization and final-turn evaluation. They scored 21.230 and 18.915 privately, closely matching their public results. Literal-marker exfiltration attacks scored much higher publicly but all failed privately, supporting the decision to prioritize authorization failures.

solution_summary: The author ultimately used a random forest with engineered features and selection focused on reducing overfitting. Insights from a disclosed train-test relationship led to removing earthquakes 5 and 6 because their split reflected a different stress threshold. The author also reduced the training weight of short earthquakes to account for a train-test distribution mismatch. Extensive RNN experimentation was abandoned, and computationally expensive Matrix Profile statistics offered little benefit.

The author adapted a public multi-model image matching baseline by tuning ALIKED and LightGlue parameters. The final configuration used 8192 features, a detection threshold of 0.005, at least 100 matches, and resizing to 1500. Image pair shortlisting used a similarity threshold of 0.08. These changes improved the public score by 0.01 and private score by 0.0018; the tested TTA alternative did not outperform 8192 features.

The author submitted a PolyBERT regression model and an ensemble combining PolyBERT with ChemBERTa. The approach used official and competition-shared data, runtime molecular augmentation, separate scaling for each target, and pooled transformer outputs feeding a regression head. Training used mean squared error with missing labels masked, while predictions were clipped to physically or mathematically valid ranges. Attempts at label balancing, learned target scaling, pseudo-labeling, and tabular modeling did not improve sufficiently to enter the final approach.

The author described solutions to several capture-the-flag challenges using model probing, serialization behavior, OCR-mediated XML injection, and adversarial attacks. Single-pixel probes exposed class activation patterns, while matching MobileNetV2 weights enabled accurate reproduction of a challenge model. For the passphrase challenge, a sentiment-score search combined a carefully chosen initialization with equal-length words and an NLTK vocabulary sweep. The author reported reaching 24 challenges, while Hush, CIFAR, and Granny 3 remained unsolved.

The described portion combined whole-video predictions, three five-frame models, and a label-conditioned localization network. The five-frame models comprised one DBoF and two VLAD networks pretrained on the previous year's sequences and fine-tuned on current annotated fragments. An LSTM localization model processed frame sequences concatenated with target-label embeddings while masking unannotated frames. Weighted geometric combination produced fragment scores, and the team's final submission used a ranked-sum ensemble with the teammate's contribution.

The solution generated search queries from CPC codes and title words using document frequencies. Tokens were scored by their frequency among neighboring patents divided by their global document frequency, and the top 25 were joined with OR. Experiments with code pairs yielded only a small score improvement, with final inclusion unspecified. Applying the same approach to claims, abstracts, and descriptions failed, possibly because it ignored repeated occurrences within documents.

solution_title: From Soundtracks & Signatures to Stars & Galaxies: Ali Hassaïne and Eu Jin Lok on finishing third on the Mapping Dark Matter Challenge
solution_summary: The team predicted galaxy ellipticity with a linear fit over a large collection of diverse image features. Morphological operations used structuring elements derived from star images, followed by quadrupole moment measurements. Geometrical descriptors inspired by handwriting and signature analysis added further signals from thresholded galaxy and star images. The implementation used C++ and OpenCV.

The solution combined 29 models into four local ensembles and averaged those ensembles equally. All models used 512-pixel inputs, with diversity supplied by architectures, training losses, augmentation, and ensemble construction. The author's FastAI models used staged unfreezing, while the PyTorch models used extra training data, bi-tempered loss, and mixed augmentation techniques. Public pretrained competition models and test-time augmentation further expanded the ensemble.

solution_title: General Intelligence - Open source framework for structural pattern learning (my ARC approach)
solution_summary: The author describes an unfinished ARC reasoning approach released after missing the competition deadline. The General Intelligence framework uses active, self-organizing knowledge for structural pattern learning. It is described as interpretable, compositional, and able to work with tiny datasets, but no measured competition results are provided.

solution_title: A ConvNet for Kaggle Statoil/C-CORE Iceberg Classifier Challenge
solution_summary: The solution uses a ConvNet with separate metadata and two-channel radar image inputs. Its augmentation pipeline supports HH and HV images directly and applies flips, rotations, shifts, and zooms. The author reports scores around 0.194–0.205+ and suggests further training and optimizer tuning as possible improvements.

The team combined improved GPS baseline positions and inter-point displacements with post-processing and averaging. The baseline work filtered poor pseudoranges, smoothed them with carrier-phase measurements, and used Doppler measurements to bridge short carrier-phase interruptions. Satellite uncertainty adjustments and removal of suspected multipath measurements helped, particularly in downtown areas. Reference-based differential positioning failed, while self-relative positioning and satellite coordinate corrections did not provide the hoped-for gains.

The solution combined diverse recurrent and convolutional text networks with LightGBM and XGBoost models using extensive engineered features. Frozen pretrained embeddings and a locally trained FastText embedding supplied complementary text representations, with FastText also imputing missing embeddings. Eight-fold out-of-fold predictions supported fold-specific HillClimb weighting and nonlinear XGBoost stacking. The final blend weighted HillClimb and the stacker 4:1, with neural networks contributing 54% and boosted trees 46%.

solution_summary: The solution uses XGBoost with varied feature combinations and 10-fold training predictions. Features include row statistics, manifold representations, and class-specific distance distribution percentiles. Previous model predictions are also reused as features, and a genetic algorithm selects an ensemble with replacement. The author monitors new submissions against the best existing submission as a proxy for overfitting and reports a leaderboard score of 0.40327.

The team treated landmark recognition as instance search because classes had limited internal variation and were numerous. A kNN classifier combined global CNN descriptors with geometric matching of local features. They learned GeM descriptors on the competition training set and used DELF features with ASMK indexing for geometric verification.

solution_summary: The approach reranks the base model's top-five text-span candidates with a model that predicts each candidate's Jaccard score. A RoBERTa-base model takes sentiment, tweet, and candidate text as input and is trained with mean squared error against measured Jaccard scores. The final ranking score adds the predicted Jaccard score to the average of the base model's softmax start and end scores. Reranking improved cross-validation and private leaderboard scores by 0.003–0.005, with public leaderboard gains of 0.001–0.003.

solution_title: 20th Place Solution; XLM-Rs, xtune, hacky postprocessing
solution_summary: The solution ensembled nine XLM-RoBERTa-large question-answering models built using five training recipes. Diversity came from alternative prediction heads, multilingual external QA datasets, additional MLM pretraining, and staged fine-tuning. Five-fold language-stratified validation supported early stopping and seed selection. Postprocessing converted eligible Hindi numerals to Arabic digits, favored earlier answer spans, and penalized spans near chunk boundaries. The ensemble scored 0.811 on the public leaderboard and 0.755 on the private leaderboard.

solution_title: 98th place: Cell tracking with a LightGBM division classifier

A small neural head predicted bounded coordinate shifts from local decoder features, and its output was averaged equally with a second head. A LightGBM classifier replaced fixed division rules using 19 geometric, tracking, and network-derived features. The coordinate ensemble raised the private score to 0.921, and the division classifier at threshold 0.01 raised it to 0.929; several locally promising changes failed to transfer.

solution_summary: The final prediction averaged four similar Keras networks combining Dense and bidirectional GRU processing with WaveNet and Dense classification layers. Inputs included Gaussian-mixture signal encodings, segment-group features, and stacked predictions from random forest and histogram gradient boosting classifiers. Automatic sinusoidal drift removal and exclusion of outliers in training batch 8 supported the pipeline. Training used Adam, stochastic weight averaging, and a one-cycle schedule, with checkpoints selected by validation F1. Five-fold validation balanced batches and used a seed chosen for similar target distributions across folds.

solution_summary: The final system combined eight U-Net and FPN segmentation models with EfficientNet-B5, SE-ResNeXt50, and InceptionV4 encoders. Single-channel adaptation of pretrained weights, larger batches, and carefully sampled ensemble pseudo-labels helped training. Predictions used horizontal-flip TTA, minimum defect-area thresholds, and per-pixel conflict resolution. RMS averaging improved the public score but reduced the final private score to 0.90274; rerunning the ensemble with arithmetic averaging scored 0.90975. An abandoned classifier-based threshold adjustment produced the author's best private score of 0.91023.
