solution_title: A User Customized WAF solution - ADD your message !
solution_summary: The author presents a WAF challenge solution that constructs a Shellshock-style payload invoking Bash with a customizable message. The payload is Base64-encoded and submitted as the input field of a JSON request to the scoring endpoint. The code prints the server response, but the writeup provides no score or confirmation of success.

solution_title: 11th place solution (with updated code on github)
solution_summary: The pipeline converted DICOM slices into three channels using brain, blood/subdural, and soft-tissue windows, with metadata corrections for erroneous intercepts. ImageNet-pretrained SE-ResNeXt-50 and SE-ResNeXt-101 models were trained across eight folds, with pixel-offset augmentation, five-way TTA, and averaging of predictions from two epochs. A second-level ensemble used each slice's predictions alongside predictions from nine neighboring slices on either side. Averaging LightGBM, CatBoost, and XGBoost predictions improved the first-stage public score, with immediate neighbors providing the strongest contextual features.

The author selected an XGBoost model after testing several model families and searching feature subsets with five-fold CV. Predicting the log1p-transformed target improved results compared with predicting the raw target. Optuna followed by manual tuning improved the hyperparameters, and adding original data improved both CV and public leaderboard performance. The team's predictions were ultimately combined through a weighted average.

solution_title: 1st place solution: everyone can be a winner!
solution_summary: The author describes the approach as a modified version of their winning solution from two years earlier. The only stated change is an experiment with pseudo-labeling. The post links to the earlier solution but gives no further pipeline details or results for the modification.

The authors identify field-aware factorization machines as a powerful model in their Avazu and Criteo CTR competition work. They provide links to their competition code and supporting document. They also release LIBFFM to make the model available for use on other datasets, but the post gives no feature engineering, validation, or training details.

The solution fine-tuned a single Nemotron model with LoRA on compact reasoning traces generated by deterministic symbolic teachers across nine task categories. The largest gains came from matching the bit-manipulation teacher to the underlying rotate-and-shift structure and improving numerical-operator inference using corpus statistics. Training emphasized fragile examples through duplication and targeted demonstrations, while validation compared model accuracy with teacher accuracy. The selected full-training run achieved 0.880 on the private leaderboard, with teacher coverage and trace learnability identified as the main limitations.

solution_title: 8th place solution - a densely connected GNN
solution_summary: The core solution was a custom graph neural network built around SchNet interactions, using one model across all coupling types. It added richer edge and molecule features, edge updates, dense connections, squeeze-and-excitation blocks, and a deep stack of interactions. Training used molecule-grouped cross-validation, inverse-frequency-weighted log-MAE, Adam, and cyclic cosine scheduling. The final blend combined differently configured versions of this network with a small MegNet contribution and optimized blending by coupling type, achieving a private score of -3.001.
compute: GTX1080Ti; optimized starter MPNN from 15 minutes to 90 seconds per epoch; graph preprocessing took 40 minutes.

solution_summary: The solution ensembled three MixNet models predicting either three or six possible future trajectories. Performance depended on sample filtering, extensive training data, and raster inputs containing irregularly spaced history frames, semantic maps, traffic-light history, and available future-frame information. Training used Adam, learning-rate decay, and auxiliary velocity and yaw targets. A custom confidence-weighted fixed-point optimization reduced twelve candidate trajectories to three, producing a public score of 11.788 and validation score of 11.61.
compute: Best MixNet-L trained on 34.4M samples: 215 epochs × batch size 64 × 2500 iterations; ensemble optimization ran on GPU.

solution_summary: SSD-generated bounding boxes for the cervical os provided the largest improvement, using annotations supplied by Paul. The final ensemble combined VGG-19, Xception, ResNet50, and InceptionV3 models through linear regression with three-fold cross-validation. VGG-19 with seven frozen layers and Xception with two frozen layers were strongest, while weaker models added a small ensemble benefit. A separate submission incorporating leak features performed much worse, and the whole pipeline took five days on a GTX 970.
compute: GTX 970; five days for the whole pipeline; strongest two models took 1.5 and 2 days each.

solution_summary: The solution combined target-specific spectral preprocessing with small neural networks. Spectra were low-pass filtered, decimated by eight, and reduced by removing uninformative features; the first four targets additionally used differences, centering, and variance-based feature scaling. MATLAB neural networks with two hidden layers were trained using Levenberg–Marquardt optimization. Averaging 100 models across repeated five-fold cross-validation stabilized otherwise noisy validation errors.

The solution adapted the Center-Resnet starter with mask and position inputs, focal-loss heatmaps, and revised regression targets. It predicted image-plane offsets and log depth, and doubled regression loss weights to improve balance with heatmap learning. Position jitter, Gaussian noise, and brightness and contrast augmentation supported training, while masks suppressed invalid predictions. The final submission scored 0.086 on the private leaderboard; several changes failed to improve results, and a locally promising head modification was discarded based on its public score.

The final submission combined EfficientNet-B7 with an average of EfficientNet-B6 and Inception-ResNet-v2, giving B7 half the total weight. Larger images, Noisy Student weights, training without a validation holdout, and horizontal and vertical flips were the main successful choices. The featured submission achieved a private score of 0.978 and a public score of 0.982. Several additional augmentations and regularization experiments provided little benefit or worsened results.

The solution used a two-stage workflow with LightGBM models followed by optimized linear blending of submissions. First-stage training used shuffled stratified folds, early stopping, out-of-fold predictions, and averaged test predictions. Preprocessing and hyperparameter optimization were implemented as separate reusable components, with predictions saved for later blending. Cross-validation metrics guided the blend optimization.

The final pipeline used 36 tiles of 256×256 pixels per slide, with transpose and flip augmentation applied both to individual tiles and concatenated inputs. EfficientNet B0 and B1 models were trained with Adam, gradual warmup, and cosine annealing. Inference combined 32 test-time augmentations across two tile-generation modes and ensembled B0 fold 0 with B1 folds 0 and 1. Tile resolution, test-time augmentation, and fold selection based on agreement between cross-validation and leaderboard scores mattered most; removing white space reduced training loss without improving quadratic weighted kappa.
compute: GPU limitations restricted model size; inference TTA was constrained by the competition's submission runtime limit of under 9 hours.

solution_summary: The performance solution blended public notebook predictions with a DeBERTa-v3-xsmall model trained on reconstructed essays. Common anonymized words were added to its tokenizer, and its first six layers were frozen while token embeddings remained trainable. The efficiency solution combined five model families across five folds and reduced feature loading costs through feature selection. Validation used alternating half-data holdouts around five-fold training; post-processing attempts did not work well.
compute: Efficiency ensemble inference ran in under 2 minutes.

solution_summary: The solution blends nine ArcFace embedding models and matches topics to content using cosine similarity. Text inputs are supplemented with topic ancestry and content text to compensate for missing or weak descriptions. Seven models use topic-based labels and two use content-based labels, providing complementary predictions. Threshold tuning and several matching heuristics refine the output, while second-stage text and LightGBM models were dropped. A separate efficient two-model submission achieved 0.72 in 22 minutes using shorter inputs, multiprocessing and ONNX.
compute: Separate efficiency submission: two smaller models with shorter token lengths, 22 minutes inference using multiprocessing and ONNX.

solution_title: 2nd Place Solution (One model is all you need) - Team Ujjwal Pandey
solution_summary: After extensive experiments with boosted trees and neural networks, the author settled on an ensemble of CatBoost models. Newton-based scoring, a lower learning rate with longer training, duplicate removal, and feature binning improved validation performance. Models trained with different splits and random states were averaged using validation scores, followed by a community trick whose mechanics were not described. The final submission scored 0.89788 publicly and 0.89753 privately.
compute: Tuning used 2 P100s, one Colab L4, and one local RTX 4070; CatBoost tuning took about 10 hours and a fold required about 48 GB RAM after training.

solution_summary: The agent combines a tested Rust simulator and feature pipeline with a Python deep reinforcement learning system. Extensive hidden-state inference and ten-observation histories feed a residual CNN with squeeze-excitation layers, trained using PPO. At inference, it averages policies across symmetry transformations and samples actions stochastically. The final ten-million-parameter model trained for approximately 300 million game steps over eight days; a vision transformer alternative showed promise but had unstable training.
compute: AMD Ryzen 9950X (16 cores/32 threads), 64GB RAM, RTX 3090 and RTX 2070 Super; final model approximately 8 days and 300 million game steps, at 430 steps/second.

solution_summary: The solution combined ensembles of four NFFM submissions, seven LightGBM models, and seven embedding neural networks using weights of 0.25, 0.5, and 0.25 respectively. LightGBM relied on filtered categorical values, frequency encodings, update-date differences, and disk-capacity features, with choices supported by time-split validation. The neural network compressed embeddings within semantic variable groups before combining them with numerical features. The final ensemble achieved a reported public leaderboard score of 0.707, while the LightGBM pipeline reached 0.718 validation AUC.
compute: Seven LightGBM models: 50 CPU hours; seven neural networks: 50 GPU hours. One neural network took 7 hours on a Kaggle Tesla P100 GPU.

solution_summary: The solution learns features with spherical k-means on whitened patches extracted convolutionally from contrast-normalized spectrograms. Max-pooled features feed several classifiers, with random forests performing best. Fast experimentation enabled random search over spectrogram, patch, and normalization settings. Predictions from several of the best models were averaged.

solution_title: What worked for me -- and by how much
solution_summary: The solution blended six tuned LightGBM, XGBoost, and CatBoost models built around chains of residual regressors. Restricting each regressor's features aimed to capture calendar patterns without introducing absolute-date interactions that would generalize poorly. Day-of-year and day-of-week features produced the largest measured gains, followed by a two-year cycle and annual baseline normalization. Most 2020 training data was excluded, and log targets, repeated residual fitting, and holiday features added smaller gains; shop normalization was retained despite a slightly negative final ablation.

solution_title: 13th Place Solution – Mean Co-Teachers and Noisy Students
solution_summary: The author addressed missing audio labels through progressive pseudo labeling across three training stages. Mean Teacher models with a ResNet34 sound event detector generated initial out-of-fold pseudo labels, and DenseNet121 co-teaching models filtered noisy pseudo labels while preserving provided labels. A final stage used stronger augmentation and heavy spectrogram mixup, reaching 0.940 public score with five folds. A geometric-mean ensemble of roughly 90 models increased the public score to 0.943.
compute: Final-stage training: 80 epochs; preceding two stages: approximately 32 epochs each.

solution_title: Completes but scores blank — and why our 90-point attack scored private zero
solution_summary: The public approach optimized single-message sentinel exfiltration through replay overfill, live candidate filling, and control tokens that reduced reasoning overhead. Experiments showed that throughput and evaluator structure dominated performance, while multi-call fanout reduced scores. The selected finals also included a marker-free confused-deputy email strategy as a private hedge. The exfiltration leg fell from 89.945 publicly to zero privately, while the selected email leg transferred from 14.460 to 14.685.
compute: Companion notebooks run on a CPU kernel without GPU or internet.

solution_summary: The author trained LightGBM models using summary statistics of raw signals and FFT-denoised signals. A second variant incorporated peak-width features from the host's papers. Both submissions achieved a private score of 0.694 despite public scores of 0.365 and 0.511. Local cross-validation scores were 0.63991 and 0.67035, illustrating substantial disagreement between public evaluation and the other estimates.

The solution ensembled eight DenseNet-201 and EfficientNet-B7 models trained across two validation splits and two repeated runs per architecture. It used 512×512 images, blockout and horizontal-flip augmentation, pretrained weights, and external flower data. Predictions were combined in logit space, with separately optimized architecture weights for original and flipped images. A final weighting between the two inference views achieved a validation F1 score of 0.970367.
models_pretrained: ["DenseNet-201 with ImageNet weights", "EfficientNet-B7 with Noisy Student weights"]
compute: TPU training; DenseNet runs used 35 and 50 epochs, EfficientNet runs used 35 and 40 epochs.

solution_summary: The author describes a learning-focused competition approach involving CatBoostRegressor and LGBMRegressor. Feature scaling and transformation selection are mentioned as techniques they aimed to explore, without implementation details. The post links a solution notebook but does not describe the final pipeline, validation, ensemble, or scores.

solution_title: [25th Place] DPC Solution: Contextual ByT5-Large Ensemble, Chunking, and MBR
solution_summary: The final system trained contextual ByT5-large on an adapted row-wise corpus plus a smaller full-sequence auxiliary corpus. The largest gains came from corpus construction and adapting generated translations to the compact style of the competition data. Inference split long transliterations with a learned chi-square chunker, supplied neighboring context, combined four checkpoints, and used MBR reranking and deterministic editing. Reported ablations attributed substantially more benefit to data adaptation than to ensembling or post-editing; the provided writeup ends during the training description.
external_data: ["OARE", "CDLI Old Assyrian tablets", "DPC - Larsen by MPWARE"]

solution_summary: The post humorously asks how many placement-based solution writeups are waiting for final results. It provides no competition approach or implementation details. No methods or results are described.

The solution added 512 features extracted by a shared 3D-ResNet10 to tabular inputs and used them across neural networks and retrained public models. A branched neural network separately processed loading, connectivity, and image features before predicting five targets. Target-specific loss weights were optimized with Optuna, and averaged neural predictions contributed to the final blend. Site detection enabled small site- and target-specific prediction multipliers, improving the score by about 0.0003; the final private score was 0.15729.

The solution engineered application-level features from auxiliary tables using recent time windows and subsets defined by approval and account status. More than 10,000 features were reduced through LightGBM importance rankings and random selection of remaining features, yielding about 500 features per model. Around 200 out-of-fold predictions fed a two-layer stack with diverse first-layer models and a LightGBM second layer, improving cross-validation from about 0.800 for the best single model to 0.803. Binary log loss performed better than AUC as the LightGBM evaluation metric.

solution_title: Why shouldn't you even consider using LB probing in Playground Competitions
solution_summary: The solution used shared five-fold out-of-fold predictions to guide a class-weighted tree ensemble, with small neural contributions for diversity. Fold-local exact-value target encoding and missingness augmentation addressed representation limits and concentrated errors in incomplete rows. Two final candidates used either constrained model-group blending or a 95% tree blend with 2.5% each from RealMLP and TabM. The simpler candidate scored 0.95060 privately, while all 176 fixed label-flipping tests reduced OOF balanced accuracy.

The post announces the release of the authors' competition solution and links to its GitHub repository. It says a PDF explains the model and notebooks contain the code. The supplied text contains no technical description of the approach or results.

The final prediction was a weighted average of variants from an autoencoder-pretrained GNN/attention/CNN family and a GRU/LSTM family. The author emphasized preprocessing, using multiple RNA folding engines to generate additional structures, loop types, and base-pair probability matrices. Features captured pairing strength, pair types, neighboring pairs, and entropy, alongside sample weighting and clustering-based validation. Training with padded 130-base sequences and reversed sequences provided little standalone improvement but helped the ensemble slightly, which achieved a private score of 0.34471.

The solution combined lab-specific XGBoost classifiers and convolutional neural networks, selecting the strongest cross-validated model for most labs. XGBoost used engineered pose, motion, interaction, metadata, and neighboring-frame features with action-specific thresholds. The neural network used masked, class-weighted training across all labs followed by lab-specific fine-tuning. Three labs instead used frame-wise majority voting across the three model variants.

The solution first predicted broad patient-level ROI crop coordinates with a DINOv3 ViT, retaining over 95% of annotated aneurysm locations. A CoaT-Lite-Medium classifier learned from localized positives and slices from negative patients despite severe imbalance. Rotation, neighboring-slice inputs, and soft pseudo-distillation improved performance, followed by an ensemble with MaxViT. Inference classified every slice and used maximum aggregation for patient predictions, reaching reported CV of 0.896 and private score of 0.84.
compute: Started with 14 days remaining; reached the reported gold medal threshold in 8 days.

solution_title: 4th place solution: Stacking with XGB + Pseudo labeling + metric optimizing.
solution_summary: The solution stacked diverse model probabilities alongside the original training features using an XGBoost meta-model. It combined competition and original data and used two feature-engineering pipelines with binning, transformations, encoding, and polynomial features. Base models included AutoXGB, AutoGluon, LightAutoML, and custom boosted-tree pipelines with and without pseudo-labeling. Training optimized log loss, followed by accuracy-oriented probability adjustment. Final predictions used a class vote across nine diverse prediction sets, including two public notebooks.

The team built a minimal SAINT+ encoder-decoder transformer using question metadata, aggregate accuracy and timing features, and shifted user responses. Quantile transformation of timing inputs improved convergence, while larger embeddings and a smaller learning rate improved results. The single model achieved AUC scores of 0.792 on CV, 0.793 publicly, and 0.795 privately. Ensembling it with a public LightGBM approach trained on the last 20–30 million rows added approximately 0.004, while ELO and FTRL received zero ensemble weights.
compute: Kaggle GPUs; 20–30 minutes per epoch and 5–6 hours per model. Four training runs exhausted a weekly GPU quota.

solution_summary: The solution centered on COCO-pretrained EfficientDet-D6 with default anchors and losses, extensive augmentation, and eight-way test-time augmentation fused with weighted boxes fusion. Validation used relative detection loss on a manually cleaned 20% stratified split. Features included aggregation statistics, feets outputs, regression coefficients, and custom peak-shape measurements. Concatenating noisy copies of the training data improved the score by about 0.04 and reduced the CV-to-leaderboard gap. Separate galaxy- and DDF-specific models fed additional stacks, which were combined through a weighted geometric average, with a community equation and minor leaderboard probing used for class 99.

solution_title: 3rd source code(To fulfill requirement of prize)
solution_summary: The post links to a separate competition solution discussion. It also provides a GitHub repository containing code. No methods, training details, or results are described in the supplied text.

The author used a standard scikit-learn support vector machine with default parameters and reported 89.6% AUC. Several classifier combinations were explored, and naive Bayes with Bernoulli priors performed better in cross-validation. Despite weaker cross-validation and midterm leaderboard results, the SVC performed substantially better on the actual dataset.

The solution used XLM-RoBERTa with an LSTM and max-pooling head, followed by an ensemble of these models. Popular comment templates helped identify bot comments. Language-specific offsets applied to prediction logits improved the final private score to 0.9482. The author considered the ensemble stage overfit and lacked a reliable cross-validation strategy.

The final submission combined eight candidate trajectories using a segment-wise dynamic ensemble that predicted model reliability with ExtraTrees and mixed adaptive weights with a global linear prior. V171 supplied residual corrections from a TCN–Transformer–TCN network over a particle-filter baseline, with smoothing-correction decomposition and spatial augmentation providing important improvements. Two GeoFM models contributed complementary trajectories by predicting local TVT rates and integrating them from the last known TVT, supported by geological cross-attention and masked-GR pretraining. Well-held-out validation showed that the dynamic ensemble reduced OOF RMSE from 6.0253 to 5.8795; its private leaderboard RMSE was 6.763.

The solution combines targeted feature engineering with LightGBM cross-validation. Weather data is included alongside the competition data. The short writeup provides setup instructions but does not describe the features or validation splits.

The solution fine-tuned BERT with an evidence-gathering module that pooled noisy signals from heuristic and pretrained coreference systems. Coreference clusters masked last-layer BERT embeddings before attention-based evidence aggregation and final classification. Augmentation targeted the underrepresented neither class, while label smoothing addressed annotation noise. Ensembles averaged folds, five seeds, cased and uncased language models, and alternative label-cleaning treatments; the two submitted variants differed in whether unsanitized-label models were included.
models_pretrained: ["BERT, cased and uncased", "Lee et al. coreference model"]

solution_title: One silver solution - XBM + Query Expansion + k-reciprocal
solution_summary: The solution learned image retrieval embeddings with a CGD head, MultiSimilarity loss, and Cross-Batch Memory, with EfficientNet-B4 identified in the final submission overview. Models were trained at 224×224 and fine-tuned at 512×512, while TF-IDF supplied useful text similarity. TF-IDF-weighted query expansion, image-distance filtering, and adding clear reciprocal neighbor sets progressively improved the reported leaderboard score to 74.4%. Five-fold validation used held-out queries against the entire dataset to better match leaderboard behavior.

The final solution ensembled a tabular neural network, a graph-based tabular learner, PyCaret models, RAPIDS SVM predictions, and other tabular models. The graph learner represented each patient with 53 nodes, using functional correlations as edge weights and atlas-derived spatial-map features as node inputs. Graph features were combined with functional connectivity and loading features before dense prediction layers. Multiplying ensembled age predictions by 1.01 provided an approximately 0.002 improvement.

The pipeline extracted transit boundaries and physics-based wavelength estimates, then trained neural networks to correct their residual errors and estimate uncertainty. A composite Gaussian process stabilized downstream predictions, although physics-derived uncertainty estimates were ineffective. Gradient boosting adjusted uncertainty scales separately for FGS and AIRS, improving the leaderboard score by about 0.01. Pseudo-labeling test residual predictions added approximately 0.004.

The post congratulates successful competitors and thanks the organizers and teammates. It invites participants to share their ideas, code, and reasoning. It mentions competition challenges but provides no concrete solution pipeline.

The solution ensembled BERT, XLM-R, and NB-SVM models trained with diverse datasets and training procedures. Translated multilingual data, pseudo-labeled test examples, pseudo-labeled OpenSubtitles, and MLM-adapted models supplied complementary predictions, with ensemble weights chosen through intuition and public leaderboard probing. Language-specific scaling and quantile-based score adjustment improved the prediction distribution across languages. Additional useful changes included a single extra dense layer and more balanced training data, while monolingual XLM-R and logistic-regression ensemble additions did not help.

solution_title: Learnings From the Competition ,  39th Place Solution
solution_summary: The final ensemble combined five-fold NFNet_l0 and two five-fold ResNeXt50 variants trained on seven-second mel spectrograms, with and without delta channels. RMS-based audio cropping and delta stacking helped, while sigmoid-level ensembling fed a post-processing layer that provided the largest improvement. Hardware and time constraints led to training on saved spectrograms without audio-level augmentation. An unselected submission scored 0.66 on the private leaderboard.
compute: Approximately 10 days available; attempted SED training required one hour per epoch and at least 35 epochs to converge.

solution_summary: The solution generated 754 features, including features describing individual rounds within game sessions. Removing duplicate and nearly identical variables left 649 features. Three cumulative binary LightGBM classifiers were trained with five-fold cross-validation, and their predictions plus assessment title fed a linear regression model. Final thresholds were optimized with Nelder–Mead initialized by a golden-section search, which generally outperformed either method alone.

solution_title: Kaggle TGS Salt Identification Challenge 2018 4th place code
solution_summary: The solution used several encoder-decoder segmentation networks with deep supervision and Lovasz softmax, trained across 10 folds and multiple cycles. Model and cycle predictions were combined by voting, then refined with handcrafted rules based on 2D and 3D jigsaw reconstruction. Pseudo-label training split test images into two halves, trained on one half while predicting the other, and balanced original and pseudo-labeled samples in minibatches. The final three-model pseudo-label ensemble with post-processing scored 0.887 publicly and 0.8953 privately.

The solution blended XGBoost, LightGBM, and generalized additive models using stratified cross-validation with four to ten folds. Log-transformed features and selected interaction features improved the inputs, while small boosting trees and manually tuned regularization controlled overfitting. Generalized additive models showed smaller training-to-validation loss gaps than boosted trees. Calibration was unnecessary in CV, and Random Forest, Extra Trees, and logistic regression attempts did not improve the final approach.

The solution combined neural networks, TabNet, per-target SVMs, and XGBoost using drug-aware multilabel validation. Features included summary statistics, CELL-only PCA, selected pairwise differences, and quantile transformation. A second stage averaged CNN stacking with an optimized weighted blend, achieving CV 0.01647 and private leaderboard loss 0.01600. Drug-ID-based label replacement slightly improved CV but worsened the private score.
compute: Training and inference were almost entirely performed on Kaggle kernels; hardware and runtime were unspecified.

solution_summary: The post announces that the leaderboard is finalized and links to a solution notebook. It says the solution summary is contained in the notebook rather than providing technical details in the post. The author also thanks the organizers and congratulates the winners.

The team blended five CQT image models with a waveform-based 1D CNN. They standardized signals using full-dataset statistics and added sum and difference channels from the LIGO signals. Waveform mixing, scaling augmentation, test-time augmentation, and soft pseudo-labels supported training and inference. Optimizing blend weights on out-of-fold predictions produced CV 0.8812 and private leaderboard score 0.8805.

solution_title: 6th Place Solution: An Attempt to Bet Responsibly
solution_summary: The author used a bookmaker-aligned goto-conversion baseline with all overrides removed. They then concentrated risk on two first-round games, favoring St. Mary’s over Vanderbilt and McNeese State over Clemson. Choosing one favorite and one underdog was intended to reduce correlation with other submissions while maximizing the probability of reaching a desired rank threshold. Risk magnitude was chosen intuitively rather than through a quantitative optimization.

The final solution used a two-level stack of 78 CatBoost, XGBoost, LightGBM, random forest, and ridge models, followed by a ridge regression meta-model. Both levels used 10-fold cross-validation, with shared folds across first-level models and saved fold predictions to construct the second-level data. Random parameter searches supplied diverse models that handled noise differently, while ridge regression accommodated their highly correlated predictions. The author trusted cross-validation over a stronger public leaderboard single model, achieving a cross-validated RMSE of 0.84159 and a public score of 0.84190.
compute: Around 36 hours across two machines: 3rd-generation Core i5 with 24 GB RAM, and Ryzen 5 3600X with 32 GB RAM and GTX 1060 GPU.

solution_summary: The solution ensembled five configurations of Hypercolumns U-Net with ResNet34 and EfficientNet-B7 backbones, each trained across four folds. Training used combined binary cross-entropy and Dice loss, cyclic learning-rate phases, and selection of the best Dice checkpoints; self-attention models added ensemble diversity despite weaker individual scores. Inference used horizontal-flip augmentation and connected-component filtering based on mean predicted probability. The reported final scores were 0.8568 in Stage 2 and 0.8763 in Stage 1.

The solution combined extensive feature engineering with diverse boosted trees and neural networks. More than 447 engineered features provided the largest improvement, while 11-fold cross-validation guided model selection. Predictions from multiple seeds and residual-focused models were stacked with logistic regression and combined through weighted blending. The final public leaderboard score was 0.97733; synthetic minority oversampling did not work.

solution_title: 13th place solution: Ensemble context ensemble model
solution_summary: The solution combined retrieval from two Wikipedia versions and a 270,000-item dataset with an ensemble of DeBERTaV3-Large models. Wikipedia retrieval used bge-small-en embeddings and sharded exact FAISS indexes, followed by TF-IDF reranking. Models predicted separately from three retrieved contexts and combined predictions using maximum probability. Retrieval had the largest reported impact, while index compression, PEFT, and a large Platypus model were unsuccessful.
compute: Rejected Platypus2-70B-instruct retrieval configuration exceeded nine hours during submission.

solution_summary: The solution relied heavily on categorical interactions, especially two-way and three-way combinations involving v22. Numerical rounding, reconstruction of integer-valued features, target-based categorical transformations, and grouped aggregate features supplied additional gains. The best single XGBoost model used more than 7,500 features and achieved a private score of 0.4242. The team also built models using different categorical representations and refined a 223-model ensemble into a second-level combination involving extra trees, neural networks, and XGBoost.
compute: Many CPU cores; quantity and runtime unspecified.

solution_summary: The pipeline prioritized image-pair recall before progressively removing false correspondences. DINOv2 pair filtering fed rotation-aware ALIKED and LightGlue matching at three resolutions, with DBSCAN-guided crops and RANSAC improving precision. COLMAP reconstructed scenes and estimated camera poses through incremental reconstruction and bundle adjustment. Balanced execution across two T4 GPUs reduced processing time, and the selected configuration scored 41.08 publicly and 44.69 privately.
compute: 2× T4 GPUs; workload balancing shortened some pipelines by up to about 15%.

solution_title: [3rd place solution with code] 17 layers squeezeformer with timerduce and ROPE
solution_summary: The solution used a Squeezeformer with rotary position encoding and temporal downsampling on landmark sequences resized to 320 frames. Inputs combined original and normalized coordinates with absolute position, while retaining frames without hands. Heavy temporal masking, stochastic depth, and adversarial weight perturbation supported training on competition and downweighted supplemental data, followed by competition-only fine-tuning. PyTorch accelerated experiments, and nobuco converted the model to Keras for deployment.
compute: 4090 GPU; PyTorch reported as 3–4 times faster than TensorFlow.

solution_summary: The author used Gemini to generate ranked misconception labels from question-answer target frequencies and training-fold examples. Ground truth was promoted to the first position in these rankings, which then served as decoder training targets. Qwen decoders encoded labels as separate special-character tokens and combined probability distributions from three output positions. The final ensemble combined three encoders with two Qwen3-4b-instruct-2507 decoders, one trained with Gemini labels; the added labels improved CV by about 0.0005 but slightly reduced the public leaderboard score.
compute: One Gemini pass over all training samples cost close to $100.

solution_summary: The solution focused on identifying related transaction sequences, treating fraud as a pattern across similar samples. Grouping keys used V307, device and identity information, card identifiers with adjusted D features, and amount with day and address. A two-stage modeling pipeline improved the score by about 0.001. Grouping the card-and-D key across training and test data together, followed by rule-based result processing, provided a substantial further gain, reaching a reported leaderboard score range of 0.9600–0.9630.

The author extended a public ECG digitization pipeline with high-resolution homography, refined grid detection, and rectification. Two cascaded heatmap CNNs refined grid points using manually labeled examples, with a reported validation localization error of 0.146 pixels for the second network. Signal extraction used doubled image width, subpixel soft labels, coordinate features, and a ten-seed ensemble. Final signals combined overlapping lead-II estimates and applied Einthoven error correction.

The solution fed LightGBM classifier probabilities into a LightGBM regressor to improve prediction diversity and essay scoring. Word and character count n-grams were combined with engineered quotation, spelling-error, and sentence vocabulary features. Feature-importance filtering and modest hyperparameter tuning supported consistent private scores around 0.823, with the selected solution scoring 0.82397. TF-IDF and a Bayesian-regression extension were explored but not retained for the main solution.
compute: Approximately 96 seconds for submission predictions; final leaderboard reported 114 seconds. Classifier inference took 9–10 seconds and regressor inference about 2 seconds.

solution_title: 1st Place Solution for the AIMO3 Competition
solution_summary: This research-based account describes an inference pipeline for GPT-OSS-120B on a single H100 using memory optimizations and coordinated reasoning. It combines shared-prefix caching, 8-bit KV caches, and entropy-weighted aggregation of parallel generations. Persistent Jupyter kernels execute generated code and return verification feedback, while adaptive scheduling manages the notebook deadline. The author emphasizes prompt quality and inference engineering but provides no quantitative competition result.
compute: Single NVIDIA H100 80GB GPU

solution_summary: The final approach used an EfficientNet B3 initialized with Noisy Student weights and three classification heads on original 137×236 images. Switching from cropped to uncropped images was a major improvement, followed by aggressive Mixup and Cutmix. Training used weighted cross-entropy, AdamW, a one-cycle schedule, and three final epochs without augmentation. The author trained five folds and reported a score of 0.985 with a small validation-to-leaderboard gap.

The pipeline retrieved 160 misconception candidates per question-answer pair and reranked them to select 25. It fine-tuned an SFR-Embedding-2_R retriever and a quantized Qwen 32B reranker with LoRA, using question-grouped cross-validation and downsampled negatives. The reranker scored candidates through forced Yes/No token probabilities, with vLLM prefix caching accelerating repeated prompts. Hard-example mining improved validation but not leaderboard results, while several alternative input and quantization approaches did not work.

The solution used gradient boosting on mostly raw forecast features without preprocessing. Each station received all 75 forecasts from its four nearest mesos, supplemented by month, distance, and latitude differences. Eleven models were trained, one per forecast member, and averaged to optimize MAE. Validation used three contiguous blocks of years.

The solution combined 2D CNNs that used neighboring CT slices as channels or combined their feature maps to classify the middle slice. Preprocessing corrected gantry tilt and applied a manually designed nonlinear HU transform, which outperformed alternative windowing schemes. Models used patient-separated five-fold training, RAdam, spatial augmentation, fold ensembling, and test-time augmentation. A second-level linear model combined predictions from neighboring slices, giving a small gain over averaging; a segmentation-trained model was retained for diversity despite little log-loss benefit.

The solution prioritized simplicity and stability with a four-layer dense neural network. It trained on later training periods plus supplemental training data, transformed the target logarithmically, and removed 127 target outliers. Features were processed with a quantile transformer without additional feature engineering. Training used Adam and mean squared error with custom 20-fold validation and a 10-time-ID purge.

The solution combined EfficientNet study and opacity classifiers with three YOLOv5 detection models. NIH chest X-ray pretraining, soft-label self-distillation, pseudo-labeling, and heavy augmentation improved performance, while an auxiliary segmentation head contributed to the ensemble. Detection predictions were fused with weighted boxes fusion and combined with a blended None-class prediction. The final total score was 0.644 public and 0.617 private; the study ensemble improved cross-validation and public results but underperformed the best single model privately.

The solution combined HandyRL self-training with Monte Carlo Tree Search. Training for 5,000 epochs with a large minibatch produced a best score of 1112, while ensembling models from several epochs scored around 1100. The author found extended training and MCTS important, whereas larger models, parameter changes, player-centered inputs, and ensembling without MCTS did not work.

solution_title: [4th Place Solution] Conformer Encoder-Decoder Ensemble with beam search and edit_dist optimization
solution_summary: The solution ensembles two encoder-decoder models with adapted 12-layer Conformer encoders and small two-layer Transformer decoders. Normalized landmark coordinates and temporal differences were combined with extensive spatial, temporal, and token augmentation. Training used cross entropy followed by minimum error rate fine-tuning to better match character edit distance. Cached beam search improved the final ensemble by about 0.005, and replacing predictions for severely corrupted samples with a fixed string yielded another 0.005.
compute: Local RTX 3090; about two days per full 12-layer encoder training run; most experiments used shallower models on approximately 20% of the data.

solution_title: 137th place solution, ProtoSSM + 3 SED models ensemble(Private 0.94386)
solution_summary: The team blended diverse sound-event detection models with a ProtoSSM pipeline built on Perch embeddings. The SED models used EfficientNet, ConvNeXt, and MobileNet backbones with attention pooling over spectrogram features. Official-data overlays, Xeno-canto recordings, and pseudo-label mixup expanded training diversity, with pseudo-labeled models helping the ensemble even when their individual scores were weaker. Final combinations were selected using public scores because local validation correlated poorly, and the ensemble achieved 0.955 public and 0.944 private.

The solution relied on translated training data and an ensemble of models trained on different data variants. Adding XQuAD and MLQA helped, while translating Natural Questions provided further gains. The author compared logit averaging with span-score voting that supports different tokenizers. Models trained with iterative HardEM denoising and negative sampling remained useful for ensemble diversity despite weak standalone results. Several alternative pretrained models, architectures, translation models, and ensemble methods were tried without improving results.

The solution used a single 39 MB sequence model trained with intermediate CTC loss, without ensembling. Inputs included three-dimensional coordinates from both hands, eyes, lips, and pose landmarks, with pose and z coordinates improving the score. The network combined a dense layer, four Conv1D layers, and six Branchformer layers with relative multi-head attention and stochastic depth. Training ran for 150 epochs using Adam with Lookahead, cosine decay with warmup, and adversarial weight perturbation.

The team combined several ResNet variants, a multi-head model, staged models, and an ImageNet-pretrained EfficientNet B7 using image sizes of 512, 640, and 736 pixels. EfficientNet B7 was trained with different losses and used four folds from a ten-fold split. They applied a referenced post-processing trick and compared ensemble weights based on leaderboard scores versus cross-validation scores. Both weighting approaches achieved a private score of 0.972, with the final submission scoring 0.969 publicly.

The team fine-tuned a Bengali wav2vec CTC model after filtering noisy competition samples using transcription error rates. A five-gram language model trained on external Bengali text improved decoding. Inference used length-based batching and selectively applied Demucs denoising according to preliminary transcript token counts. XLM-RoBERTa punctuation models provided the largest stated improvement, exceeding 0.030 on the leaderboard.
external_data: ["indicCorp v2", "Common Voice transcripts", "FLEURS transcripts", "OpenSLR transcripts", "OpenSLR37 transcripts", "OSCAR text"]

solution_summary: The solution used only text, combining parsed HTML with supplied and independently extracted boilerplate. More than 100 tag-weighted text sets were transformed into over 300 representations and modeled with logistic regression before ensembling. Writing-style metadata scored reasonably alone but added no useful ensemble improvement. The selected submission achieved a private score of 0.88817, while an unselected candidate achieved 0.88915.

solution_title: My best single model and solution
solution_summary: The solution emphasized feature engineering by separating listing attributes into manager and building groups, then linking and comparing them. It incorporated the published image-time leak and trained diverse classification and regression models across four feature datasets. Multiple stacking levels combined cross-validated predictions, with a weighted geometric blend of XGBoost and neural networks mixed with Extra Trees, followed by averaging two final stacks. The best single model scored 0.50379 publicly and 0.50500 privately; a description-source feature helped publicly but hurt privately, while prior correction contributed only a tiny gain.
compute: About four hours to generate four expensive features; a precomputed timeout.csv was provided.

solution_summary: The solution used DenseNet121 to classify 1,108 categories from 512×512 images. Training included geometric and brightness/contrast augmentation, normalization, Adam, and a decreasing learning rate. The authors averaged predictions and reported using plate leakage, controls, and several classification losses.

solution_title: 13th Place (Final) 1st Place (6 Weeks In) Final Solution
solution_summary: The solution combined LightGBM and Keras neural networks using 17 features built from lagged market statistics, timestamp averages, and asset identity. Its central improvement was reconstructing two targets and switching between their models according to whether missing asset observations forced the beta component to zero. Expanding temporal validation across different market regimes guided model selection, while additional Binance currencies provided small consistent gains. The best ensemble scored 0.0565 on the original test period and 0.0475 on the supplemental period.

external_data: ["Public exchange API data from Binance, FTX, Coinbase, and Kucoin", "Additional Binance currencies including XRP and ZEC"]

solution_summary: The solution converted the expression matrix into long format and ensembled tabular neural networks, random forests, XGBoost models, and fine-tuned transformers. PCA denoising improved the tabular networks, while their learned categorical embeddings provided stronger tree features than directly added biological information. Transformer regressors used different input wording for DeBERTa and TinyBioBert, and multiple seeds diversified the ensemble. The final ensemble scored 0.553 on the public leaderboard and 0.753 on the private leaderboard.
compute: SaturnCloud A10 GPU; DeBERTa 20–25 epochs took 48–60 hours, and TinyBioBert 20–30 epochs took 24–30 hours, both with batch size 256.

solution_summary: The team fully fine-tuned Gemma 2 and ArmoRM-Llama3 classifiers using prompt-grouped validation and additional deduplicated training data. Training both response orders together improved performance, and a teacher ensemble generated 240,000 pseudo-labeled examples for a second training stage. Final supervised fine-tuning produced a two-model ensemble with a 2:1 ratio and an old-leaderboard score of 0.868. Padding-free sequence packing and optimized attention kernels accelerated training and inference.
compute: 4× A100 80 GB for experiments during the final 10 days; inference on 2× T4 in FP16.
external_data: ["Deduplicated 33k dataset, 21k examples used", "lmsys-1m, 110k examples", "Other unnamed datasets, 130k examples"]

solution_summary: The solution combined pretrained MatchFormer, QuadTreeAttention, two scales of SuperPoint plus SuperGlue, and Patch2Pix. Match caps balanced the contributions of the matchers and reduced runtime, while MAGSAC estimated the fundamental matrix. Fixed-seed validation on 80 and 800 images guided implementation checks, although its correlation with leaderboard scores was weak. Patch2Pix provided only a slight improvement, and several refinement and filtering approaches failed to help.

The team emphasized signal preprocessing: aligning the test distribution with training through cross-correlation and removing 50 Hz sine noise. Their ensemble contained six WaveNet variants, two CNN2d-WaveNet hybrids, one CNN2d, and one LightGBM model. The strongest models used either a CNN2d-WaveNet hybrid or WaveNet with cleaned signal, signal differences, and rolling minimum and maximum features. They excluded a noisy portion of the eighth training batch and blended fold predictions, with EMA decay providing a substantial benefit.

The solution averaged three small CNNs trained on normalized images with either white-region removal or duplicate-region removal. Short training, label smoothing, and class-balanced binary cross-entropy helped limit overconfidence in a low-signal task. Four-flip test-time augmentation was followed by probability rescaling and clipping. This calibration improved the reported CV loss from 0.655 to 0.640, with a private leaderboard loss of 0.666.

The final solution averaged ECA-NFNet-L1 and EfficientNet-B2/B6/B7 predictions across several input resolutions, using original and horizontally flipped inputs. All six cadence tiles were stacked and resized through a nearest-neighbor enlargement followed by area downsampling, which was important for benefiting from larger inputs. Training used LAMB, warm restarts, lightly weighted cross-entropy, MixUp, and horizontal flips. Normalized data from the earlier competition version and soft pseudo-labels for the new test set improved performance; the best single model achieved 0.79648 private AUC.
compute: Local RTX 3070, later RTX 3080 Ti; Kaggle TPUs for EfficientNet-B6/B7; seven training epochs with warm restarts.

solution_title: 11th place solution: Transformer with MFE distance embeddings (with code)
solution_summary: The solution modified Hugging Face BERT with RNA structure features, BPP attention injection, interleaved one-dimensional CNNs, and relative distance embeddings. Eternafold supplied the most useful folding features, while CapR accelerated convergence and bpRNA had uncertain benefit. Most final models shared a two-dimensional CNN within each transformer block to balance accuracy and training time. A single model scored approximately 0.1432 publicly, and averaging slightly different models brought the score below 0.14.

solution_title: 63rd Place Solution for the RSNA 2023 Abdominal Trauma Detection
solution_summary: The solution ensembled a single-stage CT-Net architecture covering all organs with a multi-stage pipeline for the kidneys, liver, and spleen. The multi-stage pipeline used EfficientNet-v1b0 to predict sub-volumes before applying CT-Net. The single-stage model alone achieved a leaderboard score of 0.61 without tuning. The author describes the final architecture as only partially finished.

The approach used JAN BRE's Baskfins and Fullbody datasets with EfficientNet models trained using ArcFace loss at 768-pixel resolution. Embeddings from nine models were combined, and cosine distance between training and test images supported identification; weaker ConvNeXt and water-removed-data models also contributed to the ensemble. Training ran for 30–50 epochs with five warm-up epochs followed by cosine learning-rate decay. A single validation fold achieved 0.72 without new_individual and 0.86 with a 0.6 threshold, after which models were retrained on all training data and the test threshold was increased to 0.65.
compute: TPU; limited available training time.
external_data: ["Baskfins and Fullbody datasets by JAN BRE"]

solution_summary: The author first trained a simple neural network and used its out-of-fold predictions to relabel the top 5% of suspected mislabeled examples. Retraining on corrected labels improved the reported leaderboard score from about 0.749 to 0.75010. A further round using pseudo-labels for 5% of the data reached about 0.75070, before blending with a shared post-processing kernel. Predictions were converted to percentile ranks before blending to reconcile differing model probability scales for AUC.

The submission combined 19 models spanning multiple architectures and fold strategies. Most models split images into left and right streams and fused pretrained backbone features through Mamba blocks before predicting three biomass components and deriving aggregate targets. Heavy augmentation, reduced backbone learning rates, and output scaling supported performance, while metadata supervision and test-time augmentation were dropped. Individual model sets generally exceeded 0.64, with the final three-backbone set reaching 0.67.

The solution ensembles LightGBM with XGBoost, combining Tweedie regression and classification predictions. Important components included pseudo-labeling samples without sii labels and percentile-based threshold optimization fitted within each training fold. Features included sequential statistics and dual categorical/numeric representations, with fold-specific median imputation. Evaluation and submission used five stratified folds across ten seeds, with per-seed Optuna tuning and voting to reduce seed sensitivity.

solution_title: Multi-Attempt Tool-Augmented LLM for Olympiad-Level Math Reasoning
solution_summary: The solution used an unnamed large language model served through vLLM to explore multiple mathematical reasoning trajectories. Each attempt could execute Python in a persistent Jupyter sandbox for symbolic computation and numerical verification. Final answers were extracted and range-checked, then combined through inverse-entropy weighted voting with early stopping on agreement. Dynamic time allocation, cached prefixes, and reusable sandbox kernels supported budget-aware parallel inference; no numerical evaluation result was reported.
compute: Tensor-parallel GPU inference with GPU memory utilization configured to 0.96; hardware and runtime unspecified.

solution_summary: The pipeline converts fluorescence recordings into spike trains using MATLAB and oopsi, then constructs pairwise correlation features under multiple spike and row filtering thresholds. Each correlation matrix is also transformed with the ND algorithm, retaining both original and transformed features. Features are Z-normalized before training random forest and gradient boosting models separately on normal-1 and normal-2 data. The four trained models feed a submission-generation script, although the writeup does not explain how their outputs are combined.
compute: Feature generation requires more than 32GB RAM and takes approximately 24–48 hours.

solution_title: [7th solution, my part] Single Stage Model Wins!
solution_summary: The solution combined a two-stage crop-and-classify model with a one-stage model intended to capture whole-image context and correlations across spinal levels. The one-stage model predicted level-point heatmaps and pixelwise grades, then pooled grades using the heatmaps to obtain levelwise predictions. Training exposed competition between localization and grading objectives, which the author associated partly with imprecise point labels and L5/S1 confusion. The final blend weighted the two-stage model at 0.75 and the one-stage model at 0.25, improving on the two-stage model despite implementation and training bugs.
compute: HP Z8 Fury-G5 Data Science Workstation

solution_title: 4th Place Solution for the Regression with an Abalone Dataset
solution_summary: The author adapted an existing notebook using OpenFE and a logarithmic target transformation. AutoGluon trained only tree-based models with a custom RMSLE metric. The final prediction was an equal-weight average of the adapted solution and the original notebook's output.

The solution combined LightGBM models trained on several target transformations using weighted averaging. Production and consumption were modeled separately, with residual targets based on historical values and an installed-capacity-normalized production target. Validation used a single February–May 2023 holdout, and historical-weather-derived features were excluded. The models were retrained once at the end of January 2024.

The author trained Keras CNN, LightGBM, and CatBoost models across multiple cleaned datasets and feature configurations. Removing simultaneous zero readings across meters at a site appeared more valuable than most feature engineering, while neural and tree models provided complementary predictions. One selected submission averaged over 30 experiments after correlation-based selection. The best private result instead used LightGBM to stack roughly ten leak-free predictions with meter identity, training the stacker on leaked target rows despite a worse public score.
compute: Zero-reading cleaning script ran for a few hours.

solution_title: 19th place solution: Loosen up, add a tree, and let the sparrows explore
solution_summary: The author built larger tree packings by slightly expanding an existing packing, inserting one overlapping tree, and using sparrow to resolve the overlap. Multiple random seeds and expansion factors produced candidates, with unsuccessful starts discarded early. The best candidates were compressed with sa_fast_v2 and eazy, yielding the author's best packings for most tree counts above 60.
compute: One illustrated sparrow overlap-resolution run took 70 seconds.

solution_title: 18th Place Solution: LGM with the mean of 3 months as targets
solution_summary: The solution used LightGBM regression with about 20 features derived from historical targets. Lagged values and rolling-window calculations captured temporal patterns at different offsets and window sizes. Predicting the mean of the three future months worked better than forecasting each month separately. The same predicted value was submitted for every forecast month within each county.

The solution combined three-fold, five-second SED models using three backbones with online Perch v2 embedding distillation and pseudo-labeled soundscapes. GRU, LSTM, LightGBM, and XGBoost stackers incorporated soundscape context, site/hour priors, and temporal features, with separate strategies for sonotype labels. Temporal smoothing and maximum-score propagation within related sonotype groups completed the pipeline. The final public and private scores were 0.94751 and 0.95675, with distillation, pseudo-labeling, and stacking each improving results.
compute: CPU inference for OpenVINO SED backbones; PyTorch heads and stackers.

solution_title: 326th Place Solution: AI Agent Security - Multi-Step Tool Attacks
solution_summary: The team reverse-engineered the deployed scoring predicates and tested attack recipes against real target models and reconstructed guardrails. A forged analysis-channel framing increased public-score throughput, but its exfiltration submission scored zero privately as anticipated. Their second final submission allocated roughly 80% to destructive writes and 20% to obliquely requested email actions, achieving 8.01 privately. Only the email component survived, exposing a costly allocation error despite their correct prediction of public/private divergence.
compute: Evaluator live-exploration budget: 9,000 seconds per model; targets run as quantized GGUFs.

solution_summary: The solution forecast monthly density multipliers with a small TensorFlow GRU rather than directly predicting density values. It first adjusted historical densities to a common census population basis and constructed overlapping county sequences. Training used the largest 90% of counties with county-grouped validation, while smaller counties received last-value predictions before adjustment. Public leaderboard probing supplied multiplier corrections that substantially improved the forecasts; a linear model with the same postprocessing was also submitted.

solution_title: RL PPO Light Layer on Base Layer; Final Rank 1231/10148 (4362.2 Final Score)
solution_summary: The solution added a small policy to the public Pipe-16 agent to choose among eight strategy options at four game stages. Exact simulator branching evaluated counterfactual actions on the same game state, removing seed noise that prevented ordinary PPO and GRPO from learning reliably. Search distillation followed by VinePPO improved close mirror matches, although wheat carry strategies remained vulnerable against an older opponent. The final agent performed better in 14 paired games and worse in seven against the previous best, and settled about 100 rating points higher live.

The team combined one-stage and two-stage solutions, with the described two-stage branch locating spinal keypoints before classifying cropped regions. One classifier fused sagittal and axial features, while another used single-view 3D regions centered on predicted coordinates. Multiple backbones and view-specific flip augmentation contributed to the ensemble. The described branch reported CV 0.373, public LB 0.35, and private score 0.40.

solution_title: FLG's Approach - Deep Reinforcement Learning with a Focus on Performance - 4th place
solution_summary: The agent used a custom DoubleCone convolutional network trained through self-play reinforcement learning, with imitation-learning experiments guiding architecture selection. Its observations combined current board features with three turns of history, while collision prevention and randomized communication costs made learning more practical. Training progressed from resource-focused shaped rewards to mostly outcome-focused zero-sum rewards, using Vtrace and a delayed teacher. CPU inference constraints led to a smaller final model, supplemented by a tiny transferred model and pattern matching to build longer action queues.
compute: Competition inference used CPU-only VMs, mostly appearing single-core; the imitation-learning dataset was around 300 GB.

solution_summary: The author averaged a single CatBoost model with predictions from two public notebooks. Feature engineering emphasized polar coordinates between P_2 and other features, together with statistics and interactions for groups sharing similar means or high correlations. Target encoding, PCA, binning, and lagged-data aggregations supplemented these features, while null importance reduced roughly 2,200 features to 1,200. The standalone model achieved mean CV and public leaderboard scores of 0.795; averaging improved the public score to 0.799 and the private score to 0.807.

The final submission ensembled five models each from Qwen3-8B, gemma-2-9b-it, and Hunyuan-7B-Instruct, including merged LoRA adapters. Concatenating adapter bottlenecks reduced causal-language-model inference cost while retaining much of the benefit of seed ensembles. Labels were reduced to 37 classes, prompts listed question-specific candidates, and affine output alignment supported combining causal and classification models. Shared frozen classification heads mitigated severe classification-model merging degradation, although gains remained inconsistent, and vLLM was excluded after slow T4 inference.
compute: T4x2 instance used for vLLM inference experiments

solution_summary: The post asks whether others are eagerly awaiting writeups from the leading competitors. It expresses interest in learning their approaches. It provides no solution methods or implementation details.

The approach used CenterNet-style detection with heatmap, offset, depth, and trigonometric pose heads, plus an auxiliary width-height task. ImageNet-pretrained ResNet18 and KITTI 3DOP-pretrained DLA34 backbones with FPNs benefited strongly from increased input resolution. Five-fold models were trained with geometric and color augmentation, RAdam, and cosine learning-rate annealing, then ensembled by averaging raw output maps. Mask filtering, distance-based suppression, duplicate-image ensembling, and score filtering completed inference; the ensemble achieved validation mAP 0.2736 and a private score of 0.115.
models_pretrained: ["ResNet18 pretrained on ImageNet", "DLA34 pretrained on KITTI 3DOP"]

solution_summary: The solution averaged six EfficientNet experiments, pairing larger networks with lower-resolution inputs to reduce overfitting. Images were cropped from gray borders, transformed into a common image type during training, and heavily augmented. Models were pretrained on the full 2015 dataset before five-fold training on the 2019 data, with eight-way dihedral augmentation at inference. The more diverse final ensemble replaced two models with variants trained using Ben's preprocessing and achieved a private score of 0.933.
compute: Approximately 10 minutes for 40 prediction passes over 1,928 images; six-model ensemble took 50 minutes for committing and 6 hours for submitting.
external_data: ["2015 diabetic retinopathy dataset, train and test"]

solution_summary: The solution trained Faster R-CNN and Cascade R-CNN detectors through MMDetection, with ImageNet-pretrained ResNeXt101 in the best single model. Fine-tuning on six class-frequency subsets addressed imbalance and improved the public score by approximately 0.05. Horizontal flips, multi-scale inference, parent-class expansion, and weighted ensembling produced a final public score of 0.608. Increasing the per-image detection limit to 600 also formed part of the final submission.
compute: Approximately 20 days to train Faster R-CNN + ResNeXt101 for 24 epochs; hardware unspecified.

solution_title: 45th place with XGBoost in first Kaggle competition
solution_summary: The solution used XGBoost throughout a two-stage pipeline, with AUC guiding optimization and tuning. Statement histories were summarized using 16 aggregations per numerical feature, including Hull and exponential moving averages. First-stage models generated out-of-fold predictions for two next-month delinquency outcomes, which were aggregated and added to roughly 3,000 features for the final XGBoost Pyramid model. The final training used the full dataset with round counts informed by CV early stopping, and the submitted standalone model scored 0.80798 on the private leaderboard.
compute: GPU used; GPU resources and remaining time were limited, with about 48 hours left for first-stage OOF prediction.

solution_summary: The pipeline corrected image orientation, pruned candidate image pairs with a trained scene classifier, and supplemented retrieval using NetVLAD. It extracted RDD features at two resolutions, matched them with LightGlue, and merged the matches. Pair pruning mainly saved runtime, enabling multiscale matching that raised the reported public/private scores to 48.02/47.88. Alternative pair classifiers and mixing other keypoint detectors with RDD descriptors did not work.

The author built regression models with holiday indicators and log relative GDP features, eventually selecting Extra Trees. Setting relative GDP to 0.4 for every country in 2022 produced the largest improvement, reducing public MAPE to about 7.5. Integer conversion and subtracting one further improved the author's predictions to about 6.13 public MAPE. The final solution combined these predictions with an adjusted public submission using weights of 0.175 and 0.825, then rounded the result, achieving about 5.93 private MAPE and 5.00 public MAPE.

The solution uses a fairly simple neural network classifier. It achieved approximately 81.818% classification accuracy. TF-IDF, spelling normalization, and neural network hyperparameter optimization were suggested as future improvements rather than reported experiments.
compute: GeForce GT 755M; Python 2.7 under Ubuntu 14.04

solution_summary: The final submission blended four models with different validation strategies and training-data partitions. The models used time-series or grouped cross-validation and were split by week, by category, or left unsplit. Grouping by year and month worked on both leaderboard splits, while the blend scored 0.56715 in cross-validation and 0.60101 on the private leaderboard.

solution_title: Bronze Solution: Robust LoRA Adapter Selection and Packaging
solution_summary: The final submission packaged a public LoRA adapter for the official Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B-BF16 model, prioritizing compatibility and reproducibility. The pipeline discovered candidate adapters, normalized their formats, checked module and rank constraints, and produced the required submission archive. Because vLLM was unavailable in the final environment, it selected the preferred huikang_tinker adapter without validation-backed candidate selection. Additional supervised fine-tuning remained disabled because small runs could improve some task families while degrading others.
models_pretrained: ["Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B-BF16", "huikang_tinker adapter", "huikang_v27 adapter", "huikang_v20 adapter", "kienngx_submit adapter", "kienngx_v13 adapter", "kienngx_v4_small adapter", "llkh0a_unsloth adapter"]

solution_summary: The pipeline combined signal calibration and noise reduction with transit modeling and neural networks. Temporal binning, smoothing, normalization, and subtracting dark current before nonlinearity correction improved signal preparation. Pairing signals with all calibration files expanded training diversity. Modeling used a CNN with filter kernels and a projection layer alongside transit and tree-model stacking, although robust postprocessing remained unresolved.

The post describes cleaning and feature engineering for trip classification without specifying a final model. The author removed NULL-description rows when other descriptions were available within a visit and aggregated scan counts by visit and UPC to reconcile reversed scans. They inferred day and within-day visit features from the combined train and test sequence. UPC processing, count vectorization, and aggregate counts and sums completed the described approach.

The final submissions used diverse nine-model ensembles of fine-tuned language models with Nelder-Mead weighting. Custom heads combined hidden-layer averaging, an LSTM, vocabulary-level dense features, and handcrafted text statistics. Reinitializing upper transformer layers, removing dropout, and clipping gradients improved validation performance. Both selected ensembles achieved a private score of 0.452.
compute: 1× GeForce RTX3090

solution_summary: The solution identified 7,820 leaked test targets using 34 feature sets. Its machine-learning component stacked three XGBoost models: a tuned version of a shared kernel, a selected-column model, and a principal-component model. Feature engineering emphasized time-series structure in sorted column sets. The tuned shared-kernel component reportedly achieved 1.37.
The post links to the author's code and prompts in a Kaggle notebook. It requests feedback and explanations of MNIST hints. No solution methods or results are described in the provided text.

The final approach used a regularized Random Forest trained on the competition data and an additional obesity risk dataset. It retained all original features and added BMI and BMI prime multiplied by physical activity frequency; BMI was particularly important. The author tuned parameters with 300 Optuna trials using five-fold stratified group cross-validation, taking approximately four hours on CPU. The overview reports a CV score of 0.8892 and a private leaderboard score of 0.8825, although subsequent experiment tables report slightly different scores.
compute: CPU only; approximately 4 hours for training with 300 Optuna trials.

solution_summary: The project classifies crime descriptions into 39 category labels using a hybrid TextCNN and GRU network. It implements training and prediction with TensorFlow 2.x Keras and exports a model, vocabulary, label mapping, and training parameters. Prediction primarily loads the best validation checkpoint. No evaluation scores or comparison with alternative approaches are reported.

solution_title: How to drop more than 500 places!
solution_summary: The author adapted a shared benchmark into R and tuned radial-kernel support vector machines using repeated five-fold cross-validation. Most targets achieved RMSE between 0.3 and 0.4, while phosphorus remained substantially harder. Adding untransformed satellite data slightly improved pH and sand predictions, which were combined with the original predictions for one final submission. A second final submission ensembled the phosphorus SVM with a random forest, but leaderboard results were disappointing despite the validation estimates.

The solution used a single-stage video event model combining a mostly 2.5D EfficientNetV2 backbone with late 3D convolutions. Grayscale frame stacks provided temporal context across 15 frames while enabling efficient cached inference. SoccerNet pretraining improved the score by roughly 0.02, and fixed-video validation reached 0.857 with strong leaderboard correlation. The final system retrained on all available data and blended two models on alternating frames, taking about five hours to run.
compute: Inference used both CPU cores with threading; 2.5 hours per model, 25 minutes per video, approximately 5 hours for the final two-model solution.

solution_summary: The author used a single T5 generative model to map topics directly to lists of document identifiers. Training combined document-to-identifier memorization with topic-to-document recommendation, with memorization needed before recommendation could work. An additional task predicting a topic's position in the topic tree did not improve results. The approach achieved a public leaderboard score of 0.25 and was described as computationally demanding and highly sensitive to hyperparameters.

The solution ensembled DeBERTa-v3-large and DeBERTa-v3-base models trained with target-specific prediction heads, combining full-data and fold-trained models. Back-translation pretraining, Feedback Prize 2 pretraining, and pseudo-labeling improved performance, with particularly strong vocabulary gains from back-translation. Pearson and ranking losses helped harder targets, while target-specific ensemble weights balanced differences between models. The selected pseudo-labeling and Optuna ensemble achieved a reported private score of 0.43363, although tuning on all training OOF predictions made validation optimistic and a manually weighted alternative performed slightly better.
compute: Inference took 2 hours 20 minutes on 2 NVIDIA T4 GPUs for 23 full-training models and 23 fold models.

solution_summary: The team built a CatBoost-centered ensemble with DeepTables neural networks, combining augmented and non-augmented models through CV-based hill climbing. Validation used StratifiedGroupKFold grouped by the first letter of the game ruleset name and repeated three times. Agent-swapping augmentation, target transformation, one-hot encoding, and restrained feature engineering and selection contributed to the approach. Prediction scaling and sign-dependent blending with quantile models gave similar improvements of about 0.004–0.005, while discrepancies between CV and leaderboard performance complicated model selection.

The solution uses hierarchical Bayesian linear regression with Student-t observation noise and only daily-return inputs. It predicts the next two daily returns while setting minute-return predictions to zero. The Stan implementation places normal priors on regression coefficients and inverse-gamma priors on variance parameters, with Student-t degrees of freedom specified as 2.6. The author reports relatively consistent performance across cross-validation and leaderboard evaluations.

The solution used a publicly shared BERT masked language model as its foundation. External datasets from @mlconsult substantially improved the public score without hurting private performance. The two final submissions, with and without these datasets, scored almost identically at 0.372 and 0.373. The nine-hour kernel training limit constrained further training and model development.
compute: 9-hour kernel training time limit

solution_summary: The solution ensembled four EfficientNetV2 models across three image resolutions, including two large models trained with different seeds at 768 pixels. Geometric augmentation, geometric test-time augmentation, dropout, stochastic depth, focal loss, and pseudo labels for time steps 3 and 5 were useful. The ensemble scored 0.6936 on the validation folder, compared with roughly 0.690–0.692 for its first three individual models. Additional pseudo-label rounds, broader appearance augmentation, and several temporal 2.5D or 3D architectures did not help.

The author used brute-force computation to estimate whether each starting cell was alive or dead from a centered 7×7 block of stopping cells. The algorithm incorporated quarter-turn rotational symmetry and inversion symmetry. Computation ran across a 376-core Xeon cluster using OpenMP and MPI. An SSE implementation was left unfinished, and a GPU implementation was suggested but not attempted.
compute: 376-core cluster with E5420 Intel Xeon 2.5GHz processors

solution_summary: The post links to an external article explaining the features used in the team's final model. The author describes this as the team's first NLP problem and Kaggle competition. The post itself provides no concrete features, models, or implementation details and thanks the community.

solution_title: Temporal Modeling Approaches for Large-scale Youtube-8M Video Understanding
solution_summary: The authors provide data providers and model configurations for temporal video understanding approaches used in the competition.
